The documentation page on Auto capture does not list licensing requirements, mailbox types, regional restrictions or technical limits, so those points need to be confirmed in the related setup and licensing material before a rollout is planned.

Typical situations for Auto capture include sales teams that handle many email threads and meetings per opportunity or account, where logging each item manually is tedious and often skipped. Reviewing a short list of suggestions on the timeline is quicker than creating each activity record by hand, and it supports more complete records for forecasting, handovers and account reviews. Decisions around the feature usually concern when to enable it, which users should work with it, and how sellers are guided to review suggestions regularly so that the timeline stays accurate.

Auto capture is part of the wider set of intelligence capabilities in Dynamics 365 Sales Insights. The M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Sales Insights - Simply Explained" (2026-08-17) explains Sales Insights in plain English and covers how Microsoft uses AI, activity signals, relationship data, predictive scoring, conversation intelligence and forecasting to help sales teams focus their attention. In that discussion, Auto Capture is listed alongside the Sales Insights assistant, Email Engagement, predictive lead and opportunity scoring, Sales Accelerator, relationship intelligence, Who Knows Whom, Talking Points, Conversation Intelligence, notes analysis, forecasting, Microsoft 365 integration, Microsoft Teams and LinkedIn Sales Navigator. The excerpt places Auto Capture among these capabilities and shows that it connects the Microsoft 365 mailbox and calendar side with the customer data held in the CRM.

autogen.desc: AutoGen is an agent framework named in M365.FM episodes on multi-agent design, Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio scaling, AI agent governance and Microsoft Agent Framework.

faq.a: AutoGen is an agent framework that M365.FM episodes describe as supporting multi-agent systems, where several AI agents cooperate on tasks. It is named alongside LangGraph, CrewAI, Haystack and Semantic Kernel.
faq.q: What is AutoGen?

faq.a: According to the episode with Andre Baltieri, Microsoft Agent Framework brings together capabilities associated with Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. It adds tools for workflow orchestration, MCP, RAG and data ingestion.
faq.q: How does AutoGen relate to Microsoft Agent Framework?

faq.a: The episode on production AI agents says the Azure AI Foundry SDK supports AutoGen along with Semantic Kernel, CrewAI, LangGraph and LlamaIndex, so teams can choose the framework that fits their needs.
faq.q: Can AutoGen be used with Microsoft Foundry?

autogen.long:
AutoGen is a framework for building AI agents and coordinating several of them to work on a shared task. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, AutoGen appears as one of the named frameworks used for multi-agent systems, alongside LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Haystack and Semantic Kernel. The sources in this knowledge base do not give a formal product definition, so the description here rests on how the episodes place AutoGen in the wider Microsoft ecosystem.

The episode "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide" groups AutoGen with LangGraph as a framework that supports emergent cooperative behavior between agents. In that context the episode describes message passing and shared memory as the means of communication between agents. Dynamic coordination and task decomposition let agents split up work. The episode lists role assignment, specialization (skill-based specialists and role-based team members), and modular, observable graphs for orchestration, which it says improve scalability and fault tolerance. Its practical tip is to assign roles and tasks to agents based on their skills and to use modular graphs to scale the system.

The episode "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" uses AutoGen as an example of a multi-agent framework. According to the episode, such frameworks divide work, allow agents to reason in parallel and adapt to changing needs. It cites AutoGen and Haystack as examples of how organizations apply these strategies to software development and compliance tasks. The episode's point is that integrating AI agents into structured workflows gives better control and reliability, and that multi-agent workflows help automate complex processes while keeping control as an organization grows. The same episode stresses that deploying agents at scale requires meeting governance, security and compliance obligations.

In "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]", AutoGen is listed among the frameworks supported by the Azure AI Foundry SDK, together with Semantic Kernel, CrewAI, LangGraph and LlamaIndex. The episode presents this as a choice: teams can pick the tools that suit them while using Foundry's built-in tooling for rapid agent development. It also mentions that Foundry supports open protocols such as MCP and A2A, which let agents connect to external systems and work across platforms.

The episode "How AI Changed Software Development Forever — Building the Agentic Future with Andre Baltieri [MVP]" connects AutoGen to Microsoft Agent Framework. Andre Baltieri explains, according to the episode, that Microsoft Agent Framework brings together capabilities associated with Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. It gives developers tools for connecting models, orchestrating workflows, using MCP, implementing RAG, handling data ingestion and exposing application functionality to AI. The episode notes that for .NET developers this can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Governance is the fourth theme. The episode "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" names AutoGen and LangChain as frameworks that can help streamline reporting on AI agent activity. It describes such tools as providing visibility into what agents do, which makes it easier to track performance and compliance. The episode recommends a designated owner responsible for each agent's actions, clear documentation of agent operations and decisions, and continuous monitoring through regular audits against established policies.

Taken together, the episodes treat AutoGen as a framework choice within a larger set of decisions: how to structure cooperating agents, which SDK or platform hosts them, how they connect to external systems, and how their behavior is observed and governed. Related topics include Microsoft Agent Framework, Semantic Kernel, Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, MCP, A2A and AI agent governance.

automatic-attack-disruption.desc: Automatic attack disruption is a Microsoft Defender XDR capability that uses high-confidence signals to contain compromised devices or accounts and stop attacks such as ransomware.

faq.a: It correlates signals into a high-confidence incident, identifies the assets under attacker control and runs response actions such as isolating a device, disabling a user or revoking sessions in Microsoft Entra ID. The goal is to stop an attack like ransomware before it spreads.
faq.q: What does automatic attack disruption do?

faq.a: Yes. According to Microsoft Learn, the security team keeps control of investigation and recovery, and every automatic action can be undone.
faq.q: Can the automatic actions be reversed?

faq.a: Containment applies to devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint, and disabling Active Directory accounts relies on domain controllers with the Defender for Identity sensor. The documentation page does not list specific license requirements.
faq.q: What is needed for containment to work?

automatic-attack-disruption.long:
Automatic attack disruption is a capability built into Microsoft Defender XDR that detects ongoing attacks and automatically contains the assets affected by them. It uses high-confidence signals to stop an attack in progress, such as ransomware, before it spreads further through an environment. It sits under the broader Microsoft Defender family of security products and is part of the response side of the Defender XDR platform.

The purpose of the capability is to limit lateral movement early, reduce the impact of an attack and give the security team time to carry out full remediation. According to Microsoft Learn, it assesses the whole attack at incident level rather than reacting to single indicators of compromise. The security team keeps control of investigation and recovery, and every automatic action can be undone, so containment does not remove the team's ability to decide how an incident is resolved.

According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, the capability works in three stages. First, signals from endpoints, identities, email and collaboration tools, and SaaS apps are correlated into a high-confidence incident. Second, the assets that are under the attacker's control are identified. Third, response actions are run in the relevant Defender products. The actions described include containing or isolating a device, containing or disabling a user, revoking sessions in Microsoft Entra ID, and handling OAuth app compromise. Integrations with Okta and AWS IAM are noted as being in preview.

Predictive shielding is related to the same approach. It applies protective measures, such as hardening, in advance so that assets are better protected before an attack reaches them. In the M365.FM overview of endpoint protection types, automatic attack disruption and predictive shielding are grouped together under autonomous protection, which is described as proactively protecting endpoints. The same overview lists other categories next to it, including endpoint detection and response, next-generation protection with ransomware prevention, attack surface reduction and vulnerability management.

There are practical prerequisites to consider when planning for the capability. Containment applies to devices that are onboarded to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Disabling Active Directory accounts relies on domain controllers that have the Microsoft Defender for Identity sensor. The documentation page does not list specific license requirements, so organizations typically check their Defender licensing separately when deciding how broadly to deploy the underlying products. Because the capability draws on several signal sources, coverage of endpoints, identities, email and SaaS apps affects how complete the correlated view of an incident can be.

Typical situations in which the capability is relevant include a ransomware attempt that begins on one device and could spread to others, or a compromised user account that an attacker uses to move between systems. In such cases, containing the device or disabling the user can interrupt the attack while analysts investigate. Because actions are reversible, a team can restore an asset if the detection turns out to need review.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" mentions automatic attack disruption as part of the autonomous protection layer of Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, alongside predictive shielding, within a breakdown of the types of endpoint protection on offer.

autonomous-agent.desc: An autonomous agent is an AI agent that runs on triggers or schedules instead of in a conversation, and may use reasoning to decide its next steps.

faq.a: An autonomous agent is an AI agent that runs on its own in response to triggers or schedules rather than in a conversation with a user, for example in Copilot Studio. It can use reasoning to decide its next steps.
faq.q: What is an autonomous agent?

faq.a: The episode on Excel RFI responses contrasts the agent with macros and step-by-step automation, since the agent interprets the questions in a file and generates answers from defined knowledge. The Dynamics 365 episode adds that the agent chooses from allowed next steps toward a defined goal.
faq.q: How does an autonomous agent differ from traditional automation?

faq.a: The episodes recommend a narrowly defined job, least-privilege and scoped permissions, approvals for sensitive actions, human oversight, and a dedicated identity with an independent audit trail and lifecycle management for each agent.
faq.q: What controls do the episodes recommend for autonomous agents?

autonomous-agent.long:
An autonomous agent is a type of AI agent that runs on its own in response to triggers or schedules rather than in a conversation with a user. Copilot Studio is one example of a platform where such agents can be built. Because it is not waiting for a person to type a prompt, it can start work when an event occurs, such as a file arriving, and it can use reasoning to decide what to do next. In the topic hierarchy it sits under the broader concept of the AI agent.

The M365.FM episodes describe autonomous agents mainly through concrete work scenarios. In "Automate Excel RFI Responses with an Autonomous Agent", the agent watches for incoming Excel files, interprets the questions inside them, generates responses from defined knowledge, writes the answers back into the spreadsheet and sends the result onward. The episode contrasts this with macros or step-by-step automation, because the agent interprets content instead of following a fixed script. It also says that when inputs are malformed or expectations are not met, the system should fail cleanly and alert humans rather than break silently.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Autonomous Agents - Simply Explained" gives a definition in a business-application setting: an autonomous agent is a specialized AI tool designed to perform a narrow business job. It can review business information, choose from allowed next steps and carry out work toward a defined goal. The episode stresses that the word "defined" matters, since an autonomous agent is not given unrestricted control of a business process. Organizations determine its job, the information it can access and the actions it can perform. The same episode distinguishes autonomous agents from Copilot and from traditional automation, and says that permissions, guardrails, approvals and human oversight remain essential.

Security and identity are a recurring theme. "Security Agent Fabric: Autonomous AI for Cyber Defense" describes autonomous agents as able to execute tasks without human intervention, with examples such as phishing triage and identity protection, including risk-based decisions made in real time. The same episode warns that agents with broad access can become targets for attackers, that unauthorized actions and lateral movement can occur if strict permissions are not enforced, and that the identity fabric should be used to limit agent access and to monitor all agent activity.

Two further episodes focus on governance. In "From Copilot Rollout to AI Workplace: Adoption, Agents & Real Business Value with Christoffer Besler Hansen [MVP]", the discussion covers which actions require explicit approval, what an agent can delete, which systems it can access and what permissions it receives. The episode emphasizes least privilege and approval controls, and gives the example that giving an autonomous agent Global Administrator privileges without restrictions would create obvious risks. It also notes that enterprise-wide agents need an intake process and quality control, unlike a personal agent used by one employee. "The Copilot Credit Trap- Why Your AI Economy is Already Broken" recommends that agents have independent identities rather than shared user accounts, each with a dedicated identity, scoped permissions, least-privilege access, an independent audit trail and lifecycle management. This makes it possible to distinguish human actions from autonomous agent behavior and supports accountability.

Taken together, the episodes treat the autonomous agent as a pattern with two sides. One side is the capability: event-driven or scheduled work, interpretation of content and decisions about next steps without a person in the loop. The other side is control: a narrowly defined job, limited data access and actions, approvals for sensitive operations, a separate identity and an audit trail. Decisions around the concept therefore usually concern how narrowly to scope the agent, which actions need human approval and how to give it a traceable identity.

availability-sets.desc: Availability sets are an Azure feature that spreads virtual machines across fault domains and update domains inside one datacenter to limit correlated failures.

faq.a: An availability set is a logical grouping of virtual machines that spreads them across fault domains and update domains within one datacenter. This lowers the chance that a single hardware fault or maintenance restart affects all related machines at once.
faq.q: What is an availability set in Azure?

faq.a: Fault domains share a power source and network switch, so they represent hardware failure boundaries. Update domains are groups of machines that can be restarted together during planned maintenance, with only one update domain restarted at a time.
faq.q: What is the difference between fault domains and update domains?

faq.a: No. They do not protect against operating system or application faults, they remain exposed to some shared infrastructure outages, and they offer less resilience than availability zones. For new designs, Microsoft Learn points to scale sets in flexible orchestration mode.
faq.q: Do availability sets protect against everything?

availability-sets.long:
An availability set is a logical grouping of virtual machines in Microsoft Azure that lowers the chance of a correlated failure affecting all related machines at once. It works inside a single datacenter and is one of the older tools for building resilience into virtual machine workloads. The idea is simple: if several machines serve the same application, they should not all sit on the same power source, the same network switch, or the same maintenance schedule.

The mechanism relies on two kinds of domains. Fault domains are groups of hardware that share a power source and a network switch, so a hardware problem in one domain affects only the machines placed there. Update domains are groups of machines that can be restarted together during planned platform maintenance. When maintenance happens, only one update domain is restarted at a time, and the platform allows a recovery pause before moving on to the next one. Placing machines from the same application in different fault domains and update domains means that a single hardware fault or a single maintenance restart should not take down every instance.

Several constraints apply. The number of fault domains and update domains cannot be changed after the set is created, so the choice has to be made up front. For the platform's availability SLA to apply, a set needs at least two virtual machines. A managed availability set accepts only machines that use managed disks. There is no extra charge for the availability set itself beyond the cost of the virtual machines, and latency between machines can be lower than with availability zones, which is sometimes a reason to consider them.

The limits matter as much as the benefits. Availability sets do not protect against faults in the operating system or in the application running on the machines. They also remain exposed to some shared infrastructure outages in the datacenter, because all machines stay within one datacenter. Compared with availability zones, which place resources in separate physical locations within a region, availability sets give less resilience. For new designs, Microsoft Learn points to scale sets in flexible orchestration mode instead.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Availability Zones - Simply Explained" covers availability sets as "the older tool" within a broader walk through Azure resilience. The episode outline starts with regions and the idea of a region, then looks inside a region at availability zones and explains why one datacenter is not enough. It then places availability sets next to zonal versus zone-redundant services, and goes on to what SLAs actually mean, designing for resilience, region pairs, and the costs and trade-offs. The episode starts from the point that putting an app in the cloud does not by itself keep it running no matter what.

In practice, the decision around availability sets usually comes down to scope of protection. Spreading machines across fault and update domains addresses hardware faults and planned maintenance within one datacenter. If the requirement is to survive the loss of an entire datacenter, availability zones or other region-level designs are the relevant topics, as the episode's structure suggests. Availability sets therefore sit as a narrower, lower-level option under the broader Microsoft Azure resilience toolbox.

availability-zones.desc: Availability zones are physically separate locations inside an Azure region, each with its own power, cooling and networking, used to keep workloads running if one zone fails.

faq.a: Availability zones are physically separate locations within an Azure region, each with its own power, cooling and networking. They let a workload be spread so that a failure in one zone does not affect every instance.
faq.q: What are availability zones in Azure?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Availability Zones - Simply Explained", every region that supports zones contains at least three separate buildings. The episode also says Azure runs more than 70 regions.
faq.q: How many zones does an Azure region have?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention the Standard Load Balancer, zone-redundant storage (ZRS) for disks, Managed Disks redundancy options and Azure Traffic Manager, which operates across multiple availability zones and regions.
faq.q: Which Azure services work with availability zones?

availability-zones.long:
Availability zones are physically separate locations within a Microsoft Azure region. Each zone has its own power, cooling and networking, so a failure in one zone does not take down every instance of a workload. The idea is to spread a workload across these zones instead of placing everything in a single datacenter.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Availability Zones - Simply Explained" places zones in the context of the wider Azure footprint. It says Azure runs more than 70 regions and that every region that supports zones contains at least three separate buildings. The episode also challenges a common assumption: placing an app in the cloud does not by itself keep it running no matter what. Resilience depends on how the workload is designed and deployed, and zones are one of the building blocks for that. The episode structure covers regions as the big picture, the role of availability zones inside a region, and why a single datacenter is not enough.

In practice, zones matter when a workload has to tolerate the loss of one facility. Spreading instances across zones means that a power, cooling or networking problem in one location affects only part of the deployment. The remaining zones continue to serve requests, which reduces downtime compared with a design that depends on a single location. Because the zones sit within one region, they are a different tool from multi-region designs, which address failures that affect an entire region.

Several other Azure services in the M365.FM catalog interact with availability zones. In "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained", the Standard Load Balancer is described as offering features such as session persistence and availability zones. Health probes check server status to prevent downtime, and traffic is distributed automatically so that no single server is overloaded. Combining a load balancer with instances in several zones is a typical way to keep an application reachable when one zone has problems.

Storage is another area where zones appear. The episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" notes that Azure keeps three copies of each disk in different places within the same region to guard against hardware problems and outages. It also mentions zone-redundant storage (ZRS), which adds protection across different availability zones. "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" lists availability zones and redundancy options among the topics a disk design has to consider, alongside disk types, snapshots, backups, encryption, resizing and shared disks, and integration with Azure Backup, Azure Site Recovery and virtual machine scale sets.

At the traffic-routing level, "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained" says the service operates across multiple availability zones and regions to provide resilience during outages. It monitors endpoint health and, when an endpoint becomes unhealthy, reroutes traffic to healthy ones or to a backup endpoint. This shows how zone-level and region-level designs are combined: zones protect against the loss of a single facility, while DNS-based routing helps users reach a working endpoint when a larger failure occurs.

Typical decisions around availability zones include which services and disks should be zone-redundant, how many zones a workload should span, and how load balancing and failover are configured on top. Because the sources describe zones as part of Microsoft Azure's regional structure, the concept is relevant to administrators, cloud architects and DevOps engineers who plan for resilience and to anyone preparing for Azure-related Microsoft certifications.

aws-direct-connect.desc: AWS Direct Connect is an Amazon Web Services offering that provides a dedicated private network connection from on-premises or colocation facilities to AWS.

faq.a: AWS Direct Connect is an Amazon Web Services offering that provides a dedicated private network connection from on-premises or colocation facilities to AWS.
faq.q: What is AWS Direct Connect?

faq.a: No. It is described as a connection that does not traverse the public internet, linking on-premises or colocation facilities directly to AWS.
faq.q: Does AWS Direct Connect use the public internet?

faq.a: This entry does not include those details. They are available in the official AWS documentation.
faq.q: Where can details such as pricing or supported capacities be found?

aws-direct-connect.long:
AWS Direct Connect is an Amazon Web Services offering that provides a dedicated private network connection from on-premises or colocation facilities to AWS without traversing the public internet.

In practice, organizations use a dedicated connection of this kind to link their own data centers or colocation environments directly to AWS. Because traffic does not travel over the public internet, the connection is described as private. This type of setup is typically considered when a hybrid architecture requires a defined network path between local infrastructure and cloud resources.

On M365.FM, AWS Direct Connect is catalogued as a product entity within the broader coverage of the Microsoft ecosystem and neighboring cloud platforms. No related topics or episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no further technical details are recorded here beyond the definition above. For specifications, supported capacities, locations and pricing, the official AWS documentation is the authoritative source.

aws-iam.desc: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the web service that controls authentication and authorisation for AWS resources through users, roles and policies.

faq.a: AWS IAM is a web service that controls access to AWS resources. It handles authentication (who is signing in) and authorisation (what that identity may do) across AWS accounts, using users, roles and policies.
faq.q: What does AWS IAM do?

faq.a: No. The AWS IAM User Guide strongly recommends against using the root user for daily tasks. It advises creating other identities, such as administrators, analysts and developers, with only the access they need.
faq.q: Should the AWS root user be used for everyday work?

faq.a: IAM, IAM Identity Center and STS are free; customers pay only for the other AWS services they use. Some IAM Access Analyzer checks carry charges.
faq.q: Does AWS IAM cost anything?

aws-iam.long:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a web service for securely controlling access to AWS resources. It covers two related tasks: authentication, which verifies who is signing in, and authorisation, which decides what an authenticated identity is allowed to do. These controls apply across AWS accounts. The product summary also names IAM Identity Center, which adds single sign-on and multi-factor authentication (MFA) across AWS accounts.

IAM is built around users, roles and policies. Every AWS account starts with a root user that has full access to everything in the account. The AWS IAM User Guide strongly recommends not using the root user for daily tasks. Instead, other identities such as administrators, analysts and developers are created and given only the access they need. This least-privilege approach is the main design decision when setting up IAM in a new account.

Access works as a sequence of steps. A user signs in and is matched to a trusted principal. A principal can be an IAM user, a federated principal from AWS STS (the AWS Security Token Service), an IAM role or an application. The principal then sends a request to access a resource. AWS checks the identity of the requester and the policies that enforce the access level. Once the request is authorised, the principal can act, for example by launching an EC2 instance or deleting S3 buckets. Requests can originate from the same account or from a trusted other account, which is how cross-account access is handled.

Some operational properties are worth knowing. IAM is eventually consistent, so changes take time to replicate across the service. For that reason, IAM changes should not sit in critical code paths. On cost, IAM, IAM Identity Center and STS are free of charge; customers pay only for the other AWS services they use. Some IAM Access Analyzer checks, however, carry charges.

In mixed Microsoft and AWS environments, IAM is often compared with Microsoft Entra, and the M365.FM episode "AWS vs Microsoft Entra for Enterprise Cloud Identity" (26 February 2026) takes up that comparison. The episode frames identity and governance as critical for maintaining security and compliance in hybrid cloud environments, and it says control plane failures can lead to widespread disruptions, affecting services such as eCommerce and streaming. According to the episode, AWS IAM has limitations that can hinder effective identity management across hybrid setups. It also states that gaps in the control plane can create security and compliance risks, which makes continuous monitoring essential.

The episode's practical recommendations follow from those points. It says that implementing redundant and distributed control mechanisms can enhance resilience in cloud operations, and that multi-cloud management tools can improve operational resilience. These statements reflect the episode's own assessment and are not part of the AWS documentation summarised above.

In practice, teams working with IAM typically decide how to separate administrative, analyst and developer identities, whether workloads should use roles rather than long-lived users, how cross-account trust is granted, and how single sign-on and MFA are rolled out through IAM Identity Center. Where AWS runs alongside Microsoft services, an additional decision is how identity and governance are coordinated between the two platforms, and how the control plane is monitored so that gaps are found before they become compliance problems.

az-104.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate (AZ-104) is an associate-level Microsoft certification for managing Azure identities, storage, compute, networking and monitoring.

faq.a: It is an associate-level Microsoft certification for managing Azure identities, storage, compute, networking and monitoring. It is earned by passing the exam AZ-104.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate (AZ-104)?

faq.a: The episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" says there are no formal prerequisites. It recommends at least six months of hands-on experience administering Azure and notes that the Azure Fundamentals certification (AZ-900) can be beneficial.
faq.q: Are there prerequisites for AZ-104?

faq.a: AZ-104 matches the daily tasks of an Azure administrator, while the higher-level Azure Solutions Architect Expert certification (AZ-305) covers design work. Several M365.FM episodes mention both exams together for listeners planning a path from administration toward architecture.
faq.q: How does AZ-104 relate to AZ-305?

az-104.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate is an associate-level certification developed by Microsoft. It is earned by passing the exam AZ-104 and covers the day-to-day management of Microsoft Azure: identities, storage, compute, networking and monitoring. The certification is aimed at people who run and maintain Azure environments, and it is often referred to simply by its exam code, AZ-104.

The content of the certification matches the daily tasks of an Azure administrator rather than the design work of an architect. Design-oriented topics sit in the higher-level certification Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305), and many candidates treat AZ-104 as a practical foundation before specializing further. The administrator role described here includes provisioning and operating resources, controlling access through identities, choosing suitable storage services, and watching the health of workloads through monitoring.

Preparation is discussed in the M365.FM episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect". The episode says that candidates should have at least six months of hands-on experience administering Azure before attempting AZ-104. It notes that there are no formal prerequisites, but that completing the Azure Fundamentals certification (AZ-900) can be beneficial. According to the episode, the average time to progress from Azure Fundamentals to Azure Administrator Associate is approximately four months, including about four weeks for the AZ-900 certification. The same episode gives an example of a typical administrator decision: Azure Blob Storage is described as suited to large amounts of unstructured data, while Azure Files provides a fully managed file share in the cloud. Beyond exam topics, the episode presents a seven-level maturity model that reframes administrators as architects of a distributed decision system, with a focus on governance and identity-driven control.

Several other M365.FM episodes mention AZ-104 as a relevant certification for their audience. "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" is aimed at listeners preparing for AZ-104 or AZ-305, and it explains where Azure Load Balancer fits into an Azure networking strategy, what its limitations are, and how it improves availability and scalability for virtual machines, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and enterprise workloads. "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" addresses Azure administrators and developers and covers secretless authentication for services such as Logic Apps and containerized workloads, including how managed identities reduce the risk of credential leaks and simplify secure communication between Azure services.

"Azure Arc - Simply Explained" names AZ-104 alongside AZ-305 for listeners who work as cloud architects, Azure administrators or DevOps engineers. The episode describes managing servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases on-premises, at the edge or in other clouds from a single control plane, and mentions the use of Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Policy and Azure Update Manager to simplify hybrid cloud operations. "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" lists AZ-104 together with AZ-204 and explains Microsoft's serverless platform for containerized applications, which removes the need to manage Kubernetes clusters or virtual machines, and its integration with Azure Container Registry, Azure Monitor, GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps.

Taken together, these episodes show the range of topics that surround the certification in practice: identity and governance, storage choices, networking and load balancing, hybrid management with Azure Arc, and container hosting. The official exam page on Microsoft Learn is the reference for the current exam skills outline and for the exact scope of AZ-104.

az-140.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Virtual Desktop Specialty (AZ-140) is a Microsoft specialty certification for planning, delivering and managing Azure Virtual Desktop.

faq.a: It covers planning, delivering, managing and monitoring virtual desktop experiences and remote apps on Azure. The exam is organized into four areas: infrastructure, identity and security, user environments and apps, and monitoring and maintenance.
faq.q: What does the AZ-140 certification cover?

faq.a: It is aimed at server or desktop administrators who design, implement, manage and maintain Azure Virtual Desktop. Candidates are expected to have experience with Azure compute, networking, identity, storage and resiliency.
faq.q: Who is Microsoft Certified: Azure Virtual Desktop Specialty (AZ-140) intended for?

faq.a: The certification must be renewed, and according to Microsoft Learn the renewal is free through an online assessment on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: How is the certification renewed?

az-140.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Virtual Desktop Specialty (AZ-140) is a specialty certification developed by Microsoft. It is earned by passing the AZ-140 exam and covers planning, delivering, managing and monitoring virtual desktop experiences and remote apps on Azure, so that users can reach them from any device. According to Microsoft Learn, it is an intermediate-level credential for administrators.

The certification targets server or desktop administrators and engineers who design, implement, manage and maintain Azure Virtual Desktop. Because the service runs on Azure infrastructure, the certification is tied to Microsoft Azure, and candidates are expected to have experience with Azure compute, networking, identity, storage and resiliency. Working knowledge of the Azure portal and scripting tools is also expected. The documentation names no formal prerequisites or licensing requirements.

The AZ-140 exam is organized into four areas: planning and implementing the infrastructure, planning and implementing identity and security, planning and implementing user environments and apps, and monitoring and maintaining the infrastructure. These areas follow the lifecycle of a virtual desktop deployment, from initial design through setup to ongoing operation. The split between identity and security on one side and user environments and apps on the other reflects the fact that a working deployment needs both a sound platform and a usable experience for end users.

Typical situations in which the topic comes up include organizations that want to give employees secure access to a managed desktop from any device, teams that need a consistent workspace for remote or temporary staff, and IT departments that want to centralize desktop images and updates instead of maintaining individual physical machines. Candidates usually work in roles where they plan such environments, set them up and keep them running over time, which is why the exam combines design decisions with day-to-day operations.

On the practical side, the exam is proctored, may include interactive components, is offered in several languages and is booked through Pearson VUE. Microsoft Learn recommends using a personal Microsoft account for registration rather than a work or school account. Pricing depends on country or region, and retakes are possible after a waiting period. The certification has to be renewed, and renewal is free through an online assessment on Microsoft Learn, which avoids retaking the full exam.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so no episode-based guidance on preparation or exam strategy is available here. For candidates, the official certification page on Microsoft Learn is the primary source for the current exam skills outline, languages and scheduling details.

az-305.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305) is Microsoft's expert certification for designing identity, data, continuity and infrastructure solutions on Azure.

faq.a: The certification is earned by passing the exam AZ-305. The exam and its details are documented on Microsoft Learn.
faq.q: Which exam leads to the Azure Solutions Architect Expert certification?

faq.a: AZ-104 belongs to the administrator-focused Azure Administrator Associate certification, while AZ-305 is expert-level and concentrates on designing solutions, such as choosing services and balancing security, availability and cost.
faq.q: How does AZ-305 differ from AZ-104?

faq.a: It centers on designing identity, data, business-continuity and infrastructure solutions on Azure. One episode excerpt also lists compute, storage, networking, identity and access management, governance and disaster recovery.
faq.q: What areas does the certification cover?

az-305.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert, earned by passing the exam AZ-305, is an expert-level certification developed by Microsoft. It covers Microsoft Azure and focuses on designing identity, data, business-continuity and infrastructure solutions. The credential is aimed at people who plan Azure architectures and make design decisions, rather than those who only operate an existing environment.

Within the Azure role path, the certification sits above the administrator-focused Azure Administrator Associate certification (AZ-104). Where AZ-104 centers on running and managing Azure resources, the Azure Solutions Architect Expert certification concentrates on choosing suitable services and balancing requirements such as security, availability and cost. Practical Azure knowledge, for example hybrid management and workload identities, feeds directly into the kind of design questions that AZ-305 addresses. Official details about the exam are published on Microsoft Learn on the exam page for AZ-305.

One episode excerpt describes the scope of the certification as covering compute, storage, networking, identity and access management, governance, and disaster recovery. It also stresses hands-on experience through real-world projects and scenario-based learning as a way to prepare for the exam. According to that excerpt, passing AZ-305 leads to the title of Microsoft Certified Azure Architect Expert, and employers look for Azure architects to lead cloud adoption, design solutions and solve complex problems.

The episode "5 Microsoft Certifications That Boost Salary—and 3 to Skip" places AZ-305 among the high-value certifications, alongside SC-100, CISSP, AWS Certified Solutions Architect and PMP. The episode argues that many certifications validate task execution but not architectural authority, and that credentials demonstrating architecture skills tend to matter more for job prospects. It recommends weighing the cost of a certification against potential salary increases, aligning choices with long-term career goals, staying aware of industry demand, and combining certifications with real-world experience. It also warns against common pitfalls such as procrastination and resource overload when pursuing certifications.

Several technical episodes in the catalog reference AZ-305 as relevant background for Azure design topics. "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" describes how Azure Arc extends Azure management, security and governance to servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases outside Azure, together with Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Policy and Azure Update Manager, and mentions AZ-104 and AZ-305 as relevant certifications for the audience. "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" explains how Azure can create and manage identities for resources so that applications do not store usernames, passwords or secrets, and why Microsoft recommends secretless authentication. "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" covers where Azure Load Balancer fits into an Azure networking strategy, what its limitations are, and how it improves availability and scalability, again naming AZ-104 and AZ-305 as related preparation.

Taken together, these topics illustrate the design perspective of the certification: identity choices such as managed identities, hybrid governance through Azure Arc, and availability decisions involving load balancing are all areas where an architect has to select and justify a solution. The Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate episode also lists the certification in the context of advancing to cloud roles. Candidates deciding whether to pursue it typically consider their current role, whether they already hold AZ-104, and whether architectural design responsibility is part of their career plan.

az-400.desc: Microsoft Certified: DevOps Engineer Expert (AZ-400) is an expert-level Microsoft certification covering DevOps with Azure DevOps and GitHub, pipelines and delivery.

faq.a: It is an expert-level Microsoft certification for people who design and run DevOps practices with Azure DevOps and GitHub, with a focus on pipelines, source control and software delivery. The exam code is AZ-400.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Certified: DevOps Engineer Expert (AZ-400) certification?

faq.a: It covers Microsoft Azure as the platform on which build, release and infrastructure processes typically run, alongside the tools Azure DevOps and GitHub. The certification is developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: Which platform does the AZ-400 certification cover?

faq.a: The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" refers to a study guide for Exam AZ-400, learning materials for Microsoft Azure aimed at beginners, and the DevOps resource center for Azure DevOps as places to learn about DevOps practices.
faq.q: How can candidates prepare for AZ-400 according to M365.FM?

az-400.long:
Microsoft Certified: DevOps Engineer Expert (AZ-400) is an expert-level certification from Microsoft for people who design and run DevOps practices with Azure DevOps and GitHub. The matching exam carries the code AZ-400, and the credential is commonly referred to by that code. It focuses on pipelines, source control and the delivery of software, and it is aimed at engineers who connect development and operations work into one repeatable process.

The certification is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure as the platform on which build, release and infrastructure processes typically run. Candidates are therefore expected to combine knowledge about source control and automation with an understanding of how Azure resources are provisioned and operated. In practice, the credential sits at the point where code management, automated build and release workflows, and the cloud environment that hosts the result come together.

Typical situations in which the topic becomes relevant include teams that want to replace manual release steps with automated pipelines, organizations that want source control and delivery handled in a consistent way, and engineers who want to document their skills in this area with a recognized expert-level credential. Because the certification covers both Azure DevOps and GitHub, it is relevant for teams that use either tool or a combination of the two. The decision to pursue it usually follows from a role that already involves pipelines, branching strategies, release management or infrastructure automation, rather than from a purely theoretical interest.

Microsoft publishes official learning material for the exam. The M365.FM episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" points to a study guide for Exam AZ-400, described as a comprehensive guide on Azure DevOps solutions. It also refers to learning materials for Microsoft Azure as a compilation of resources for beginners, and to the DevOps resource center for Azure DevOps as a central hub for learning about DevOps practices. These pointers suggest a preparation path that starts with the platform fundamentals and then moves to the exam-specific study guide.

The same episode gives the working context on which the certification builds. It describes Azure DevOps as Microsoft's all-in-one platform for planning, developing, testing and delivering software, and explains that it replaces separate tools for project management, source control, build automation, testing and deployments. The episode also stresses that the platform helps development and operations teams collaborate and automate repetitive tasks. Among the benefits it lists are quick release cycles for deploying new systems and applications, and built-in security and compliance, so that security and control are applied directly in the pipelines.

In relation to other topics on M365.FM, the certification is closely tied to Microsoft Azure as the covered platform and to Microsoft as the vendor that defines the exam. Anyone reading about Azure DevOps features, pipelines or release practices will find that the AZ-400 exam objectives follow the same themes: planning and tracking work, managing source code, building and releasing automatically, and keeping security and compliance part of the delivery process rather than an afterthought.

az-700.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700) is an associate-level Microsoft certification for designing, implementing and maintaining Azure networking solutions.

faq.a: AZ-700 is the exam code for Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate, an associate-level certification developed by Microsoft. It covers designing, implementing and maintaining Azure networking solutions.
faq.q: What is the AZ-700 certification?

faq.a: The certification covers Microsoft Azure, with a focus on networking. Network security services such as Azure Firewall belong to this topic area.
faq.q: Which technology area does AZ-700 cover?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" describes Azure Firewall as a cloud-native, fully managed network security service. It also lists study resources, including the Microsoft Press AZ-700 cert prep course, a demo repository, documentation and a deployment tutorial.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Azure Firewall offer for AZ-700 preparation?

az-700.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft that focuses on designing, implementing and maintaining networking solutions in Azure. The related exam code is AZ-700, and the credential is often referred to simply by that code. It addresses professionals who plan how Azure workloads are connected, secured and made reachable.

The certification covers Microsoft Azure and is developed by Microsoft. Networking is a foundation for almost every other Azure workload, which is why the subject matters well beyond dedicated network teams. Architects, administrators and engineers who need to understand how traffic flows between cloud resources, on-premises environments and users are the typical audience. Decisions about how services are connected and protected tend to shape the reliability and security of an entire Azure environment, and AZ-700 is positioned as the credential that addresses this area.

In practice, the role described by the certification covers three broad activities that are reflected in its short description: designing networking solutions, implementing them, and maintaining them over time. Design involves deciding how Azure resources should be connected and exposed. Implementation turns those decisions into working configurations. Maintenance covers keeping the network operating as workloads and requirements change. The certification is aimed at people who carry responsibility across all three activities rather than only one of them.

Network security is a central part of this topic area. The M365.FM episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" (July 2026) touches on it directly. The episode presents Azure Firewall as Microsoft's cloud-native, fully managed network security service that protects Azure workloads from internal and external threats. Instead of deploying and maintaining traditional firewall appliances, teams get centralized traffic filtering, threat intelligence and application-aware security that scales with the environment. The episode also points to a modular economic model that allows scaling based on network traffic. For anyone preparing for AZ-700, this gives a practical view of how network protection is delivered as a managed service rather than as hardware or self-maintained software.

The same episode lists learning resources for people who want to go deeper. Among them is a course titled "Designing and Implementing Microsoft Azure Networking Solutions (AZ-700) Cert Prep" by Microsoft Press, which is named as a way to study the exam content. The episode also mentions a demo repository for quick deployment of Azure Firewall, the Azure Firewall documentation, and a step-by-step tutorial for deploying and configuring it. These resources are presented as tools for strengthening both understanding and hands-on implementation, which fits the implement-and-maintain emphasis of the certification.

Typical situations in which this certification becomes relevant include building a structured learning path in Azure networking, validating existing hands-on experience with a recognized credential, or preparing for roles in which responsibility for connectivity and network protection in Azure is part of the job. The official Microsoft Learn page for the AZ-700 exam is the place to check the current exam details, such as the skills measured, since those are maintained by Microsoft and may change over time.

az-800.desc: Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-800 is a Microsoft certification exam on hybrid Windows Server administration, retired on 30 September 2026; successor: AZ-802.

faq.a: No. The catalog data and a warning on the Microsoft Learn page state that AZ-800 was retired on 30 September 2026 and can no longer be taken for the certification. The successor named in the catalog is AZ-802.
faq.q: Is exam AZ-800 still available?

faq.a: The exam covers AD DS in on-premises and cloud settings, hybrid server and workload management, virtual machines and containers, on-premises and hybrid networking, and storage and file services. Tools named include Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor and Azure Update Manager.
faq.q: What topics does AZ-800 cover?

faq.a: Both are exams of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification. AZ-800 deals with core infrastructure, while AZ-801 covers advanced services, and the catalog data lists both as retired on the same date.
faq.q: How does AZ-800 relate to AZ-801?

az-800.long:
Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-800 is a Microsoft certification exam for administrators who run Windows Server in on-premises and hybrid environments. It is one of the two exams of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification, the other being AZ-801. According to the catalog data, AZ-800 was retired on 30 September 2026, and AZ-802 is named as its successor. The exam is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure, because the hybrid scenarios connect local Windows Server infrastructure with cloud services.

The Microsoft Learn exam page, titled "Administering Windows Server Hybrid Core Infrastructure", describes the role behind the exam. It concerns deploying, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server, including servers running in Azure, migrating workloads, and handling identity, security, compute, networking, storage and monitoring. The exam is aimed at candidates with several years of Windows Server experience, and the pass mark is 700. The related exam AZ-801 covers advanced services, while AZ-800 addresses the core infrastructure side.

The skill areas measured by AZ-800 are grouped around a few themes. These include Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) in on-premises and cloud settings, hybrid server and workload management, virtual machines and containers, on-premises and hybrid networking, and storage and file services. The tools named in the documentation include Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products. Together they show the typical shape of the work: managing servers and identity services consistently across a data center and the cloud rather than treating the two as separate worlds.

In practice, candidates preparing for hybrid administration tend to combine the official Microsoft Learn material with hands-on practice in a test environment, since many of the subjects, such as joining servers to Azure management through Azure Arc or applying policy and update management to hybrid machines, are operational skills. The exact skills measured should always be taken from the current Microsoft Learn exam page rather than from older study guides, because exam outlines change over time.

Retirement is the most important point for anyone planning a certification path. A warning on the Microsoft Learn page states that the exam was retired on 30 September 2026, after which it can no longer be taken for the certification. The scheduling section of the same page still shows no retirement date, so the two statements on the page do not fully line up, and the warning text and the catalog data should be treated as the reference. Anyone starting now should orient themselves on AZ-802 and check how it relates to AZ-801, which is retired on the same date according to the catalog data.

No M365.FM episode in the catalog is currently linked to this exam, so there is no episode commentary to summarize here. The topic connects most directly to Microsoft Azure, the platform that the hybrid scenarios of this certification build on. The documentation page names no license requirements and no price for the exam, so those details should be checked through Microsoft directly.

az-801.desc: AZ-801 is the Microsoft exam on advanced Windows Server hybrid services, part of the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate; retired 30 September 2026, successor AZ-802.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it covers advanced Windows Server administration in on-premises and hybrid setups: securing Windows Server, high availability, disaster recovery, migration to Azure, and monitoring and troubleshooting.
faq.q: What does the AZ-801 exam cover?

faq.a: No. The catalog data records that AZ-801 was retired on 30 September 2026, and AZ-802 is listed as its successor.
faq.q: Is AZ-801 still available?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn page names Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products.
faq.q: Which tools are associated with AZ-801?

az-801.long:
Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate – exam AZ-801 is a Microsoft certification exam, titled "Configuring Windows Server Hybrid Advanced Services" on Microsoft Learn. It belongs to the Windows Server Hybrid Administrator Associate certification, alongside AZ-800, and is aimed at administrators who run Windows Server in on-premises and hybrid infrastructures. The catalog data records that AZ-801 was retired on 30 September 2026, with AZ-802 listed as the successor.

The exam is developed by Microsoft and covers Microsoft Azure, because hybrid administration means extending on-premises Windows Server environments with Azure services. According to the Microsoft Learn page, AZ-801 deals with advanced services for administering Windows Server, including migration of servers and workloads to Azure. The role it describes is about keeping servers secure, available and recoverable across on-premises and cloud locations.

The skills measured fall into several areas: securing Windows Server, implementing and managing high availability, implementing disaster recovery, migrating servers and workloads, and monitoring and troubleshooting Windows Server environments. The Microsoft Learn page names a range of tools in this context, among them Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Policy, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager and the Defender products. In practice, these cover tasks such as hardening servers, planning failover and backup strategies, moving workloads to Azure, and tracking the health of a mixed server estate.

On the preparation side, Microsoft Learn recommends several years of Windows Server experience and gives the pass mark as 700. The page lists no formal prerequisites; AZ-800 appears only as a related exam. A free practice assessment, a study guide and an exam sandbox are offered for candidates. Details such as exam duration, number of questions, format and certificate validity are not stated on the page.

The retirement matters for anyone planning a certification path. A warning on the Microsoft Learn page states that the exam was retired on 30 September 2026, after which the certification can no longer be earned or renewed through it, although the scheduling section of the page still shows no retirement date. Candidates who encounter older AZ-801 study material should therefore compare it with the current AZ-802 outline on Microsoft Learn, since earlier skills outlines may no longer apply.

Within the wider Microsoft certification landscape, AZ-801 sits in the infrastructure branch, in contrast to the Microsoft 365 administrator exams, which focus on the productivity cloud. No M365.FM episode is linked to AZ-801 in the catalog, so there are no episode statements to report for this topic.

az-802.desc: Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate (AZ-802) is a 2026 consolidated exam for Windows Server hybrid administration, replacing AZ-800 and AZ-801.

faq.a: AZ-802 is the exam for the Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate certification. It validates skills in deploying, implementing, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server workloads in on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments.
faq.q: What is the AZ-802 exam?

faq.a: According to the facts provided, AZ-802 is a new consolidated exam from 2026 that replaces AZ-800 and AZ-801. The official Microsoft documentation should be consulted for the current status of those older exams.
faq.q: Does AZ-802 replace AZ-800 and AZ-801?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn page recommends experience with Windows Admin Center, Hyper-V, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AD DS basics. No formal prerequisites are listed.
faq.q: What experience is recommended for AZ-802?

az-802.long:
Microsoft Certified: Windows Server Administrator Associate (AZ-802) is an associate-level certification from Microsoft for Windows Server hybrid administration. It is built around the exam code AZ-802 and, according to the facts available, was introduced in 2026 as a consolidated exam that replaces the earlier AZ-800 and AZ-801 exams. The certification covers Microsoft Azure alongside Windows Server, reflecting the way many administrators run servers in their own data centers while also using cloud services.

The exam is described on Microsoft Learn as validating skills in deploying, implementing, managing and troubleshooting Windows Server workloads in on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments. Its content areas include deploying and managing AD DS, managing Windows Server instances and workloads in hybrid settings, managing virtual machines, implementing on-premises and hybrid networking, managing storage and file services, securing the Windows Server infrastructure, and monitoring and troubleshooting. Merging two earlier exams into one puts these areas under a single credential, which matches the idea that they belong together in the daily work of a server administrator.

The documentation lists recommended experience rather than formal prerequisites. The recommended background covers Windows Admin Center, Hyper-V, PowerShell, Azure Arc, Azure Monitor, Azure Update Manager, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AD DS basics. This mix shows how hybrid administration is framed: classic server roles and virtualization on one side, and Azure-based management, update, monitoring and security services on the other. Typical scenarios for the topic include running core server roles in an existing infrastructure, connecting on-premises servers to cloud management services, and planning the availability and recovery of important systems.

On the practical side, the exam is available in English and is booked through Pearson VUE. The price depends on the country. Microsoft offers a course called Administer Windows Server that supports preparation. The official exam page does not list formal prerequisites, license requirements, a validity period or renewal rules, and it states no retirement date for the exam, so candidates who need those details should check the current Microsoft documentation directly.

For administrators who had already started preparing for AZ-800 or AZ-801, the main decision is how that earlier preparation maps to the new exam. Because AZ-802 is stated to replace both, the official Microsoft documentation is the place to confirm the current status of the older exams and the transition. The topic areas listed for AZ-802 give a way to compare earlier study material against what the new exam covers.

The M365.FM episodes in the current data do not cover this certification directly, so there are no episode statements to report on AZ-802. The certification is relevant to listeners of M365.FM mainly through its connection to Microsoft Azure and to the hybrid server administration topics that surround the Microsoft ecosystem.

az-900.desc: Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) is Microsoft's entry-level certification covering basic cloud concepts and core Azure services.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it covers describing cloud concepts, describing Azure architecture and services such as compute, networking and storage, and describing Azure management and governance, including security, governance and administration tools.
faq.q: What does the AZ-900 exam cover?

faq.a: No formal prerequisite is listed. Microsoft Learn recommends experience in an IT area such as infrastructure, database administration or software development, but this is not required.
faq.q: Are there prerequisites for Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals?

faq.a: The exam is proctored, offered in many languages, and booked through Pearson VUE, or through Certiport for students and educators. Microsoft lists a practice assessment, an exam sandbox and a study guide as preparation options.
faq.q: How is the AZ-900 exam taken?

az-900.long:
Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals is an entry-level certification developed by Microsoft. It is earned by passing the exam with the code AZ-900, and the exam code is often used as the short name for the certification itself. It covers basic cloud concepts and core services of Microsoft Azure and is aimed at people who are new to cloud computing or to Azure, for example in business, sales or early IT roles.

According to Microsoft Learn, the certification demonstrates foundational knowledge of cloud concepts in general and of Microsoft Azure in particular. It is described as a common starting point for a career in the Azure space. Microsoft Azure is the cloud platform on which many Microsoft 365 integrations, data services and AI services run, which is one reason a fundamentals-level overview of the platform is useful for people working anywhere in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The exam covers three areas. The first is describing cloud concepts. The second is describing Azure architecture and services, including compute, networking and storage. The third is describing Azure management and governance, which includes security, governance and administration tools. The scope is conceptual and descriptive rather than deeply hands-on, which fits the fundamentals level.

No formal prerequisite is listed for AZ-900. Microsoft Learn notes that experience in an IT area such as infrastructure, database administration or software development is recommended but not required. The exam is proctored and offered in many languages. It is booked through Pearson VUE, or through Certiport for students and educators. Preparation options listed by Microsoft include a practice assessment, an exam sandbox and a study guide. The documentation reviewed here does not state a passing score, a question count or renewal rules, so those details should be checked on the official exam page before booking.

In practice, AZ-900 is typically chosen as a first step before more specialized, role-based Azure exams, or as a way for non-engineering staff to learn the vocabulary used by cloud teams. Typical decisions around it include whether the learner needs only a conceptual overview or a path toward administration and architecture roles, and which preparation materials to use.

The M365.FM catalog has no episode dedicated solely to AZ-900, but the episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" places the certification at the start of a career progression. The episode excerpt lists, as a key takeaway, to start the Azure journey with the AZ-900 certification, since it provides essential knowledge of cloud concepts and Azure services. It also stresses understanding key Azure terms such as subscriptions, resource groups and workloads in order to manage resources effectively, and mentions managing Azure subscriptions to control costs and ensure compliance, with strategies such as rightsizing and autoscaling. The episode further says that professionals who excel in Azure administration can move into roles like Solutions Architect or DevOps Engineer, and it describes a seven-level model from beginner to cloud architect, in which a fundamentals exam such as AZ-900 marks the beginning.

azure.desc: Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform offering compute, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI services for running applications and data workloads.

faq.a: Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform with services for computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI. It lets organizations run applications and store data without operating their own data centers.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Azure?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained", it runs the same models but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with their own keys, limits and privacy rules.
faq.q: How does Azure OpenAI Service differ from ChatGPT?

faq.a: Related topics include Azure Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Azure landing zone, Azure Virtual Desktop and Bicep, the language used to describe Azure resources as code.
faq.q: Which services are related to Azure on M365.FM?

azure.long:
Microsoft Azure, often shortened to Azure, is Microsoft's cloud platform. It provides services for computing, storage, networking, databases, analytics and AI. Organizations use it to run applications, store data and build solutions without operating their own data centers. Microsoft develops the platform, and on M365.FM it is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a cloud platform.

Azure is not a single product but a broad collection of services that can be combined. Several of them are linked to the platform on M365.FM: Azure Logic Apps and Azure Functions for automation and event-driven logic, Azure Virtual Desktop for delivering desktops from the cloud, and the Azure landing zone as a foundation for structuring an Azure environment. Bicep, the language used to describe Azure resources as code, is part of the same ecosystem. Many Microsoft 365 solutions depend on Azure services, for example for identity, automation and AI, which is why Azure appears so often in discussions of the wider Microsoft ecosystem.

The M365.FM episodes in the "Simply Explained" series describe individual Azure services in plain language. "Azure OpenAI Service - Simply Explained" says the service is not ChatGPT with a Microsoft logo on it. It runs the same models, but Microsoft hosts them inside the customer's own Azure space, with the customer's own keys, limits and privacy rules. The episode covers topics such as deployments as your own copy of a model, endpoints and keys, built-in content filtering, data privacy, and how the service differs from the OpenAI API.

"Azure SQL Database - Simply Explained" describes a relational database that Microsoft runs for you in its cloud. The episode walks through the two ways to pay for it, how to pick a service tier, elastic pools described as a timeshare trick, and which tasks Azure handles so the customer does not have to. It also touches on security.

"Azure Data Factory - Simply Explained" compares the service to a courier for company data: it picks up raw information from wherever it lives, cleans it on the way, and delivers it somewhere reports can use it. The episode explains the building blocks, including pipelines and activities, linked services and datasets, integration runtimes, triggers and scheduling, and mapping data flows for transformation.

"Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" covers the part of Azure that tells apps what has already happened. A file lands in storage, a device connects or an order comes in, and instead of code asking repeatedly, Event Grid delivers the news. The episode discusses why event-driven designs keep coming up, the different kinds of topics, push versus pull delivery, retries and dead-lettering when delivery fails, and how Event Grid compares with Service Bus and Event Hubs.

Azure also appears in an industry context. The episode "Predictive Maintenance on Azure for Manufacturers: What You Actually Need Before the Model" is aimed at maintenance managers, reliability engineers, plant and production leaders, OT and IT architects, and data teams planning predictive maintenance, condition monitoring and industrial AI on Microsoft Azure in manufacturing. It stresses the preparation needed before a model is built and the maintenance process technicians already follow.

Typical decisions around Azure include which service fits a workload, how to structure the environment through a landing zone, how to define resources as code with Bicep, and how to handle data privacy and access for AI services. The linked topics and episodes above give entry points for each of these areas.

azure-ad-b2c.desc: Azure AD B2C is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing apps, configured with user flows or XML custom policies and succeeded by Microsoft Entra External ID.

faq.a: Azure AD B2C is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing apps. According to the M365.FM episodes, it is used for sign-in to customer portals and multi-tenant SaaS platforms, including social accounts, tenant-specific credentials and single sign-on.
faq.q: What is Azure AD B2C used for?

faq.a: It is configured with user flows or with XML-based custom policies. User flows cover common scenarios, while custom policies allow more tailored identity journeys.
faq.q: How is Azure AD B2C configured?

faq.a: Microsoft Entra External ID succeeds Azure AD B2C. The episode "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth" covers migration realities and how organizations can modernize without abandoning existing CIAM investments.
faq.q: What replaced Azure AD B2C?

azure-ad-b2c.long:
Azure AD B2C (Azure Active Directory B2C) is Microsoft's earlier customer identity service for consumer-facing applications. It is part of Microsoft Azure and handles sign-up and sign-in for external users such as customers, rather than for an organization's own workforce. The service has been succeeded by Microsoft Entra External ID, which is why most current discussion of it concerns existing deployments, comparison with its successor, and migration.

The service is configured in one of two ways: with user flows or with XML-based custom policies. User flows are the predefined route for common scenarios, while custom policies are written in XML and allow more tailored identity journeys. Choosing between the two is a typical design decision, since it affects how much of the sign-in experience can be adapted and how much configuration effort is involved. Official documentation describes the service in its overview pages on Microsoft Learn.

The M365.FM episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" discusses Azure AD B2C in the context of multi-tenant software-as-a-service platforms. According to the episode, Azure AD B2C works well for such platforms because tenants can use their own credentials or connect with social accounts, which it describes as giving flexibility and strong security. The episode adds that user flows, policies and branding can be managed for each tenant, and that the service supports single sign-on (SSO), which makes the login process smoother for users. It also mentions custom identity providers as a further option and stresses tenant-specific authentication and authorization, with separation between tenants to support privacy and legal requirements.

The episode "Build Customer Portals with Power Pages and Dataverse" places Azure AD B2C in a customer portal setting. Its field guide lists external identities, either Azure AD B2C or local authentication, combined with multi-factor authentication as the authentication layer of a portal. Access is then controlled through web roles such as Customer, Partner and Manager, mapped to Dataverse table permissions scoped by Contact or Account, so that users read and write only their own records. The episode also lists a go-live checklist covering authentication, data scope, branding and audit, including sign-in logs, data access logs and change history.

The relationship to its successor is covered in "Microsoft Entra External ID for Digital Trust and Growth". The episode describes Microsoft Entra External ID as the layer for external identities and Verified ID as the means of portable trust through verifiable credentials. It says that together they help organizations modernize customer and partner identity without abandoning existing CIAM (customer identity and access management) investments. The same episode addresses Azure AD B2C migration realities, governance challenges, digital sovereignty, lifecycle management and the balance between user control and enterprise policy enforcement.

The broader positioning appears in "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform". The episode notes that what used to be several consoles, including Azure AD, Azure AD B2C and B2B, is now a coordinated platform under the Microsoft Entra umbrella for managing users, devices and apps from a single control plane. For readers searching for Azure AD B2C, the practical takeaways from the episodes are that the service remains relevant for understanding existing customer-facing sign-in setups, that its policy-based configuration model shapes migration planning, and that Microsoft Entra External ID is the direction Microsoft has taken for external identities.

azure-ad-graph.desc: Azure AD Graph is the legacy Microsoft directory API, part of Microsoft Azure, that was deprecated and retired in favor of Microsoft Graph.
