According to the episode, it allows organizations to manage public and private DNS zones, automate DNS management, and provide fast, reliable name resolution for cloud and hybrid environments, all without maintaining their own DNS servers. The episode is part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format.

For planning, the main decisions revolve around which zones are public and which are private, how on-premises name resolution connects to Azure through the Private Resolver, and whether query filtering at virtual network level is required. Because Azure DNS uses the same management model as other Azure resources, it fits teams that already administer their infrastructure through Azure tools and want DNS handled in the same way.

azure-elastic-san.desc: Azure Elastic SAN is a managed Azure storage area network that pools block storage into volume groups and volumes, which workloads attach to over iSCSI.

faq.a: Azure Elastic SAN is a managed storage area network service in Microsoft Azure that provides pooled block storage. It is organized into volume groups and volumes, and workloads connect to volumes over iSCSI.
faq.q: What is Azure Elastic SAN?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, Azure Elastic SAN can serve as shared backend storage for Azure Virtual Machines, Azure VMware Solution and Azure Kubernetes Service.
faq.q: Which Azure services can use Azure Elastic SAN as storage?

faq.a: It supports encryption at rest, LRS or ZRS redundancy, private endpoints, VNet-restricted access and snapshots. Encryption in transit and soft delete are not supported, and a single volume can reach up to 80,000 IOPS as an upper bound.
faq.q: What features and limits does Azure Elastic SAN have?

azure-elastic-san.long:
Azure Elastic SAN is a managed storage area network service in Microsoft Azure that provides pooled, high-performance block storage. Microsoft Learn describes it as a fully integrated SAN offering that simplifies provisioning, scaling and managing a storage area network, with cloud capabilities such as high availability built in. Workloads connect to its volumes over iSCSI. It belongs to Microsoft Azure and is aimed at performance-heavy workloads and large databases.

The service addresses a problem that often appears only after an Azure environment grows. One virtual machine with one Managed Disk is simple, but as more virtual machines, databases and applications appear, each workload can end up with its own disks, its own performance limits and its own capacity decisions. The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" describes the resulting inefficiency: one workload may pay for storage performance it rarely uses while another needs additional capacity or performance. Consolidating many IO-intensive workloads onto one SAN, instead of managing storage separately for each compute resource, can be more cost-efficient, according to the documentation.

Azure Elastic SAN is organized into three levels. The Elastic SAN itself is the top-level resource, where redundancy and provisioned capacity are set. Volume groups sit beneath it and pass settings, such as virtual network rules, down to the volumes they contain. Volumes are the partitions of capacity that clients attach to over iSCSI. Because performance is shared across all volumes in the SAN, volumes typically do not need to be overprovisioned individually. According to the documentation, a single volume can reach up to 80,000 IOPS depending on the SAN's limits and the volume's size, and these figures are upper bounds rather than guarantees.

Azure Elastic SAN can act as shared backend storage for several Azure compute services: Azure Virtual Machines, Azure VMware Solution and Azure Kubernetes Service. This makes it relevant for scenarios where many workloads draw on one storage pool and where sizing each disk separately would lead to stranded capacity or unused performance.

The documented feature set includes encryption at rest, locally redundant storage (LRS) or zone-redundant storage (ZRS) redundancy, private endpoints, access restricted to virtual networks, and snapshots. Two limits are worth noting when planning: encryption in transit and soft delete are not supported. Teams evaluating Azure Elastic SAN against per-VM Managed Disks should weigh the pooled-performance model against these constraints, as well as the redundancy option chosen at the SAN level.

The second episode, "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365", places Azure Elastic SAN within a wider architectural discussion. It covers centralized, scalable resource pools as an alternative to isolated storage silos and fixed allocations, alongside concepts such as Azure SQL Hyperscale, elastic storage pools, shared performance layers and tenant-wide scaling models for multi-tenant Microsoft 365 environments. The episode also discusses automation, orchestration, governance and dynamic scaling as ways to improve operational efficiency and reduce infrastructure waste.

In short, Azure Elastic SAN is a pooled block-storage option in Azure where capacity and performance are provisioned at the SAN level and distributed across volumes, rather than assigned workload by workload.

azure-event-grid.desc: Azure Event Grid is a managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure that routes events from publishers to subscribed handlers over HTTP or MQTT.

faq.a: Azure Event Grid is a fully managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure that routes events from publishers such as Azure services or custom apps to subscribed handlers. It supports HTTP and MQTT, with push and pull delivery.
faq.q: What is Azure Event Grid?

faq.a: According to the episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem", IoT Hub Message Routing is designed around preserving and distributing operational data, while Event Grid is designed around notifying systems that something changed and may require a response.
faq.q: How does Azure Event Grid differ from IoT Hub Message Routing?

faq.a: The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" compares Event Grid with Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs to help listeners decide which messaging service fits a given situation.
faq.q: Which Azure services are compared with Event Grid in the episodes?

azure-event-grid.long:
Azure Event Grid is a fully managed publish-subscribe service in Microsoft Azure. It routes events from publishers, such as Azure services or custom applications, to subscribed handlers. Delivery works over HTTP or MQTT, and both push and pull delivery are supported. The service is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented on Microsoft Learn.

The core idea is event-driven design. The M365.FM episode "Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" describes Event Grid as the part of Azure that tells applications what has already happened. A file lands in storage, a device connects, or an order comes in, and instead of application code asking over and over whether something changed, Event Grid delivers the news. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" makes the same point: instead of constantly polling for changes, Event Grid delivers notifications in real time, which lets services react instantly when something happens.

In practical terms, a publisher emits an event, and subscribers register interest in the events they care about. Event Grid sits between the two and moves the event from source to handler, so publishers and handlers do not need to know about each other directly. The episode "Azure Event Grid - Simply Explained" structures its explanation around a small set of terms, including why event-driven architecture keeps coming up, what the service actually is, and the kinds of delivery it supports. The episodes frame Event Grid as a building block for cloud-native, serverless and microservices architectures, where components respond to changes rather than checking for them on a schedule.

A frequent design decision is choosing between Event Grid and other Azure messaging services. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" compares Event Grid with Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs so listeners can judge when each service is the right choice. A second episode theme concerns separating telemetry from events. In "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem", the hosts follow a manufacturing scenario in which a press line continuously sends temperature, vibration, cycle count, energy consumption and machine-state data through an industrial gateway. That stream forms an operational history that engineers, data teams and maintenance teams may need to analyze later. A device disconnect is different, because it is a discrete change that may require a response.

According to that episode, Azure IoT Hub Message Routing and Azure Event Grid solve different problems. One path is designed around preserving and distributing operational data. The other is designed around notifying systems that something changed and may require a response. The episode warns that treating the two as interchangeable can lead to expensive workflows processing routine sensor data, or to important signals buried inside a telemetry pipeline that nobody is actively watching. It also notes that treating routine measurements as discrete events can create noisy workflows, incomplete production histories, unnecessary processing, and systems that react without enough context.

Event Grid also appears in the modernization discussion in "Replace Legacy Middleware with Policy-Driven Architecture". That episode names Microsoft Azure Event Grid and Service Bus as enabling real-time, event-driven architectures that reduce what it calls the coordination tax of legacy middleware, and links modernization to faster response to market changes and improved customer experience.

In summary, Azure Event Grid is the routing layer for "something happened" notifications in Azure. It is most relevant where applications should react to state changes from Azure services or custom sources, and less suited to being used as a store or pipeline for continuous measurement data, a distinction the M365.FM episodes return to repeatedly.

azure-event-hubs.desc: Azure Event Hubs is Microsoft's big-data streaming and event ingestion service in Azure, handling millions of events per second and compatible with Apache Kafka.

faq.a: Azure Event Hubs is Microsoft's big-data streaming platform and event ingestion service in Microsoft Azure. It receives and processes millions of events per second and is compatible with Apache Kafka.
faq.q: What is Azure Event Hubs?

faq.a: According to the episode "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service", Event Hubs focuses on stream processing and high-volume data movement via partitions and consumer groups. It does not manage device lifecycles, firmware or desired configurations.
faq.q: How does Azure Event Hubs differ from IoT Hub?

faq.a: The episodes mention Azure Functions, Azure Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Explorer, Apache Kafka, Event Grid, Microsoft Graph change notifications and Fabric Data Activator as integrations or related services.
faq.q: Which services work with Azure Event Hubs?

azure-event-hubs.long:
Azure Event Hubs is a big-data streaming platform and event ingestion service developed by Microsoft and offered as part of Microsoft Azure. It receives and processes millions of events per second and is compatible with Apache Kafka. In everyday usage it is often shortened to Event Hubs. Microsoft documents the service in its Azure documentation, and it is classified as a Microsoft tool within the wider Azure portfolio.

The core purpose of Event Hubs is high-throughput, low-latency movement of event data from many producers to many independent readers. The episode "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service" describes it as a data highway that focuses entirely on stream processing and high-volume movement. According to that episode, its primary job is keeping traffic moving efficiently through partitions and consumer groups. Partitions and consumer groups are therefore central concepts: they allow data to be spread across parallel streams and read by several consumers independently.

An important distinction made in the same episode is what Event Hubs does not do. It does not manage device lifecycles, firmware or desired configurations. Those responsibilities belong to a device-management service, and the episode contrasts Event Hubs with Azure IoT Hub, where individual gateways can be identified, authenticated, enabled or disabled. For example, a single suspect gateway on a production line can be isolated without shutting down the whole plant's telemetry path. The episode's argument is that manufacturers often choose the wrong service by overlooking this difference between a device-aware service and a pure streaming pipeline.

The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" presents the service as a high-throughput event streaming platform for cloud-native applications, IoT solutions, real-time analytics and large-scale data pipelines. It also covers how Event Hubs integrates with Azure Functions, Azure Stream Analytics, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Explorer, Apache Kafka and other analytics platforms to support real-time processing and insights. Kafka compatibility is relevant for teams that already use Kafka-based tooling and want to work with an Azure-hosted streaming endpoint.

Event Hubs also appears as a building block in other Microsoft services covered by M365.FM. In "Microsoft Graph Change Notifications - Simply Explained", Event Hubs is named as an alternative to webhooks for receiving change notifications: webhooks suit instant push notifications, while Event Hubs is the choice for handling large volumes of notifications securely and reliably. In "Event Grid - Simply Explained", Azure Event Hubs is listed as an example of an event publisher that sends events to Event Grid, alongside Azure Blob Storage. In "Power BI Alerts vs Fabric Data Activator", it is mentioned as one of the sources, along with Power BI, that Fabric Data Activator can connect to in order to watch live data and trigger alerts or actions, such as messages in Teams, emails or workflows.

Taken together, the episodes position Event Hubs as an ingestion and streaming layer rather than a complete solution on its own. Typical decisions around it concern whether device management is needed (pointing to IoT Hub), whether volume justifies Event Hubs over webhooks for notification delivery, and which downstream consumers, such as Stream Analytics, Functions, Fabric or Data Explorer, will process the incoming events.

azure-file-sync.desc: Azure File Sync caches Azure Files content on local Windows servers, giving on-premises users local performance while Azure Files stays the source of truth.

faq.a: Azure File Sync caches files from Azure Files on local Windows servers. On-premises users get local performance, while Azure Files remains the source of truth.
faq.q: What is Azure File Sync?

faq.a: Azure Files is the managed file share service in Azure Storage, and Azure File Sync replicates those shares to Windows Server for performance and caching. The M365.FM episodes describe it as part of hybrid file-server setups.
faq.q: How does Azure File Sync relate to Azure Files?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity" says many organizations still rely on X.509 certificates and SAS tokens, which it describes as possession-based secrets. It recommends Managed Identity with least-privilege roles on the storage account and shares.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode say about authentication for Azure File Sync?

azure-file-sync.long:
Azure File Sync is a product within Microsoft Azure that caches files from Azure Files on local Windows servers. On-premises users work with files at local performance, while the Azure file share remains the source of truth. The service connects a managed cloud file share with Windows Server, which makes it relevant for hybrid file-server scenarios.

The purpose of Azure File Sync is to combine the characteristics of Azure Files with the behavior of a traditional on-premises file server. Azure Files is a managed file share service within Azure Storage that supports SMB and NFS shares. The M365.FM episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" describes how businesses increasingly replace or extend on-premises file servers with this managed service, and it lists Azure File Sync among the key concepts alongside redundancy options, authentication, security, snapshots, backups and performance tiers. In that framing, Azure File Sync is the component that links hybrid Windows Server environments to the cloud share.

The episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" places Azure File Sync in the context of Azure Files within a storage account. It describes the feature as a way to replicate Azure file shares to Windows Server, improving performance and caching. Other use cases named there for Azure file shares include file sharing across teams and departments, backup solutions, and application migration, where applications that expect a file share are moved to the cloud without major changes. Azure File Sync fits into these scenarios when a local copy of the data is still needed for speed or compatibility.

Authentication is a recurring topic in the M365.FM coverage. The episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity" notes that many organizations still run Azure File Sync on older authentication based on local X.509 certificates and SAS tokens. The episode characterizes these as possession-based secrets: whoever holds them is treated as the legitimate identity. According to the episode, such secrets tend to spread into scripts, backups, repositories and logs, can expire without notice, and a leaked credential allows silent data exfiltration with valid credentials.

The proposed alternative in that episode is Managed Identity. It describes the migration as assigning least-privilege roles to the storage account and shares, with the stated outcomes of fewer open URLs, no secrets to rotate, uniform logging and governance that scales. The episode "Managed Identities - Simply Explained" lists Azure File Sync among the Azure services that integrate with managed identities, alongside Azure Data Factory and Azure Service Bus. It adds that such integrations allow authentication and access control without hardcoded credentials, and that prerequisites include an Azure subscription with permission to create storage accounts and assign Azure RBAC roles.

In practice, decisions around Azure File Sync therefore involve several layers: the Azure Files share and its storage account, the Windows Server that acts as the local cache, and the identity model used for access. Related topics covered by M365.FM include Azure Files, Azure Storage Accounts, Managed Identities and, for adjacent Azure storage knowledge, Azure Managed Disks, whose episode lists the Azure File Sync migration episode as related listening. Official documentation for the product is available through Microsoft Learn under the Azure Storage section on file sync.

azure-files.desc: Azure Files is Microsoft's fully managed cloud file share service, reachable via SMB and NFS and extendable to on-premises servers with Azure File Sync.

faq.a: Azure Files is a Microsoft Azure service that offers fully managed cloud file shares accessible via SMB and NFS. It lets organizations provide shared storage without maintaining traditional file servers.
faq.q: What is Azure Files?

faq.a: Azure File Sync provides on-premises caching for Azure file shares. According to the episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity", syncing between Azure file shares and on-premises servers can also be used to achieve geographic redundancy.
faq.q: What is Azure File Sync used for?

faq.a: The episodes mention RBAC for access control, soft delete against accidental deletion, share snapshots for point-in-time recovery, and Azure Backup, which covers Azure Files among other workloads.
faq.q: How can data in Azure Files be protected?

azure-files.long:
Azure Files is a Microsoft Azure service that provides fully managed file shares in the cloud. It is developed by Microsoft, belongs to Microsoft Azure, and is accessed through the familiar SMB and NFS protocols. Because the service is managed, organizations can create secure, scalable and highly available file shares without maintaining traditional file servers. Azure Files can be combined with Azure File Sync, which provides on-premises caching of cloud file shares.

The main purpose of Azure Files is shared file storage for both cloud-native and hybrid environments. As the episode "Azure Files - Simply Explained" describes, the use of SMB and NFS allows Windows, Linux and macOS systems to reach the same shared storage from anywhere. This makes the service relevant wherever applications or users expect a conventional file share but the underlying infrastructure should not be operated by the organization itself. In the broader context of Azure storage, Azure Files is one of several storage options. The episode "7 Levels of Azure Administration: Beginner to Cloud Architect" lists Azure Blob Storage, Azure Files and Azure Disk Storage side by side. According to that episode, Blob Storage is suited to large amounts of unstructured data, while Azure Files provides a fully managed file share in the cloud, and disk storage serves virtual machine disks.

Azure Files is delivered as part of a storage account. The episode "Azure Storage Accounts - Simply Explained" covers how storage accounts organize and manage data and names Azure Files among the services they provide, alongside Blob Storage, Queue Storage, Table Storage and managed disks. The same episode touches on concepts that apply at the storage account level, including redundancy options, performance tiers, access tiers, encryption, networking and lifecycle management. It also describes how storage accounts integrate with services such as Azure Virtual Machines, Azure Functions, Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Backup, Azure AI and Microsoft Fabric.

Security and data protection are recurring themes in the episode material. The episode "Migrate Azure File Sync to Managed Identity" notes that role-based access control (RBAC) can be used to define specific permissions for users and applications, so that only authorized individuals can reach sensitive data. It also describes redundancy options that protect data from events such as hardware failures and natural disasters, with geographic redundancy achievable by syncing between Azure file shares and on-premises servers. For protection against mistakes, the episode points to soft delete, which guards against accidental deletion of files, and share snapshots, which allow point-in-time recovery. The title of that episode also shows that Azure File Sync can be migrated to use a managed identity, in line with the episode's emphasis on modern authentication.

Backup is a related decision area. The episode "Azure Backup - Simply Explained" presents Azure Backup as automated, secure and scalable protection for virtual machines, databases, Azure Files and many other workloads, managed directly from Azure. It addresses risks such as accidental deletion, hardware failures, ransomware and disasters, and explains Recovery Services Vaults and Backup Vaults. For Azure Files, this means that share snapshots and soft delete can be complemented by a dedicated backup service.

Typical decisions around Azure Files include choosing between SMB and NFS depending on the client systems, deciding whether to keep a copy of the data on-premises through Azure File Sync, selecting redundancy and tier settings at the storage account level, and defining how access and recovery are handled through RBAC, snapshots, soft delete and backup. Official documentation for the service is available from Microsoft Learn under the Azure Storage Files section.

azure-firewall.desc: Azure Firewall is Microsoft's cloud-native, managed network firewall in Microsoft Azure that filters virtual network traffic by address, port and protocol.

faq.a: Azure Firewall is Microsoft's cloud-native, fully managed network security service in Microsoft Azure. It protects Azure virtual network resources by inspecting addresses, ports and protocols and provides centralized traffic filtering and threat intelligence.
faq.q: What is Azure Firewall?

faq.a: No. Azure Firewall and Azure Web Application Firewall are different services. Azure Firewall is a network firewall for virtual network traffic.
faq.q: Is Azure Firewall the same as Azure Web Application Firewall?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained" describes NSGs and Azure Firewall as parts of layered security architectures. NSGs provide simple network filtering, while Azure Firewall covers more advanced security controls.
faq.q: How does Azure Firewall relate to network security groups?

azure-firewall.long:
Azure Firewall is a cloud-native network firewall service that protects Azure virtual network resources by inspecting addresses, ports and protocols. It is part of Microsoft Azure and is described in M365.FM material as a fully managed network security service that protects Azure workloads from both internal and external threats. It is a different service from Azure Web Application Firewall, and the two should not be mixed up when planning a security architecture.

The central idea is to replace traditional firewall appliances that must be deployed and maintained by the customer with a managed service. According to the episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained", Azure Firewall provides centralized traffic filtering, threat intelligence and application-aware security that automatically scales with the environment. In practice, this means that traffic rules, threat-based filtering and application-level controls can be managed in one place instead of being spread across individual virtual machines or appliances.

Azure Firewall rarely works in isolation. It sits inside a wider set of Azure networking services, and several M365.FM episodes describe those relationships. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" lists Azure Firewall among the services that integrate with virtual networks, alongside Azure VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Load Balancer, Private Link, Azure Bastion and Azure Kubernetes Service. Virtual networks provide the subnets, IP address spaces, route tables, peering and DNS on which a firewall deployment builds. The episode "Azure Virtual WAN - Simply Explained" describes Azure Firewall as one of the components used together with SD-WAN solutions, ExpressRoute, Azure VPN Gateway and Azure Virtual Networks to create a resilient, centrally managed network architecture, for example when connecting multiple offices, supporting remote workers or linking Azure workloads across regions.

A common decision is when to use Azure Firewall and when simpler controls are enough. The episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained" covers network security groups (NSGs) with inbound and outbound rules, priorities, service tags, application security groups, default security rules, stateful filtering, and associations at subnet or network interface level. It also discusses the differences between NSGs and Azure Firewall and stresses that understanding when to use simple network filtering and when to implement more advanced security controls is essential. NSGs and Azure Firewall are presented as parts of layered security architectures rather than as alternatives that exclude each other.

Another scenario appears in the episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure". The episode says that Azure Firewall and Application Gateway can be used in parallel for both web and non-web workloads. In that setup, inbound traffic can be inspected, and egress traffic can be filtered based on Fully Qualified Domain Names (FQDN). The episode ties this to custom security layers in virtual networks: protecting inbound application flows and limiting outbound flows to only the internet endpoints that are necessary. It also links network isolation to compliance goals, naming standards such as SOC2 and ISO27001, and the aim of keeping sensitive data inside a controlled environment.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure Firewall as the managed filtering and threat-protection layer in Azure network designs. It is used to centralize rules, to control traffic between and out of virtual networks, and to complement NSGs, Application Gateway and the hybrid connectivity services. Because it is separate from Azure Web Application Firewall, design discussions typically need to state clearly which of the two is meant and which type of traffic each is expected to cover.

azure-front-door.desc: Azure Front Door is a global Azure service combining content delivery and layer 7 load balancing at Microsoft edge locations, with a built-in web application firewall.

faq.a: Azure Front Door is a global Azure service that combines content delivery and layer 7 load balancing at Microsoft edge locations, with a built-in web application firewall. The M365.FM episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained" describes it as Microsoft's global application delivery network.
faq.q: What is Azure Front Door?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained", Azure Load Balancer distributes traffic within a region, Azure Front Door acts as a global application delivery network, and Azure Traffic Manager operates at the DNS layer to route users to endpoints.
faq.q: How does Azure Front Door differ from Azure Load Balancer and Azure Traffic Manager?

faq.a: The episodes mention caching, SSL offloading or termination, DDoS protection, and built-in protection against web attacks through its web application firewall. It is also often placed in front of regional Application Gateways.
faq.q: What does Azure Front Door provide besides load balancing?

azure-front-door.long:
Azure Front Door is a global Azure service that combines content delivery and layer 7 load balancing at Microsoft edge locations. It is part of Microsoft Azure and includes a built-in web application firewall. In the M365.FM episode "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained" it is described as Microsoft's global application delivery network that improves the performance, availability, and security of web applications.

The core idea is that user traffic is routed through Microsoft's worldwide edge network instead of travelling directly to the application's origin. According to the episode, this approach delivers faster response times, intelligent load balancing, SSL offloading, and built-in protection against web attacks, all from a single managed service. Another M365.FM episode, "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures", describes the same behaviour in architectural terms: Azure Front Door improves global performance by routing user requests to the nearest healthy backend, and it offers caching, SSL termination, and DDoS protection.

Typical situations in which Azure Front Door is considered involve web applications with users in several geographic regions, applications that need to stay reachable when a back end fails, and workloads that need a central point for security filtering. The "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" episode says Front Door helps reduce latency and mitigate the performance impact of back-end failures. It also describes it as a way to troubleshoot and isolate connectivity issues. Because it works at layer 7, it makes routing decisions based on web traffic rather than on raw network connections. It is also often placed in front of regional Application Gateways, which lets a global entry point sit above region-specific load balancing.

A recurring theme in the episodes is how Azure Front Door differs from neighbouring Azure networking services. The episode "Azure Load Balancer — Simply Explained" covers the Layer 4 service that distributes traffic within a region and discusses when to choose Azure Load Balancer over Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door. The episode "Azure Traffic Manager - Simply Explained" contrasts the three: Load Balancer distributes traffic within a region, Front Door acts as a global application delivery network, and Traffic Manager operates at the DNS layer to route users to endpoints. That episode also notes that Traffic Manager integrates with Azure Front Door, among other Azure services and hybrid environments that include on-premises applications. Choosing between these services therefore comes down to the layer at which routing should happen and whether the scope is regional or global.

Azure Front Door also comes up in the context of API exposure. The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" explains when Azure API Management should be used instead of Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door, and how API management fits into enterprise architectures, hybrid environments, and AI-powered applications that rely on secure API access. In that framing, Front Door is a delivery and protection layer for web applications, while API Management is a management layer for APIs such as Azure Functions, App Services, Kubernetes workloads, and legacy APIs.

In summary, the M365.FM material presents Azure Front Door as a managed, global entry point for web applications: it routes users to the nearest healthy back end, terminates SSL, caches content, and adds web application firewall and DDoS-related protection. Related topics worth reading alongside it are Azure Load Balancer, Azure Traffic Manager, Azure Application Gateway, and Azure API Management, since architecture decisions often involve combining or choosing between them.

azure-functions.desc: Azure Functions is Microsoft's serverless compute service in Azure for running event-driven code, used for APIs, Power Apps back ends and MCP servers.

faq.a: Azure Functions runs event-driven code in Azure without server management. The episodes mention uses such as back-end logic for Power Apps, heavy processing, integration with third-party APIs and plugins for Microsoft Copilot.
faq.q: What is Azure Functions used for?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, a function is exposed as an HTTP endpoint that Power Apps can call, often through a custom connector and Azure API Management.
faq.q: How do Azure Functions connect to Power Apps?

faq.a: Azure Functions can be exposed as an MCP server, for example through Azure API Management, so that the functions can serve as tools in AI agent scenarios.
faq.q: How does Azure Functions relate to the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

azure-functions.long:
Azure Functions is the serverless compute service of Microsoft Azure. It lets developers write small pieces of code, called functions, that run in response to events such as an HTTP request, a timer or a file upload, without setting up or managing servers. Microsoft develops the service, which is classed as a developer tool and is part of Microsoft Azure. It is offered as a paid service, and the official documentation is available on Microsoft Learn.

The core idea is event-driven execution. A function starts with a trigger, for example an HTTP call or a schedule. The developer then writes the logic in a language such as C#, JavaScript or Python and publishes the function to an Azure environment. According to the episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions", the code runs in the cloud without server setup, and the functions can scale with the needs of a business. The episode describes typical jobs for such functions: handling big files, performing complex calculations, or connecting to other systems, for example checking a credit score or updating a database.

Getting started is covered in the episode "Azure Functions - Simply Explained". It walks through creating a Function App in the Azure portal: selecting Create a resource, choosing Function App, and then picking a hosting option before deploying the first function. This makes the service a common first step for people who want to move custom logic into the cloud without owning infrastructure.

Azure Functions is often combined with other services. The episode "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions" describes a pattern in which Power Apps send requests through a custom connector to Azure API Management, which forwards them to an Azure Function and then to an external system. API Management adds a secure layer that controls access, monitors usage and applies security rules. The episode describes this as a low-code front end with a pro-code backend, suited to scenarios that need secure server-side logic, heavy processing or integration with third-party APIs, and to building scalable plugins for an organization. Azure API Management can also be used to expose Azure Functions as an MCP server, which links the service to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and to AI agent scenarios.

A frequent design decision is where custom code should run. The episode "Copilot Studio Code Interpreter vs Azure Functions" discusses Python running natively inside Power Platform through the Copilot Studio Code Interpreter. It argues that "runs natively" does not mean "runs anywhere", describes the Code Interpreter as a sealed environment for code, and points to practical limits such as flows timing out and files reaching 512 MB. In that comparison, Azure Functions is the option for workloads that outgrow those limits.

Azure Functions also sits alongside Azure Logic Apps, a related Azure service. Logic Apps is aimed at workflow automation, while Azure Functions is where custom code is written and hosted. Together with Azure API Management and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), these services form the typical set of related topics around Azure Functions in the Microsoft ecosystem.

azure-image-builder.desc: Azure Image Builder is a managed Azure service that builds standardized virtual machine images from a defined configuration, using HashiCorp Packer behind the scenes.

faq.a: Azure Image Builder is a fully managed Azure service, built on HashiCorp Packer, that builds customized virtual machine images from a configuration you submit and then distributes them.
faq.q: What is Azure Image Builder?

faq.a: According to Microsoft's documentation, the output can be stored in an Azure Compute Gallery, as a managed image, or as a VHD.
faq.q: Where can the finished images be stored?

faq.a: The documentation lists availability in a defined set of regions, restricted Trusted Launch and Confidential VM combinations, no support for moving the image template resource, and no support for Azure Hybrid Benefit.
faq.q: What are known limitations of Azure Image Builder?

azure-image-builder.long:
Azure Image Builder, documented by Microsoft as Azure VM Image Builder, is a fully managed service within Microsoft Azure for creating customized virtual machine images. Instead of preparing an image by hand, an administrator submits a configuration that describes the desired result. The service then builds the image and distributes it. It is built on HashiCorp Packer, which does the underlying build work, while Azure handles the platform-specific steps around it.

The problem it addresses is the manual creation and maintenance of standardized images. The M365.FM episode "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" describes the traditional process: an administrator starts with a clean virtual machine, installs Windows updates, applications, monitoring agents, security tools and certificates, and applies configuration changes. The machine is then tested, generalized and captured as an image. The episode notes that this approach can work but depends heavily on people remembering every step. When updates or requirements change, the process has to be repeated, and small differences can appear between images that are supposed to be identical.

With Azure Image Builder, the configuration takes the place of those remembered steps. Builds start from Windows or Linux images in the Azure Marketplace or from custom images the organization already owns. The configuration defines the customizations to apply, and the service produces the finished image. The output can be stored in an Azure Compute Gallery, kept as a managed image, or exported as a VHD. The service also performs Azure-specific tasks such as generalization (Sysprep), so this step does not need to be handled manually.

Typical uses named in Microsoft's documentation include standardized golden images, baseline security images and images for Azure Virtual Desktop. Because the service can plug into existing customization scripts and CI/CD pipelines, image creation can become a repeatable, automated part of an existing delivery process rather than a separate manual task. Teams that already maintain scripts for installing software or applying settings can reuse them within a build.

During a build, the service creates a staging resource group and temporary build resources, and removes most of them afterwards. Access to artifacts is controlled through managed identities and Azure RBAC, and everything remains in the customer's own subscription. Compute, network and storage used during builds are billed at normal Azure rates, so the cost depends on the resources a build consumes.

There are limits to consider when planning its use. The service is available in a defined list of regions. Some combinations involving Trusted Launch and Confidential VMs are restricted. The image template resource cannot be moved, and Azure Hybrid Benefit is not supported. These points matter when choosing target regions, designing image templates and deciding how builds fit into a subscription layout.

Azure Image Builder is part of Microsoft Azure and sits alongside the other services used to deploy and manage virtual machines. Its place in an environment is as the step that produces consistent, versionable images before machines are deployed from them. The M365.FM episode "Azure Image Builder - Simply Explained" frames it as the answer to the growing difficulty of keeping standardized images consistent as environments grow.

azure-integration-services.desc: Azure Integration Services is a set of Microsoft Azure services for connecting applications, automating processes and managing APIs, including Logic Apps and Service Bus.

faq.a: Microsoft's description lists Azure Logic Apps, Azure API Management, Azure Service Bus, Azure Event Grid, Azure Data Factory and Azure Functions. Whether Azure Functions counts as part of the collection depends on the definition used.
faq.q: What does Azure Integration Services include?

faq.a: It is used to connect applications and cloud systems, automate business processes and manage APIs. Typical scenarios include cross-product process automation, decoupling services with message brokers and events, and exposing AI models behind an API gateway.
faq.q: What is Azure Integration Services used for?

faq.a: "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]" covers Logic Apps and Service Bus in a Dynamics 365 integration context. "AI Turns Integration into an Organism as a Service" discusses how AI could change Logic Apps-based integration.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes relate to Azure Integration Services?

azure-integration-services.long:
Azure Integration Services is Microsoft's collection of Azure services for enterprise integration. It belongs to Microsoft Azure and is positioned as an integration platform that connects applications and cloud systems, automates business processes and manages APIs. Microsoft describes it as a way to link older systems with newer technologies. The exact membership of the collection depends on the definition used, since Azure Functions is counted as part of it in some descriptions and not in others.

The collection brings together several distinct services, each covering a different integration need. Azure Logic Apps provides workflows and automation. Azure API Management is used to publish, secure and govern APIs in the cloud and on premises. Azure Service Bus handles messaging, while Azure Event Grid is a publish-subscribe service for event-driven designs. Azure Data Factory is named for hybrid data integration, and Azure Functions supplies event-driven serverless code. A large library of prebuilt connectors and templates is mentioned for the workflow side of the platform.

Typical scenarios described by Microsoft include process automation across products, decoupling services with message brokers and events, and exposing AI models behind an API gateway. In the decoupling case, a message broker such as Service Bus or an event service such as Event Grid sits between systems so that they do not depend directly on each other. API Management also offers features aimed at AI workloads, such as token limits, token tracking, semantic caching and load balancing for large language models. The source material names no specific licensing model or technical limits and refers readers to the Azure pricing pages for cost details.

In practice, choosing between the services in the collection is a design decision. Workflows with triggers, conditions, transformations, retries and exceptions fit Logic Apps. Publishing and protecting interfaces points to API Management. Asynchronous exchange between systems points to Service Bus or Event Grid, and custom code that reacts to events points to Azure Functions. Because the services are separate, solutions often combine several of them rather than relying on a single one.

The M365.FM episode "D365FO Integration Architecture with Anitha Eswaran [MVP-MCT]" places Azure Integration Services next to Power Platform components such as Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Power Virtual Agents. The episode describes Logic Apps as a tool for automating workflows across multiple applications and for setting up event-driven processes, such as real-time notifications or multi-step approvals. It says Logic Apps connects Dynamics 365 to cloud services, on-premises systems and partner platforms, and that it offers flexibility to scale an integration as a business grows. The same episode also covers Azure Service Bus within this architecture.

The episode "AI Turns Integration into an Organism as a Service — How Azure Logic Apps Are Changing Enterprise Integration with Sonny Gillissen [MVP]" looks at how AI may change the integration layer. It starts from the traditional approach in which architects define triggers, conditions, transformations, retries, exceptions and destinations in advance. The guest, an Azure Integration Services specialist with a focus on Azure Logic Apps, discusses a concept he calls "Organism as a Service." According to the episode, the idea is that enterprise integration could evolve from static workflows into systems that interpret context, respond to unexpected situations, choose appropriate actions and potentially recover from failures more intelligently.

Taken together, the sources show Azure Integration Services as both an established toolkit for connecting systems and a place where AI-related changes to integration are being discussed. Readers evaluating it typically look at which of the individual services match their scenario, how they connect to surrounding products such as Dynamics 365 or the Power Platform, and where the Azure pricing pages apply.

azure-iot-edge.desc: Azure IoT Edge is a feature of Azure IoT Hub that runs containerized modules on edge devices, managed remotely from the cloud and able to work offline.

faq.a: Azure IoT Edge is a feature of Azure IoT Hub that deploys, runs and monitors containerized modules on edge devices. It is managed from the cloud and can keep working offline.
faq.q: What is Azure IoT Edge?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn names three parts: IoT Edge modules (Docker-compatible containers), the IoT Edge runtime on each device, and a cloud interface for remote monitoring and management.
faq.q: What are the main parts of Azure IoT Edge?

faq.a: The episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" says Azure IoT Edge suits requirements focused around a gateway or individual device, where modules collect data, apply local logic, buffer it and send it upstream through Azure IoT Hub.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode position Azure IoT Edge against Azure IoT Operations?

azure-iot-edge.long:
Azure IoT Edge is a device-focused runtime for deploying, running and monitoring containerized workloads on edge devices. It is a feature of Azure IoT Hub and belongs to Microsoft Azure. Its core idea is to move analytics and logic closer to the devices that produce data, so that decisions can be made quickly, even when there is no connection to the cloud. When connectivity returns, the edge device synchronizes telemetry and configuration with the cloud.

According to Microsoft Learn, the solution consists of three parts. The first is IoT Edge modules, which are Docker-compatible containers. A module can run an Azure service, a partner service or custom code, and several modules can be chained into a processing pipeline. The second part is the IoT Edge runtime, which runs on each device. It installs and updates modules, keeps them running, enforces security standards and reports module health. The third part is a cloud interface used for remote monitoring and management of the devices and their workloads.

One reason to use Azure IoT Edge is to process data locally. Raw data can be cleaned and aggregated on the device, and only the results are sent to the cloud, which lowers bandwidth use. Typical scenarios named in the documentation include anomaly detection on production lines, gateway devices that aggregate data from local equipment, and running machine learning or Stream Analytics at the edge. Linux is the native platform, and Windows is supported through IoT Edge for Linux on Windows. The feature is available in both the free and standard tiers of Azure IoT Hub, where the free tier is intended only for testing and evaluation. The documentation also lists which long-term-support versions are current and which have reached or will reach end of support, a point worth checking when planning a deployment.

The M365.FM episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" places Azure IoT Edge in an industrial data context. The episode compares it with Azure IoT Operations as two Microsoft approaches for running industrial edge workloads. It says Azure IoT Edge works well when the requirement is focused around a gateway or an individual device. In that setup, containerized modules can collect data, apply local logic, buffer information and send it upstream through Azure IoT Hub. The episode describes this as a practical choice for a defined cell or smaller scope.

The same episode also draws a boundary for what edge logic should do. It states that the edge should add facts it knows with confidence. It should not guess which production order is active based on stale information, and it should not quietly create business context that belongs to MES, ERP, planning or quality systems. This frames the edge as a place for reliable local collection, buffering and basic logic rather than for inventing business meaning.

In practice, the decision around Azure IoT Edge often comes down to scope and operating model. A single gateway or device that needs local processing, offline tolerance and cloud-managed module deployment fits the device-focused design described in the documentation. Wider industrial edge scenarios may call for comparison with Azure IoT Operations, as the episode discusses. Because Azure IoT Edge is tied to Azure IoT Hub, module deployment, monitoring and telemetry flow through that service.

azure-iot-hub-device-provisioning-servic.desc: Azure IoT Hub Device Provisioning Service (DPS) checks a device's identity against enrollment rules on first boot and assigns it to an IoT hub.

faq.a: It is a helper service for Azure IoT Hub that verifies a device's proof of identity against enrollment rules on first boot and assigns the device to an IoT hub using an allocation policy. This enables zero-touch, just-in-time provisioning without manual steps.
faq.q: What does Azure IoT Hub Device Provisioning Service do?

faq.a: DPS supports X.509 and TPM-based attestation. Allocation policies include lowest latency, evenly weighted and static, plus custom allocation through Azure Functions webhooks.
faq.q: Which attestation methods and allocation policies does DPS support?

faq.a: No. After provisioning, the device talks to its assigned IoT hub directly. DPS only becomes involved again for reprovisioning.
faq.q: Does a device keep contacting DPS after it is provisioned?

azure-iot-hub-device-provisioning-servic.long:
Azure IoT Hub Device Provisioning Service (DPS), also referred to as IoT Hub Device Provisioning Service or Device Provisioning Service, is a helper service for Azure IoT Hub. It enables zero-touch, just-in-time provisioning of devices to the right IoT hub without manual steps. In practice, it answers a question that becomes harder as fleets grow: which hub should a given device talk to, and how does that device get registered there without anyone configuring it by hand?

The process follows a defined sequence. The manufacturer stores credentials and the DPS endpoint on the device. In the cloud, enrollments define which devices are valid and how they are provisioned. On first boot, the device contacts DPS and proves its identity. DPS checks that proof against the enrollment list, assigns the device to a hub using an allocation policy, and registers it there. After that, the device communicates with the hub directly. DPS only becomes involved again if a device needs to be reprovisioned.

The service supports X.509 and TPM-based attestation, which are the mechanisms a device can use to present cryptographic proof of its identity. Enrollments come in two forms, individual and group, so that a device can be listed on its own or as part of a larger set. Allocation policies decide which hub receives a device: lowest latency, evenly weighted and static are available, and custom allocation is possible through Azure Functions webhooks. Devices can connect over HTTPS, AMQP or MQTT.

Typical scenarios named in the documentation are load balancing across multiple hubs, multitenancy, geo-sharding and reprovisioning. Several operational points matter when planning a deployment. Each API call is a billable operation, and per-subscription limits apply, for example to the number of instances, enrollments and linked hubs. Provisioning of nested IoT Edge devices is not supported. These constraints are relevant when estimating cost and capacity for large rollouts.

The M365.FM episode "Azure DPS: Why Provisioning 100,000 IoT Devices Is an Architecture Problem" frames DPS as an architectural decision rather than a configuration detail. According to the episode, DPS acts as the secure reception desk for a cloud estate, standing between unconfigured hardware and the specific IoT hub that will handle its daily traffic. Instead of hard-coding endpoints into firmware, devices contact a global provisioning endpoint on first boot, present their cryptographic proof, and receive the details of their assigned hub.

The episode also stresses a separation between a device's manufacturing identity, meaning where and how the unit was built, and its operational identity, which determines how and where the device connects to the cloud. The episode says this separation keeps device images portable across different customer environments and deployment waves. This ties directly to how DPS works: the image carries credentials and the provisioning endpoint, while the hub assignment is decided later in the cloud through enrollments and allocation policies.

DPS is part of Azure IoT Hub's ecosystem and is closely related to it. IoT Hub handles the ongoing device communication, while DPS handles the initial assignment and registration. For teams planning large device populations, the relevant decisions are the attestation method, the choice between individual and group enrollments, the allocation policy, and whether reprovisioning will be needed over the device lifetime.

azure-iot-operations.desc: Azure IoT Operations is a Microsoft edge data platform on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes with OPC UA connectivity, a local MQTT broker and data flows.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft edge data platform that runs on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and provides OPC UA connectivity, a local MQTT broker and data flows for industrial sites. It is part of Microsoft Azure.
faq.q: What is Azure IoT Operations?

faq.a: According to the episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics", Azure IoT Edge works well for a gateway or individual device using containerized modules that send data upstream through Azure IoT Hub. The episode compares this with Azure IoT Operations as the other Microsoft approach to industrial edge workloads.
faq.q: How does Azure IoT Operations differ from Azure IoT Edge?

faq.a: The episode "Azure IoT Operations at Scale: Managing Hundreds of Sites With Azure Arc" says this needs repeatable deployment and central oversight. It covers rollout, configuration management and monitoring across sites using Azure Arc.
faq.q: How are many sites managed with Azure IoT Operations?

azure-iot-operations.long:
Azure IoT Operations is a Microsoft edge data platform for industrial sites. It runs on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and provides OPC UA connectivity, a local MQTT broker and data flows. It is part of Microsoft Azure, and its documentation is published on Microsoft Learn. The product is aimed at manufacturing and similar environments in which machine and sensor data has to be collected, processed and forwarded close to the point where it is produced.

The three capabilities named in the product description map to common needs on a plant floor. OPC UA connectivity covers the link to industrial equipment and automation systems. The local MQTT broker gives an on-site messaging layer, so that data can be exchanged at the edge without a round trip to the cloud. Data flows move and route that data onward, for example towards cloud analytics. Because the platform sits on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, sites running the platform can be treated as Azure-managed resources, which matters when many locations need consistent handling.

The M365.FM episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" looks at the architecture around these protocols. According to its description, the episode starts from a lack of trust in manufacturing data, even where ERP, MES and Azure systems are already in place. It discusses the difference between MQTT and OPC UA, why semantic contracts such as types, units and lineage are important, and how Sparkplug B adds industrial rules to MQTT, such as defined topics and birth and death lifecycle state. The episode places Azure IoT Operations together with Microsoft Fabric in this picture.

The episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" follows the path of machine data from OPC UA towards real-time analytics. It states that the edge should add facts it knows with confidence and should not guess which production order is active based on stale information, nor quietly create business context that belongs to MES, ERP, planning or quality systems. The same episode compares Azure IoT Edge with Azure IoT Operations. Azure IoT Edge, it says, works well for a gateway or individual device, with containerized modules that collect data, apply local logic, buffer information and send it upstream through Azure IoT Hub. This can suit a defined cell or a smaller workload.

Operating the platform across many locations is the subject of "Azure IoT Operations at Scale: Managing Hundreds of Sites With Azure Arc", part of the iFAKT series. The episode states that managing hundreds of sites needs repeatable deployment and central oversight. It covers architecture, rollout, configuration management and monitoring across sites, with the aim of standardizing deployments and keeping control as the footprint grows. This is where the Azure Arc foundation becomes relevant in practice.

A related design question is covered in "Edge or Cloud? Where Industrial Workloads Should Actually Run", also from the iFAKT series. It builds a decision framework for placing manufacturing workloads based on latency, bandwidth, resilience, security and cost, and it discusses the role of Azure Arc and Azure IoT Operations. The episode frames the core question as which production decisions belong near the machine and which belong in the cloud, and it describes architecture patterns that hold up as the setup grows.

Taken together, the episodes position Azure IoT Operations as the edge layer in a larger Microsoft manufacturing architecture. It connects equipment through OPC UA, distributes data locally through MQTT, and forwards it through data flows, while Azure Arc supplies the management model and Microsoft Fabric appears as a downstream analytics destination. Decisions around it typically concern how much logic stays at the edge, how sites are rolled out and monitored in a standard way, and how data is given reliable meaning before it reaches analytics.

azure-key-vault.desc: Azure Key Vault is Microsoft's Azure service for securely storing secrets, keys and certificates, with access controlled through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC.

faq.a: Azure Key Vault is used to securely store and manage secrets, keys and certificates such as passwords, API keys, connection strings and encryption keys. Applications read these values from the vault instead of having them embedded in code or configuration files.
faq.q: What is Azure Key Vault used for?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained", access is tightly controlled through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC, so the vault follows the same identity model as the rest of an Azure environment.
faq.q: How is access to Azure Key Vault controlled?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]" notes that Bicep can be used to define secure resources such as Azure Key Vault, which supports repeatable and consistent deployments.
faq.q: How does Azure Key Vault relate to Infrastructure as Code?

azure-key-vault.long:
Azure Key Vault is a service for securely storing secrets, keys and certificates. It was developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft Azure, and counts both as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool. Typical contents are passwords, API keys, connection strings, certificates and encryption keys, which are the kinds of sensitive values that applications need at runtime but that should not be visible to everyone who can read code or configuration.

The core idea is to separate sensitive values from the application itself. Instead of embedding secrets directly into application code or configuration files, they are placed in a protected vault, and applications read them from there. Access to the vault is tightly controlled. According to the episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained", this control runs through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC, so the vault uses the same identity and permission model as the rest of an Azure environment. This means that who or what may read a secret can be defined and reviewed in one consistent place rather than being scattered across files and pipelines.

In practice, Azure Key Vault appears in many Azure scenarios. The episode "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions" lists strong security measures such as HTTPS and Azure Key Vault as ways to protect data and maintain compliance with industry standards when building plugins on Azure Functions. The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" mentions leveraging Azure Key Vault for managing secrets securely, alongside other practices such as Infrastructure as Code, strict access controls, HTTPS for Azure Functions, Network Security Groups, Zero Trust principles and monitoring with Azure Monitor and Azure Network Watcher. In that context the vault is one building block among several network and identity controls rather than a standalone solution.

The service also connects to infrastructure automation. In "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", the discussion of Bicep notes that it integrates with Azure services and can be used to define secure resources such as Azure Key Vault to protect sensitive information. Defining the vault through code allows the same configuration to be deployed repeatedly, which supports consistency and reduces manual errors. Terraform is described in the same episode as another widely used tool for Azure infrastructure as code that works across multiple cloud providers.

Key management is another area where the episodes mention the service. "Cryptographic Agility for Post-Quantum Security" states that Microsoft 365 and Azure Key Vault can help centralize key management and provide visibility into a cryptographic landscape. The episode frames this within crypto-agility: keeping an up-to-date inventory of cryptographic assets is described as the first step, because assets that cannot be seen cannot be protected. Tools that centralize keys make it easier to track and manage those assets as the environment changes.

Typical decisions around Azure Key Vault include which applications and identities should be allowed to read which values, how secrets are kept out of source code and configuration files, and how the vault fits into network design and deployment automation. The episodes consistently place it as part of a layered approach: identity-based access through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC, secured transport with HTTPS, restricted network exposure, and deployment through Infrastructure as Code, with the vault holding the sensitive values that these layers protect.

In summary, Azure Key Vault serves as the central place within Microsoft Azure for storing and managing secrets, keys and certificates, replacing the practice of hard-coding such values into applications. Its role in the M365.FM episodes ranges from a basic explanation of how it works to its use in Azure Functions plugins, networking security, infrastructure automation and cryptographic governance.

azure-kubernetes-service.desc: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is Microsoft's managed Kubernetes offering in Azure, where Microsoft runs the control plane and customers manage worker nodes.

faq.a: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is Microsoft's managed Kubernetes offering in Azure. Microsoft runs the control plane, while customers choose and pay for the worker node virtual machines that run their containers.
faq.q: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?

faq.a: Microsoft takes care of the control plane, updates, monitoring and much of the operational complexity, according to the M365.FM episode on AKS. Customers choose and pay for the worker node virtual machines that run their containers.
faq.q: Who is responsible for what in AKS?

faq.a: Both run containers in Azure. The episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" discusses when to choose Azure Container Apps over AKS, App Service or Azure Container Instances, for example for microservices, APIs, background jobs and AI workloads.
faq.q: How does AKS relate to Azure Container Apps?

azure-kubernetes-service.long:
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is Microsoft's managed Kubernetes platform within Microsoft Azure. It is used to deploy, operate and scale containerized applications without having to build and maintain a Kubernetes cluster entirely from scratch. In AKS, Microsoft runs the Kubernetes control plane, while customers choose and pay for the worker node virtual machines that run their containers. This split of responsibility is the core idea behind the service.

According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) - Simply Explained", Microsoft takes care of the control plane, updates, monitoring and much of the operational complexity. The stated benefit is that developers and IT teams can concentrate on building applications rather than on maintaining clusters. The official documentation for the service is published under the title "What is AKS" in Microsoft Learn.

Kubernetes itself is the underlying technology that AKS builds on. The episode "Kubernetes - Simply Explained" describes real-world scenarios where Kubernetes is used, from hosting microservices and APIs to powering enterprise applications and AI workloads across on-premises environments and public clouds such as Microsoft Azure. That episode also covers how Kubernetes integrates with AKS, supports rolling updates with minimal downtime, recovers automatically from failures and enables highly scalable cloud-native applications. AKS is therefore the way these Kubernetes capabilities are consumed as a managed service in Azure.

A recurring decision around AKS is whether it is the right place to run a given container workload. The episode "Azure Container Apps - Simply Explained" frames this as a comparison: it explains when to choose Azure Container Apps over Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), App Service or Azure Container Instances. Azure Container Apps is presented there as an easier way to run modern cloud-native applications such as microservices, APIs, background jobs and AI workloads, with concepts like revisions, ingress, environments, autoscaling, scale-to-zero, KEDA and Dapr. The contrast helps in understanding that AKS is a Kubernetes-based option with cluster-level responsibilities on the customer side for the worker nodes, whereas other Azure container services abstract more of that away.

Operations around AKS can also be automated. The episode "Azure Automation - Simply Explained" mentions that Azure Logic Apps can automate the lifecycle of Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) based on business hours, and that Azure DevOps Pipelines can run jobs on a schedule to control cluster states. The same episode stresses state verification in automated workflows, so that actions only occur when necessary and redundant operations or errors are avoided. This is relevant for AKS because worker node virtual machines are a billable resource, and controlling when clusters run is a typical cost and maintenance consideration.

In summary, AKS sits within Microsoft Azure as the managed Kubernetes option. Its defining characteristics, as given in the sources, are that Microsoft operates the control plane and handles updates and monitoring, while the customer selects and pays for the worker node virtual machines on which containers run. Related topics in the M365.FM catalog include Kubernetes fundamentals, Azure Container Apps as an alternative container platform, and Azure Automation for scheduling and lifecycle control. The episode "Dynamics 365 Customer Service - Simply Explained" also lists the AKS episode among related recommended listening, pointing to its place in the wider Microsoft technology discussion on the show.

azure-landing-zone.desc: An Azure landing zone is a pre-configured Azure environment with management groups, networking, policy and identity that gives workloads a secure, scalable foundation.

faq.a: An Azure landing zone is a pre-configured Azure environment with management groups, networking, policy and identity that gives workloads a secure, scalable foundation. It is also referred to as Azure Landing Zones, ALZ or Landing Zone.
faq.q: What is an Azure landing zone?

faq.a: They are usually deployed and maintained as code, which ties the concept closely to Infrastructure as code. This keeps the foundation consistent instead of relying on manual portal configuration.
faq.q: How are Azure landing zones usually deployed?

faq.a: The episode "How to Secure an AI Landing Zone in Microsoft Azure" describes an AI landing zone as a structured environment that provides governance, security and compliance for AI solutions. It recommends the Azure Landing Zones framework for enterprise AI deployments.
faq.q: How do landing zones relate to AI workloads?

azure-landing-zone.long:
An Azure landing zone, also written as Azure Landing Zones, ALZ or simply Landing Zone, is a pre-configured Azure environment that gives workloads a secure and scalable foundation. It typically bundles management groups, networking, policy and identity, so that new workloads are placed into an environment that already follows the organization's rules instead of every team inventing its own setup. The concept belongs to Microsoft Azure and is documented as part of the Cloud Adoption Framework guidance on getting an environment ready for workloads.

The purpose of a landing zone is to prepare the ground before workloads arrive. The M365.FM episode "Azure Landing Zones - Simply Explained" describes it this way: rather than simply creating subscriptions and resources, a landing zone establishes the core architecture, including identity, networking, security, governance, management and compliance. Every new workload then starts from a consistent, enterprise-ready baseline. The episode compares this to preparing the ground before building a house, because without a solid foundation everything built on top becomes harder to manage and secure.

The episode "Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework - Simply Explained" uses a similar image. A building needs electricity, doors, network connectivity, security, shared facilities and rules, and it would make little sense to move hundreds of employees into an empty building and tell each department to design its own electrical system and security model. Azure landing zones apply the same principle to cloud infrastructure: common foundational decisions are prepared before workloads arrive. Identity is named as one of those foundational components. Microsoft Entra ID controls digital identities and helps determine who or what can access Azure resources, and users should receive only the permissions required to perform their work.

In practice, a landing zone is closely tied to Infrastructure as code. Landing zones are usually deployed and maintained as versioned code rather than assembled manually in the portal, which supports repeatability and consistent configuration across environments. The topic also sits within Governance, since structure and policy are at its core. A stricter variant exists as the Sovereign landing zone, which is listed as a related concept for organizations with additional sovereignty requirements.

The episode "Azure Platform Engineering, Azure Landing Zones, Cloud Adoption Framework & Building Enterprise Cloud Platforms" with Microsoft MVP Jev Suchoi places landing zones in the context of platform engineering. According to the episode, moving workloads into Microsoft Azure is only the beginning of a cloud journey, and building a platform that is secure, scalable, automated and developer-friendly requires a different mindset. Platform engineering is presented as a way to build reusable cloud foundations that enable innovation while maintaining governance and security.

Landing zones also come up in hybrid and AI scenarios. The episode "Azure Local and Landing Zones: How to Build Hybrid Cloud the Right Way" with Christoffer Klarskov Jakobsen [MVP] discusses how Azure Local can become part of a broader Azure architecture rather than another isolated on-premises platform, alongside Infrastructure as Code, automated deployment pipelines and Azure Landing Zones. Some workloads need to stay close to factories, offices, regulated environments or latency-sensitive systems. The episode "How to Secure an AI Landing Zone in Microsoft Azure" defines an AI landing zone as a structured environment for deploying AI solutions, ensuring proper governance, security and compliance while integrating AI with existing systems. It recommends the Azure Landing Zones framework to streamline enterprise AI deployments and states that strong governance is about creating a safe foundation that allows innovation to thrive rather than slowing progress.

azure-lighthouse.desc: Azure Lighthouse is an Azure service that lets a service provider or enterprise manage resources in other Azure tenants through delegated resource management.

faq.a: Azure Lighthouse lets a service provider or enterprise manage resources in other Azure tenants through delegated resource management, without having accounts in those tenants. Customers decide which subscriptions or resource groups are delegated and can revoke access at any time.
faq.q: What is Azure Lighthouse used for?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn there is no additional cost, and any Azure customer or partner can use it. EA, CSP and pay-as-you-go licensing are supported.
faq.q: Does Azure Lighthouse cost extra?

faq.a: No. Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is a separate offering. Azure Lighthouse concerns delegated management of Azure resources across tenants.
faq.q: Is Azure Lighthouse the same as Microsoft 365 Lighthouse?

azure-lighthouse.long:
Azure Lighthouse is a service that is part of Microsoft Azure. It allows a service provider, or an enterprise with several tenants, to manage resources in other Azure tenants through delegated resource management, without needing accounts in those tenants. The aim is multitenant management with greater automation and governance across resources. According to Microsoft Learn, Azure Lighthouse is a non-regional service.

The problem it addresses is often described as the "two houses" problem: an outside company has to work in a customer's Azure environment, but handing over passwords or creating separate accounts in every customer tenant is cumbersome and hard to control. The M365.FM episode "Azure Lighthouse - Simply Explained" frames it this way: an outside company can manage an Azure setup without ever holding the customer's password. The episode outline covers what Azure Lighthouse is, how the connection between the two sides is created ("The Handshake: How the Door Gets Built"), who uses it and who approves it, and the security question of who really holds access.

The mechanism is Azure Delegated Resource Management. A customer delegates a subscription or a resource group to users and roles in the managing tenant, and the managing users then work on those resources from their own tenant. The customer stays in control of who has access, which resources can be reached and what actions are permitted. The delegation can be revoked at any time. Onboarding can be done with Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates, or through managed service offers published in the Microsoft Marketplace.

Visibility is handled in the Azure portal. A "My customers" view gives the service provider cross-tenant information, while a "Service providers" view lets customers review the delegations they have granted. The activity log in the customer tenant shows who made changes, which supports auditing of delegated work. Other services work together with Azure Lighthouse, including Azure Policy, Microsoft Sentinel and Azure Arc, so that governance, security monitoring and hybrid resources can be handled across tenants.

Several practical points are stated in the documentation. There is no additional cost for Azure Lighthouse, and any Azure customer or partner can use it.
