It says Azure Bastion supports both Windows and Linux virtual machines within an Azure virtual network, works through the Azure Portal in a web browser without client software, and uses a secure management tunnel over HTTPS. The episode also states that it can reduce the need for public IP addresses and simplify management.

Virtual networks also appear in desktop and hybrid scenarios. In "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]", network connectivity to an Azure virtual network (vNet) is listed as a requirement so that Windows 365 Cloud PCs can join Active Directory like traditional workstations, alongside Hybrid Azure AD Join and planning of network and internet access. The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" explores how Virtual Network integration, private endpoints and network isolation allow Azure Functions to reach private resources without exposing services to the public internet, and it also covers Azure Virtual Network Manager and Infrastructure as Code for automating secure, scalable environments.

In practice, planning around Azure Virtual Network involves choosing address ranges, dividing them into subnets, deciding how workloads reach private services, and defining how users and administrators connect. The official documentation overview for Azure Virtual Network is the reference for the service itself, while the episodes above show how it fits into wider designs for private access, remote management and hybrid identity.

azure-virtual-network-manager.desc: Azure Virtual Network Manager is a centralized Azure service for grouping, configuring and managing virtual networks across subscriptions at scale.

faq.a: It is used to group, configure and manage virtual networks centrally across subscriptions. Its documented areas are IP address management, connectivity, security admin rules and routing.
faq.q: What is Azure Virtual Network Manager used for?

faq.a: The episode "Azure ExpressRoute - Simply Explained" states that up to 400 UDRs are allowed by default and up to 1,000 with Azure Virtual Network Manager, so the service can raise the route limit.
faq.q: How does Azure Virtual Network Manager relate to user-defined routes?

faq.a: According to the episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure", security policies can be defined at scale with the service and applied across multiple virtual networks, contributing to effective network isolation.
faq.q: How does Azure Virtual Network Manager support network isolation?

azure-virtual-network-manager.long:
Azure Virtual Network Manager is a centralized Azure service for grouping, configuring and managing virtual networks across subscriptions. According to the official overview, it covers IP address management, connectivity, security admin rules and routing. It is part of the Azure Virtual Network family of services and is aimed at organizations that run many virtual networks and need a consistent way to administer them instead of configuring each network one by one.

The core idea behind Azure Virtual Network Manager is central management at scale. Virtual networks are grouped, and configurations are then applied to those groups rather than to each network individually. The four areas named in the description each address a different administrative task: IP address management helps coordinate address space across networks, connectivity configurations define how virtual networks communicate with each other, security admin rules define centrally managed security policy, and routing controls how traffic flows between networks. Because the service works across subscriptions, it suits environments where workloads are spread over several subscriptions but should follow shared network rules.

Typical decisions around the service concern governance and consistency. Teams that operate larger Azure estates often have to decide how to keep security policy uniform across many virtual networks and how to limit the manual effort of maintaining routes. Azure Virtual Network Manager gives these questions a single management plane. This is relevant to the way Azure networking is discussed in the M365.FM episodes, where the service appears as one building block in secure and automated cloud designs rather than as a topic on its own.

The episode "Secure Azure Networking with Rex de Koning [MVP-MCT]" describes how modern Azure networking has moved well beyond simply connecting virtual machines. It names Azure Functions, Azure Virtual Network Manager and Infrastructure as Code as the ingredients for building secure, scalable and fully automated cloud environments. In that context, the episode covers how Azure Functions can reach private resources without exposing services to the public internet, using virtual network integration, private endpoints and network isolation. Azure Virtual Network Manager is presented as part of this approach to managing networks in an organized, repeatable way.

The episode "Run Azure Application Gateway Without Public IP Exposure" connects the service to network isolation. It explains that communication can be limited to the front-end tier, which includes the Application Gateway, and that the gateway has restricted privileges on back-end machines, which reduces the attack surface. The episode adds that security policies can be defined at scale using Azure Virtual Network Manager. These policies apply across multiple virtual networks and contribute to effective network isolation, helping to keep applications protected from unauthorized access.

The episode "Azure ExpressRoute - Simply Explained" touches on the routing side. For active traffic management, it recommends creating custom user-defined routes (UDRs) instead of modifying default routes, and managing them through a route table associated with subnets. The episode states that this approach allows up to 400 UDRs by default and up to 1,000 with Azure Virtual Network Manager, which shows how the service can extend routing limits in larger environments that use ExpressRoute for private, dedicated connectivity.

Taken together, the episodes place Azure Virtual Network Manager in three situations: applying security policy at scale across virtual networks, supporting isolation designs such as an Application Gateway without public IP exposure, and raising the number of user-defined routes available for hybrid connectivity. Its relation to Azure Virtual Network is that of a management layer on top of the underlying networking primitives, giving administrators a central place to organize and govern them.

azure-virtual-wan.desc: Azure Virtual WAN is a Microsoft Azure networking service that unites site-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, user VPN and hub-and-spoke routing in a global hub architecture.

faq.a: Azure Virtual WAN is a Microsoft Azure networking service that combines site-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, user VPN and hub-and-spoke routing in one global hub architecture. It is designed to connect branch offices, remote users, virtual networks and on-premises datacenters through the Microsoft global backbone.
faq.q: What is Azure Virtual WAN?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode on ExpressRoute, ExpressRoute integrates with Azure Virtual WAN in hybrid networking scenarios. Azure Virtual WAN can bring ExpressRoute connections together with VPN-based connectivity in a single hub architecture.
faq.q: How does Azure Virtual WAN relate to Azure ExpressRoute?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" says the model is consumption-based, so organizations pay only for the connections they use. Exact prices are not given in the episodes and should be checked in official Microsoft documentation.
faq.q: How is Azure Virtual WAN priced according to the episodes?

azure-virtual-wan.long:
Azure Virtual WAN is a networking service from Microsoft that is part of Microsoft Azure. It brings site-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, user VPN and hub-and-spoke routing together in one global hub architecture. Instead of building and maintaining separate gateways and routing setups for each connection type, the service offers a centralized platform for connecting different kinds of locations and users. Microsoft documents the service on its Learn site under the Virtual WAN section.

According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Virtual WAN - Simply Explained", Azure Virtual WAN is Microsoft's global networking service that simplifies connecting branch offices, remote users, virtual networks and on-premises datacenters through the Microsoft global backbone. The episode describes the core idea as replacing the individual management of multiple VPN gateways, ExpressRoute connections and complex routing configurations with a single platform for building secure, scalable and high-performance enterprise networks.

In practical terms, the service is used when an organization has several connectivity needs at once: branch offices that connect over site-to-site VPN, remote users who need user VPN access, datacenters that rely on private connectivity, and multiple virtual networks in Azure that need to exchange traffic. The hub-and-spoke model places a hub at the center, with the connected sites, users and virtual networks acting as spokes. Routing between these parts is handled through the hub rather than through manually maintained configurations on each connection.

The relationship to Azure ExpressRoute is a central one. The episode "Azure ExpressRoute - Simply Explained" states that ExpressRoute integrates with Azure Virtual Networks, Microsoft 365, Azure Virtual WAN and hybrid networking scenarios. It also contrasts ExpressRoute with Azure VPN Gateway: VPN Gateway offers encrypted connectivity over the public internet, while ExpressRoute provides a dedicated private connection with more consistent latency and higher throughput, according to that episode. Azure Virtual WAN is the layer that can combine these connection types into one architecture.

Cost and operations are another theme in the episodes. The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" says the consumption-based pricing model of Azure Virtual WAN allows organizations to pay only for the connections they use, which removes the need for expensive dedicated circuits and reduces operational complexity. It adds a note that the economic case strengthens as deployment scale increases, because savings from unified management, automated routing and eliminated hardware ownership compound over time. These are statements from the episode and are not figures from official pricing documentation.

Security is addressed in the episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained", which says Azure Firewall integrates with Azure Bastion, Azure Virtual WAN, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor and Azure Policy to form a layered security strategy for enterprise workloads. In that context, Azure Virtual WAN is one of several Azure services that work together with centralized, scalable network protection. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop - Simply Explained" lists the Virtual WAN episode among related listening, reflecting that networking decisions often sit alongside workload decisions.

Typical decisions around Azure Virtual WAN include whether a unified hub architecture is preferable to managing individual gateways, how private connectivity through ExpressRoute should be combined with VPN-based access, and how firewall and monitoring services fit into the same design. The M365.FM episodes treat the service as a building block for hybrid and global enterprise networking and position it as a way to reduce the number of separate components that administrators handle individually.

azure-web-application-firewall.desc: Azure Web Application Firewall is a Microsoft Azure service that inspects web requests and blocks attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

faq.a: It inspects web requests and blocks common attacks against web applications, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
faq.q: What does Azure Web Application Firewall protect against?

faq.a: It runs on Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door, and it can operate in detection mode or in prevention mode.
faq.q: Where does Azure Web Application Firewall run?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Web Application Firewall - Simply Explained", a normal firewall mostly watches where traffic is going, while Azure Web Application Firewall reads what the traffic says.
faq.q: How does it differ from a normal firewall?

azure-web-application-firewall.long:
Azure Web Application Firewall is a security service in Microsoft Azure that inspects incoming web requests and blocks common attacks against web applications, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It is often shortened to WAF. The service is part of Microsoft Azure and is documented in the Microsoft Learn overview for the web application firewall.

The episode "Azure Web Application Firewall - Simply Explained" draws a clear line between this service and the kind of firewall most people picture first. A conventional firewall mostly watches where traffic is going, while Azure Web Application Firewall reads what the traffic says. That difference explains why a website needs its own kind of firewall: web attacks are carried inside ordinary-looking requests, so protection has to look at the content of those requests rather than only at their source and destination.

Azure Web Application Firewall does not run as a standalone appliance. It runs on Azure Application Gateway or on Azure Front Door, so the choice of where to deploy it follows the choice of how web traffic enters the environment. It can operate in detection mode or in prevention mode. In detection mode, suspicious requests are identified and recorded; in prevention mode, matching requests are blocked. Teams typically weigh these two modes when introducing the service, since detection helps observe what would be affected before blocking is enforced.

The service appears in several related M365.FM episodes. In "Azure Front Door - Simply Explained", Azure Web Application Firewall is named among the services that Azure Front Door works with, alongside Azure App Service, Azure CDN, Azure Firewall and Azure Monitor. That episode describes Azure Front Door as a cloud service for improving application resilience, protecting against DDoS and web attacks, and optimizing user experiences across multiple Azure regions, and it frames the integration as a way to build secure, highly available cloud applications.

The episode "Azure DDoS Protection - Simply Explained" connects the web application firewall to DDoS defence. Among the steps it lists for protecting Azure resources are deploying an Azure Web Application Firewall policy and implementing a WAF Playbook that blocks attacker IP addresses based on incidents created by DDoS analytic rules. In that scenario the web application firewall acts as an enforcement point, while the DDoS analytics and the Azure DDoS Sentinel Solution supply the detection signal.

The episode "Copilot in Microsoft Entra ID - Simply Explained" lists Azure Web Application Firewall among the Microsoft security products that Security Copilot can work with. The episode describes the service there as one that protects web applications from common threats, next to Azure Firewall, which provides network security for Azure resources, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which protects cloud resources from threats. This placement shows how the web application firewall fits into a layered setup: network-level filtering, web-request inspection, DDoS protection and cloud posture monitoring each cover a different part of the attack surface.

In practice, Azure Web Application Firewall is relevant to anyone who publishes web applications through Azure and needs protection against the common web attack categories named above. Decisions around it usually concern the hosting entry point (Application Gateway or Front Door), the mode (detection or prevention), and how its events are monitored and combined with other security services.

azure-well-architected-framework.desc: The Azure Well-Architected Framework is Microsoft's design guidance for building quality Azure workloads that are resilient, available and recoverable.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's design guidance for building quality Azure workloads. It explains design patterns, such as the circuit breaker, that help make solutions resilient, available and recoverable.
faq.q: What is the Azure Well-Architected Framework?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, the two complement each other. The Cloud Adoption Framework supports the wider adoption journey, while the Well-Architected Framework helps architects design highly available, secure, reliable, performant and cost-optimized workloads.
faq.q: How does the Azure Well-Architected Framework relate to the Cloud Adoption Framework?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Well-Architected Framework - Simply Explained" describes five pillars that help teams design, operate and continuously improve Azure workloads.
faq.q: How many pillars does the Azure Well-Architected Framework have?

azure-well-architected-framework.long:
The Azure Well-Architected Framework is Microsoft's design guidance for building quality workloads on Microsoft Azure. It describes how architects, operations teams and security specialists can design, operate and continuously improve a workload, and it includes explained design patterns, such as the circuit breaker, that help make solutions resilient, available and recoverable. The framework is part of the wider Microsoft Azure guidance and is documented on Microsoft Learn.

The central idea is that a successful Azure workload depends on more than selecting the right cloud services. According to the M365.FM episode "Azure Well-Architected Framework - Simply Explained", reliability problems, security gaps, unexpected costs, weak operational processes and poor performance often come from the architectural decisions surrounding those services rather than from the services themselves. The framework addresses this by organizing guidance into five pillars, which help teams balance business requirements and technical risk while they design and run a workload.

In practice, the framework is used as a shared reference during design reviews and while a workload is running. Architects use it to shape highly available, secure, reliable, performant and cost-optimized solutions. Design patterns such as the circuit breaker are examples of the concrete techniques the guidance explains: they show how a solution can keep working, or recover cleanly, when a dependency fails. Because the guidance covers both design and operation, it also supports continuous improvement after a workload has been deployed, not only the initial architecture.

The framework is closely connected to other Azure guidance. In the episode "Azure Platform Engineering, Azure Landing Zones, Cloud Adoption Framework & Building Enterprise Cloud Platforms Jev Suchoi [MVP]", the discussion covers how organizations should gradually introduce the framework without overwhelming teams, so that architects, operations teams and security specialists can focus on the areas most relevant to their roles. The same episode describes the Azure Well-Architected Framework as complementing the Cloud Adoption Framework: the Cloud Adoption Framework supports the broader adoption journey, while the Well-Architected Framework helps architects design the individual workloads.

Governance is another area where the framework appears. In "Azure Governance at Scale with Vladimir Stefanovic [MVP-MCT]", the episode notes that a Cloud Center of Excellence often uses frameworks such as the Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework to guide governance efforts. It places this alongside Azure Blueprints, policy rules for requirements such as HIPAA, GDPR and PCI DSS, and landing zones designed with compliance in mind, which the episode says reduce risk and make audits easier. Reporting and remediation through Azure Policy are described as part of keeping the environment healthy.

The episode "Use Azure CAF to Select Your First Cloud Workloads" treats Azure Landing Zones and the Azure Well-Architected Framework as the foundation for scalable, secure cloud deployments. It describes landing zones as simplifying setup and aligning with governance, networking, identity and security requirements, and it links the framework to practices such as Azure Policy, compliance controls, cost management, Azure Monitor and continuous optimization for long-term operational excellence.

A typical decision around the framework is when and how to introduce it. The episodes suggest a gradual approach, where each role concentrates on the pillars most relevant to its responsibilities, and where the framework is used together with the Cloud Adoption Framework and landing zones rather than in isolation. Teams also decide which design patterns apply to a given workload, for example whether a circuit breaker is needed to protect a solution from failing dependencies.

barcode-scanning.desc: Barcode scanning reads printed barcodes or QR codes with a camera or scanner to capture data in a structured way instead of manual typing, as covered on M365.FM.

faq.a: Barcode scanning is reading printed barcodes or QR codes with a camera or scanner to capture data in a structured way instead of typing it manually.
faq.q: What is barcode scanning?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Track Inventory with Power Apps Barcode Scanning" describes it as a way to ingest accurate data into Dataverse once, instead of typing it twice, and to enforce referential integrity at the point of capture.
faq.q: How does barcode scanning relate to Power Apps and Dataverse?

faq.a: Episodes describe it in Dynamics 365 Warehouse Management and Supply Chain Management, where it connects physical warehouse activities with digital inventory records, and in Business Central for receiving with automated validation.
faq.q: Where is barcode scanning used in Dynamics 365?

barcode-scanning.long:
Barcode scanning is the practice of reading printed barcodes or QR codes with a camera or a dedicated scanner so that data is captured in a structured way instead of being typed in manually. The scanned value is passed directly into an application or database, which removes a common source of transcription errors and keeps records consistent with the physical item that was scanned.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, barcode scanning appears most often in inventory and warehouse scenarios. The M365.FM episode "Track Inventory with Power Apps Barcode Scanning" frames it as more than a convenience feature. According to the episode, many inventory systems are in practice just Excel sheets acting as ERPs, which leads to lost assets, failed audits and spreadsheets nobody trusts. The episode argues that barcode scanning in Power Apps is a way to ingest clean data into Dataverse once, rather than having it typed twice, and that its value lies in enforcing referential integrity at the point of capture rather than in using a phone camera as a novelty.

The same episode ties the topic to the wider goal of inventory control. It states that effective inventory control reduces costs by limiting overstocking and carrying expenses, and that accurate inventory management helps prevent costly mistakes and keeps operations running smoothly. In this view, scanning is the entry point that makes the downstream records dependable, because each transaction starts from a code that identifies the item exactly instead of a free-text entry.

Barcode scanning also plays a role in the larger business applications covered on M365.FM. The episode "Dynamics 365 Warehouse Management - Simply Explained" lists barcode scanning among the capabilities that connect receiving, put-away, storage, replenishment, picking, packing, shipping, cycle counting, returns and quality management with the wider Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management platform. Warehouse work happens physically, and scanning is one of the mechanisms that links those physical steps to the digital system and to the instructions workers receive about what to do next.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management - Simply Explained" describes the same relationship in more detail. Barcode scanning and mobile devices can connect physical warehouse activities with digital inventory records: when employees receive, move, pick or pack an item, the corresponding transaction can update the operational record. The episode stresses that this connection between physical processes and digital information is essential, while also noting that technology provides workflows, instructions and controls, but inventory accuracy still depends on how the processes are carried out.

Barcode scanning is mentioned for Dynamics 365 Business Central as well. The episode "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Business Central" lists inbound operations as a key capability, describing improved receiving through barcode scanning and automated validation. In that context, scanning supports receiving, while inventory activities enable real-time tracking of on-hand quantities and adjustments, and Copilot for Supply Chain uses predictive alerts to identify and address issues proactively.

Taken together, the episodes treat barcode scanning as a data-capture method rather than a standalone product. It is typically considered when an organization wants to replace manual entry with scanned input, whether in a custom Power Apps solution built on Dataverse or in the warehouse and receiving functions of Dynamics 365 and Business Central. The recurring theme is accuracy at the source: scanned data is meant to keep physical stock, system records and audit evidence aligned.

bitlocker.desc: BitLocker is the full-volume drive encryption feature built into Windows; it can be managed by SCCM and Intune and counts toward Microsoft Secure Score.

faq.a: BitLocker is the full-volume drive encryption feature built into Windows. It protects the data on a disk, for example when a device is lost or stolen.
faq.q: What is BitLocker?

faq.a: Yes. On a dev box the disk is already encrypted, so enabling BitLocker manually can lock users out. Existing encryption should be checked first.
faq.q: Can enabling BitLocker manually cause problems?

faq.a: According to the episodes, SCCM offers BitLocker Management for Windows devices, and Intune compliance policies can enforce BitLocker for Windows. Secure Score also awards points in proportion to the share of managed devices with BitLocker enabled.
faq.q: How is BitLocker managed in Microsoft environments?

bitlocker.long:
BitLocker is the full-volume drive encryption feature built into Windows. It encrypts the contents of a disk so that data stays protected if a device is lost or stolen. Because the encryption is part of the operating system, it is usually treated as a baseline endpoint control rather than an add-on product.

One practical point from the available notes concerns developer virtual machines. On a dev box the disk is already encrypted, so enabling BitLocker manually can lock users out. Before turning the feature on by hand, an administrator therefore needs to check whether the environment already applies encryption, since a second, manual activation can cause the access problem described above.

In managed environments BitLocker is rarely configured device by device. The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" lists BitLocker Management among the security features of SCCM, next to Endpoint Protection through Microsoft Defender and compliance monitoring based on SQL queries and built-in reporting. According to the episode, SCCM can manage BitLocker encryption for Windows devices so that sensitive data remains secure, and it fits on-premises environments with strict compliance needs, though it requires skilled administrators.

The cloud-based counterpart is covered in "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained". The episode describes compliance policies that enforce platform-specific requirements, naming BitLocker for Windows and FileVault for macOS. In this model, encryption is one of the conditions a device must meet. Combined with Conditional Access, the device state can be checked before access to enterprise apps is granted, which fits the Zero Trust design the episode describes.

The same idea appears in "Zero Trust Across Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365". There, Full Disk Encryption is listed as a device-level measure: BitLocker or FileVault protects lost or stolen devices. It sits in a list with enforcing device integrity checks such as Secure Boot and TPM, blocking non-compliant devices through Conditional Access, deploying Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and limiting admin access to secure endpoints. In this framing, BitLocker is one layer of a broader device-trust approach and not a standalone safeguard.

BitLocker also matters for measurement. "Microsoft Secure Score - Simply Explained" explains that some recommendations award partial credit in proportion to coverage. The example given is that if BitLocker encryption is enabled on 80% of managed devices, Secure Score awards approximately 80% of the available points. This lets an organization see progress while it gradually extends encryption across its device fleet. The episode also notes that not every organization should aim for a score of 100%.

Finally, "Windows 365 Link - Simply Explained" mentions BitLocker encryption among the technologies that work together with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Intune, Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Secure Boot, Microsoft Defender and strict application controls. The episode describes how these elements protect both the access device and the cloud-hosted desktop environment, supporting a secure endpoint with reduced operational complexity.

Taken together, the episodes position BitLocker as a built-in Windows encryption feature that is typically governed centrally through SCCM or Intune policy, assessed through compliance rules and Secure Score, and combined with TPM and Secure Boot in Zero Trust designs. The main caution from the notes is that existing encryption, such as on dev boxes, should be verified before BitLocker is enabled manually.

border-gateway-protocol.desc: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the standard routing protocol for exchanging routing and reachability information between networks, used by Azure VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute.

faq.a: BGP exchanges routing and reachability information between networks. In Azure, VPN gateways and ExpressRoute use it to share routes dynamically with on-premises networks instead of relying on static routes.
faq.q: What is Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) used for in Azure?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn, using BGP with a VPN gateway is optional. If it is used, the gateway must be route-based and the on-premises VPN device must support BGP.
faq.q: Is BGP required for an Azure VPN gateway?

faq.a: With several active tunnels between a virtual network and an on-premises site, the routes of a failed tunnel are withdrawn and traffic shifts to the remaining tunnels.
faq.q: How does BGP help when a VPN tunnel fails?

border-gateway-protocol.long:
Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the standard routing protocol used on the internet to exchange routing and reachability information between two or more networks. In the Microsoft ecosystem it appears mainly in two places: Azure VPN Gateway connections and Azure ExpressRoute. In both cases it replaces manually maintained static routes with dynamic routing, so that connected networks learn about each other's address ranges automatically.

According to Microsoft Learn material on BGP with Azure VPN Gateway, the VPN gateway and the on-premises VPN device act as BGP peers, also called neighbors, and exchange routes and prefixes with each other. Prefix updates happen automatically. A peer only needs to declare a minimal prefix over the tunnel, and further changes are propagated by the protocol. Using BGP with a VPN gateway is optional; static routing remains an alternative. BGP requires a route-based VPN gateway, and the on-premises device must support BGP.

One practical use is resilience. When several tunnels are active between a virtual network and an on-premises site, the routes of a failed tunnel are withdrawn, and traffic shifts to the remaining tunnels. Another use is transit routing: gateways can learn prefixes from various networks and pass them on, which allows connectivity between sites or between virtual networks through the gateway. A constraint to plan for is that a BGP prefix may not be identical to a virtual network prefix, because such routes are rejected. Larger prefixes that contain the virtual network's address space are allowed.

In the context of ExpressRoute, BGP provides the routing layer between an on-premises network and Microsoft cloud services. The M365.FM episode "Azure ExpressRoute - Simply Explained" lists Dynamic Routing as one of the service's characteristics and says that ExpressRoute uses Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) for dynamic routing between the on-premises network and Microsoft cloud services, supporting efficient data flow. The same episode describes Layer 3 connectivity through connectivity partners, which gives address-level access to Azure resources, and notes that connections can reach services such as Azure and Microsoft 365.

The episode "Azure Virtual Network - Simply Explained" places BGP among the protocols available for external communication from Azure Virtual Networks. It describes BGP as the protocol that shares routing details with external networks and thereby establishes connectivity. The episode lists it alongside IPsec/IKE tunnels, which provide secure communication between Azure and an internal network, and Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), which encapsulates traffic so that only intended traffic reaches its destination. In this framing BGP handles route exchange, while IPsec/IKE and GRE address how traffic is protected or encapsulated.

Typical decisions around BGP include whether to use dynamic or static routing for a VPN connection, whether the on-premises device supports BGP, whether the gateway type is route-based, and how address prefixes should be advertised so they do not collide with virtual network prefixes. For hybrid designs with multiple tunnels or multiple sites, BGP reduces manual route maintenance because routes are learned, shared and withdrawn automatically. For ExpressRoute, dynamic routing through BGP is part of how circuits and gateways share routes without manual configuration.

bring-your-own-device.desc: Bring your own device (BYOD) is the practice of employees using personally owned phones, tablets or laptops for work, with corporate data kept separate and protected.

faq.a: BYOD is the practice of employees using personally owned phones, tablets or laptops for work. It requires separating and protecting corporate data on those devices.
faq.q: What is Bring your own device (BYOD)?

faq.a: The episodes link BYOD to Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender, Conditional Access and Windows 365. The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" says Intune supports a BYOD policy by allowing management of various devices.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tools are associated with BYOD in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: According to the episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained", secure BYOD strategies are one of its business scenarios. It gives employees secure access to a familiar Windows environment from anywhere, managed centrally.
faq.q: How does Windows 365 relate to BYOD?

bring-your-own-device.long:
Bring your own device (BYOD) is the practice of employees using personally owned phones, tablets or laptops for work. Because these devices belong to the user rather than the organization, they sit outside the traditional model in which IT buys, configures and controls every endpoint. The central requirement of a BYOD approach is therefore to separate and protect corporate data on those devices, so that company information can be secured without taking over the personal side of the device.

In practice, BYOD is a deployment scenario within endpoint management rather than a single product. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained" lists BYOD alongside other common scenarios such as corporate-owned devices, frontline workers, remote employees and hybrid work environments. The episode describes how Microsoft Intune works together with Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender, Conditional Access, Windows 11, Apple Business Manager, Android Enterprise and Microsoft 365 to deliver a secure and unified endpoint management experience. It also explains how organizations can balance security, user productivity and compliance while simplifying endpoint administration across multiple operating systems, which is the core trade-off BYOD brings: protecting data without making the device unusable for its owner.

BYOD also shapes the choice of management tooling. The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" notes that Intune offers cloud-based management, which suits remote work and diverse operating systems, and that Intune supports a BYOD policy by allowing management of various devices. SCCM, by contrast, is described as automating software distribution and patch management, enhancing operational efficiency in complex environments. The episode advises considering the organization's infrastructure needs when choosing between the two, and mentions that both can be used together in a co-management setup for flexibility. For organizations whose workforce relies on a mix of personal devices, the cloud-native approach is presented as a better match, and the episode adds that it can lead to lower costs.

A third angle appears in the episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained", which treats secure BYOD strategies as one of several business scenarios for Windows 365, next to remote work, contractors, hybrid employees and disaster recovery. The idea described is that employees gain secure access to a familiar Windows environment from anywhere, with central management through Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender and Microsoft 365. The episode frames Windows 365 as extending the workplace rather than replacing every physical PC, which is relevant to BYOD because the corporate Windows environment can be reached from a device the organization does not own.

Typical decisions around BYOD include which devices and operating systems are allowed, how much control the organization needs over a personally owned device, how corporate data is separated from personal content, and how access is governed through identity and compliance checks. The sources summarized here do not detail specific policy settings, enrollment methods or licensing for BYOD, so those choices depend on the organization's own requirements and on the capabilities of the tools in use.

In summary, BYOD describes both a working practice and a management challenge. It is supported by cloud-based endpoint management with Microsoft Intune, by identity and security controls from Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender and Conditional Access, and by virtualized options such as Windows 365. The M365.FM episodes referenced above place it among the standard scenarios that modern device management is expected to handle, alongside corporate-owned and remote or hybrid work setups.

bulkhead-pattern.desc: The Bulkhead pattern isolates resources such as connection pools, worker capacity or queues per dependency or workload, so one failure cannot exhaust resources others need.

faq.a: It prevents an overloaded or unresponsive service from tying up shared resources, such as connection pools, and thereby causing calls to other services to fail. By isolating resources per dependency or workload, a failure stays contained at its origin.
faq.q: What problem does the Bulkhead pattern solve?

faq.a: Common approaches include separate connection pools per called service, grouping service instances into partitions, and using separate queues for asynchronous services. Microsoft's guidance also mentions processes, thread pools and semaphores, containers and VMs, and Kubernetes resource requests and limits.
faq.q: How can the Bulkhead pattern be implemented?

faq.a: Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center recommends combining it with Retry, Circuit Breaker and Throttling. The pattern's trade-offs include less efficient resource use and the need to choose partition granularity and monitor each partition.
faq.q: Which other patterns are combined with the Bulkhead pattern?

bulkhead-pattern.long:
The Bulkhead pattern is a resilience design pattern that separates the elements of an application into isolated pools of resources, so that a failure in one element does not take down the rest. Resources that can be partitioned in this way include connection pools, worker capacity and queues. The name comes from the partitions in a ship's hull: when a leak occurs, only one section floods while the rest of the vessel stays afloat.

The pattern addresses a specific failure mode. When a service becomes overloaded or unresponsive, calls to it can tie up shared resources, such as a common connection pool. Once those shared resources are exhausted, calls to other, healthy services start to fail as well, and a local problem turns into a cascading failure. Assigning each dependency or workload its own pool of resources keeps the damage contained at its origin. The M365.FM episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" describes the goal in similar terms: the bulkhead pattern in microservice architecture is used to prevent faults in one part of a system from taking down the entire system, effectively locking down the failure to its origin.

In practice, the isolation can be applied at several levels. Service instances can be grouped into partitions based on consumer load and availability needs, and a consumer can hold a separate connection pool for each service it calls. Asynchronous services can be isolated through separate queues. Implementation mechanisms mentioned in Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center guidance include processes, thread pools and semaphores, containers and virtual machines, and resource requests and limits in Kubernetes. Which mechanism fits depends on how strong the isolation needs to be and what the platform offers.

The documented benefits are protection against cascading failure, partial functionality during an outage, and differentiated service quality. If one partition is saturated or failing, the other parts of the application can keep working, so users may still reach a reduced set of features instead of losing everything. Partitioning by consumer or workload also allows different levels of service, for example giving critical callers capacity that cannot be consumed by less important ones.

The pattern also involves trade-offs that need to be weighed. The strength of isolation, the cost and the operational effort have to be checked against the risk being addressed. Resource use can become less efficient, because capacity reserved for one partition cannot be borrowed by another when it sits idle. The granularity of the partitions is a design decision: too coarse and failures still spread, too fine and the overhead grows. Each partition also needs its own monitoring so that saturation or failure in one of them becomes visible.

The Bulkhead pattern is generally not used alone. Microsoft's guidance recommends combining it with Retry, Circuit Breaker and Throttling. The "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" episode places the bulkhead alongside the circuit breaker, which can stop requests from reaching unhealthy services based on thresholds for errors and timeouts and reroute traffic when a service fails. In that combination, the circuit breaker limits calls to a failing service, while the bulkhead ensures that whatever load still reaches it cannot consume resources that other parts of the system depend on.

burnout.desc: Burnout is occupational exhaustion and disengagement from chronic workplace stress, discussed in M365.FM episodes on work design, isolation, notifications and HR analytics.

faq.a: Occupational burnout is a state of exhaustion and disengagement resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.
faq.q: What is occupational burnout?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus" cites a Microsoft finding of a 26% jump in stress levels for employees facing frequent digital interruptions and describes how constant alerts can lead to mental fatigue.
faq.q: How do notifications relate to burnout according to M365.FM?

faq.a: The episode "HR Analytics with Fabric and Dynamics 365 Human Resources" describes dashboards, alerting and predictive insights on burnout and attrition risk so HR can act early rather than report late.
faq.q: Can data help identify burnout risk?

burnout.long:
Burnout, in its occupational sense, is a state of exhaustion and disengagement that results from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It is treated as a condition tied to how work is organized and experienced over time, rather than a short-lived reaction to a single busy week. In the context of the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept appears in discussions about how digital tools, collaboration habits and data practices shape the working day.

The topic matters to individuals, managers and HR teams alike. For individuals, it concerns workload, focus, energy and the sense of connection to colleagues. For organizations, it concerns well-being, engagement, performance and retention. Several M365.FM episodes return to burnout from different angles, which shows how many parts of working life it touches: planning, communication, culture and measurement.

One recurring theme is the effect of constant digital interruptions. The episode "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus" describes cognitive load and burnout as a consequence of frequent alerts. It cites a Microsoft finding that employees facing frequent digital interruptions experience a 26% jump in stress levels, and explains that expecting a message at any moment keeps the mind on high alert, which leads to mental fatigue and can leave people anxious or irritable. The same episode frames notification overload as a drain on both time and team energy.

A second theme is social connection. The episode "Why High Performers Burn Out from Workplace Isolation" links burnout to isolation and loneliness. It describes how, without mentors, stress can build, creativity can stall and loneliness can deepen, and it lists self-doubt, quiet loneliness, increased imposter syndrome and burnout, and feeling invisible or stuck without growth opportunities as possible outcomes. It cites a CDC report that 32.1% of people feel lonely, with 43.3% among younger adults aged 18 to 34, and notes that focusing mainly on achievement can crowd out quality social bonds.

A third theme is time and task management. In "Use the Eisenhower Matrix with Microsoft 365 Copilot", burnout is mentioned in connection with respecting natural energy rhythms. The episode suggests planning urgent tasks for the times of day with the most energy and saving routine work for low-energy moments, so that burnout is avoided and work actually gets done. It also points out that rigid to-do lists handle sudden changes poorly, such as a new project from a manager or a meeting that runs long.

A fourth theme is organizational policy and measurement. "The Future of Work with Fabio Bonolo [MVP]" lists prioritizing employee mental health among its recommendations for a future-of-work strategy. It suggests offering resources and flexible arrangements to support well-being and reduce burnout, measuring progress with key metrics such as engagement and performance, and encouraging feedback so employees feel safe to share ideas and suggest improvements.

Finally, "HR Analytics with Fabric and Dynamics 365 Human Resources" treats burnout as something that data can help surface early. The episode describes a reference architecture in Microsoft Fabric that brings HR data into one lakehouse, with dashboards for headcount, onboarding, leave balances, DEI and attrition, plus alerting and predictive insights on burnout and attrition risk. The stated aim is for HR to act early rather than report late.

Taken together, the episodes treat burnout as a concept that connects several decisions: how notifications are configured, how tasks are prioritized, how people are supported socially, how well-being is included in strategy, and how HR data is used to spot risk. They present it as a workplace and design question as much as a personal one.

business-central-extensions.desc: Business Central extensions are installable apps written in AL that add fields, pages, actions, rules and integrations to Dynamics 365 Business Central without changing its base application.

faq.a: They are separate installable apps, written in AL, that add fields, pages, actions, rules and integrations to Dynamics 365 Business Central without modifying the standard base application.
faq.q: What are Business Central extensions?

faq.a: Older approaches often changed the original application code, which had to be reconciled with Microsoft's new code after updates. Extensions keep the standard application in place and add custom functionality as a separate application, though updates still require testing.
faq.q: How do extensions differ from older customization approaches?

faq.a: Extensions are written in AL, stored in .al files, and developed in Visual Studio Code with the AL Language extension. The result is bundled in a .app package with a manifest containing name, publisher and version.
faq.q: What tools and file formats are used to build extensions?

business-central-extensions.long:
Business Central extensions are separate, installable applications written in the AL language that add functionality to Dynamics 365 Business Central without modifying the standard base application. They can add fields, pages, actions, business rules and integrations. Because the custom functionality sits beside Microsoft's application rather than inside it, the standard code stays unchanged.

The extension model exists because no two organizations operate in exactly the same way. Business Central already covers finance, sales, purchasing, inventory, projects and other core business processes. A company may still need specialized shipping, local financial reports, additional approval rules, bank integrations, electronic invoicing or a connection to another business system. Extensions are the mechanism for adding such requirements on top of the standard product.

Technically, extensions are the programming model in which functionality is defined as an addition to existing objects instead of a change to the base code. The model is object-based. Developers create new objects or extend existing ones such as tables, pages, reports, enums and code flows. The objects are written in AL and stored in .al files, with one object per file recommended. Typical object types are tables for schema, pages for the user interface, codeunits for logic, and reports. Table extensions and page extensions add or override parts of existing objects. A .app package bundles these artifacts together with a manifest that holds the name, publisher and version.

Development is done in Visual Studio Code with the AL Language extension, which provides compiler validation, snippets, IntelliSense and publishing to a tenant. Telemetry can be connected to an Azure Application Insights resource. For extensions intended for the marketplace, Microsoft Learn recommends working through a checklist before submission, and the AppSourceCop analyzer can be enabled.

The main decision around extensions concerns upgrades. According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Business Central AL Development", older development approaches frequently involved modifying the original application code. That could work until the underlying application was updated, after which Microsoft's new code and the organization's modifications had to be compared and reconciled. With extensions, the standard application remains in place while custom functionality sits beside it as a separate application. The episode notes that updates still require testing, but developers do not need to recreate every customization inside Microsoft's original source code. The same episode uses an office-building analogy, with Business Central as the building, to explain this separation.

The episode "Dynamics 365 Business Central Extensions - Simply Explained" approaches the topic from the business side. It describes the kinds of requirements that extensions address, such as local financial reports, extra approval rules, bank integrations, electronic invoicing and links to other systems, and explains the idea in plain terms.

Extensions sit under the broader topic Dynamics 365 Business Central. Anyone evaluating how to adapt the product to specific processes will encounter them as the supported route for custom fields, pages, actions, rules and integrations, while AL and the .app package structure define how that work is built and delivered.

business-email-compromise.desc: Business email compromise (BEC) is a fraud attack in which an attacker impersonates or takes over a trusted mailbox to trick people into moving money or sharing data.

faq.a: BEC is a fraud attack in which an attacker impersonates or takes over a trusted mailbox to trick people into moving money, for example by changing bank details or approving payments. It can also be used to get employees to share sensitive information.
faq.q: What is business email compromise (BEC)?

faq.a: According to the episode "Exchange Online Protection (EOP) - Simply Explained", EOP focuses on spam, malware and basic phishing, and BEC and executive impersonation often slip through. The episode lists BEC as not covered and recommends more advanced threat protection.
faq.q: Does Exchange Online Protection (EOP) stop BEC?

faq.a: The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" says that email addresses, writing style and even voice messages are no longer reliable trust signals because attackers can imitate people with AI-generated content. It argues for identity verification instead of trust based on appearance.
faq.q: Why are deepfakes relevant to BEC?

business-email-compromise.long:
Business email compromise (BEC) is a fraud attack in which an attacker impersonates or takes over a trusted mailbox in order to trick people into moving money. Typical examples are changing the bank details of a supplier or getting a payment approved. Because the message appears to come from someone the recipient already trusts, such as an executive or a vendor, BEC relies on social engineering rather than on malicious attachments or obviously suspicious links.

The M365.FM episode "Detect Microsoft 365 Attack Chains with Entra and Sentinel" describes BEC as a sophisticated attack that targets organizations through their email systems. Attackers impersonate trusted individuals, such as executives or vendors, to manipulate employees into transferring funds or sharing sensitive information. The episode presents it as one stage in a wider set of Microsoft 365 attack chains, alongside topics such as OAuth app abuse, and stresses that understanding BEC tactics is essential for protecting an organization.

BEC is difficult to stop with basic email filtering. The episode "Exchange Online Protection (EOP) - Simply Explained" says that EOP primarily filters spam, malware and basic phishing attempts. It states that advanced phishing, Business Email Compromise and impersonation of executives often slip through EOP's defenses, and its coverage table lists BEC as not covered by EOP. The episode concludes that such threats call for more advanced threat protection measures on top of the baseline filtering.

One such measure is covered in "Microsoft Defender for Office 365 - Simply Explained". The episode explains that the system analyzes incoming messages in real time to identify potential phishing attempts, and it cites a Microsoft-reported 99.995% accuracy rate in detecting malicious intent and around 140,000 BEC emails blocked daily. The detection methods it names include anti-phishing policies that can be configured against impersonation and phishing, with adjustable thresholds for detecting phishing emails, and real-time scanning of links and attachments so that malicious content does not reach the inbox.

Sender authentication is another layer. In "SPF, DKIM and DMARC - Simply Explained", the hosts explain why anyone can send email as someone else: legacy SMTP protocols were built for an era of trust, and the hidden envelope address can differ from the visible "From" line. The episode walks through SPF, DKIM and DMARC as a blueprint for protecting an email infrastructure, framed explicitly for administrators of a Microsoft 365 tenant and for organizations that want to protect themselves from BEC, so that a stranger cannot use the company's name.

The newest development discussed is the use of AI. The episode "Stop Deepfake Business Email Compromise with Verified ID" explores how deepfake-enabled BEC attacks are becoming more convincing and dangerous. It says that traditional trust signals, such as email addresses, writing style or even voice messages, are no longer reliable because attackers can imitate executives and employees with AI-generated content. The episode argues that organizations should move away from trust based on appearance and adopt identity verification as a core principle, with Verified ID in the title as the approach it examines.

Taken together, the episodes treat BEC as a problem that spans several layers: baseline filtering, advanced anti-phishing protection, authentication of sending domains, detection of attack chains, and verification of identity for sensitive requests such as payments and bank detail changes. Typical decisions for administrators include whether EOP alone is sufficient, which anti-phishing policies and thresholds to configure, and how to authenticate email so the company's domain cannot be easily spoofed.

business-performance-analytics.desc: Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is a Microsoft add-on that turns Dynamics 365 ERP data into prebuilt Fabric and Power BI reports and exposes it to agents via MCP.

faq.a: Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is a Microsoft analytics offering for Dynamics 365 ERP data. It provides prebuilt reports on Fabric and Power BI and exposes ERP analytics to AI agents through an MCP server.
faq.q: What is Business Performance Analytics?

faq.a: It is a preview MCP server that supports natural-language queries, DAX generation by AI agents and role-based row-level security. According to the documentation, it integrates with Visual Studio Code and Copilot Studio.
faq.q: What is the ERP Analytics MCP server?

faq.a: The documentation lists reporting over a maximum of eight quarters, data volume bound by the Power BI Embedded A6 capacity, and refreshes twice a day. Near real-time analysis and predictive insights are announced for later releases.
faq.q: What limits apply to Business Performance Analytics?

business-performance-analytics.long:
Business Performance Analytics (BPA) is an analytics offering for Dynamics 365 ERP data. It builds prebuilt reports on Microsoft Fabric and Power BI and exposes ERP analytics to agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which is why it is also known as the ERP Analytics MCP. Microsoft developed it as part of Dynamics 365, and it is classified as a Microsoft tool and an analytics and BI tool. It is listed as an add-on.

The purpose of Business Performance Analytics is to turn an organization's operational and financial data into actionable insights without building every report and data model from scratch. According to Microsoft's documentation, it works with Dynamics 365, Dataverse and Power BI. The documented goals are consolidating key performance indicators, automating reporting and allowing custom analysis. Typical business areas named in the documentation are finance, supply chain, project operations and commerce reporting. The offering is related to Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations, whose data it analyses.

The offering provides preconfigured reports and interactive dashboards for several business areas. It also provides dimensional data models that can be used in a SaaS or data-as-a-service approach. Teams that need more than the standard content can build custom models on top of these models, for example in Microsoft Fabric. Access to the data lake relies on shared Dataverse permissions, so existing security concepts carry over to the analytical layer.

The link to agents is a distinguishing part of Business Performance Analytics. A preview ERP Analytics MCP server supports natural-language queries, lets AI agents generate DAX, and applies row-level security based on roles. The documentation names integration with Visual Studio Code and Copilot Studio. This means an AI agent can ask questions about business performance in plain language while the results respect the same role-based access rules as the reports. Because this server is described as a preview, its behaviour and scope may change, and current documentation should be consulted before relying on it.

Several limits are documented. Reporting covers a maximum of eight quarters, data volume is bound by the Power BI Embedded A6 capacity, and data refreshes twice a day. Near real-time analysis and predictive insights are announced for later releases rather than being part of the current scope. These points matter in practice: organizations that need long history, very large data volumes or frequent refreshes should check whether the limits fit their requirements, and may consider custom models in Fabric for needs beyond the prebuilt content.

On licensing, the documentation states that the capability is included in the Dynamics 365 Finance license scope, while the product is also described as an add-on. Anyone evaluating it should verify current licensing and availability in Microsoft's own documentation. Typical situations in which it is considered include finance and operations teams that want standard ERP reports in Power BI without a custom data project, analysts who want to work with ERP data in Fabric, and scenarios in which AI agents answer questions about business performance through the MCP server.

No M365.FM episode is currently recorded for Business Performance Analytics, so this description relies on the product's own documentation and metadata. Related topics on the site include Dynamics 365 Finance and Operations, Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and AI agents, which together describe the data sources, the analytical platform and the agent access that the offering combines.

caching.desc: Caching keeps frequently accessed data in fast memory so repeated requests avoid slower storage; it is a core performance lever in APIs, cloud apps and Microsoft Fabric.

faq.a: Caching keeps frequently accessed data in fast memory so repeated queries or requests do not have to read from slower storage. It improves response times and reduces load on the underlying system.
faq.q: What is caching?

faq.a: The episodes name Redis and Memcached for in-memory caching, content delivery networks (CDNs) for caching static assets closer to users, API gateway caching such as in Azure API Management, and semantic caching for AI agents.
faq.q: Which technologies do the M365.FM episodes mention for caching?

faq.a: The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" says that semantic caching reduces API calls, which can lower costs and improve response times for AI agents.
faq.q: How does caching help with AI agent costs?

caching.long:
Caching is the practice of keeping frequently accessed data in fast memory so that repeated queries or requests do not have to read from slower storage every time. It is used wherever the same information is requested again and again: in analytics platforms such as Microsoft Fabric, where it is described as a key lever for query performance, but also in API gateways, application back ends and cloud-hosted services.

The basic idea is simple. When data is requested for the first time, it is fetched from its original source, such as a database or a backend service. A copy is then held in a faster layer. Later requests for the same data can be answered from that copy, which shortens response times and takes load off the underlying storage or service. The main decisions around caching therefore concern what to keep, where to keep it, and how long the stored copy should be considered valid.

The M365.FM episodes place caching in several contexts. In "API Gateway - Simply Explained", caching is listed alongside authentication, authorization, rate limiting, request routing, logging and monitoring as one of the capabilities an API Gateway provides while simplifying access to multiple backend services. The episode "Azure API Management - Simply Explained" covers caching in the same way, as one of the concepts of Azure API Management, which acts as a secure gateway between applications and backend services. There it appears together with products, subscriptions, policies, rate limiting, authentication, transformations, versioning and revisions.

The episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" treats caching as a way to address scaling problems and improve performance. It says that database calls and API responses can be cached to reduce load on the backend, and that the data store used for caching should be selected based on need. Redis and Memcached are named as popular choices. The episode also says that fragments can be cached based on their volatility and update frequency, which means that data that changes rarely can be held longer than data that changes often.

The episode "High-Performance Azure Cloud Governance to Reduce Waste" lists caching strategies for cloud applications. It states that storing frequently accessed data in a cache reduces the time needed to retrieve information. Suggested approaches include in-memory caching solutions such as Redis or Memcached to speed up data retrieval, and content delivery networks (CDNs) that cache static assets closer to users. In that episode, caching is one part of keeping a cloud environment responsive and efficient, including during peak usage.

Caching also appears in the context of AI workloads. The episode "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" recommends semantic caching to reduce API calls, and says this strategy can lower costs and improve response times for AI agents. It is mentioned together with other cost measures such as prompt compression to minimize token usage, choosing the right billing model in Azure, and monitoring resource usage with alerts for spending spikes.

Across these sources, caching serves two goals: faster responses and reduced load on or cost of the backing system. The choice of layer depends on the situation, whether that is a gateway policy in front of backend services, an in-memory store such as Redis or Memcached, a CDN for static assets, or a semantic cache in front of AI calls. In each case the trade-off is the same: cached data is quicker to read, but its freshness has to be managed according to how often the underlying data changes.

calculated-column.desc: A calculated column is a Power BI table column defined by a DAX formula, computed row by row and stored in the model, which adds to model size and refresh work.

faq.a: According to the episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]", a calculated column adds data to each row, is static and is used for data preparation, while a measure calculates values based on filters, is dynamic and is used for analysis.
faq.q: What is the difference between a calculated column and a measure?

faq.a: Yes. Its values are computed row by row and stored in the model, which increases model size and adds work to each refresh. The episode "Power BI Calculated Columns vs Measures - Simply Explained" discusses this as a memory cost.
faq.q: Does a calculated column affect model size?

faq.a: The episode "Implement Power BI Row-Level Security in Microsoft Fabric" lists a calculated column used for identity as a pitfall because it has no per-user effect, and suggests moving that logic into role filter DAX over model tables.
faq.q: Can a calculated column be used for row-level security by user identity?

calculated-column.long:
A calculated column is a column added to a table in a Power BI model using a DAX formula. The formula is evaluated for every row of the table, and the resulting values are stored in the model alongside the imported data. Because the values are materialized rather than computed at query time, a calculated column increases the size of the model and adds work to each data refresh. Microsoft's documentation covers the creation of calculated columns in a Power BI Desktop tutorial.

The central idea behind a calculated column is that it adds data to each row. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" contrasts it with a measure in a simple comparison: a calculated column adds data to each row, is static, and is used for data preparation, whereas a measure calculates values based on filters, is dynamic, and is used for analysis. In practice this means a calculated column behaves like any other column in the table. It can be placed on an axis, used in a slicer, or used as a field in a visual, because its value already exists on every row.

The episode "Power BI Calculated Columns vs Measures - Simply Explained" frames the difference as a question of where the calculation stands. It describes the two options as ways of doing something similar that behave very differently, noting that a calculated column is stored inside the data model and follows every single row. The episode also addresses the memory cost of that storage, which it describes as a bill that can lead to a slow report, and it lists common beginner mistakes around choosing between the two. It places the topic in the wider context of Microsoft 365, Fabric and Azure.

Choosing between a calculated column and a measure is a recurring modeling decision. When a value must exist per row, for example to categorize or prepare data, a calculated column fits. When a value should respond to the filters applied in a report, a measure is the appropriate tool. The episode "Bulk Rename Power BI Measures with PBIP" touches on this decision when it discusses replacing a measure: the process includes analyzing the existing DAX and deciding between a new calculated column or a revised measure, then updating visuals so results remain accurate. The same episode mentions common troubleshooting issues such as broken visuals, context-related errors and performance bottlenecks, and covers DAX fundamentals including functions like CALCULATE, VAR, SUM and SWITCH.

Calculated columns also appear in the context of security. The episode "Implement Power BI Row-Level Security in Microsoft Fabric" lists a calculated column used for identity as a pitfall, noting that it has no per-user effect. Its suggested fix is to move that logic into the role filter DAX over model tables instead of relying on calculated columns. This illustrates a limit of the concept: because a calculated column is stored and static, it does not adapt to the identity of the person viewing the report.

In day-to-day work, the main trade-offs are model size, refresh duration and flexibility. Since every calculated column is stored, adding many of them to large tables grows the model and lengthens refresh. Testing DAX before using it in reports is recommended in the first episode, which mentions DAX Studio as a way to check formulas, find errors and improve performance. Taken together, the episodes position the calculated column as a data-preparation tool whose convenience should be weighed against its storage and refresh cost.

calculation-groups.desc: Calculation groups are a tabular model feature that applies reusable DAX calculation items, such as time intelligence, to many measures at once.

faq.a: A calculation group is a tabular model feature that applies reusable DAX calculation items, such as time intelligence, to many measures. This reduces the number of redundant measures in a model.
faq.q: What is a calculation group?

faq.a: According to the episode "Power BI Calculation Groups - Simply Explained", models often accumulate dozens or hundreds of measures that are copies of one another for different periods. Calculation groups define the variation once and apply it to the base measures.
faq.q: Which problem do calculation groups solve?

faq.a: The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" describes calculation groups as a way to keep time intelligence, KPIs, and business rules centralized and auditable within a semantic model reused across reports and teams.
faq.q: How do calculation groups relate to semantic models in Microsoft Fabric?

calculation-groups.long:
Calculation groups are a feature of tabular models, available in Power BI semantic models, that lets a modeler define reusable DAX calculation items and apply them to many measures. Instead of building a separate measure for every combination of a base figure and a variation, such as the current period, year to date, or prior year, the logic is written once as a calculation item and then applied to whichever measures a report uses. The main purpose is to reduce redundant measures and keep repeated logic in one place.

The problem they address is a familiar one in growing models. The episode "Power BI Calculation Groups - Simply Explained" describes a model with dozens of measures, most of them copies: one sales number is built, then rebuilt for this month, this year, and last year, until nobody can tell which version is right. A simple report turns into a hundred measures. A calculation group replaces that pattern by separating the base measure from the variation applied to it, so the base measure is defined once and the variations are defined once.

In practice, a calculation group is a table-like object in the model that contains calculation items. Each item holds a DAX expression that modifies how a selected measure is evaluated. A typical use is time intelligence, where items such as YTD, QTD, and TTM sit in a single group and can be combined with any measure in the model. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" names this use directly: calculation groups remove the need for endless YTD/QTD/TTM variants and keep time intelligence, KPIs, and business rules centralized and auditable.

Calculation groups also fit into a wider modeling approach. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" presents the semantic model as an enterprise asset, a single definitional layer reused across reports, workspaces, and teams, with row-level security enforced in the model. In "Extend Microsoft Fabric with Custom APIs and Power BI Models", the semantic model is described as a contract: business logic goes into measures rather than reports, calculation groups handle time intelligence, and KPI definitions are centralized. Keeping logic in the model rather than in individual reports is what allows several reports to show consistent numbers.

The topic also appears in discussions of DAX practice. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" lists calculation groups among recommended practices for scalable analytics models, alongside variables for readability, efficient data types, pattern-based measure design for modularity and reusability, and a star schema. In "Bulk Rename Power BI Measures with PBIP", the connection is to maintenance: tools such as Tabular Editor can support bulk edits and advanced features like calculation groups, which centralize logic and reduce repeated formulas, and the episode stresses validating changes and refreshing datasets afterwards.

Typical decisions around calculation groups concern where repeated patterns exist. If a model contains many measures that differ only by a time period or a similar transformation, a calculation group is a candidate for consolidation. If a model has few measures, the added concept may not be needed. Because calculation groups are defined at the model level, they are usually created and maintained with modeling tools rather than inside individual reports, and changes should be tested against existing measures and visuals. Official documentation on calculation groups is available from Microsoft Learn under the Analysis Services tabular models section.

canvas-app.desc: Canvas app: a Power Apps app type where the maker designs the screen layout freely, like a slide, and connects it to data with Power Fx formulas.

faq.a: A canvas app is a Power Apps app type where the maker designs the screen layout freely, like a slide, and connects controls to data using Power Fx formulas. Data can come from many sources through connectors.
faq.q: What is a canvas app in Power Apps?

faq.a: A model-driven app is generated from the Dataverse data model, while a canvas app starts from the screen design chosen by the maker. The episode "Canvas Apps vs Model-Driven Apps - Simply Explained" says the right choice depends on the business requirements.
faq.q: How does a canvas app differ from a model-driven app?

faq.a: Power Fx is the formula language used to define behavior and connect data in a canvas app. It is closely related to Power Apps and the Power Platform.
faq.q: Which language is used to build logic in a canvas app?

canvas-app.long:
A canvas app is one of the two primary app types in Power Apps. The maker designs the screen layout freely, in a way comparable to arranging objects on a slide, and then connects the controls on those screens to data by writing Power Fx formulas. The name is also written "Canvas apps" or, in German, "Canvas-App". Because the starting point is the visual design rather than a data model, canvas apps are the Power Apps option where the maker decides exactly how each screen looks and behaves.

In practice, canvas apps are used for task-focused business applications that need a specific design. Typical examples mentioned in the M365.FM material on Power Apps include employee onboarding, asset management, inspections, help desk solutions, inventory tracking, approval processes and field service applications. Data can be brought in through connectors from many different sources, and the apps can integrate with Microsoft 365 services such as SharePoint, Teams, Excel, Outlook, Dynamics 365 and Azure. The freedom of the layout comes with a trade-off: the maker is responsible for how the screens are arranged and how they respond.

The two building blocks that define a canvas app are the screen design and Power Fx. Controls are placed on screens, and Power Fx, the formula language of the Power Platform, defines behavior, data connections and logic. A canvas app therefore sits inside Power Apps as its broader platform and relies on Power Fx for everything that goes beyond the visual layout.
