The main decision around canvas apps is the choice against the other app type, the model-driven app. A model-driven app is generated from the Dataverse data model, while a canvas app starts from the screen design. The episode "Canvas Apps vs Model-Driven Apps - Simply Explained" presents these as the two primary ways to build business applications with Microsoft Power Apps and says the right choice depends entirely on the business requirements. It is aimed at IT professionals, citizen developers and Microsoft partners who need to know when each approach delivers the most value. The episode "Power Apps - Simply Explained" places both app types within the wider Power Platform, alongside Power Automate, Power BI, Dataverse and Power Pages.

Several episodes look at how canvas apps relate to newer approaches and to data governance. "Canvas App UI vs Generative Pages: Which Should You Use?" compares manual canvas work with Generative Pages, which turn plain-English prompts into responsive, Dataverse-aware React pages. The episode describes the upside as speed, consistency, accessibility and governance through Dataverse metadata and roles, and the downside as possible fragility, such as read-only generated output, prompt ambiguity and hidden licensing. It also says the technical debt shifts from messy one-offs to platform dependency and regeneration discipline.

"Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" describes Code Apps as a way to build modern React-based web applications with familiar tools such as Visual Studio Code while keeping Power Platform features like Dataverse, Microsoft Entra authentication, connectors, security policies and managed deployments. The episode contrasts them with traditional canvas apps and model-driven apps, and says they extend the platform rather than replace low-code development.

"Move Canvas Apps from SharePoint to Dataverse" addresses where a canvas app's data lives. The episode describes a fork between a fast personal Copilot lane and a governed enterprise Power Platform lane, and discusses stopping accidental data exposure, the point that Copilot amplifies whatever governance already exists, and the role of sensitivity labels in protecting a tenant. For makers, this frames moving a canvas app's data from SharePoint to Dataverse as a governance decision as much as a technical one.

capable-to-promise.desc: Capable to promise (CTP) is an order promising approach that derives a delivery date from current factory capability rather than from a static lead time.

faq.a: Capable to promise is an order promising approach that sets a delivery date based on what the factory can currently do, given material, routing, resource, labor and shipping limits, instead of a static lead time.
faq.q: What is capable to promise (CTP)?

faq.a: According to the Infor LN documentation, CTP is a group of techniques that includes basic ATP checks on standard items as well as approaches such as capacity CTP, component CTP, channel ATP and family CTP, each drawing on a different source of availability.
faq.q: How does CTP differ from available to promise (ATP)?

faq.a: The Infor LN documentation states that with multisite functionality active, CTP and ATP calculations run per planning cluster. If a cluster is linked to several sites, the checks use the combined supply across those sites.
faq.q: How does CTP work in multisite setups?

capable-to-promise.long:
Capable to promise (CTP) is an order promising approach in which the delivery date offered to a customer is derived from what the factory can currently do, given constraints such as material, routing, resources, labor and shipping, rather than from a fixed, static lead time. The idea is to answer a sales question with a date that reflects real production conditions instead of a standard estimate that may no longer hold.

In practice, CTP is used when a salesperson or customer service team needs to know whether a quantity of an item can be delivered by a requested date, how soon a quantity could arrive, or how much could ship before a month ends. Because the answer rests on the state of supply and capacity at the time of the request, it can change from one request to the next as orders, stock and resource loads change.

The Infor LN documentation describes CTP as a group of order-promising techniques rather than a single method. They range from basic available-to-promise (ATP) checks on standard items to more advanced approaches, and each one draws on a different source of availability. Standard ATP uses supply that is already planned for the product. Capacity CTP looks at capacity that could be converted into deliverable supply. Component CTP uses the ATP of components linked to the product. Channel ATP considers the maximum volume that can be sold through a particular channel, and family CTP supports long-term promising at product-family level. The same documentation notes that CTP is also supported for customised items.

These variants matter for the decision of which technique to apply. A check against planned supply answers a different question than a check that converts spare capacity into new supply, and a check that depends on component availability answers yet another. The choice depends on what limits delivery for a given product: finished stock already planned, free production capacity, or the availability of the parts that go into it. Family-level promising, by contrast, serves longer-term commitments where item-level detail is not yet available.

Multisite environments add a further consideration. According to the Infor LN documentation, when multisite functionality is active, CTP and ATP calculations run per planning cluster. If a cluster is linked to several sites, the checks use the combined supply across those sites, so a promise can reflect more than a single location.

The documentation identifies the kinds of information consulted when a promise request is answered, but it does not describe step by step how a delivery date is calculated. This page therefore stays at the level of the concept: CTP ties a promise date to present capability and supply, in contrast to relying on a static lead time, and it sits alongside ATP as part of the wider set of order-promising techniques. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this topic at present.

carbon-removal.desc: Carbon removal (carbon dioxide removal) is the deliberate extraction of CO2 from the atmosphere and its durable storage in land, ocean, geological reservoirs or products.

faq.a: Carbon removal, or carbon dioxide removal (CDR), is the deliberate removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and its durable storage in geological, land or ocean reservoirs, or in products. It is also called greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions.
faq.q: What is carbon removal?

faq.a: Carbon capture and storage at point sources such as power plants cuts new emissions but does not lower CO2 already in the air. Carbon removal takes CO2 out of the atmosphere itself.
faq.q: How is carbon removal different from carbon capture and storage?

faq.a: Land-based methods include planting forests, improving soil carbon, bioenergy with carbon capture, and direct air capture with storage. Ocean and water-based methods include ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, wetland restoration and blue carbon management.
faq.q: Which methods count as carbon removal?

carbon-removal.long:
Carbon removal, also called carbon dioxide removal (CDR), greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions, is the deliberate removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and its durable storage in geological, land or ocean reservoirs, or in products. It is a human-led activity: the aim is to lower the amount of CO2 already present in the air, not only to avoid adding more. Organisations buy removal credits to counterbalance residual emissions in net claims, which is why the term appears in corporate climate and sustainability reporting.

The methods fall into two broad groups. Land-based approaches include planting forests, improving soil carbon through farming, bioenergy combined with carbon capture, and direct air capture with storage. Ocean and water-based approaches include ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, wetland restoration and blue carbon management. The approaches differ in where the carbon ends up and in how reliably it stays there.

Permanence is a central point when comparing methods. Biological stores such as forests are considered volatile, because fire, disease or policy shifts can release the stored carbon again. Geological and mineral storage can last far longer. For anyone evaluating removal credits, the type of storage therefore matters as much as the quantity claimed.

According to the source material, CDR currently removes about 2 gigatons of CO2 per year, roughly 4 percent of annual human greenhouse gas emissions, mostly through reforestation. Studies suggest that methods deployable today could reach around 10 gigatons per year. The same material notes that measuring removals precisely is difficult, which affects how credible and comparable removal claims are.

Carbon removal should be distinguished from carbon capture and storage at point sources such as power plants. Point-source capture cuts new emissions but does not lower CO2 that is already in the atmosphere. Removal, by contrast, works on the existing stock of atmospheric CO2. In practice the two address different parts of the problem, and net claims typically refer to removal when counterbalancing emissions that remain after reductions.

In a business and sustainability context, the typical decisions around carbon removal concern which method to fund, how durable the storage is, how the removal is measured and verified, and how purchased credits are described in net claims. Choosing between volatile biological stores and longer-lasting geological or mineral storage is one of the main trade-offs.

No M365.FM episodes are currently linked to this entry, and no related topics are listed for it. The description above rests on the general definition and the figures from the cited reference article.

cardinality.desc: Cardinality in Power BI data modeling describes how often values repeat on each side of a relationship: one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one or many-to-many.

faq.a: It describes how often values can repeat on each side of a relationship between two tables. The options are one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many.
faq.q: What does cardinality mean in a Power BI relationship?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" says high cardinality in a column can inflate model size and slow performance. "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" adds that high-cardinality text keys in relationships can degrade performance compared with surrogate integer keys.
faq.q: Why does high cardinality matter for Power BI performance?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" suggests keeping only the necessary columns, testing splitting columns or replacing decimal columns with whole numbers, and limiting rows to what the report needs.
faq.q: How can cardinality be reduced in a data model?

cardinality.long:
Cardinality is a concept in Power BI data modeling that describes how often values can repeat on each side of a relationship between two tables. The common settings are one-to-many, many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many. The term also has a second, related meaning: it can refer to the uniqueness of the values in a single column. Both meanings appear in the M365.FM episodes, and they matter for how a semantic model behaves and performs.

When a relationship is defined, the cardinality tells the model whether one row on one side matches a single row or many rows on the other side. A one-to-many relationship, for example, lets multiple records from one table be related to a single record in another. The episode "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS" notes that managing cardinality is essential when working with lookup functions: the relationships between tables must be defined correctly to avoid errors, and a one-to-many relationship allows multiple records to be pulled from one table into another, for instance when customer details from a separate table are added to a sales report.

In Power BI Desktop, relationships are created and reviewed in a visual interface. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" describes dragging fields between tables to define relationships, using the relationship view to check for errors or missing links, and adjusting cardinality and cross-filter direction for more advanced modeling. Choosing between one-to-many and many-to-many relationships is part of this modeling work, alongside formatting tasks such as naming tables and fields and setting data types, which the episode says make a model easier to maintain.

Cardinality also affects performance and model size. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" defines cardinality as the uniqueness of data values in a column and states that high cardinality can inflate the data model size and slow down performance. Its suggested strategies include keeping only the columns a report needs, testing ways to lower column cardinality such as splitting columns or replacing decimal columns with whole numbers, and limiting rows to what is required. The episode attributes to Shahid Umar the remark that performance bottlenecks are often caused not just by large datasets but by how those datasets are structured.

The same point appears in the context of relationship keys. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" says that using high-cardinality text keys in relationships can degrade performance, and that replacing them with surrogate integer keys in a star schema usually yields much faster joins and a smaller model. In a star schema, relationships between a fact table and its dimension tables are typically many-to-one, so the choice of key column and its cardinality directly influences how efficiently those joins run.

In the episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric", cardinality is listed among the design factors behind performance tuning. The episode says that suboptimal model design, cardinality, or a lack of appropriate aggregations can cause slow queries and an inconsistent user experience in semantic models. Reviewing relationship cardinality and column uniqueness is therefore part of making a semantic model reusable across reports.

In practice, decisions around cardinality come down to a few checks: whether each relationship uses the intended setting, whether the key columns are as lean as possible, and whether unnecessary high-cardinality columns can be removed or simplified. The episodes treat these as routine modeling tasks rather than one-off fixes, since relationship definitions and column uniqueness shape both the correctness of results and the resource use of a model.

certificate-authority.desc: A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted entity in a public key infrastructure that issues and signs digital certificates, binding identities to public keys.

faq.a: A certificate authority issues and signs digital certificates that bind an identity to a public key. It hashes the certificate content, signs the hash with its private key and embeds the signature in the certificate.
faq.q: What does a certificate authority do?

faq.a: A root CA typically anchors trust in the hierarchy, while an issuing CA signs certificates for devices and users. The root CA publishes its public key in a self-signed CA certificate.
faq.q: What is the difference between a root CA and an issuing CA?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" describes Key Vault sending a TLS/SSL certificate request to the CA, which responds with an X509 certificate that is then merged to complete the certificate creation.
faq.q: How does a CA relate to Azure Key Vault?

certificate-authority.long:
A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted entity in a public key infrastructure (PKI) that issues and signs digital certificates. In a typical hierarchy, a root CA anchors trust, while an issuing CA signs certificates for devices and users. According to Microsoft Learn, the certification authority is the trusted third party that acts as the root of trust, offering services that authenticate the identity of people, computers and other entities on a network.

The problem a CA addresses is one of ownership. Someone who receives a public key cannot be sure that it truly belongs to the claimed sender, because a third party on the communication channel might have swapped it for another. The CA resolves this by binding an identity to a public key through a certificate. A public key infrastructure as a whole is described as a set of software and hardware elements that lets a trusted third party establish the integrity and ownership of a public key, and the CA is the central element of that arrangement.

The mechanism rests on digital signatures. To issue a certificate, the CA hashes the certificate content, signs that hash with its private key and embeds the signature in the certificate. The CA publishes its own public key in a self-signed CA certificate. A recipient who wants to verify a certificate decrypts the signature with the CA's public key and compares the resulting hash with a hash of the certificate content. If the two match, the content has not been altered and the certificate was signed by that CA. Trust in the whole chain therefore depends on the CA verifying identities correctly before it issues a certificate.

A CA usually operates together with other PKI components. The Microsoft Learn material lists a registration authority, which in Microsoft PKIs is usually called a subordinate CA, a certificate database, a certificate store on the local computer and a key archival server. The split between a root CA and subordinate or issuing CAs reflects the hierarchy described above: the root anchors trust, and the issuing CAs sign the certificates that devices and users actually present.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the CA appears wherever certificates are requested and consumed. The M365.FM episode "Azure Key Vault - Simply Explained" walks through how certificates are handled in Azure Key Vault and shows where the CA fits into that process. According to the episode, the steps are: create a certificate by starting with a key in the Key Vault; have Key Vault send a TLS/SSL certificate request to the certificate authority; let the application poll Key Vault to see whether the certificate is ready; receive an X509 TLS/SSL certificate from the CA; and complete the creation by merging the CA's X509 certificate. The episode presents this as a simple way to manage secrets, keys and certificates in one place.

Seen from a decision-making perspective, the key points are which CA is trusted and how its identity checks are performed. Because every certificate inherits its credibility from the CA that signed it, the choice of root and issuing CAs, the protection of their private keys and the way identities are validated determine how much confidence relying parties can place in the certificates. The sources treat the underlying signing and verification process in simplified form, and the details of a real deployment can be more involved.

In summary, a certificate authority provides the trust anchor for certificate-based security. It signs certificates with its private key, publishes its public key in a self-signed certificate, and lets others verify that a public key belongs to the identity named in the certificate. Services such as Azure Key Vault rely on this relationship when they request and receive TLS/SSL certificates from a CA on behalf of an application.

change-notifications.desc: Change notifications and webhooks are a Microsoft Graph pattern that pushes a message to an endpoint when data changes, replacing repeated polling.

faq.a: With polling, an application repeatedly asks Microsoft Graph whether data has changed, which often returns nothing new. With change notifications, the application registers a subscription and Microsoft Graph sends a message to its endpoint when the data changes.
faq.q: What is the difference between change notifications and polling?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Microsoft Graph Change Notifications and Webhooks" names a mishandled validation echo as the most common reason: the endpoint must return the raw token within the first five seconds, without JSON or wrappers. It also points to subscription renewals and monitoring as safeguards.
faq.q: Why do Microsoft Graph webhooks sometimes stop delivering notifications?

faq.a: The episodes recommend combining them. Delta query retrieves the changes since a previous point in time, and a saved deltaLink allows continued tracking, while webhooks supply the real-time trigger.
faq.q: How are change notifications related to delta query?

change-notifications.long:
Change notifications and webhooks are a Microsoft Graph pattern in which an application is told when data changes instead of asking for it repeatedly. The application registers a subscription, and Microsoft Graph then sends a message to the application's notification endpoint when the relevant data changes. This replaces constant polling, which, as the episode "Microsoft Graph Webhooks - Simply Explained" notes, often returns nothing new. The pattern is part of Microsoft Graph, the API that connects data across Microsoft 365.

The main purpose is to let applications respond almost immediately to events, such as calendar updates or document modifications. According to the episode "Microsoft Graph Change Notifications - Simply Explained", notifications can cover create, update and delete changes on various resources such as users, groups and security entities. Creating a subscription requires three settings: the resource to watch, the notification endpoint, and the change types. The request is then sent to the Microsoft Graph API. The same episode describes a choice of delivery channel: webhooks for instant push notifications, or Azure Event Hubs for handling large volumes of notifications securely and reliably.

Operating a subscription involves several recurring tasks. The episode says subscriptions should be renewed automatically so that notifications are not interrupted and no manual effort is needed. Incoming notifications should be processed quickly and securely, which includes validating the data, responding within 30 seconds and monitoring the status of the subscription. The episode also covers troubleshooting of common issues.

The episode "Fix Microsoft Graph Change Notifications and Webhooks" focuses on the situation where webhooks go silent, for example when SharePoint updates stop arriving. It names the most frequent cause as a validation echo that the endpoint handles incorrectly within the first five seconds: the endpoint is expected to return the raw token, with no JSON and no wrappers. The episode then lists measures that make the pipeline more reliable, compliant and auditable: thorough token checks, smart retries, automated subscription renewals and real monitoring.

Change notifications are frequently combined with delta query. The episode "Microsoft Graph Delta Queries - Simply Explained" describes delta queries as a way to query for changes in resources without retrieving the whole dataset, tracking additions, deletions and updates. It advises saving the deltaLink after the first request in order to keep tracking changes, and recommends combining delta queries with webhooks for real-time updates and better performance. In this combination, the notification signals that something changed, and the delta query retrieves what exactly changed.

The pattern also appears in architecture guidance. The episode "Microsoft Graph Automation Architecture: Beyond Scripts" lists webhooks for real-time notifications as one element of a governance-first automation design, alongside batching of requests and regular audits of permissions and access. Webhooks there let systems respond instantly to changes in Microsoft 365.

Typical decisions around the topic include whether push notifications are needed at all or polling is sufficient, whether webhooks or Azure Event Hubs suit the expected notification volume, how subscription renewal is automated, and how the endpoint is monitored. The episodes address administrators, architects and business stakeholders and stress safe implementation and operational value alongside the technical mechanics.

chaos-engineering.desc: Chaos engineering is the practice of injecting controlled failures into a system to test resilience hypotheses and find weaknesses before real outages occur.

faq.a: Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting controlled failures into a system to test hypotheses about its resilience and to find weaknesses before real outages occur.
faq.q: What is chaos engineering?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" describes Azure Chaos Studio as Microsoft's chaos engineering service for safely simulating failures in Azure environments, such as virtual machine failures, network latency, CPU stress and service outages.
faq.q: Which Microsoft service is associated with chaos engineering?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build Resilient Azure Architecture for Regional Outages", simulating failures lets teams validate that recovery mechanisms work during disruptions, and regular chaos testing builds confidence in the system's resilience.
faq.q: How does chaos engineering relate to disaster recovery?

chaos-engineering.long:
Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting controlled failures into a system in order to test hypotheses about its resilience and to find weaknesses before real outages occur. Rather than waiting for an incident to expose a gap in an architecture, teams create disruptions on purpose, observe how the system responds and recovers, and use the results to improve the design. The approach treats resilience as something that has to be verified by experiment, not assumed from the architecture diagram.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, this practice is most closely tied to Azure. The M365.FM episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" describes Azure Chaos Studio as Microsoft's chaos engineering service, which helps organizations build more resilient cloud applications by safely simulating failures before they happen in the real world. The episode compares it to a fire drill for an Azure environment: failures are rehearsed in a safe, controlled way so that teams know how systems behave when something actually goes wrong. According to the episode, such experiments can simulate virtual machine failures, network latency, CPU stress, service outages and many other real-world scenarios.

The core idea is the same regardless of tooling. A team states an expectation about how a system should behave under a given fault, introduces that fault in a controlled way, and compares the observed behavior with the expectation. If the system does not respond as hoped, the experiment has revealed a weakness that can be fixed while the stakes are still low. The word controlled matters: the goal is not to cause damage but to learn, so experiments are scoped and deliberate rather than random.

Chaos engineering also appears as one element of wider resilience and disaster recovery work. The episode "Build Resilient Azure Architecture for Regional Outages" places chaos engineering and testing alongside topics such as warm standby, automated failover and infrastructure as code. It says that chaos engineering helps find weaknesses in a cloud architecture, that simulating failures shows how a system responds, and that the practice lets teams validate recovery mechanisms and confirm they work during disruptions. The episode also states that regular chaos testing builds confidence in a system's resilience and that it identifies gaps in architectural resilience. In the same context, it notes that disaster recovery improves when failover is monitored and tested regularly.

The practice is also named in the context of migration and long-term operation. In "Move Legacy Systems to Azure Without Disrupting Work", chaos engineering is listed among ongoing optimization strategies after a move to Azure, next to continuous testing frameworks, load and stress testing, performance tuning with Azure Application Insights, recommendations from Azure Advisor, autoscaling based on real-time metrics and storage and network optimization. Here it serves to test system resilience by simulating failures once workloads are running in the cloud.

A further mention comes from the episode "Build an Auditable Multi-Agent Copilot in Microsoft 365", where chaos engineering scenarios appear in a list of compliance and governance mechanisms for multi-agent systems, alongside circuit-breaker mechanisms that isolate non-compliant agents and behavior baselining that detects compliance drift. In that list, chaos engineering scenarios are described as testing compliance resilience during disruptions or failures. This shows the concept being applied beyond infrastructure, to the behavior of agent-based systems as well.

Typical decisions around chaos engineering include which failures to simulate, how to keep experiments safe and controlled, and how to connect the findings to concrete changes such as failover design, standby capacity or monitoring. Because the episodes frame it as a recurring activity rather than a one-time test, it fits naturally into regular resilience reviews and continuous testing routines.

chargeback.desc: Chargeback is a FinOps practice in which each team or cost center is billed for allocated technology costs through an internal budget transfer.

faq.a: Showback reports costs back to the consuming teams, while chargeback actually bills them through an internal budget transfer. The episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs" notes that reporting without consequence often fails to change behavior.
faq.q: What is the difference between showback and chargeback?

faq.a: The episodes point to consistent tagging, such as cost center, project and environment tags, to attribute costs accurately. They also mention Azure Policy to enforce tagging and Azure Cost Management to analyze usage.
faq.q: What is needed to run a chargeback model for cloud resources?

faq.a: The episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" mentions the Fabric Chargeback App, which attributes compute usage to organizational units to make cost allocation easier.
faq.q: Is there a chargeback tool for Microsoft Fabric?

chargeback.long:
Chargeback is a FinOps practice in which each team or cost center is actually billed for the technology costs allocated to it. The billing happens as an internal budget transfer: money moves from the budget of the consuming unit to the budget of the central IT or platform owner. This separates chargeback from showback, which only reports costs back to the consumer without moving any money.

The practice is used in enterprise IT cost management for cloud and Microsoft 365 workloads. Its purpose is to make the people who drive consumption responsible for what that consumption costs. Several M365.FM episodes treat chargeback as part of a larger cost-accountability setup rather than a stand-alone control, and they connect it to tagging, cost allocation, monitoring and governance.

The episode "Showback vs Chargeback for Cloud and Microsoft 365 Costs" challenges the common belief that showback and chargeback alone create accountability. According to the episode, many organizations introduce showback dashboards or reports and expect behavior to change, only to find that business units ignore, dispute or game the numbers. The core message of the episode is that transparency without consequence is not enough. It argues that cost reporting needs clear ownership, meaningful incentives and integration into enterprise processes in order to influence decisions and deliver sustainable cost optimization. The discussion begins by defining showback as reporting costs back to the consuming units and then contrasts it with chargeback, where those costs are actually billed.

A recurring prerequisite for chargeback is the ability to attribute costs accurately. The episode "Azure Service Bus - Simply Explained" recommends consistent tagging strategies for Service Bus namespaces, including cost center, project and environment tags. The episode states that such tags enable accurate cost allocation and support chargeback models, and that tagging allows cost attribution across shared infrastructure, including structured chargeback for multi-tenant Service Bus deployments. It also suggests using Azure Cost Management to analyze message volume patterns and operation counts, so that tier selection rests on data.

The episode "Azure Policy - Simply Explained" links chargeback to governance. It lists cost management as one use of Azure Policy and says that enforcing tagging supports cost control and ownership, which aids chargeback and lifecycle management. In this view, policies that require tags on resources create the data foundation on which allocation and billing between teams can be built.

For Microsoft Fabric, the episode "Reduce Microsoft Fabric Costs by Optimizing Compute Workloads" mentions the Fabric Chargeback App. According to the episode, the app enables financial accountability by attributing compute usage to organizational units, which makes cost allocation easier. It is listed alongside the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics App, which is used for operational monitoring, so that usage can be observed technically and also assigned to the units responsible for it.

The episode "Build an Automated Azure Cleanup Engine to Reduce Cloud Waste" places chargeback in the context of waste reduction. It notes that many organizations use chargeback or showback practices to encourage teams to manage their own costs, and it pairs them with dashboards, budgets, automated alerts, native recommendations and regular reviews of budget and usage metrics. The aim named in the episode is to motivate teams to optimize their own usage.

Taken together, the episodes describe chargeback as one element of a FinOps approach. It depends on reliable allocation data such as tags, on tooling that attributes usage to organizational units, and on ownership and incentives that give the resulting numbers consequences. A typical decision is whether to start with showback reporting or to bill teams directly, and the episodes caution that either choice depends on those supporting elements to change behavior.

chart-of-accounts.desc: A chart of accounts is the list of general ledger accounts, usually with a name and number, that categorizes money movements such as sales income, rent or supplier debt.

faq.a: It is the list of accounts used in a company's general ledger, each typically with a name and number. The accounts categorize money movements such as sales income, rent or supplier debt.
faq.q: What is a chart of accounts?

faq.a: The episode "Why Your Business Central Won't Scale to Finance & Operations" advises designing the chart of accounts and dimensions with future consolidation in mind for organizations that may grow through acquisitions.
faq.q: Why does the chart of accounts matter for consolidation?

faq.a: According to "Financial Forecasting with Dynamics 365 Finance and Fabric", the chart of accounts is standardized in the transform step using translation tables, and an account dimension (DimAccount) is part of the semantic model alongside a general ledger fact table.
faq.q: How is the chart of accounts used in forecasting with Fabric?

chart-of-accounts.long:
A chart of accounts is the list of accounts used in a company's general ledger. Each account typically carries a name and a number, and together the accounts categorize money movements such as sales income, rent or amounts owed to suppliers. The chart of accounts defines the categories used to organize financial activity, so every posting can be placed in an appropriate account and later summarized for reporting.

The purpose of the chart of accounts is to answer one basic question for every transaction: what kind of financial activity was this? The episode "Dynamics 365 Finance - Simply Explained" gives examples of accounts an organization might have: sales revenue, rent, software costs, travel, salaries, taxes, cash, money owed by customers, and money owed to suppliers. If the organization pays office rent, that amount belongs in the account designed for rent. Because rent, wages, travel, taxes, inventory costs and other financial movements are all recorded in the appropriate account, the general ledger can bring these records together so that Finance can understand the organization's overall financial position.

In Dynamics 365, the chart of accounts sits at the center of the general ledger. The episode "Dynamics 365 General Ledger - Simply Explained" presents the general ledger as the company's master financial record and lists the chart of accounts first among the topics it explains in plain English, alongside financial dimensions, subledgers, posting profiles, vouchers, journals, allocations, tax, period close and consolidation. In that picture, the chart of accounts provides the account structure, while the other elements describe how transactions reach those accounts and how the results are reviewed and closed.

The chart of accounts also matters when planning for growth. The episode "Why Your Business Central Won't Scale to Finance & Operations" recommends that organizations that may eventually grow through acquisitions design the chart of accounts and dimensions with future consolidation in mind. It pairs this with establishing consistent customer, vendor, product and general ledger master data, considering future Dataverse requirements, and documenting customizations when they are created. The stated aim is not to over-engineer Business Central but to avoid making a later transition harder than necessary.

The chart of accounts is also treated as master data in AI and analytics scenarios. In "Use Copilot in Dynamics 365 Business Central", the data readiness step asks that master data, including customers, vendors, items and the chart of accounts, be clean, consistent and accessible to Copilot features. In "Financial Forecasting with Dynamics 365 Finance and Fabric", the transform step in Power Query in Fabric standardizes the chart of accounts, cost center, business unit and project codes using translation tables, and maps subledger dimensions to general ledger dimensions. The model then includes an account dimension, DimAccount, alongside cost center, business unit, project, vendor, customer and period dimensions, and a general ledger fact table, FactGL.

Typical decisions around the chart of accounts therefore include how detailed the account list should be, how accounts relate to financial dimensions such as cost center or project, and whether account structures will stay consistent across entities and systems. Consistency becomes more important when data from several sources must be combined, whether for consolidation after an acquisition, for Copilot features that rely on clean master data, or for forecasting models that need standardized account mappings.

chatbot.desc: A chatbot is a conversational interface that answers user questions by retrieving or generating responses, typically for FAQs and support ticket deflection.

faq.a: A chatbot is a conversational interface that answers user questions by retrieving or generating responses. It is typically used for FAQs and for support ticket deflection.
faq.q: What is a chatbot?

faq.a: According to the episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents", chatbots answer questions, while digital twins model the underlying business reality, including relationships, dependencies, rules and context. The episode says AI agents need such structured representations to make decisions and orchestrate actions.
faq.q: How does a chatbot differ from a digital twin or an AI agent?

faq.a: The episode "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" says Microsoft Copilot is not just a chatbot. It describes deep integration with Microsoft 365, working across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Copilot a chatbot?

chatbot.long:
A chatbot is a conversational interface that answers user questions by retrieving or generating responses. It is typically used for frequently asked questions and for support ticket deflection, where a user receives an answer directly instead of opening a request with a support team. The term describes the interaction pattern, a question in natural language followed by an answer, rather than a single product, and it appears throughout the Microsoft ecosystem in discussions of Microsoft 365, Copilot, Dataverse and Fabric.

In practice, a chatbot can work in two broad ways. It can retrieve an existing answer from a prepared source, or it can generate a response based on the question and the data it can reach. The quality of the answer depends on the underlying content and on how access to that content is governed. This is why several M365.FM episodes treat the chatbot less as a standalone feature and more as the visible surface of a larger data and governance design.

The episode "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken" frames the issue from the data side. It argues that organizations invest significant resources in enterprise data infrastructure yet often do not see the promised value, and that the problem often lies not in the technology itself but in an approach that fails to deliver the scalable governance and security the organization requires. In that view, a chatbot is only as useful as the data strategy behind it.

The episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" contrasts chatbots with digital twins. According to its description, chatbots answer questions, while digital twins model the underlying reality of the business, including relationships, dependencies, rules and context. The episode recommends treating business knowledge as an architecture problem rather than a chatbot project, which it links to better scalability, governance and long-term maintainability. It also points to a broader shift toward agentic systems, where AI agents need structured, trustworthy representations of business operations to make decisions and orchestrate actions, and it concludes with the advice to stop investing exclusively in chatbot experiences.

Reliability is another recurring theme. In "Build an Auditable Multi-Agent Copilot in Microsoft 365", the episode notes that AI hallucinations can occur without any intent to deceive and stresses the need for a multi-layered approach. It cites examples involving chatbots: Air Canada's chatbot fabricated a bereavement fare policy, which led to a legal case when a customer relied on it, and Google's Bard chatbot incorrectly claimed something about the James Webb Space Telescope during a public demonstration, causing a significant drop in stock value. The episode also lists common errors such as outdated API parameters or incorrect configuration instructions, which can waste time and reduce trust.

The episode "Govern Microsoft Fabric Data Agents in Copilot Studio" discusses AI chatbots that work on enterprise data. Its list of surprising facts states that such integrations can improve data quality, not only access, by surfacing inconsistencies, duplicate records and missing fields while answering queries, and that privacy safeguards can be stronger than human workflows when role-based access, data masking and auditing are configured correctly. It also recommends continuously improving security measures by updating policies, training and monitoring tools as new threats appear.

Finally, "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" distinguishes Microsoft Copilot from a simple chatbot. The episode says Microsoft Copilot is not just a chatbot because it integrates deeply with Microsoft 365 and works across Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook, so users do not need to switch contexts. It describes Copilot as built into Windows, Microsoft 365 and Azure and as acting as a unified system for workplace AI automation.

Taken together, the episodes show a consistent decision point. A chatbot suits question-and-answer scenarios such as FAQs and ticket deflection, while tasks that need decisions, orchestration of actions or reliable business context call for structured data, governance and agent-based design behind the conversational interface.

chatgpt.desc: ChatGPT is OpenAI's AI chat assistant, often compared with Microsoft 365 Copilot in enterprise planning, pricing and persistent-context architecture.

faq.a: ChatGPT is an AI chat assistant from OpenAI that answers questions and produces drafts, summaries or explanations from natural-language instructions. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is listed as a paid product.
faq.q: What is ChatGPT?

faq.a: The two assistants are often compared because they rely on similar kinds of language models, and GPT-5 is related to both. Microsoft 365 Copilot is embedded in Microsoft 365 applications and works with a tenant's own data, while ChatGPT is a more general conversational AI solution.
faq.q: How does ChatGPT relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: One episode says the choice should depend on integration needs, with Copilot preferred where embedded functionality across Microsoft products and enterprise data connectors are required. Other episodes compare pricing tiers and report user-preference figures, which should be verified against current sources.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about choosing between ChatGPT and Copilot?

chatgpt.long:
ChatGPT is an AI chat assistant from OpenAI. Users type questions or instructions in natural language and receive written answers, drafts, summaries or explanations. It was released in November 2022 and is listed in the M365.FM knowledge base as a paid product. In the Microsoft ecosystem it appears mostly as a reference point for Microsoft 365 Copilot, the assistant built into Microsoft's own applications.

ChatGPT is related to two other topics in the knowledge base. The first is GPT-5, the OpenAI model generation used in ChatGPT and in Microsoft Copilot. The second is Microsoft 365 Copilot itself. The two assistants are often discussed side by side because they rely on similar kinds of language models. The difference lies in the surrounding context: Microsoft 365 Copilot is embedded in Microsoft 365 applications and works with a tenant's own data, while ChatGPT is a more general conversational AI solution. That difference in integration and control is usually what matters when organizations weigh the two.

The episode "Persistent Context Architecture for Copilot and ChatGPT" treats ChatGPT in an architectural setting. According to the episode, persistent context is not a convenience feature but a foundational layer that determines whether AI systems can scale reliably and productively in the enterprise. The host argues that many organizations treat AI as a session, where each interaction starts from scratch, and that this episodic approach slows people down. The episode also names tooling for context management, such as memory modules and retrieval mechanisms, and graph-based workflows with memory handling.

Pricing and licensing are another recurring theme. "The Copilot Tax: Hidden Costs of Enterprise AI Strategy" compares ChatGPT with Microsoft Copilot across tiers. According to the episode's table, ChatGPT has a free tier based on a smaller GPT-4o model with limits, a Plus plan at $20 per month, a Pro plan at $200 per month, and a Team plan at $25 per seat per month. Microsoft Copilot is shown with a basic free tier, Copilot Pro at $30 per month and an M365 add-on at $30 per seat per month. The same episode places such figures in a wider frame of operational complexity, governance overhead and architectural debt that can accompany enterprise AI beyond licenses and adoption numbers. These are the episode's figures and should be checked against current vendor pricing.

Several episodes describe how users and organizations choose between the tools. "Is Microsoft 365 Copilot Worth the Cost?" contrasts the two on integration: Microsoft Copilot is built for Microsoft 365 and works inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams, so users do not need to copy and paste content between apps. "Fix 10 Data Problems That Weaken Microsoft Copilot" cites market-share figures from the episode. These say Microsoft Copilot's share among U.S. paid AI subscribers fell from 18.8% in July 2025 to 11.5% in January 2026. They also say that when both Copilot and ChatGPT are available, 18% of users choose Copilot and 76% prefer ChatGPT. When Gemini is also an option, the episode reports 8% for Copilot, 70% for ChatGPT and 18% for Gemini.

For deployment decisions, "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" addresses whether Copilot is comparable to ChatGPT Enterprise. The episode says that Copilot is deeply integrated into Microsoft 365 and enterprise data flows, whereas ChatGPT Enterprise is a more general conversational AI solution. It advises choosing based on integration needs: where embedded Copilot functionality across Microsoft products and enterprise data connectors are required, Copilot is the preferred option. Together, the episodes frame ChatGPT less as a standalone tool review and more as a benchmark for questions about context, cost, governance and integration in enterprise AI strategy.

chunking.desc: Chunking splits documents into smaller, coherent pieces before embedding and indexing, which strongly influences how precise RAG answers are.

faq.a: Chunking is the splitting of documents into smaller, coherent pieces before they are embedded and indexed for retrieval. It strongly influences the precision of RAG answers.
faq.q: What is chunking in RAG?

faq.a: The episode "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" recommends chunking methods for document processing to improve search accuracy and speed when handling large volumes of data.
faq.q: Why does chunking matter for search accuracy and speed?

faq.a: According to the episode "Scaling Microsoft Copilot to 35 Million Pages: The Epstein Files", it is an approach that breaks documents down while respecting their natural structure. The episode says it improves context fragmentation by 40% and semantic clarity by 35%.
faq.q: What is recursive structure-aware chunking?

chunking.long:
Chunking is the practice of splitting documents into smaller, coherent pieces before those pieces are embedded and indexed for retrieval. It is a preparation step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and it strongly influences the precision of the answers a RAG system produces. Because a retrieval system returns individual pieces rather than whole documents, the way a document is divided determines what information can be found and how well it fits the question being asked.

In a typical RAG process, documents are ingested, divided into chunks, converted into vector embeddings, stored in a vector database or search index, and then retrieved when a user submits a query. The episode "RAG on Azure — Simply Explained" walks through this flow and lists chunking alongside vector search, embeddings, semantic search, Azure AI Search, Azure OpenAI and the grounding of AI responses in an organization's private knowledge. The episode "How to Build Private RAG with SharePoint and n8n" likewise names chunking strategies as one of the core architectural elements of a private RAG solution, next to document ingestion, vector embeddings, semantic search and AI response generation. In both cases chunking sits between collecting the content and making it searchable.

The central decision around chunking is how to split content so that each piece stays meaningful on its own. A chunk that cuts through a sentence, a table or a section can lose the context needed to match a query or to support a correct answer. The episode "Scaling Microsoft Copilot to 35 Million Pages: The Epstein Files" discusses recursive structure-aware chunking, an approach that breaks documents down while respecting their natural structure, such as the hierarchy of a complex document. The episode says this method improves context fragmentation by 40% and semantic clarity by 35%, and presents it as producing clearer, more meaningful chunks. These figures are attributed to that episode and relate to its specific scenario of a very large document collection.

Chunking also matters for speed and scale, not only accuracy. The episode "Scaling Copilot Studio with Isha Kapoor [MVP]" recommends using chunking methods for document processing to improve search accuracy and speed when handling large volumes of data. In that discussion it appears alongside other scaling practices for Copilot Studio, such as modular agent design, integration with Power Platform, clear communication protocols among agents, governance and security, and regular monitoring of agent performance with user feedback. Chunking is therefore treated as one practical lever among several for keeping retrieval workable as the amount of content grows.

The topic is also placed in a wider architectural context. The episode "The Copilot Assumption That's Holding You Back — Agentic RAG" describes traditional RAG as focusing heavily on documents, embeddings, chunking and vector search, and contrasts this with agents that increasingly need access to callable enterprise systems. It points to the Model Context Protocol as a standardized pattern for connecting AI agents to tools and systems, moving the discussion beyond making documents searchable toward making enterprise capabilities accessible. In this framing, chunking remains a defining part of document-centred RAG, while agentic approaches add further ways of reaching enterprise information.

In practice, teams working with chunking weigh several points: how the source documents are structured, whether the split should follow headings and sections or a fixed size, and how retrieval quality is checked after changes. The episodes treat these as design choices within the larger pipeline rather than isolated settings, since chunking affects what the embeddings represent, what the index contains, and ultimately which passages are passed to the model to ground its answer.

ci-cd-pipeline.desc: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence of trigger, build, test, artifact and deploy steps that runs the same way whenever software changes.

faq.a: A CI/CD pipeline is described as a fixed sequence of steps: trigger, build, test, artifact and deploy. This sequence runs the same way every time software changes.
faq.q: What are the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes name Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as tools for automating the steps that move an app from development to production. In Azure DevOps, a pipeline can be defined with a sample YAML configuration.
faq.q: Which tools can be used to set up a CI/CD pipeline?

faq.a: Automated tests run as part of the pipeline and check for errors, broken workflows and security issues before changes reach users. The episodes also recommend adding integration tests early, plus smoke and contract tests, to the pipeline.
faq.q: How do tests fit into a CI/CD pipeline?

ci-cd-pipeline.long:
A CI/CD pipeline is an automated, fixed sequence of steps that runs the same way every time software changes. It combines continuous integration with continuous delivery or deployment. The typical stages are a trigger, a build, tests, the creation of an artifact, and a deployment. Because the sequence is defined once and then repeated, every change passes through the same checks before it reaches users.

The main purpose of a CI/CD pipeline is to deliver updates quickly and safely. Instead of building, testing and releasing by hand, a team describes these steps in a pipeline and lets tooling run them. The episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" says that CI/CD pipelines help automate the process of building, testing and deploying changes, and that automated testing ensures each change meets quality standards before it reaches users. In that episode, tests run as part of the pipeline and check an app for errors, broken workflows and security issues, so problems can be caught early and fixed before they affect users.

Pipelines are usually set up with a hosted DevOps tool. The same episode names Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as tools for automating the steps needed to move an app from development to production. The episode "Azure DevOps - Simply Explained" describes the setup in Azure DevOps as a short sequence: create a new project, which becomes the foundation for the development work, then create a new pipeline, which is where the build and deployment are defined. It suggests starting from a sample YAML configuration for the application, noting that YAML keeps the definition easy to read and maintain as code.

Testing is a central part of any pipeline, and the choice of test type affects how the pipeline is used. In "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing", the advice for integration tests is to start them early and add them to the CI/CD pipeline. The episode also recommends practical habits for that setup: use a test database rather than the real one, reset services before each test, and use mocks for outside services to save cost and keep tests isolated. It adds smoke and contract tests as a way to catch large changes quickly and keep APIs working as an app grows.

Scripting tools are often what a pipeline calls to perform deployment work. The episode "Azure CLI vs PowerShell: Which Should You Use?" lists Azure CLI as a good fit for fast tasks and for CI/CD pipeline integration, because it makes automation easier, while PowerShell is presented as better suited to complex automation, reusable modules and detailed control with object-based output. The episode also notes that both can be used together, combining the speed of one with the depth of the other.

Repository structure can influence how well a pipeline performs. The episode "The Monorepo Myth: Why Your Architecture Is Fragmented" says that CI/CD pipeline performance may suffer in large monorepos, with longer build times and coordination challenges as teams grow. It suggests investing in specialized tools to streamline processes and reduce bottlenecks, and it points to deployment complexities such as coordinating releases and managing rollbacks. As alternatives, it mentions service-oriented repositories or microservices, and it recommends evaluating the architecture against these trade-offs.

Taken together, the episodes treat a CI/CD pipeline as the automation backbone that connects code changes, tests and releases. Decisions around it typically concern which tool defines the pipeline, where tests run, which scripting tool performs the deployment steps, and how the repository layout affects build time and release coordination.

claude-code.desc: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool, discussed on M365.FM as a terminal-native agent and as a platform that can run portable agent skills.

faq.a: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. M365.FM episodes describe it as a terminal-native agent, in the same group as Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and Copilot CLI.
faq.q: What is Claude Code?

faq.a: The episode "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills" names Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and Copilot Studio as platforms that can run portable agent skills. Skills use progressive disclosure to reduce what the episode calls the Context Tax.
faq.q: How does Claude Code relate to agent Skills?

faq.a: The episode "THE DEATH OF THE PROXY" lists Claude Code among the AI clients an enterprise may deploy. It argues that a proxy per client creates separate authentication, connection pools, monitoring and failure domains that become hard to manage at scale.
faq.q: Why does Claude Code appear in the Dataverse proxy episode?

claude-code.long:
Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, it appears in two roles: as one of several terminal-native AI agents used by developers, and as one of the platforms that can run portable agent skills alongside GitHub Copilot and Copilot Studio. The knowledge base has no official documentation for the product on file, so this page restates only what the episodes say.

The episode "Agentic Developer Stack: AI Agents in the Terminal" places Claude Code in a group of tools that also includes Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and Copilot CLI. According to the episode, these terminal agents run shell commands, modify files, run tests and manage workflows. The episode presents this approach as a way to raise productivity and reduce reliance on traditional IDE-centric workflows, and says terminal agents offer flexibility that traditional IDEs cannot match. It also contrasts them with IDE-based platforms such as Cursor 2.0, where agent orchestration is a primary feature, and notes that developers can choose between classic IDE views and agent-driven workflows depending on their needs.

In "The End of AI Bloat: Why Modern Agents Need Skills", Claude Code is named together with Microsoft Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot as platforms across which Skills are becoming an architectural foundation for modern AI agents. The episode describes a problem it calls the Context Tax: an agent starts with a small system prompt covering role, tone, business rules and guardrails, and then accumulates policies, compliance rules, business procedures, examples, edge cases and department-specific instructions. The episode explains how modular Skills address this through progressive disclosure, instead of one monolithic prompt. Claude Code is relevant here because skills of this kind are described as portable between the platforms listed.

The episode "THE DEATH OF THE PROXY: Architecting Dataverse for the Agent Fabric" treats Claude Code as one of several AI clients an enterprise may deploy. The excerpt lists Claude Desktop, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Copilot CLI, custom orchestration services and internal AI assistants. Its argument concerns the proxy architecture, which it says assumes a single developer. The episode states that each proxy creates independent authentication, separate connection pools, individual infrastructure, separate monitoring and isolated failure domains, and that operational complexity grows sharply as an organization moves from ten developers to hundreds or thousands. In that framing, Claude Code is one of the clients that multiplies the number of proxies an administrator would otherwise have to manage.

The interview "Building Modern Microsoft 365 Solutions with SharePoint Framework, Microsoft Graph, PnPjs & Great User Experiences with Julie Turner [MVP]" mentions Claude Code in a discussion of open-source software and AI-assisted development, together with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Copilot. According to the episode summary, Julie Turner explains why AI should enhance rather than replace developer expertise, how experienced developers can use AI as a collaborative assistant instead of an automated replacement, and why logical thinking and software architecture remain essential skills. The same conversation touches on the future relationship between low-code and pro-code development.

Taken together, the episodes treat Claude Code as part of a broader agentic developer stack in the Microsoft ecosystem rather than as a Microsoft product. It sits next to GitHub Copilot, Copilot CLI and Copilot Studio, and the decisions the episodes raise around it concern where agents run (terminal or IDE), how instructions are packaged (monolithic prompts versus portable Skills), and how access to enterprise data is governed when many different AI clients are in use.

clean-core.desc: Clean core is an SAP extension approach that keeps standard code unmodified and extends the system through released APIs and side-by-side apps, so upgrades stay predictable.

faq.a: Clean core is an extension approach that avoids modifying SAP standard code. Extensions use released APIs and side-by-side apps instead, so that upgrades stay predictable.
faq.q: What does clean core mean in SAP?

faq.a: Only released objects, such as released public APIs, BAdIs and RAP business object extension points. Unreleased objects are not allowed, and the ABAP Cloud model enforces this through syntax checks.
faq.q: Which objects may clean core extensions use?

faq.a: Tier 1 uses only ABAP Cloud and the cloud extensibility model and is mandatory for Public Edition. Tier 2 wraps unreleased objects in released ones for Private Edition and on-premise systems. Tier 3 covers classical extensions, which are discouraged because they are likely to disrupt upgrades.
faq.q: What are the three tiers of the clean core model?

clean-core.long:
Clean core is an SAP extension approach in which the standard SAP code is left unmodified. Custom requirements are instead met through released interfaces and through apps that run beside the core system. The aim is that upgrades stay predictable, because extensions are kept separate from SAP code and therefore do not interfere with it. In SAP Learning material on clean core extensibility, this is summed up as keeping extensions clean so that they stay separate from SAP code, upgrades run smoothly and the system remains maintainable.

The approach covers several practical rules. According to the SAP Learning unit "Decouple Extensions from Standard", extensions should be avoided where standard features or configuration already meet the need. Where an extension is justified, approvals should be governed with documented reasons and value. The guiding principle is two-sided: extensions must never break upgrades, and upgrades must never break extensions. An organization that follows this principle treats every request for custom code as a decision to be assessed, not as a default.

Two families of extension are described. On-stack extensions are created inside S/4HANA Cloud and include key user extensions and developer extensions. Side-by-side extensions are built on SAP Business Technology Platform and run outside the core system. In both cases, extensions may use only released objects, such as released public APIs, BAdIs and RAP business object extension points. Unreleased objects must not be used. The ABAP Cloud model enforces this restriction through syntax checks, which means that the boundary between permitted and non-permitted objects is checked by tooling and does not depend on developer discipline alone.

A three-tier model ranks the available approaches. Tier 1 uses only ABAP Cloud and the cloud extensibility model, and it is mandatory for the Public Edition. Tier 2 wraps unreleased objects in released ones and applies to Private Edition and on-premise systems. Tier 3 covers classical extensions, which are discouraged because they are likely to disrupt upgrades. For assessing use cases and choosing a target solution, the SAP Application Extension Methodology is named as a supporting aid. Typical decisions around clean core therefore concern which tier an existing or planned extension falls into, whether a standard feature could replace it, and whether it belongs on-stack or side-by-side.

Clean core also appears outside pure SAP development topics. The M365.FM episode "Build an Enterprise AI Operating Model for Scale" (2026-01-19) lists building a clean core architecture as one of the steps for incorporating AI into an operating model. The episode names it alongside redesigning workflows to integrate machine participation, defining accountability before automation, and treating data governance as infrastructure. In that framing, clean core is presented as part of the architectural foundation that lets AI initiatives scale, and the episode describes the wider goal as turning AI from a novelty into a competitive advantage.

In summary, clean core is a discipline for how SAP systems are extended. It restricts extensions to released, supported mechanisms, prefers standard capabilities over custom code, and uses a tiered model to classify how far a given extension departs from that ideal. The result described in the sources is a system whose extensions remain separate from SAP code, so that upgrades can proceed without the extensions causing disruption.

client-credentials-flow.desc: The OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow lets a confidential client, such as a background service, authenticate with its own identity and application permissions instead of a user's.

faq.a: It is used when a confidential client, such as a background daemon, service account or backend service, needs to call an API under its own identity without any user being involved.
faq.q: When is the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow used?

faq.a: It uses application permissions, also called app roles, granted by a tenant administrator in Microsoft Entra ID, or an access control list on the resource server. Delegated permissions cannot be used because no user is involved.
faq.q: Which permissions does the client credentials flow use?

faq.a: No. The response contains a bearer access token and its lifetime, and the app requests a new token when the current one expires.
faq.q: Does the client credentials flow issue a refresh token?

client-credentials-flow.long:
The OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow is a grant type in the Microsoft identity platform that allows a confidential client, such as a web service or background daemon, to authenticate with its own credentials rather than acting on behalf of a user. It is sometimes called two-legged OAuth, because only the client and the authorization server are involved and no signed-in person takes part. The flow is suited to background daemons, service accounts and other scenarios where an application needs to call an API without human interaction.

Because no user is present, the app cannot rely on delegated permissions. Before it can request a token, the app must be authorized in another way. According to the Microsoft documentation, this can be done through an access control list maintained by the resource server, or through application permissions, also called app roles, which a tenant administrator grants in Microsoft Entra ID. The result is that the app acts under its own identity, and what it may do is determined by the permissions assigned to that identity, not by the rights of any particular user.

In practice, the app sends a request to the token endpoint using the client credentials grant type. The scope in that request is made up of the resource identifier plus the default suffix, and only one resource may be named per request. The app proves its identity in one of several ways: with a client secret, with a certificate-signed assertion, or with a federated credential from an external identity provider. The response contains a bearer access token along with its lifetime. No refresh token is issued in this flow, so the app simply requests a new access token when the current one expires.

Several practices follow from how the flow works. Credentials must never be placed in source code or in distributed native apps, since a confidential client is expected to keep its secret or certificate protected on the server side. Microsoft recommends using MSAL (the Microsoft Authentication Library) rather than making raw protocol calls, which leaves token acquisition and handling to a maintained library. Typical decisions around the flow include choosing between a secret, a certificate or a federated credential, and deciding which application permissions to grant, since these permissions apply without a user context and therefore require tenant administrator consent.

The flow also appears in the context of Microsoft Entra External ID. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Entra External ID - Simply Explained" describes machine-to-machine (M2M) communication as a capability of Entra External ID, in addition to customer identity (CIAM) and business-to-business (B2B) scenarios. According to the episode, this capability allows secure authentication through the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow: one machine can authenticate itself and obtain an access token to interact with APIs or trigger processes without human intervention. The episode gives the example of backend services communicating with payment processors or internal microservices, where the services authenticate using a client ID and secret to make secure API calls.

In summary, the client credentials flow is the standard way for a service to obtain an access token for itself. It differs from user-based flows in that it uses application permissions, issues no refresh token, and depends on a protected credential held by the client. Understanding these differences helps when designing automated integrations, background jobs and service-to-service calls in the Microsoft ecosystem.

cloud-act.desc: The CLOUD Act is a 2018 US law letting US law enforcement compel US-based providers to produce data they control, even when it is stored outside the United States.

faq.a: The CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act) is a 2018 US law that lets US law enforcement compel US-based technology providers, by warrant or subpoena, to produce data in their possession, custody or control, even when the data is stored outside the United States.
faq.q: What is the CLOUD Act?

faq.a: According to the episode "Audit Microsoft 365 Data Access Before Deploying Copilot", hosting documents in a specific country does not guarantee protection from foreign access, because the US Cloud Act requires Microsoft to comply with requests from US authorities regardless of where the data resides.
faq.q: Does storing Microsoft 365 data in a specific country protect it from the CLOUD Act?

faq.a: The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" describes it as a government access law that can allow cross-border data access under certain conditions, which can unexpectedly expose data to foreign legal systems and therefore needs to be considered alongside data residency and key control.
faq.q: Why does the CLOUD Act matter for sovereign cloud design?

cloud-act.long:
The CLOUD Act, short for Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act, is a 2018 US law. It allows US law enforcement to compel US-based technology providers, by warrant or subpoena, to produce data that is in their possession, custody or control. This applies even when the data is stored outside the United States. In discussions about Microsoft 365 and Azure, the CLOUD Act is mostly raised as a question of data sovereignty: where data is physically hosted does not by itself decide which legal system can reach it.

The central point for cloud customers is the distinction between data location and legal control. A document can be stored in a specific country or region and still fall under the reach of a foreign law if the provider operating the service is subject to that law. The CLOUD Act is a frequently cited example of this. For organizations that must meet national or regional regulations, protect sensitive information, or keep data stored and processed within the EU or other defined jurisdictions, this creates a question that goes beyond choosing a datacenter region.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" places the CLOUD Act within the wider sovereignty discussion. It describes organizations needing to meet national and regional regulations, protect sensitive data, keep data stored and processed inside the EU or other specified jurisdictions, avoid exposure to foreign cloud legal frameworks such as the CLOUD Act, and retain control of their data and key management. The episode also asks how Microsoft 365 Local options and in-country data processing can help keep Microsoft 365 data and certain services within a geographic boundary, and mentions sovereign cloud offerings from Microsoft in that context. The framing is that sovereignty involves more than technical custody of the data.

The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" treats the CLOUD Act as one of several risks in sovereign cloud design. It notes that some countries let law enforcement request data from cloud providers even if the data sits in another country, and gives the US CLOUD Act as an example of cross-border data access under certain conditions. According to the episode, this can unexpectedly expose data to foreign legal systems. The episode lists it next to financial and reputational risks, such as fines, lawsuits and loss of customer trust from failing to follow sovereignty rules, and observes that smaller organizations can be affected more because they depend heavily on their reputation.

The episode "Audit Microsoft 365 Data Access Before Deploying Copilot" brings the same law into a data ownership and compliance context. It states that hosting documents in a specific country does not guarantee protection from foreign access, and that the US Cloud Act requires Microsoft to comply with requests from US authorities for data access regardless of where the data resides. The episode ties this to compliance with data protection laws and lists it among the legal implications of data ownership, alongside risks of incomplete archiving and non-compliance with ongoing data journaling requirements.

In practice, the CLOUD Act shapes several planning decisions that the episodes mention. Organizations assess whether regional hosting is enough or whether additional controls are needed, whether to use local or sovereign deployment options, and how to retain control over encryption keys and key management. It also appears as an input to audits that review who can access Microsoft 365 data before new services such as Copilot are introduced. The sources describe it as a legal fact to account for in governance and architecture decisions rather than something a technical setting alone removes. The episodes summarized here do not give legal advice, and organizations with specific obligations would need to confirm their own situation with legal counsel.

cloud-discovery.desc: Cloud Discovery is a Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps feature that identifies cloud apps in use via Defender for Endpoint or uploaded logs and rates their risk.

faq.a: Cloud Discovery is a feature that finds the cloud apps in use across an organization and rates them against the app catalog. It analyzes traffic logs to give ongoing visibility into cloud usage and shadow IT.
faq.q: What is Cloud Discovery in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps?

faq.a: Snapshot reports are ad hoc analyses of traffic logs uploaded manually from firewalls and proxies. Continuous reports analyze logs forwarded to the service and can flag unusual behavior through machine-learning anomaly detection or custom policies.
faq.q: What is the difference between snapshot and continuous reports?
