faq.a: Continuous data can come from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint integration, a log collector using Syslog or FTP, supported secure web gateways, or the Cloud Discovery API. Snapshot reports use logs uploaded manually from firewalls and proxies.
faq.q: Which data sources can feed Cloud Discovery?

cloud-discovery.long:
Cloud Discovery is a feature of Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps that finds the cloud apps in use across an organization and rates them against the product's app catalog. It addresses a common visibility gap: employees often use cloud services that IT has not approved, a situation usually called shadow IT. By comparing network traffic logs with a catalog of cloud apps, Cloud Discovery gives security and IT teams ongoing insight into which apps are in use and how risky they are.

The feature works by analyzing traffic logs. Each log is parsed with a source-specific parser, matched against the catalog, and used to identify active users and IP addresses. The result is a risk assessment report. Each app in the catalog is scored against a large set of risk factors, so that an organization can compare apps and decide which ones to sanction, monitor or block.

There are two kinds of reports. Snapshot reports are ad hoc analyses of traffic logs that an administrator uploads manually from firewalls and proxies. They suit a one-time look at current cloud usage. Continuous reports analyze logs that are forwarded to the service on an ongoing basis, and they can flag unusual behavior through machine-learning anomaly detection or through custom policies. Continuous data can arrive through several routes: integration with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, a log collector that receives logs over Syslog or FTP, supported secure web gateways, or the Cloud Discovery API.

Typical uses center on detecting shadow IT and acting on it. Once unsanctioned apps are visible, they can be blocked through gateway integrations or block scripts. Because the report ties usage to risk scores, it also helps prioritize which apps deserve attention first, rather than treating every unapproved service as equally important.

There are limits to keep in mind. Apps that are missing from the catalog are not detected by default, so coverage depends on the catalog. Newly released log formats may not be parseable, which can cause uploads to fail. Choosing between snapshot and continuous reporting is therefore a practical decision: uploaded logs are simple to start with, while Defender for Endpoint or other continuous sources provide a steady stream of data.

Cloud Discovery is one of several capabilities of Defender for Cloud Apps. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps - Simply Explained" describes how the platform discovers Shadow IT, assesses the security of cloud services and monitors user activity for suspicious behavior. The episode lists Cloud Discovery alongside app governance, SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM), threat detection, OAuth app protection, adaptive access controls and data loss prevention (DLP). It also covers how the platform integrates with Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft 365 to provide a unified security experience.

cloud-flow.desc: A cloud flow is a Power Automate workflow that runs on Microsoft's servers, starts from a trigger and connects apps and services through connectors.

faq.a: A cloud flow is a Power Automate workflow that runs on Microsoft's servers. It starts from a trigger and connects apps and services through connectors.
faq.q: What is a cloud flow in Power Automate?

faq.a: The episode "Why Power Platform Is Your Real Automation Layer — Not Custom Code" says flows suit human approvals and cross-system processes, where visibility and adaptability matter. Transactional and high-volume operations may still need code-level performance.
faq.q: When is a cloud flow a better choice than custom code?

faq.a: Yes. According to the episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability", administrators can connect a Managed Environment to Azure Application Insights and emit cloud flow runs, triggers and action-level data for analysis.
faq.q: Can cloud flow runs be monitored?

cloud-flow.long:
A cloud flow is a Power Automate workflow that runs on Microsoft's servers. It starts from a trigger and then carries out a series of actions, using connectors to link apps and services. Because the logic executes in the cloud rather than on a local machine, a cloud flow can react to events in one service and update or notify another without manual steps. The official Microsoft Learn documentation for Power Automate provides an overview of this flow type.

In practice, a cloud flow is built from a trigger and one or more actions. The trigger defines what starts the flow, and each following step performs an operation, such as sending a message or updating a record. The episode "Power Automate - Simply Explained" walks through a simple example of building a cloud flow. It adds a new step, selects the "Send an email (V2) - Office 365 Outlook" action, fills in the recipient and subject, and inserts values from the dynamic content list, such as the name of the person who posted a tweet. This shows how data from the trigger can flow into later steps as placeholders.

Cloud flows are commonly used for repetitive business tasks. The episode "Migrate Power Automate Cloud Flows to Agent Flows" says that studies show up to 66% of knowledge workers report improved productivity from tools like cloud flows, and it describes cutting manual tasks by 10-50%. It recommends starting by identifying workflow needs, setting clear goals so success can be measured, and using flowcharts to visualize the workflow and support collaboration. The same episode frames the topic as a move from cloud flows to agent flows, which is relevant to teams that already have cloud flows in production and are deciding how to evolve them.

Approval scenarios are a typical use. The episode "Build Audit-Ready Power Automate Approval Workflows" describes an approval flow as a cloud flow, or automated cloud flow, that routes requests to approvers, waits for an approval action, and then takes follow-up steps such as an update item action or sending an email. It names documents, purchase requests and leave requests as examples, and it points to regulated industries that need consistent, auditable processes and secure records. In this context, the value of a cloud flow lies in its repeatable structure and the evidence it can leave behind.

Choosing a cloud flow over custom code is also a design decision. The episode "Why Power Platform Is Your Real Automation Layer — Not Custom Code" notes that a custom plug-in may execute faster than a cloud flow but take weeks longer to modify and deploy, while a flow may take several seconds to complete and still allow a business rule to change safely within days. According to the episode, the right architecture depends on the requirement: transactional and high-volume operations may need code-level performance, whereas human approvals and cross-system business processes usually care more about visibility and adaptability.

Operations and monitoring are a further concern. The episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability" explains that administrators can connect a Power Platform environment to an Azure Application Insights instance to analyze cloud flow telemetry, including metrics dashboards and performance diagnostics. Cloud flow runs, triggers and action-level data can be emitted to Application Insights. The setup is done in the Power Platform Admin Center, for an environment that is a Managed Environment, by providing connection details such as subscription and resource group. The episode also mentions that the right licenses are required.

Taken together, the episodes treat a cloud flow as the basic building block of Power Automate: a trigger-driven, connector-based workflow hosted by Microsoft. It suits event-driven automation, approvals and cross-system processes, can be monitored through telemetry, and is a starting point when considering newer agent-based approaches.

cloud-flows.desc: Power Automate cloud flows run in Microsoft's cloud and link services through connectors, unlike desktop flows that drive a machine's screen.

faq.a: They are Power Automate flows that run in Microsoft's cloud and connect services to each other through connectors. They differ from desktop flows, which drive a machine's screen.
faq.q: What are Power Automate cloud flows?

faq.a: The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" lists Power Automate cloud flows as part of a process solution, together with connection references, APIs, plug-ins and workflows. Organizing them this way supports deployment and reduces errors during automation.
faq.q: How are cloud flows handled in solution deployment?

faq.a: The episode "Migrate Power Automate Cloud Flows to Agent Flows" names a premium connector trap that can turn one small flow into a company-wide license bill, hidden API throttling, and AI Builder double-pay as budget concerns.
faq.q: What cost risks do the episodes mention for cloud flows?

cloud-flows.long:
Power Automate cloud flows are flows in Power Automate that run in Microsoft's cloud and connect services to each other through connectors. They are distinguished from desktop flows, which operate a specific machine's screen. Because cloud flows are hosted in the cloud rather than on a local device, they are the form of Power Automate used to move data and trigger actions between online services.

The central building block of a cloud flow is the connector. A connector is the piece that lets a flow talk to another service, and a flow strings together connector-based steps to carry out a business process. The M365.FM material on this topic also points to a cost dimension: the episode "Migrate Power Automate Cloud Flows to Agent Flows" describes a "premium connector trap", in which one small flow can turn into a company-wide license bill. The same episode lists hidden API throttling, which can slow automations without warning, and "AI Builder double-pay", where one result is charged twice, as budget concerns for teams that build automations the way they did in 2019.

Cloud flows are also a common part of larger Power Platform solutions. The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" mentions using Power Automate cloud flows to synchronize data, alongside Dataverse and Power Platform dataflows for data management across environments. That episode also notes that deployments of such apps can be automated with CI/CD pipelines using GitHub Actions, which gives teams a repeatable way to manage the apps and flows they depend on.

In application lifecycle management, cloud flows are treated as solution components. The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" lists Power Automate cloud flows within a process solution, together with connection references, APIs, plug-ins and workflows. Grouping flows with connection references in this way supports organized deployment and, according to the episode, reduces errors during automated deployment. Components can be viewed and managed in the Power Apps maker portal.

Cloud flows also appear in integration and testing discussions. The episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" names Power Automate cloud flows as a feature that helps automate business processes, next to secure custom connectors for connecting to external APIs, Dataverse Power Fx functions, and plug-ins for business rules and server logic. It describes setting up inbound and outbound integrations using Dataverse and Azure, and frames these capabilities as speeding up app development, securing data transactions and improving performance.

Reliability is a recurring theme as well. The episode "Build Reliable Power Automate Flows for Production" lists related M365.FM episodes on approval workflows and agent-based automation, including "Build Audit-Ready Power Automate Approval Workflows" and "Migrate Power Automate Cloud Flows to Agent Flows". Together, these episodes place cloud flows in a broader decision: when a flow built around connectors remains suitable, what it costs to run, and when moving to agent flows is worth considering.

Within the product family, Power Automate cloud flows are part of Power Automate. The practical choices around them usually concern which connectors a flow depends on, how it is packaged in a solution with connection references, how it is deployed across environments, and whether its licensing and throttling behavior fit the intended workload.

cloud-migration.desc: Cloud migration moves workloads, data and applications from on-premises systems to a cloud platform such as Azure, and M365.FM episodes treat it as continuous.

faq.a: Cloud migration is the move of workloads, data and applications from on-premises systems into a cloud platform. In the M365.FM episodes the platform is mostly Azure.
faq.q: What is cloud migration?

faq.a: The episode on enterprise AI readiness argues that it is a continuous process rather than a project with an end date. Planning, governance and cost control are described as ongoing concerns.
faq.q: Is cloud migration a one-time project?

faq.a: "Make Your Cloud Migration Ready for Enterprise AI" says lift-and-shift only moves technical debt elsewhere and does not give Copilot safe, governed access to data. It recommends planning the migration as an AI architecture.
faq.q: Why does the episode criticize lift-and-shift?

cloud-migration.long:
Cloud migration is the practice of moving workloads, data and applications from on-premises systems into a cloud platform. In the M365.FM material the platform in focus is mostly Azure, and the topic comes up from several angles: planning, governance, cost control, security and readiness for AI. One episode summarized here argues that cloud migration is a continuous process rather than a project with an end date, which changes how teams budget, staff and measure it.

The episodes describe migration as more than a technical task. The episode "Use Azure CAF to Select Your First Cloud Workloads" says that many cloud architects wrongly treat it as a purely technical exercise and overlook operational maturity and governance. It names the belief that "the cloud is just someone else's computer" as a mindset behind migrations that fail or become unexpectedly expensive. The Azure Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) is presented there as a way to connect business goals with technology execution and to choose which workloads to move first.

Planning is a recurring theme. According to the episode "Azure Governance Is Enforced Architecture, Not Documentation", an Azure cloud migration should start with a thorough cloud assessment that identifies suitable workloads and limits risk. It also lists setting clear objectives and KPIs to measure success, building a cross-functional team with diverse skills so that communication works during the move, selecting Azure services that fit business needs and integrate with existing systems, and developing a detailed migration roadmap. Security and compliance features are named as part of protecting data and meeting industry standards. The title of that episode points to a further position: governance should be enforced as architecture rather than left as documentation.

Cost and security are the focus of "Plan a Secure and Cost-Controlled Azure Migration". The episode says that many cloud computing problems can be prevented through good planning, together with cost controls, security, backup and monitoring. It promises a step-by-step Azure migration blueprint, a discussion of cost traps, real-world success stories and security and compliance checks that are often overlooked. It also describes a mindset shift as the way to avoid the common reasons migrations fail.

The most critical view appears in "Make Your Cloud Migration Ready for Enterprise AI". Its argument is that lift-and-shift does not modernize anything and simply moves technical debt into someone else's data center. The episode claims that an estate which is "cloud first" can still be hostile to AI, because virtual machines do not give Copilot safe, governed access to data. It calls for a roadmap that reads as an AI architecture rather than a relocation plan, and for automation so that every AI decision becomes traceable and defensible.

Migration also appears as a consulting topic. In "How to Become a High-Value Microsoft 365 Consultant", cloud migration is listed among areas where a consultant blueprint has been applied, with the episode citing reported improvements in compliance and risk management, such as policy compliance reaching 90 percent and 95 percent compliance within a week of major patching. These figures are attributed to the episode and are not independent measurements.

Taken together, the episodes suggest a sequence of decisions: assess which workloads suit the cloud, define objectives and KPIs, put governance and security in place, control costs, and design the target state with data access and AI use in mind rather than copying the on-premises layout.

cloud-pki.desc: Microsoft Cloud PKI is a cloud-based public key infrastructure in Microsoft Intune that issues and manages device certificates without on-premises CA servers.

faq.a: It automates the issuing, renewal and revocation of certificates for devices managed by Intune, using a PKI hosted in the cloud. It supports scenarios such as VPN, Wi-Fi, email, web and device identity.
faq.q: What does Microsoft Cloud PKI do?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn, it provides a dedicated PKI without on-premises servers, connectors or hardware, and it can replace an on-premises certification authority, NDES and the Intune certificate connector.
faq.q: Does Microsoft Cloud PKI require on-premises servers?

faq.a: A Cloud PKI add-on is needed on top of Intune Plan 1 or 2, either in the Intune Suite or as a standalone license. A tenant can hold at most three CAs, and the data residency option is not currently available.
faq.q: What licensing and limits apply to Microsoft Cloud PKI?

cloud-pki.long:
Microsoft Cloud PKI is a cloud service within Microsoft Intune that automates the certificate lifecycle for devices managed by Intune. It provides a dedicated public key infrastructure (PKI) for an organization without on-premises servers, connectors or hardware. The service issues, renews and revokes certificates on all platforms that Intune supports. It is developed by Microsoft and belongs to the group of Microsoft identity and security tools, as part of Microsoft Intune.

Certificates are used to prove the identity of a device or user in a way that does not rely on passwords. According to Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Cloud PKI covers scenarios such as VPN, Wi-Fi, email, web and device identity. A typical example is certificate-based Wi-Fi, where a managed device presents a certificate to authenticate to the network. Traditionally, such a setup required running a certification authority, NDES and the Intune certificate connector in the company's own environment. Microsoft Cloud PKI is designed to replace those components.

The structure of the service follows the usual PKI model. A two-tier hierarchy of a root certification authority (CA) and an issuing CA is created in the cloud. As an alternative, a bring-your-own-CA option links an Intune issuing CA to a private CA, for example one running on Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS). Devices receive trust profiles and SCEP profiles through Intune. A device generates a certificate signing request, so the private key never leaves the device, and receives the signed certificate in return. Intune hosts the certificate revocation list (CRL) and authority information access (AIA) endpoints, so no separate publishing infrastructure is needed on the organization's side.

For day-to-day operation, a dashboard reports the number of active, expired and revoked certificates. Role-based access control and scope tags apply, which allows administrative tasks to be delegated in the same way as for other Intune features. The documentation also lists several constraints that matter when planning a deployment. A Cloud PKI add-on is required on top of Intune Plan 1 or 2, either as part of the Intune Suite or as a standalone license. A tenant may hold at most three CAs. Trial CAs use software keys, and the data residency option is not currently available.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Cloud PKI - Simply Explained" presents the topic in plain English as part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series, hosted by Mirko Peters. The episode asks what certificate-based authentication in the cloud means, why certificates are needed, and whether Microsoft Cloud PKI can replace traditional on-premises PKI infrastructure. It walks through the building blocks involved, including certificates, certificate authorities, Intune and SCEP, and contrasts them with the effort of a classic setup. The episode points to the additional servers, reverse proxies, firewall rules, backups, patching, monitoring and specialist knowledge that an on-premises design can demand. For smaller IT teams, it says, even a relatively simple requirement such as certificate-based Wi-Fi can turn into a substantial infrastructure project.

In practice, the main decision is whether a cloud-hosted PKI meets the organization's needs or whether an existing private CA should remain in place. The bring-your-own-CA option offers a path for organizations that already operate AD CS but want Intune to handle issuing to managed devices. Licensing, the limit of three CAs per tenant and the unavailable data residency option are points to check before adopting the service. Because the service is part of Microsoft Intune, it applies to devices that are already managed there, and it is closely tied to Intune's profile-based deployment of trust and SCEP settings.

cloud-solution-provider.desc: The Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program lets Microsoft partners resell Microsoft cloud services and manage billing, support and provisioning for customers.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft partner authorization that lets partners sell Microsoft cloud services such as Microsoft 365, Azure and Dynamics 365, and manage billing, support and provisioning for their customers.
faq.q: What is the Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program?

faq.a: In the indirect model, a partner works through an authorized distributor. In the direct-bill model, Microsoft bills the partner directly, and the partner must meet stricter criteria such as prior indirect reselling experience, minimum trailing revenue and a capabilities assessment.
faq.q: What is the difference between the indirect and direct-bill CSP models?

faq.a: All CSP partners must pass business verification, repeat it every year, and keep a current partner profile in Partner Center. Customers must also accept the Microsoft Customer Agreement before ordering.
faq.q: What do all CSP partners have to do to qualify?

cloud-solution-provider.long:
The Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program is a Microsoft partner authorization that allows partners to sell Microsoft cloud services, such as Microsoft 365, Azure and Dynamics 365, to customers. Beyond the subscriptions themselves, partners in the program handle billing, support and provisioning on behalf of the customer. According to Microsoft Partner Center documentation, the authorization also covers other offers, including server software and perpetual software.

The program is organized around two models. In the indirect model, a partner works through a distributor, which sits between Microsoft and the reseller. In the direct-bill model, Microsoft bills the partner directly. Which model applies depends largely on the partner's size, maturity and operational capabilities, because the entry requirements differ considerably between the two.

The documentation lists several benefits of being a CSP partner: closer customer relationships, added revenue from deployment and support services, the ability to bundle Microsoft products with industry-specific solutions, and control over the full customer lifecycle. In practice, this means the partner is not only a seller of licenses but also the party that onboards the customer, supports daily operations and shapes the services wrapped around the Microsoft platform.

Eligibility requirements apply to all CSP partners. Every partner must pass business verification, repeat that verification every year, and keep a current partner profile in Partner Center. Indirect partners additionally need active membership in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program, a partner location account ID, the authority to accept legal agreements, and a relationship with an authorized distributor. Direct-bill partners face stricter criteria. These include a period of working as an indirect reseller, a minimum trailing revenue amount, a capabilities assessment covering billing, provisioning and support, a managed service or own solution offering, a solution partner designation, security requirements and an advanced support plan. On the customer side, the Microsoft Customer Agreement must be accepted before ordering.

Typical decisions around the program include whether an organization should buy through a CSP partner or directly from Microsoft, and, for a partner, whether to start as an indirect reseller through a distributor or to work toward direct-bill status. Because direct-bill status requires a track record as an indirect reseller and demonstrated capabilities in billing, provisioning and support, many partners follow a staged path rather than entering as direct-bill from the start.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) - Simply Explained" covers the program with a practical focus on what it is, how it works, and the decisions that matter for architecture, adoption, security, governance and day-to-day operations. The episode notes describe the program as simplifying how businesses acquire and manage Microsoft cloud solutions, and it frames CSPs as playing a role in connecting organizations with essential resources as demand for cloud services grows. The episode cites a projection that the global cloud services market will reach $722.9 billion by 2025, with a compound annual growth rate of 15.7%.

For organizations evaluating the program from the customer side, the practical questions center on which services the partner provides alongside the licenses, how support is organized, and how billing is handled. For partners, the central questions are which model fits their current capabilities, how to meet the annual business verification and profile requirements, and how to build managed services or own solutions that add value on top of the resold Microsoft products.

cmdlet.desc: A cmdlet is a single ready-made PowerShell command named with a verb-noun pattern, such as Get-MgUser, used to run one operation in a command line or script.

faq.a: A cmdlet is a single ready-made PowerShell command named with a verb-noun pattern, such as Get-MgUser. The verb describes the action and the noun names what it acts on.
faq.q: What is a cmdlet in PowerShell?

faq.a: The episode "PowerShell - Simply Explained" recommends the Get-Help cmdlet, which gives detailed information about any command. It also suggests community resources and books for further learning.
faq.q: How can I learn what a cmdlet does?

faq.a: According to the episode "Modern Microsoft 365 Automation Beyond PowerShell Scripts", scripts that rely on a removed or replaced cmdlet may break. Deprecation warnings, often seen after PowerShell updates or new module installs, signal that scripts need attention.
faq.q: What happens when a cmdlet is deprecated?

cmdlet.long:
A cmdlet is a single ready-made PowerShell command named with a verb-noun pattern, such as Get-MgUser. The verb states the action and the noun names the thing it acts on, which makes the purpose of a command readable from its name alone. Cmdlets are the basic building blocks of PowerShell, which the M365.FM episode "PowerShell - Simply Explained" describes as a cross-platform task automation solution that combines a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework.

Cmdlets are used to perform operations on systems and services from a command line or from a script. The episodes show several typical uses. In "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire", a table of PowerShell commands for license management lists Get-MgUser, which retrieves user information including assigned licenses; Set-MgUserLicense, which assigns or removes licenses for a user; and Get-MgSubscribedSku, which lists the subscribed SKUs for the tenant. The episode presents these as ways to assign, remove, and audit licenses, which helps control costs and maintain compliance. Example scenarios it gives include auditing the user base before major projects and updating licenses when employees change roles or need advanced tools.

The verb-noun pattern also helps with learning and discovery. "PowerShell - Simply Explained" recommends the Get-Help cmdlet for accessing detailed information about any command, and it points to community resources and books for deepening PowerShell knowledge. The same episode notes that PowerShell's cross-platform capabilities allow managing systems on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and that scripts can automate repetitive tasks to save time and reduce manual errors. Since cmdlets are the units those scripts are made of, knowing how to find and read them is central to that work.

Cmdlets also appear in scenarios that involve web APIs. "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" covers Invoke-RestMethod, a cmdlet that simplifies communication with the Microsoft Graph API by sending HTTP requests and receiving responses in a straightforward way. The episode lists limitations to keep in mind: Microsoft recommends requesting fewer than 120 results per call to avoid errors, and the cmdlet can return a 400 Bad Request error if a request is not well formed. This shows that a cmdlet is a convenient wrapper for an operation, while the rules of the underlying service still apply.

Cmdlets are also a point of comparison between tools. "Azure CLI vs PowerShell: Which Should You Use?" discusses Azure PowerShell, which exposes Azure operations through native PowerShell cmdlets. The episode says Azure CLI often performs faster for large, repeated resource operations because its lightweight REST calls are simpler, while Azure PowerShell can be heavier due to object serialization and cmdlet overhead. It also says Azure PowerShell benefits from PowerShell's tab completion, help, and pipeline features. Choosing between the two therefore depends on the kind of work, such as bulk operations versus interactive use.

Cmdlets can also become a maintenance concern. "Modern Microsoft 365 Automation Beyond PowerShell Scripts" lists deprecated cmdlets as a sign that scripts are becoming obsolete. When Microsoft removes or replaces a cmdlet, automation may break, and warnings about deprecated commands often appear after PowerShell updates or after installing new modules. The episode treats such warnings, together with frequent errors, as a prompt to audit scripts and update them. Regularly reviewing which cmdlets a script depends on is part of keeping automation reliable as technology changes.

cmmc.desc: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) is a US Department of Defense program that verifies whether defense contractors protect FCI and controlled unclassified information.

faq.a: Level 1 covers 14 basic practices for protecting FCI and uses an annual self-assessment. Level 2 covers 110 practices aligned with NIST SP 800-171 for protecting CUI, with third-party assessments every three years for critical programs. Level 3 adds a subset of NIST SP 800-172 requirements and involves government-led assessments every three years.
faq.q: What are the three CMMC levels?

faq.a: CMMC verifies the protection of controlled unclassified information (CUI) and federal contract information (FCI) on the systems of defense contractors.
faq.q: What information does CMMC protect?

faq.a: According to the cited source, enforcement awaits final rulemaking. It reports that the 48 CFR rule cleared review in August 2025 and that in July 2026 the Pentagon temporarily paused Phase 2 while a task force reviews the program.
faq.q: Is CMMC being enforced yet?

cmmc.long:
Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) is a US Department of Defense framework and certification program. It verifies whether defense contractors protect sensitive government information on their systems, specifically controlled unclassified information (CUI) and federal contract information (FCI). The model builds mainly on NIST SP 800-171, and some contracts add requirements drawn from NIST SP 800-172.

The program exists because contractors were previously expected to attest to their own security. According to the available sources, contractors were already self-assessing against NIST SP 800-171 after DFARS rules took effect in 2016 and 2017. The Department of Defense announced CMMC in 2019 following supply-chain breaches, with the aim of checking that protections are actually in place rather than only asserted. A streamlined version, CMMC 2.0, followed in November 2021, and a proposed rule was published in December 2023.

The model is organized into three levels. Level 1 covers 14 basic practices for protecting FCI and is verified through an annual self-assessment. Level 2 covers 110 practices aligned with NIST SP 800-171 for protecting CUI, with third-party assessments every three years for critical programs. Level 3 adds a subset of NIST SP 800-172 requirements on top of Level 2 and involves government-led assessments every three years. Which level applies depends on the type of information a contract involves, so the first decision for a contractor is determining whether it handles only FCI or also CUI.

In practice, preparing for CMMC means mapping the organization's systems and processes to the relevant practices, documenting how each one is met, and closing gaps before an assessment. For organizations that already self-assess against NIST SP 800-171, much of the groundwork overlaps with Level 2, though the move from self-attestation to third-party verification changes how evidence is expected to be presented. Contractors working in the Microsoft ecosystem typically have to consider how their cloud and endpoint services fit within the boundary of systems that store, process or transmit CUI.

The regulatory status has been moving. The sources report that the 48 CFR rule cleared review in August 2025 and that in July 2026 the Pentagon temporarily paused Phase 2, with a task force set up to review the program. Enforcement awaits final rulemaking, so the timing of when specific requirements will appear in contracts depends on how that process concludes. Organizations in the defense supply chain generally need to follow official Department of Defense communications for the current phase and applicability.

No M365.FM episodes are linked to this entry yet, and no related topics are recorded in the knowledge base at this time.

co-management.desc: Co-management is Microsoft's supported model for managing Windows devices with Configuration Manager and Microsoft Intune at once, using workload sliders to assign each management area.

faq.a: Co-management is a supported model in which a Windows device is managed by Configuration Manager and Microsoft Intune at the same time. Workload sliders determine which tool is the authority for each management area.
faq.q: What is co-management in Microsoft's terms?

faq.a: Co-management covers Windows devices only. Devices must be Microsoft Entra joined or hybrid joined, and devices that are only Microsoft Entra registered are not supported.
faq.q: Which devices does co-management support?

faq.a: Yes. Workloads such as compliance policies, Windows update policies, endpoint protection and client apps can be moved one at a time, and a workload can first be piloted with a separate device collection.
faq.q: Can workloads be moved to Intune gradually?

co-management.long:
Co-management is a Microsoft-supported model in which a Windows device is managed by Configuration Manager and Microsoft Intune at the same time. Workload sliders decide which of the two tools acts as the authority for each management area. According to Microsoft Learn, the approach lets organizations keep their existing Configuration Manager investment while still using cloud capabilities, such as conditional access based on device compliance.

The central idea is that management responsibility does not have to move from on-premises to the cloud in a single step. Workloads can be shifted to Intune one at a time or gradually. The workloads named in the documentation are compliance policies, Windows update policies, resource access policies, endpoint protection, device configuration, Office Click-to-Run apps and client apps. Anything that has not been switched to Intune stays with Configuration Manager, and the same applies to any feature that co-management does not support. This split makes it possible to adopt cloud management area by area instead of replacing a whole management stack at once.

A workload can first be piloted before it is applied broadly. The documentation describes using a separate device collection for this purpose, so that only a defined group of devices is affected while the change is tested. A dashboard helps monitor co-managed devices, giving administrators a view of how the devices are enrolled and which tool manages them.

How a device reaches co-management depends on its starting point. Existing Configuration Manager clients get there through hybrid Microsoft Entra join and Intune enrollment. New internet-based devices join Microsoft Entra ID, enroll in Intune automatically and receive the Configuration Manager client. In both cases the device ends up with both management agents.

There are several requirements to plan for. The documentation lists Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licensing, an Intune license for the administrator, a supported Current Branch version of Configuration Manager, and devices that are either Microsoft Entra joined or hybrid joined. Devices that are only Microsoft Entra registered are not supported. Co-management also covers Windows devices only, so other platforms are outside its scope.

Typical decisions around co-management include which workloads to move first, how large a pilot collection should be, and whether the remaining features that depend on Configuration Manager justify keeping those workloads on-premises for now. These choices tie directly into the broader question of how Configuration Manager and Intune relate to each other.

That relationship is the subject of the M365.FM episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained". According to its description, the episode compares the two platforms across software deployment, operating system management, patching, compliance, device provisioning, remote management and Windows Autopilot. Co-management is one of the topics it covers, alongside the contrast between cloud and on-premises administration. The episode also explains why Microsoft continues to invest in Intune while Configuration Manager remains an important solution for many enterprise environments, which is the situation co-management is designed to address.

code-review.desc: Code review is a software quality practice in which people other than the author examine source code changes, typically pull requests, before merging.

faq.a: Code review is a software quality practice in which people other than the author examine source code changes, typically pull requests, before they are merged.
faq.q: What is code review?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes say AI tools can introduce bugs and vulnerabilities, and they recommend rigorous code review to identify vulnerabilities in AI-generated code before deployment.
faq.q: Why does code review matter for AI-generated code?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" recommends a code review process for DAX, M and report changes before merging.
faq.q: Does code review apply to Power BI work?

code-review.long:
Code review is a software quality practice in which people other than the author examine source code changes before those changes are merged. In most modern workflows the unit under review is a pull request: a proposed set of changes that a reviewer reads, comments on and approves or sends back. The practice exists to catch defects, security weaknesses and maintainability problems early, and to keep a second pair of eyes on every change that enters a shared codebase.

In practice, code review sits between writing a change and integrating it. The author prepares the change, reviewers inspect it, and only after approval does it reach the main branch. This position makes it a natural control point in a CI/CD pipeline. The M365.FM episode "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" lists code review and approval processes among the recommended governance policies for CI-CD, with the stated aim of ensuring that all code changes undergo thorough reviews to maintain quality and security. In that episode it appears alongside role-based access control, compliance and security monitoring, automated testing and validation, and metrics and reporting, which shows how review is treated as one policy among several rather than a standalone step.

The topic also appears in the context of Microsoft analytics work. The episode "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" includes in its checklist the establishment of a code review process for DAX, M and report changes before merging. The same checklist covers versioning PBIX files with meaningful commit messages and release tags, promoting artifacts across Dev, Test and Prod through deployment pipelines or CI/CD processes, defining testing procedures such as unit tests for measures, data validation and visual QA, and creating rollback plans. Here code review is applied not only to traditional application code but to the query and measure logic that drives reports and datasets.

A further theme in the episodes is review of AI-generated code. The episode "Connect Copilot Studio to Word Policy Files" describes AI as a high-speed drafting assistant and contains a section on code review for AI-generated code. It warns that AI tools can introduce bugs and vulnerabilities and stresses awareness of common oversights so that software quality is maintained. The episode "Govern Power Apps Generative Pages After Edit Code" makes a related point for low-code environments: it recommends rigorous code review processes to identify vulnerabilities in AI-generated code before deployment, alongside governance frameworks, user training, and continuous monitoring. It names security issues such as prompt injection as one of the risks that make this scrutiny necessary.

The episode "Use GitHub Copilot Agent Mode for Multi-File Changes" addresses the same concern from the tooling side. It describes an agent that holds cross-file context and applies coordinated changes across services, bindings, dependency injection, configuration and infrastructure, presenting a before/after diff. The episode frames this as working without losing code review or CI rigor, and says the agents do not replace developers. In other words, faster generation of changes increases rather than removes the need for a human review step before merging.

Taken together, the episodes treat code review as a stable control that applies across different kinds of artifacts: application code, Power BI datasets and reports, low-code generated pages, and output from AI assistants. Typical decisions around it include which changes require review, who is authorized to approve them, how review connects to automated testing and deployment pipelines, and how much additional scrutiny AI-generated changes should receive. Review complements, rather than replaces, automated checks and governance policies.

coe-starter-kit.desc: The Power Platform CoE Starter Kit is a Microsoft toolkit that gathers inventory data on Power Platform environments, apps and flows to support governance.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft reference implementation of components and solutions for governing, monitoring and driving adoption of Power Platform. It is built on Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI, Dataverse and Copilot Studio and collects resource information from tenant environments.
faq.q: What is the Power Platform CoE Starter Kit?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Learn overview, it is no longer actively maintained and issues are not reviewed. The page adds that its core capabilities now exist in the Power Platform admin center.
faq.q: Is the CoE Starter Kit still maintained?

faq.a: The documentation names Admin for usage insight, Govern for audit and compliance processes such as inactivity notices and a DLP editor, and Nurture for community building.
faq.q: What areas does the CoE Starter Kit cover?

coe-starter-kit.long:
The Power Platform CoE Starter Kit is a Microsoft toolkit for Centers of Excellence that work with Power Platform. It is a reference implementation made of components and solutions for governing, monitoring and driving adoption of Power Platform using native low-code tools. The kit is part of the wider Power Platform topic and is aimed at organizations that want visibility into what makers are building across their tenant.

Technically, the CoE Starter Kit is built on Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI, Dataverse and Copilot Studio. It uses a Dataverse data model and workflows that collect resource information from the environments in a tenant, such as environments, apps and flows. On top of that inventory, the kit provides several apps and Power BI reports, templates and practices for typical CoE tasks, and automation for monitoring. It is distributed as sample code from a GitHub repository, which means it may need adaptation to fit a specific organization.

The kit is organized into areas. Admin focuses on usage insight. Govern covers audit and compliance processes, including inactivity notices and a DLP editor. Nurture supports community building among makers. Typical uses described in the documentation include reviewing resources and makers in a dashboard and reassigning orphaned apps, so that applications whose owners have left do not remain without responsibility.

The M365.FM episode "Govern Power Platform Environments Instead of Disabling Them" presents the kit as tooling, templates and governance practices for governing Power Platform at scale. It associates the kit with governance controls, environment strategy, monitoring, app lifecycle management and adoption strategy, and says that using it accelerates a governance strategy. The episode frames governance as a way to support compliance with security standards and to scale low-code solutions while letting citizen developers deliver value without creating shadow IT or data governance issues, rather than disabling environments.

The episode "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" mentions the kit in a different setting. There it appears among governance essentials for AI-powered apps, next to cost tags, budgets and alerts, and audits. The episode lists these as guardrails meant to keep performance predictable and compliant when moving AI features from demo to production.

An important caveat applies to anyone evaluating the kit today. The Microsoft Learn overview states that the CoE Starter Kit is no longer actively maintained and that issues are not reviewed. The same page says its core capabilities now exist in the Power Platform admin center. The episode description in the knowledge base likewise characterizes the kit as no longer receiving updates. Because of this, teams typically weigh the kit's inventory and reporting content against the capabilities available in the admin center before building on it.

The documentation also makes clear that the kit does not replace a real CoE. A Center of Excellence consists of people and processes, and the kit only supplies sample tooling to support them. Decisions around it therefore usually concern which governance tasks need custom inventory or reporting, how orphaned resources and inactive apps are handled, and who in the organization owns those processes.

cognitive-load.desc: Cognitive load is the mental effort a task places on working memory; theory splits it into intrinsic, extraneous and germane load, a lens used in platform engineering.

faq.a: Cognitive load theory distinguishes intrinsic load (the inherent difficulty of a task), extraneous load (demands added by how the task is presented or surrounded) and germane load (effort spent building understanding).
faq.q: What are the three types of cognitive load?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes say that platform engineering, including paved-road architectures and self-service solutions, reduces the cognitive load on development teams by centralizing infrastructure and tooling responsibility.
faq.q: How does platform engineering relate to cognitive load?

faq.a: The episode "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs" says organizations producing more code with AI also experience higher cognitive load, because the bottleneck moves to reviewing, validating, governing and understanding that code.
faq.q: Can AI-generated code increase cognitive load?

cognitive-load.long:
Cognitive load is the mental effort that a task places on working memory. Cognitive load theory distinguishes three kinds of load: intrinsic load, which comes from the inherent difficulty of the material or task; extraneous load, which comes from how the task is presented or surrounded by unrelated demands; and germane load, which relates to the effort of building understanding. The idea matters wherever people must hold many concepts in mind at once, and the M365.FM episodes apply it mainly to software engineering, platform design and information management in the Microsoft ecosystem.

The concept is used to explain why work feels heavy even when each individual step is manageable. When a person must keep too many concepts, tools and decisions active at the same time, less capacity remains for the actual goal. Practical decisions around cognitive load therefore tend to focus on removing avoidable demands, such as repeated infrastructure choices or time spent searching for documents, so that attention stays on problem-solving and business functionality.

In the episode "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure", cognitive load appears as a design argument for platform engineering. The episode explains how platform engineering differs from traditional DevOps and why paved-road architectures reduce cognitive load for development teams. It also states that strong governance can coexist with innovation, and that the platform itself should be treated as a product that keeps evolving to meet customer needs. The related episode "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained" lists reducing the cognitive load on developers as one of the benefits of the approach. It names centralization of responsibility for infrastructure and tools and self-service solutions among the key components, with the stated aims of consistency, scalability and fewer delays.

The episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" treats cognitive load as a central theme and calls it a crisis. According to the episode, developers already need to understand complex business domains, and adding infrastructure decisions on top dramatically increases the mental effort required before any business logic is written. The presentation introduces a concept called Concepts to Ship (CTS) and notes that a traditional DevOps environment often requires developers to handle many such concepts. The episode argues that developers end up spending more time coordinating infrastructure than delivering business functionality, and that organizations eventually stop managing infrastructure and begin managing organizational chaos.

A different angle comes from "The Productivity Illusion: Why AI is Breaking Your Engineering KPIs". The episode says that AI has shifted bottlenecks from writing code to reviewing, validating, governing and understanding it. It reports that organizations produce significantly more code while also experiencing more incidents, higher cognitive load, greater technical debt and increased developer burnout. Its central message is that more code does not automatically mean more productivity, and that output is easily confused with value. In this framing, cognitive load is one of the measures that output-based KPIs fail to capture.

The concept also surfaces in information architecture. In "Microsoft Graph Architecture Beyond Folders and Hierarchies", the episode says that adopting a graph-based approach and reducing cognitive load lets people concentrate on creativity and problem-solving instead of searching for documents. Proactive information delivery is described as anticipating needs, saving time and keeping people focused on their goals.

Across these episodes the pattern is consistent: cognitive load is treated as a practical constraint on teams, not only a psychological term. Platform engineering, paved roads, self-service tooling and graph-based information access are presented as ways to lower the demands placed on individuals, while the AI-productivity episode warns that increased output can raise the load through review and validation work.

cold-start.desc: Cold start is the extra delay a serverless platform adds when it has scaled to zero and must rebuild the environment before handling the next request.

faq.a: A cold start is the extra delay that occurs when a serverless platform has scaled down to zero and must rebuild the environment before it can handle the next request. The first request after inactivity is slower than requests served by an already running instance.
faq.q: What is a cold start in serverless computing?

faq.a: The episode "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions" says the 'always ready' feature of the Flex Consumption model reduces cold start delays by keeping instances active. "Azure Automation - Simply Explained" adds that Azure Functions aims to mitigate the issue by preemptively creating instances.
faq.q: How can cold start delays be reduced in Azure Functions?

faq.a: No. In "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search", the cold start problem means it is hard to search for new items that lack good vector representations. It is a data issue, not the scale-to-zero latency of serverless platforms.
faq.q: Is the cold start problem in vector search the same thing?

cold-start.long:
Cold start is the additional delay that occurs when a serverless platform has scaled an application down to zero and must rebuild the runtime environment before it can process the next incoming request. The first call after a period of inactivity therefore takes longer than calls that reach an instance that is already running. The term is used most often in connection with serverless compute offerings such as Azure Functions, and it matters wherever response time is part of the user experience.

The concept follows from how serverless scaling works. When no requests arrive, the platform can release instances so that nothing is running and, in the usual serverless model, nothing is being consumed. When a new request comes in, an instance has to be provisioned and prepared again. That preparation time is what users and developers perceive as the cold start. The effect is most visible for workloads with sporadic or bursty traffic, where instances are often scaled back to zero between uses.

Several M365.FM episodes touch on the topic from different angles. In "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions", the discussion centers on the Flex Consumption model. The episode lists features that help plugins handle larger workloads without slowdowns: scaling each function individually, choosing different instance sizes, and setting how many requests each instance handles. It says the 'always ready' feature reduces cold start delays by keeping instances active. The episode also notes that lower concurrency means more instances, which helps an app scale quickly when needed, and that enabling VNet injection adds very little delay, about 37 milliseconds at the 50th percentile.

The episode "Azure Automation - Simply Explained" compares serverless offerings from different providers. It describes AWS Lambda as known for delays during function execution, commonly referred to as the 'cold start' problem, and says Azure Functions aims to mitigate this by preemptively creating instances, resulting in faster execution times. The same episode adds that Azure Functions requires careful configuration for optimal scaling, especially in distributed environments, so reducing cold start effects is presented as something that depends on setup choices as well as platform behavior.

In "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures", cold start appears as part of performance troubleshooting. When requests are slow, the episode suggests using Application Insights to trace slow requests and Azure Monitor to check CPU and memory usage, then scaling out or in or moving to a higher App Service plan. It advises investigating dependencies, code-level exceptions, and cold start impacts for serverless scenarios. In that framing, cold start is one candidate cause to rule in or out, alongside network limits and application code inefficiencies.

A different use of the phrase appears in "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search". There, 'the cold start problem' refers to the difficulty of searching for new items that lack good vector representations. This is the cold start of recommendation and search systems and is unrelated to serverless scale-to-zero latency, even though the two share a name. Readers searching for the term should keep the two meanings apart: the serverless meaning concerns infrastructure that must be rebuilt after scaling down, while the search meaning concerns missing data for new items.

Typical decisions around the serverless cold start include whether to keep instances warm, how finely to scale individual functions, how many requests each instance should handle, and whether networking features such as VNet injection add acceptable overhead. The episodes frame these as trade-offs between responsiveness and the benefits of scaling down, and they point to monitoring tools as the way to confirm whether cold starts are actually the source of observed latency.

command-line-interface.desc: A command-line interface (CLI) lets users control software by typing text commands in a terminal, favoring precision, scripting and repeatability over discoverability.

faq.a: A CLI lets users interact with software by typing text commands in a terminal. It favors precision, scripting and repeatability over the discoverability of a graphical interface.
faq.q: What is a command-line interface (CLI)?

faq.a: The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" describes the Azure CLI as a tool for managing Azure resources, with commands such as azd init, azd auth login, azd up, azd show and azd down. It links this workflow to configuration files like azure.yaml and the infra folder to make deployments repeatable.
faq.q: How is the CLI used with Azure according to the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Copilot with PowerShell" says PowerShell cmdlets return .NET objects, so data can be manipulated and processed more effectively than with plain text output.
faq.q: What distinguishes the PowerShell command line from other scripting tools?

command-line-interface.long:
A command-line interface (CLI) is a way of interacting with software by typing text commands into a terminal instead of clicking through a graphical interface. Compared with a graphical tool, a CLI trades discoverability for precision, scripting and repeatability: a user has to know or look up the commands, but once a command is known it can be run the same way every time and combined into scripts.

The M365.FM episodes describe the CLI mainly as a working tool for developers and administrators. The episode "Stop Environment Drift with VS Code Dev Containers" presents CLI tools as indispensable for developers who want efficiency and automation in their workflows. According to the episode, these tools let developers interact with their systems and applications directly and bypass graphical interfaces for tasks such as building, testing and deploying software. The episode also says that using CLI tools allows developers to execute commands and scripts to carry out these tasks, which ties the CLI to automation rather than to one-off manual work.

The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" places the CLI in the context of Azure. It describes the Azure Command-Line Interface as an essential tool for managing Azure resources and names a consistent workflow built from commands such as azd init, azd auth login, azd up, azd show and azd down. The episode says this workflow supports Infrastructure as Code through configuration files like azure.yaml and the infra folder, and that with the Azure CLI a team can move from one-off deployments to repeatable workflows. In the same episode, Bicep is described separately as a declarative syntax for defining which Azure resources are required without detailing how they are created. The CLI is the tool used to run and manage such definitions, while Bicep expresses the desired state.

The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Copilot with PowerShell" covers the CLI aspect of PowerShell. It says the command-line interface of PowerShell lets users interact with a system in a powerful way and run commands quickly, which makes managing resources easier. It highlights the object-oriented nature of PowerShell: cmdlets return .NET objects rather than plain text, so data can be manipulated more effectively and processed in more complex ways. The episode frames this as useful for both local systems and complex environments such as Microsoft 365.

Taken together, the episodes show typical situations in which a CLI is chosen over a graphical interface. One is repeatable deployment, where the same sequence of commands recreates an environment reliably. Another is automation, where commands are embedded in scripts and run without manual interaction. A third is administration at scale, where text commands and returned objects can be combined, filtered and processed. The decision to use a CLI usually rests on how much repeatability and precision a task needs versus how important it is that the options are easy to discover on screen.

The related Microsoft ecosystem topics that appear in the episodes include Azure, Bicep, PowerShell, Microsoft 365, VS Code Dev Containers and Infrastructure as Code. Across them, the CLI acts as the common layer through which commands, scripts and configuration files are applied to real systems. The sources do not go into further detail about specific syntax, installation or platform support, so this entry limits itself to the role the CLI plays in the workflows the episodes describe.

communication-compliance.desc: Communication Compliance is a Microsoft Purview capability for detecting risky or inappropriate messages across Teams, Outlook, Viva Engage and Copilot.

faq.a: It is a Purview capability that detects risky, inappropriate or non-compliant communication across channels such as Teams chats, Outlook emails, Viva Engage and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Administrators use policies to find such content and review it.
faq.q: What is Communication Compliance in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", policies can detect risks and regulatory violations in Copilot chats, including inappropriate content and leaks of confidential data. Admins can monitor conversations and take action when issues are found.
faq.q: Does Communication Compliance cover Copilot interactions?

faq.a: It is listed alongside Insider Risk Management, Data Loss Prevention, eDiscovery, Audit and Data Lifecycle Management as part of the Purview portfolio. The episodes describe these as complementary controls, with Communication Compliance focused on the content of communications.
faq.q: How does Communication Compliance relate to other Purview features?

communication-compliance.long:
Communication Compliance is a compliance capability within Microsoft Purview that helps organizations detect and review risky, inappropriate or non-compliant messages across digital communication channels. Modern business communication goes well beyond email: employees collaborate through Microsoft Teams chats, Outlook emails, Viva Engage, Microsoft 365 Copilot and other platforms every day. These tools support productivity, but they also create exposure to workplace misconduct, regulatory violations, leaks of sensitive information, insider threats and inappropriate communication. Communication Compliance addresses this by letting administrators define policies that scan messages for such issues and surface them for review.

The episodes describe the capability mainly in terms of policy-based detection and follow-up. Organizations create policies to identify risks and regulatory violations in communications, including the prompts and responses exchanged with Copilot. According to the episode "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", Communication Compliance can scan Copilot chats for inappropriate content or leaks of confidential data, and administrators can monitor conversations and act when they find problems. The same episode advises reviewing compliance policies often and updating them as regulations change, so that protection keeps pace with new requirements.

Communication Compliance is one component of a broader set of Purview features. The episode "Microsoft Purview - Simply Explained" lists it alongside Data Loss Prevention (DLP), Sensitivity Labels, Information Protection, Data Lifecycle Management, eDiscovery, Audit, Insider Risk Management, Compliance Manager and Data Governance. Together these capabilities classify sensitive information, protect business data across Microsoft 365, Azure and third-party environments, and help organizations meet compliance requirements without slowing down productivity. Communication Compliance covers the conversational side of that picture, while neighbouring features handle data handling rules, retention, discovery and user-risk signals.

The relationship to Insider Risk Management is a recurring theme. Both address behavioural and conduct-related risk, and the episode "Automate Microsoft 365 Compliance Tasks with Power Automate" names both among the compliance areas that can be automated with Power Automate. For Communication Compliance specifically, that episode mentions setting up alerts and notifications for policy enforcement. This points to a typical operating pattern: detection by policy, followed by notification and a defined response process rather than purely manual checking.

In the context of AI oversight, the episode "Azure Copilot Agents: Building a Synthetic Platform Team" lists Communication Compliance among the tools used to monitor and audit AI operations responsibly. It appears there together with Purview Audit Logs, DSPM for AI, Insider Risk Management, eDiscovery, Data Lifecycle Management, Microsoft Sentinel and other monitoring and detection tools. The point made is that responsible oversight of AI relies on several complementary controls, with Communication Compliance contributing visibility into what is said in AI-assisted conversations.

The episode "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained", part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series hosted by Mirko Peters, is the dedicated introduction to the topic. It frames the capability against the shift from email-centric communication to multi-channel collaboration and the new risks that shift brings, including regulatory compliance and sensitive information handling. Typical decisions around the capability include which channels to cover, which risk categories to define in policies, who reviews flagged items, and how policies are kept current as regulations and workplace practices change. The sources provided do not give licensing details, configuration steps or version information, so those points should be checked against official Microsoft documentation.

compliance.desc: Compliance means meeting legal, regulatory and internal requirements, such as data protection and records retention, and how M365.FM episodes cover it in Microsoft 365.

faq.a: It means meeting legal, regulatory and internal requirements, for example for data protection and records retention. In Microsoft 365 this shows up as policies for communication, retention, auditing and sensitive information.
faq.q: What does compliance mean in Microsoft 365?

faq.a: Microsoft Purview is the portfolio where many compliance controls are configured, and the GDPR is one of the main regulations organizations in Europe must observe when processing personal data. Compliance itself falls under the broader topic of Governance.
faq.q: How is compliance related to Microsoft Purview and the GDPR?

faq.a: The episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" argues against treating compliance as a documentation exercise before audits. It calls for embedding compliance in daily operations through automated, architecture-driven trust.
faq.q: What does "Compliance as Code" mean according to the episodes?

compliance.long:
Compliance is the practice of meeting legal, regulatory and internal requirements, for example for data protection and records retention. In a Microsoft 365 context it is not a single feature but a set of policies and controls covering communication, retention, auditing and sensitive information. The goal is that the handling of data can be demonstrated to auditors, regulators and internal stakeholders, rather than merely intended. The topic is also referred to as AI compliance or compliance reporting, depending on the angle taken.

Compliance sits under the broader topic of Governance, which describes how an organization sets rules and ensures they are followed. It is closely related to Microsoft Purview, the portfolio where many compliance controls are configured, and to the GDPR, one of the main regulations that organizations in Europe must observe when processing personal data. Together these three links show how a legal requirement (GDPR), a management discipline (Governance) and a tooling layer (Microsoft Purview) connect in practice.

The M365.FM episode "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" describes why this matters beyond classic email. Employees collaborate through Microsoft Teams chats, Outlook emails, Viva Engage, Microsoft 365 Copilot and other digital communication platforms every day. According to the episode, these tools improve productivity but also create new risks involving workplace misconduct, regulatory compliance, sensitive information, insider threats and inappropriate communication. The episode, part of the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets format, explains how communication compliance addresses these risks.

A different perspective comes from "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust". The episode challenges the common view of compliance as a documentation exercise that organizations prepare for audits instead of embedding it in daily operations. It argues that modern enterprises should shift from manual governance to automated, architecture-driven trust, treating compliance as something designed into systems rather than assembled afterwards.

The episode "Turn Microsoft 365 Compliance into Competitive Advantage" looks at strategy. It explains why traditional governance approaches fail at scale and why embedding compliance directly into Microsoft 365 workflows is key to enabling productivity, reducing risk and supporting AI-driven tools like Copilot. In this framing, governance becomes a business enabler instead of a blocker.

Automation is a recurring theme. "Automate Compliance Workflows with Microsoft Power Automate" treats compliance processes as work that is often handled manually, which makes it slow, repetitive and prone to human error. The episode explores how Power Automate can turn manual approvals, documentation checks and policy enforcement into automated, traceable workflows, replacing reliance on spreadsheets, emails and ticket queues.

Compliance also appears in infrastructure design. "Azure Governance Architecture to Control Cost, Security, and Compliance" argues that knowing how to provision Azure services is no longer enough and that the real value lies in governance architecture. This means designing systems that prevent erosion between intended policy and actual state, so that environments stay secure, compliant and cost-efficient as they scale.

Taken together, the episodes describe compliance as a mix of policy, tooling and architecture. Typical decisions include which communication channels to monitor, how to enforce rules automatically instead of through manual review, and how to align controls with regulations such as the GDPR while keeping day-to-day work productive.

compliance-as-code.desc: Compliance as code expresses compliance requirements as machine-readable, version-controlled and tested code that is enforced automatically, so drift is found and fixed continuously.

faq.a: It is the practice of expressing compliance requirements and controls as machine-readable code that is version-controlled, tested and enforced automatically. This allows drift to be detected and remediated continuously instead of through manual reviews.
faq.q: What is compliance as code?

faq.a: Traditional compliance is often a documentation exercise prepared for audits. Compliance as code builds controls into the architecture and daily operations so that trust is verifiable and automated, as the M365.FM episode on the topic describes.
faq.q: How does compliance as code differ from traditional compliance work?

faq.a: The main episode is "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust". Related episodes such as "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" and "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" list it among suggested related listening.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover compliance as code?

compliance-as-code.long:
Compliance as code is the practice of expressing compliance requirements and controls as machine-readable code. Instead of describing a control in a document and checking it by hand, the control is written in a form that can be stored in version control, tested like other code and enforced automatically. The aim is that drift from the required state is detected and remediated continuously, rather than being discovered during periodic manual reviews.

The approach responds to a common pattern in which compliance is treated as a documentation exercise: material is prepared for an audit and then set aside until the next one. Compliance as code moves in the opposite direction. Requirements become part of the architecture and of daily operations, so that the evidence of a control is a by-product of how a system is built and run. The M365.FM episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" frames this as a shift from manual governance to automated, architecture-driven trust, and describes the goal as systems that are verifiable, auditable and trusted by design.

The core ideas can be summarised from the description of the practice. First, controls are machine-readable, which means a tool can evaluate them without a person interpreting prose. Second, they are version-controlled, so every change to a requirement has a history and can be reviewed, in the same way as application or infrastructure code. Third, they are tested, so the rules themselves are validated before they are relied on. Fourth, they are enforced automatically, so that a deviation does not depend on someone noticing it. Together these elements allow drift to be treated as an ongoing signal and not as a finding at audit time.

In practice, the topic sits next to other code-driven disciplines. The related episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" covers describing infrastructure in code, and its show notes list the compliance episode among related listening, as do notes for "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint", which deals with governance at scale in delivery pipelines. The episode "From AI Hype to AI Harness Engineering – Building AI That People Can Actually Trust with Alan Buscaglia [MVP] from Gentleman Programming" also lists the compliance episode among related M365.FM material, in a discussion centred on trust in AI. These connections suggest where the practice tends to appear: in infrastructure definitions, delivery pipelines and platform engineering, where rules can be checked as part of the normal flow of change.

Typical decisions around compliance as code concern where to start and how far to automate. Teams usually weigh which requirements are clear enough to be expressed as testable rules, how the rules are versioned and reviewed, and how a detected deviation is handled, whether by alerting, blocking a change or remediating it automatically. The sources provided here do not specify particular tools, standards or Microsoft services, so those choices depend on the environment and are not prescribed by the facts available.

The M365.FM episode on this topic is aimed at an architectural audience. Its stated argument is that, in the era of cloud computing and AI, automated governance becomes essential, and that the future of compliance lies less in more documentation and more in better architecture. Other episodes in the catalogue that reference it, including those on platform engineering and governance, treat it as a building block for making governance repeatable and scalable rather than dependent on individual reviewers.

compliance-manager.desc: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager is a Microsoft Purview solution that assesses compliance across cloud services using assessments, templates and a compliance score.

faq.a: It is a solution in Microsoft Purview that helps organizations assess and manage compliance across cloud services. It uses assessments, regulatory templates, improvement actions and a risk-weighted compliance score.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager - Simply Explained", it turns the question of whether a company is compliant into a single number that can be watched as it changes. The score is risk-weighted and moves as improvement actions are completed.
faq.q: What does the compliance score show?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards" argues that it is not, because configuration drift can occur over time.
