According to that summary, the service supports data-in-transit encryption for the data plane, and this is enabled by default with Microsoft as the responsible party. The same summary lists Azure AD authentication for data plane access as supported but not enabled by default, with the configuration responsibility on the customer side. This shows a common pattern: some data plane protections are provided by the platform, while others must be switched on and configured by the customer.

The term also shows up in streaming and IoT designs. The episode "IoT Hub Message Routing vs Event Grid — Why Telemetry and Events Are Not the Same Problem" describes Azure IoT Hub Message Routing as part of a telemetry data plane. The episode contrasts this with Azure Event Grid, which fits event-driven and reactive architectures. It argues that machine telemetry and discrete business or lifecycle events call for different patterns, that message ordering matters for manufacturing telemetry, and that Event Grid should not become the primary high-volume telemetry bus. It also says IoT Hub routing should not be forced into every notification workflow, and that the two services can work together in the same architecture.

In manufacturing and edge scenarios, the episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" refers to Microsoft's edge data plane pattern. In this pattern, modular services run on Arc-enabled Kubernetes together with Azure IoT Operations and Microsoft Fabric. The episode also discusses the boundary between the control plane and the data plane, stating that local control loops must remain independent of the cloud and that a broker is never a safety controller. It notes that a production-ready deployment of this pattern requires hybrid IT/OT skills.

A further use of the term appears in analytics. The episode "Your Machine Data Never Becomes a Decision. Here's the Missing Pipeline." describes Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric as a common data plane for ingestion, event shaping and time-series query with the KQL database, built for investigation while data is moving. Eventstream handles basic shaping, transformation and routing of streaming sources to multiple destinations, and Activator watches defined conditions across streams, dashboards or KQL results and triggers defined actions.

Taken together, the episodes use data plane to mean the path where operational traffic and data actually flow, whether that is encrypted Event Hubs traffic, routed IoT telemetry, edge messaging or real-time analytics. Decisions around it usually concern placement, authentication, encryption, and keeping the data plane separate from the control plane that governs it.

data-product.desc: A data product is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case with owners and a business description.

faq.a: It is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case. It also has owners and a business description so others can discover it and request access.
faq.q: What does a data product contain?

faq.a: They are created and managed in the Unified Catalog, within governance domains. The episode on Purview Data Governance says data product owners are assigned and users receive Unified Catalog reader permissions to view and explore them.
faq.q: Where are data products managed in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: Episodes on Fabric recommend one workspace per data product unless specific constraints justify otherwise. They describe this as moderate isolation, with multiple workspaces and strict separation of duties for high isolation.
faq.q: How do data products relate to Microsoft Fabric workspaces?

data-product.long:
A data product is a bundle of related data assets, such as tables, files and Power BI reports, packaged for a defined use case. It carries named owners and a business description, so that other people in an organization can discover it and request access to it. The idea shifts attention from individual technical objects to a collection that is organized around a business purpose and presented in terms that business users can understand.

The concept is closely tied to the Unified Catalog in Microsoft Purview, and the official documentation describes how data products are created and managed there. According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Data Map - Simply Explained", the Unified Catalog offers a more business-oriented discovery experience in which users can search for understandable data products rather than relying exclusively on technical names. In that setting, a data product acts as the unit that people look for, evaluate and ask to use.

The same episode gives an illustrative example. Finance could publish a pricing analytics data product that contains relevant source information, cleaned data in Microsoft Fabric, and the approved reporting assets used for monthly analysis. Instead of employees hunting through folders and asking colleagues which spreadsheet is correct, the data product gathers the relevant assets in one place and presents them with a description and responsible owners. This is what makes the packaging useful: the owners and the business description tell consumers what the data is for and who stands behind it.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" describes the roles and steps needed to set data products up. Users are assigned the governance domain creator role, which allows them to build governance domains. At least one governance domain is created and a governance domain owner is assigned. Data product owners are then assigned, and at least one data product is created within the governance domains. To let others explore the results, users are given Unified Catalog reader permissions, which allows them to view and explore data products within the governance domain. The episode also notes that a unified catalog helps consolidate five catalogs into one, and it lists better scale, higher adoption and faster time-to-insight among the benefits.

Data products also appear as an organizing principle in Microsoft Fabric guidance. The episode "Fix Wrong Copilot Numbers in Microsoft Fabric" recommends using one workspace per data product unless specific constraints justify otherwise. It pairs this with documenting the default pattern and approved exceptions, and with educating teams on the intent of governance, not just the rules. Similarly, "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" says that one workspace per data product gives moderate isolation, while multiple workspaces with strict separation of duties give high isolation, and that data products should be consolidated only when necessary.

In practice, decisions around a data product concern its scope, its ownership and its boundaries. Teams decide which related assets belong together for a use case, who is accountable as owner, and how the product is described so that it can be found. They also decide how it maps to Fabric workspaces and how much isolation sensitive workloads require. Taken together, the sources treat a data product as both a discovery unit in the Unified Catalog and a structuring unit for governance and workspace design.

data-provenance.desc: Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations, used to validate and audit where data came from and how it changed.

faq.a: Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations. It is used to validate and audit where data came from and how it changed.
faq.q: What is data provenance?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, lineage supports governance by making it easier to track data provenance. Weak metadata and missing lineage obscure provenance and make audits and impact analysis slower.
faq.q: How does data provenance relate to data lineage?

faq.a: The episode on auditable ESG compliance recommends documenting every data input, transformation and output so that clear audit evidence exists for verification.
faq.q: Why is data provenance important for audits?

data-provenance.long:
Data provenance is the documented history of a data asset's origin, custody and transformations. It records where data came from, who held it, and what was done to it along the way. The main purpose is to make data verifiable: when a figure, a report or a training dataset is questioned, provenance makes it possible to trace it back to its source and to check how it reached its current form. This is why the concept appears so often in discussions of audits, compliance and governance.

In practice, data provenance is rarely handled as a standalone feature. It is usually described together with related governance capabilities such as metadata management and data lineage. The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" lists data lineage tracking among OneLake's governance capabilities and states that it helps teams understand data provenance for audits. The same list includes data discovery and classification, which automatically identify and label sensitive data, and access control management with fine-grained permissions. In that framing, provenance is one element of a broader approach in which governance is managed centrally across tenants, domains and workspaces.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" connects the two ideas directly. It says that lineage supports data governance by making it easier to enforce policies and track data provenance. Combined with access controls in the data platform and Azure, lineage helps ensure that sensitive data is handled correctly and that audit trails can be tied back to specific Fabric items and processes. The same episode also points to common limitations of lineage across Fabric, such as incomplete metadata for certain sources, and discusses how these gaps can be mitigated. Provenance information is only as complete as the metadata and lineage that feed it.

Provenance also matters for compliance programs. The episode "Turn Microsoft 365 Compliance into Competitive Advantage" lists ineffective metadata and data lineage as a common pitfall. According to the episode, weak metadata management and missing lineage obscure data provenance, which makes risk assessments, audits and impact analysis slow and error-prone. The practical lesson is that provenance has to be captured as data is created and changed, because reconstructing it afterwards is difficult.

In reporting contexts, provenance is tied to audit evidence. The episode "Design an End-to-End Auditable ESG Compliance Stack" answers the question of how to create an audit trail for ESG data by recommending systems that track data provenance. It states that every data input, transformation and output should be documented, which gives auditors clear evidence for verification. The episode also describes an evidence vault that centralizes ESG data for secure storage and easy retrieval, supporting data governance and providing an audit trail for sustainability reporting.

AI governance is a further area where provenance appears. The episode "Control Rogue AI Data Risks with Microsoft Purview" includes, among its recommended controls, maintaining an approved training dataset registry and ensuring that training data provenance is captured in Purview. It also mentions using Purview metadata and lineage to support investigations, which shows the same pattern: provenance and lineage are used to support accountability and auditability when data feeds AI agents or models.

Taken together, the episodes treat data provenance as a basis for trust in data. It supports audits, impact analysis, investigations and policy enforcement, and it depends on consistent metadata, lineage tracking and documentation of each transformation step. Typical decisions around it include which platform capabilities will record lineage, which sources lack sufficient metadata, and how provenance evidence is stored for later review.

data-quality.desc: Data quality describes how complete, consistent, accurate, fresh and unique data is; in Microsoft Purview it is measured with rules and scores from columns to domains.

faq.a: Data quality covers how complete, consistent, accurate, fresh and unique data is. Each dimension addresses a different kind of defect, such as missing values, conflicting representations, outdated records or duplicates.
faq.q: What dimensions does data quality cover?

faq.a: In Microsoft Purview, data quality is measured with rules and scores. These scores roll up from columns to assets, data products and domains, so problems can be traced from a high-level view down to individual columns.
faq.q: How is data quality measured in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes state that AI cannot compensate for unreliable data. They also describe how Microsoft 365 Copilot draws on content across SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and the Microsoft Graph, which makes governance of that data important.
faq.q: Why does data quality matter for AI and Copilot?

data-quality.long:
Data quality is the degree to which data is complete, consistent, accurate, fresh and unique. It describes whether a dataset can be trusted for the purpose it is used for, whether that purpose is a report, a Power BI dashboard, an analytics model or an AI assistant. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears both as a general discipline and as a concrete capability: in Microsoft Purview, data quality is measured with rules and scores that roll up from columns to assets, data products and domains.

The five dimensions named in the definition give a practical checklist. Completeness asks whether required values are present. Consistency asks whether the same fact is represented the same way across systems. Accuracy asks whether values reflect reality. Freshness asks whether the data is recent enough for the decision at hand. Uniqueness asks whether records are duplicated. Because a score can be calculated at the column level and then aggregated upward to assets, data products and domains, owners can see where a problem originates and how it affects the larger collection of data it belongs to.

The M365.FM episodes treat data quality from several angles. "Bad Machine Data: Fixing Data Quality Before It Reaches Power BI" focuses on the pipeline side. It states that dashboards are only as good as the machine data feeding them and covers common problems such as missing values, naming, timestamps and units. The episode explains how to build data quality checks into the pipeline so that these issues are fixed before the data reaches Power BI, and it is aimed at data engineers, BI developers and manufacturing analysts.

A second perspective comes from "The 5 Pillars of Data Transformation - Simply Explained". The episode says that AI cannot compensate for unreliable data and that data governance creates trust before automation begins. It also argues that data quality should depend on the decision being made, which matches the idea of judging freshness or accuracy against a specific use rather than against an abstract standard. The same episode connects data quality to Microsoft Purview for governance and data discovery, to Microsoft Fabric for modern analytics and data platforms, to semantic models for Power BI and AI, and to business glossaries, because conflicting definitions lead to conflicting dashboards. It also names data ownership as a factor in AI readiness.

Data quality also appears in discussions of AI adoption. "From Pilot to Production: Building Enterprise AI That Actually Delivers with Leon Gordon [MVP]" lists investing in data quality and fostering collaboration as ways to overcome common challenges when moving enterprise AI from pilot to production. "Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence - Simply Explained" recommends focusing on data quality by setting clear validation rules and regularly reviewing processes, which fits streaming scenarios where problems can propagate quickly into dashboards and decisions.

The link to Microsoft 365 Copilot is covered in "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Data Quality and Leak Risks". The episode describes how Copilot draws on information across SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and the Microsoft Graph, and why that reach makes governance important. It discusses Microsoft Purview, sensitivity labels, role-based access control, retention controls and data loss prevention as the means of governing what Copilot can surface. In that context, data quality and data protection are closely related: an assistant that reads widely will repeat whatever it finds, whether that content is accurate, outdated, duplicated or overshared.

In practice, teams typically decide where to measure quality, which dimensions matter most for a given use, and who owns the data and the rules. Defining rules once, scoring the results and rolling them up lets stewards compare assets and domains consistently, while pipeline-level checks catch defects earlier. The episodes agree on the general direction: reliable data is a precondition for trustworthy analytics and AI, and governance, ownership and clear definitions support it.

data-residency.desc: Data residency covers requirements for the geographic location where data is stored and processed, often driven by regulations such as GDPR, and applies to Microsoft 365 and Azure.

faq.a: Data residency refers to requirements about the geographic location where data is stored and processed, often driven by regulations such as GDPR.
faq.q: What does data residency mean?

faq.a: No. The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" says that knowing the difference between the two helps organizations follow laws and keep control; residency concerns location, while sovereignty concerns ownership and control of data and systems.
faq.q: Is data residency the same as data sovereignty?

faq.a: Not necessarily. The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" says some metadata and management operations can be processed outside the primary storage location for operational or security reasons while still meeting compliance commitments.
faq.q: Does data residency in Microsoft 365 mean all data stays in one country?

data-residency.long:
Data residency refers to requirements about the geographic location where data is stored and processed. Such requirements are often driven by regulations such as GDPR, and they shape how organizations choose cloud regions, plan tenant architecture and document where information lives. In the Microsoft ecosystem the term appears in discussions of Microsoft 365, Azure and sovereign cloud offerings, where location of storage and processing is one of several factors in compliance planning.

Data residency is usually treated as one building block of a wider design rather than a complete answer on its own. The episode "7-Step Microsoft 365 Sovereign Tenant Governance Framework" lists data residency as an architectural principle alongside encryption and confidential computing. It describes the principle as ensuring that data remains within specific national or regional boundaries, and it names the EU Data Boundary for Azure as an example. Encryption, with customer-managed keys and HSMs, and confidential computing, which protects data in use through secure enclaves and trusted execution environments, are presented as separate principles that complement residency.

The distinction between data residency and data sovereignty comes up repeatedly. The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" says that knowing the difference between data residency and data sovereignty helps organizations follow laws and keep control. In that framing residency answers where data is held, while sovereignty is about who owns and controls data and systems. The episode also recommends strong governance rules that can adapt to new laws, and regular checking and updating of data management rules to keep sovereignty and compliance intact. It further mentions using different cloud providers as a way to improve data control and lower the risk of vendor lock-in.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" cautions against reading residency too literally. It states that data localization does not always mean data never leaves the country. According to the episode, Microsoft 365 offers controls and guarantees about data residency, but some metadata and management operations can be processed outside the primary storage location for operational or security reasons, while still meeting compliance commitments tied to business sovereignty in Microsoft 365. It also says that Sovereign Cloud variants, such as Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty or national clouds, go beyond simple regional datacenters.

In regulated sectors, residency options are weighed against stricter expectations. The episode "Prepare Microsoft 365 for German KRITIS Requirements" says that Microsoft offers regional datacenter options and data residency controls. It adds that these are not a full substitute for on-premises isolation, but that they help meet some KRITIS data sovereignty expectations. The same episode points to data classification and sensitivity labels as tools for policy-driven handling of critical infrastructure information across email, files and collaboration tools, which shows how residency is combined with other controls in practice.

The episode "Hidden Microsoft 365 and Azure Cloud Security Risks" focuses on the risk side. It says that unclear rules about where data lives and how AI is used can create significant exposure, and that without clear data protection policies organizations may break laws or lose customer trust. It notes that many countries have strict data residency rules, and that data crossing borders without control can lead to fines, failed audits and lost track of who handles the data, which can open security gaps.

Typical decisions around data residency therefore include which region or boundary offering fits the applicable regulation, which data types need location commitments, how metadata and management operations are treated, and how residency is documented for audits. The episodes consistently place residency within a governance framework that also covers encryption, classification and ongoing review, rather than treating it as a standalone setting.

data-silos.desc: Data silos are isolated data collections kept by separate teams or systems, causing duplication, diverging versions and coordination failures across an organization.

faq.a: Data silos are isolated collections of data maintained separately by different teams or systems. They lead to duplication, diverging versions and coordination failures.
faq.q: What are data silos?

faq.a: The episode "Eliminate Data Silos with Microsoft Fabric and OneLake" describes Microsoft Fabric as a response to fragmentation, combining a single identity through Entra with OneLake as a unified storage layer.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Fabric relate to data silos?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Sensitivity Labels and Data Silos for Microsoft Copilot" argues that static, incomplete labeling gives a false sense of security, and that the underlying issue is how organizations structure their data.
faq.q: Why do data silos matter for Microsoft Copilot?

data-silos.long:
Data silos are isolated collections of data that different teams or systems maintain separately from one another. Because each collection lives in its own place, the same information is often stored more than once, versions drift apart, and teams struggle to coordinate around a shared picture of the business. In Microsoft-centered environments the term comes up in discussions of analytics platforms, storage, security and AI, since each of these areas depends on data that can be found, trusted and governed consistently.

The M365.FM episode "Eliminate Data Silos with Microsoft Fabric and OneLake" treats fragmentation as the core problem behind many modern data stacks. It describes a landscape of Power BI reports, ad hoc pipelines, shadow CSV files and conflicting dashboards as entropy in disguise rather than a true platform. According to the episode, Microsoft Fabric exists as a response to this fragmentation, bringing together elements such as a single identity through Entra and a unified storage layer in OneLake. The episode also cites figures on the scale of the issue: that businesses generate 2.5 quintillion bytes of data daily and that around 60% of data remains underutilized because of poor management practices.

Storage is another place where silos appear. The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" explains how static quota models across SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Teams, Power Platform, Azure storage and multi-tenant workloads create fragmented infrastructure and what it calls dark data silos. It describes a "buffer mentality" in which organizations keep adding extra capacity to avoid outages, leaving idle resources and inflated cloud spending. The proposed direction is elastic, shared data reservoirs in place of isolated storage silos and fixed allocations.

Silos also affect governance and AI. In "Fix Sensitivity Labels and Data Silos for Microsoft Copilot", the argument is that sensitivity labels give a false sense of security when they are static, incomplete and poorly maintained, especially in AI-driven environments. The episode places the underlying issue in how organizations structure and manage their data rather than in the labeling technology itself. When data is scattered across disconnected systems, consistent classification and access control become harder, which matters once Copilot can reach that content.

The topic recurs in agent and security work as well. "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" states that Microsoft Foundry helps break down data silos so that information becomes both accessible and trustworthy, alongside reliability, scalability and Zero-Trust governance requirements for production agents. "Turn Microsoft Threat Analytics into Real Security Action" lists breaking down data silos among its recommendations, noting that it improves collaboration and allows more comprehensive threat analysis.

Across these episodes, a few practical decisions stand out. Teams weigh whether to consolidate data on a shared platform with common identity and storage, whether to replace fixed storage allocations with pooled capacity, and whether governance measures such as labeling can work without first addressing how data is organized. The episodes frame silos not as a single technical fault but as a recurring pattern that undermines analytics, cost control, security and AI readiness at the same time.

data-sovereignty.desc: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws and control of a given jurisdiction or owner, shaping where it is stored and who can access it.

faq.a: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws and control of a particular jurisdiction or owner. It affects where data may be stored and processed and who can compel access to it.
faq.q: What is data sovereignty?

faq.a: No. The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" says that understanding the difference between data residency and data sovereignty helps organizations follow laws and keep control. The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" similarly argues that technical custody, such as storing data in a European datacenter, is not business sovereignty.
faq.q: Is data residency the same as data sovereignty?

faq.a: According to the episode "Private RAG Security: Authorization-Aware Data Retrieval", data sovereignty is not the same as data security. Permissions and access controls from systems like SharePoint and Microsoft 365 need attention when documents are ingested into vector databases for RAG.
faq.q: Does data sovereignty guarantee data security in private RAG solutions?

data-sovereignty.long:
Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws and control of a particular jurisdiction or owner. In practice it shapes where data may be stored and processed, and it determines who can compel access to that data. For organizations that run workloads in the cloud, the concept moves beyond a purely technical question about datacenter location and becomes a matter of legal exposure, governance and business control.

A recurring theme in the M365.FM episodes is that sovereignty and storage location are not the same thing. The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" argues that technical custody is not business sovereignty. According to the episode, many organizations believe they have solved Microsoft 365 data sovereignty because their data sits in a European datacenter, yet they may not actually control anything. The point of the episode is that where data is physically held answers only part of the question; control over the data and the decisions made about it also matter. The episode also stresses collaboration between IT and business leaders to create a unified approach to cloud governance, and it recommends scheduling regular audits of the cloud environment so strategies can be adjusted for ongoing security.

The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" approaches the topic from the design side. It describes digital sovereignty as organizations owning their data and systems, which it calls very important in the current digital landscape. It also distinguishes data residency from data sovereignty and says that understanding the difference helps organizations follow laws and keep control. Its key takeaways recommend establishing strong rules that can adapt to new laws, using different cloud providers to improve data control and reduce the risk of vendor lock-in, and regularly reviewing and updating data management rules so that sovereignty and compliance are maintained over time.

Sovereignty also appears as a planning requirement in AI scenarios. The episode "How to Secure an AI Landing Zone in Microsoft Azure" lists understanding data sovereignty and compliance requirements among its key points and notes that different regions have varying regulations that can affect an AI deployment. In that context it points to monitoring tools such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud for protecting AI systems, and to the Azure AI Landing Zone Framework as a way to streamline deployments while limiting risk. The takeaway is that regional rules should be considered early, before AI workloads are placed.

The episodes on private AI show how the concept interacts with architecture choices. "Private LoRA for Secure AI on Proprietary Enterprise Data" covers private deployments combined with retrieval architectures, vector databases and enterprise governance controls, and lists data sovereignty alongside model isolation, security architecture, compliance requirements and intellectual property protection. It also discusses the trade-offs between public AI platforms and private AI implementations, including performance, cost and security. The episode "Private RAG Security: Authorization-Aware Data Retrieval" adds an important caveat: data sovereignty is not the same as data security. Keeping data in a controlled or regional environment does not by itself preserve the permissions and access controls that existed in the source system. The episode examines what happens when documents leave systems such as SharePoint and Microsoft 365 and are ingested into vector databases for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where organizations often focus on storage location while overlooking authorization models.

Taken together, the episodes treat data sovereignty as one layer within a broader set of decisions. Typical questions include which jurisdiction's laws apply to a given dataset, whether residency commitments are sufficient or whether additional controls are needed, how governance responsibilities are split between IT and the business, and how permissions are carried through when data is copied into new systems such as AI retrieval stores. Treating sovereignty as ongoing governance, supported by audits and by rules that can adapt to changing legislation, is the approach the episodes describe.

data-steward.desc: A data steward is a governance role that maintains metadata, maps glossary terms, monitors data quality and supports access governance and compliance for data assets.

faq.a: A data steward maintains accurate metadata, maps business glossary terms, monitors data quality and supports access governance and compliance for a set of data assets.
faq.q: What does a data steward do?

faq.a: In the sample health monitoring checklist from "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects", the data steward handles the daily alert and notification check and the weekly data scan status review.
faq.q: Which tasks does the Microsoft Purview episode assign to the data steward?

faq.a: The episodes recommend assigning data owners and stewards for datasets used by Copilot and describe the steward as managing data quality and compliance so that sensitive information is protected in generative AI projects.
faq.q: Why is a data steward relevant for Microsoft 365 Copilot and generative AI?

data-steward.long:
A data steward is a role responsible for maintaining accurate metadata, mapping business glossary terms, monitoring data quality and supporting access governance and compliance for a defined set of data assets. The role belongs to data governance work: it connects the people who own data, the administrators who operate the platform and the compliance staff who check that rules are followed. Because it describes a responsibility rather than a product feature, the same role can exist in any organisation that manages data, including those working in the Microsoft ecosystem.

In practice, a data steward looks after the day-to-day condition of the data assets assigned to them. That includes keeping descriptive metadata correct, linking business glossary terms to the assets they describe, watching quality indicators and helping to apply access and compliance requirements. The role is operational and recurring. It does not replace the data owner, who is accountable for a dataset, but it supplies the regular attention that keeps catalogued information trustworthy and usable.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" places the data steward inside a sample health monitoring checklist for a governance domain. In that checklist, the data steward is the responsible role for the daily alert and notification check and for the weekly data scan status review. Other health actions are assigned to different roles: service health review and access control validation to the administrator, the activity log audit to the compliance officer, data quality trend analysis to the data owner, and policy and rule updates to the data governance lead. The episode presents the checklist as a way to assign tasks and set a schedule for a team, so that issues are caught early and the governance domain keeps running smoothly. This shows how the steward role is expected to handle frequent, hands-on checks while other roles handle periodic or strategic ones.

The role also appears in discussions of AI and Copilot. The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Data Quality and Leak Risks" includes a checklist whose governance and ownership section recommends assigning data owners and stewards for each dataset used by Copilot. It also recommends defining and publishing data quality policies and service levels, and mapping roles and access rights for Copilot integrations, naming the data steward, the admin and the user as roles to consider. The same checklist covers cataloguing the data sources Copilot can access, such as SharePoint, Exchange, Dataverse, Teams and OneDrive, and running regular data profiling. In this framing, stewardship is one of the controls that supports data quality when an AI assistant draws on organisational content.

The episode "Govern Power Apps Generative Pages After Edit Code" describes the data steward in the context of governing generative AI. It lists the role alongside a governance committee and a security officer as part of a cross-functional structure. According to the episode, the data steward manages data quality and compliance and helps ensure that sensitive information is protected. The governance committee oversees AI projects and updates policies based on regulations and stakeholder input, while the security officer focuses on identifying and mitigating security risks. The episode's argument is that assigning such roles creates accountability and effective oversight.

Typical decisions around the role include which datasets each steward is responsible for, how stewardship tasks are scheduled, and how the steward's duties are separated from those of the owner, administrator and compliance officer. The sources reviewed here describe the role consistently as one concerned with data quality, metadata and compliance support, and they treat it as one position within a larger set of named governance roles rather than as a stand-alone function.

dataflow-gen2.desc: Dataflow Gen2 is a Microsoft Fabric item that uses Power Query to connect to, clean and shape data through a visual, low-code editor.

faq.a: Dataflow Gen2 is a Microsoft Fabric item that uses Power Query to connect to, clean and shape data through a visual, low-code editor. The episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" describes it as building on Power BI Dataflows.
faq.q: What is Dataflow Gen2?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" points to its broad connector support and familiar Power Query experience. It says this can provide a natural starting point before moving toward more engineering-oriented approaches.
faq.q: Why is Dataflow Gen2 considered a good starting point for Power BI professionals?

faq.a: According to "Microsoft Fabric Data Factory - Simply Explained", pipelines and Dataflow Gen2 are key components of Microsoft Fabric Data Factory. Pipelines automate and orchestrate data movement, transformation and loading, and Dataflow Gen2 enhances their functionality.
faq.q: How does Dataflow Gen2 relate to pipelines in Fabric?

dataflow-gen2.long:
Dataflow Gen2 is a Microsoft Fabric item that uses Power Query to connect to, clean and shape data through a visual, low-code editor. It is part of the data integration capabilities in Microsoft Fabric and is used when data from various sources has to be brought into the platform and prepared for analysis. According to the M365.FM episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2", it builds on the foundation of Power BI Dataflows, adding more flexibility and performance. The episode describes this as the ability to connect to more data sources, use advanced transformation functions and benefit from enhanced compute engines, which it links to faster processing and better scalability.

In practice, Dataflow Gen2 is one of several ways to get data into Fabric. The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" lists Shortcuts, Mirroring, Pipelines, Copy Activity, Copy Jobs, Dataflow Gen2 and notebooks as the options discussed. The episode says the right choice depends heavily on the source and the use case. It describes Dataflow Gen2 as particularly useful because of its broad connector support and its familiar Power Query experience.

That familiarity is a recurring theme. For Power BI professionals who are entering Fabric, the episode presents Dataflow Gen2 as a natural starting point, one that can be used before moving toward more engineering-oriented approaches. The same episode also touches on when PySpark becomes important, which indicates that Dataflow Gen2 and code-based notebook approaches are treated as complementary options rather than interchangeable ones. The decision typically turns on the source, the volume and the skills available in the team.

Dataflow Gen2 also appears in the context of orchestration. In "Microsoft Fabric Data Factory - Simply Explained", pipelines and Dataflow Gen2 are named as key components of Microsoft Fabric Data Factory. Pipelines automate and orchestrate data processes, including sequences of tasks for data movement, transformation and loading. The episode says Dataflow Gen2 enhances the functionality of pipelines, which positions it as the transformation-focused counterpart to the orchestration-focused pipeline item.

The episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" frames the item in terms of ETL, meaning extract, transform and load work. It also mentions lifecycle tasks such as deployments, refreshes and monitoring as part of CI/CD pipelines, and includes a comparison table of Dataflow Gen1 and Dataflow Gen2 features. These points show that the item is considered not only for building transformations but also for operating them over time.

Performance is another topic that connects Dataflow Gen2 to the rest of the platform. In "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance", the discussion of automated table statistics notes that they support Dataflow Gen2 optimizations. The episode says that keeping statistics current helps Dataflow Gen2 refresh and process large datasets more efficiently, with benefits for both queries and data pipelines. This ties the item to the Lakehouse, where prepared data is often stored.

Finally, "From Raw Data to Real Business Impact: Mastering Power BI and Microsoft Fabric with Thummalacherla Krishnakanth" places Dataflow Gen2 among the workloads of a unified platform, alongside OneLake, Lakehouse, Warehouse, Real-Time Intelligence, Fabric capacities, licensing, governance and enterprise migration strategies. The episode describes the benefit of centralizing ingestion, storage, transformation, warehousing, reporting and data science in one platform instead of managing separate services.

dataverse.desc: Dataverse is Microsoft's managed data platform behind Power Platform and Dynamics 365, storing tables, relationships, security roles and business logic.

faq.a: Dataverse is Microsoft's managed data platform behind Power Platform and Dynamics 365. It stores tables with relationships, security roles and business logic so apps, automations and agents use one governed data source.
faq.q: What is Dataverse?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Dataverse Integration - Simply Explained", Dataverse is the shared data foundation under Dynamics 365 applications such as Sales and Customer Service. Accounts, contacts, leads, cases and permissions can live in that environment rather than in a separate system.
faq.q: How does Dataverse relate to Dynamics 365?

faq.a: The episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" says security is built into the platform. Organizations control who can view, edit, create or delete data through it, with governance, compliance and scalability in mind.
faq.q: How is data protected in Dataverse?

dataverse.long:
Dataverse, also called Microsoft Dataverse, is the managed data platform behind Power Platform and Dynamics 365. It stores data in tables with relationships and combines that data with security roles and business logic, so apps, automations and agents work on one governed data source instead of separate copies. Microsoft develops Dataverse, it is part of the Power Platform, and it is offered as a paid service. The public product documentation for it sits in the Power Apps maker documentation on Microsoft Learn.

The core idea is that data, rules and access control live together in one place. Tables define the structure of business information, relationships connect those tables, security roles determine who may see or change records, and business logic enforces how the data behaves. Because these elements are part of the platform, applications built on Dataverse do not have to re-implement them individually. This is the reason the platform is described as more than a database: the episode "Dataverse - Simply Explained" presents it as secure, relational data storage with built-in business logic, security, automation and governance, which allows organizations to build business applications without managing complex infrastructure.

Dataverse is closely tied to Dynamics 365. The episode "Dynamics 365 Dataverse Integration - Simply Explained" says that Dataverse is easier to understand once Dynamics 365 and Dataverse are no longer seen as two separate systems that constantly need to synchronize customer data. For Dynamics 365 applications such as Sales and Customer Service, Dataverse provides the shared data foundation underneath the applications. Accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities, cases, activities, relationships, permissions and business rules can all live within this structured environment.

Several other products and concepts connect to Dataverse. Model-driven apps are built directly on its tables. Power Fx, the formula language of Power Platform, is related to it, as is AI Builder. In practice this means that a maker can build an app, automate a process or add AI capabilities while all of them read and write the same governed tables. A typical decision around Dataverse is therefore whether business data should be kept in one managed, relational store with shared security rather than spread across independent sources.

Security is a recurring theme. The episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" explains how Microsoft enables organizations to control exactly who can view, edit, create or delete data while maintaining governance, compliance and scalability. The episode stresses that, unlike with traditional databases, security is built directly into the platform rather than added afterwards. This matters for any scenario in which many users, apps and automations touch the same data.

The newer episodes look at Dataverse in the context of AI. "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken" argues that organizations often invest in enterprise data infrastructure without getting the expected value, and that the problem can lie in an approach that fails to deliver scalable governance and security rather than in the technology itself. The episode names governance debt, unmonitored shadow AI and uncontrolled "ghost agents" among the failure factors, alongside technical, strategic and human causes.

"THE DEATH OF THE PROXY: Architecting Dataverse for the Agent Fabric" covers the connection between AI assistants and Dataverse. According to the episode, Microsoft's recommended architecture for connecting assistants such as Claude Desktop to Dataverse long relied on a local STDIO proxy, which was simple, easy to install and suited to individual developers experimenting with AI-powered workflows. The episode says that enterprise AI has moved on to multiple clients, platforms and business systems, that this shift changes the architecture, and that the proxy model has reached its limits, with Streamable HTTP presented as the more fitting basis. Together, the episodes position Dataverse as the governed data layer that apps, Dynamics 365 and AI agents share.

dataverse-business-skills.desc: Dataverse business skills is a preview Dataverse feature for writing business procedures as natural-language instructions that agents find through the Dataverse MCP server.

faq.a: It is a preview Dataverse feature that lets business users write procedures as natural-language instructions in Dataverse. Agents can discover these instructions through the Dataverse MCP server.
faq.q: What is Dataverse business skills?

faq.a: No. According to the feature description, agents discover the skills through the Dataverse MCP server without being rebuilt or redeployed. The episode on Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP adds that skills are updated in one place and every agent benefits.
faq.q: Does an agent need to be redeployed when a business skill changes?

faq.a: The episode "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" says developer skills are not required to create AI agents that automate business processes, and that skills are written in natural language.
faq.q: Do you need to be a developer to use Dataverse Business Skills?

dataverse-business-skills.long:
Dataverse business skills is a preview feature of Microsoft Dataverse. It lets business users write procedures as natural-language instructions and store them in Dataverse. Agents can then discover those instructions through the Dataverse MCP server, without the agent being rebuilt or redeployed. In practice, the feature moves part of an agent's behavior out of its code or configuration and into business-owned content that sits alongside the data it describes.

The core idea is separating business knowledge from agent construction. A skill describes how a task is done in an organization: a process, a policy or an operating rule, written in plain language rather than in a programming language or a flow designer. Because the agent finds the skill at the Dataverse MCP server, the people who own the process can change the instructions where they live. Neither a developer nor a new deployment is needed to update the way an agent handles that process.

This matters for organizations building agents on Microsoft Power Platform, where the same business rules often have to be applied consistently across several agents, apps and departments. The episode "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" says that Dataverse Business Skills define reusable business logic, that the skills describe an organization's processes and policies in natural language, and that they can be updated in one place so every agent benefits from the change. According to that episode, this approach supports consistency and saves time, and creating AI agents that automate business processes does not require being a developer.

The feature sits within a wider discussion of how Dataverse is used as more than a place for tables and columns. The episode "Dataverse Business Skills for Scalable Power Platform Solutions" frames business skills as one of the most important capabilities for organizations building scalable solutions on Power Platform. It describes how Dataverse can capture business knowledge, processes and operational logic, and how well-designed Dataverse structures help maintain consistency, improve governance and reduce technical debt as applications scale across departments and business units.

Typical decisions around the feature concern where a piece of logic should live. Rules that rarely change and need strict technical enforcement may belong in application or platform logic. Procedures that business owners adjust frequently, and that several agents need to follow, are the kind of content the episodes associate with business skills. Because the capability is in preview, teams evaluating it should treat it as an evolving feature and verify its current behavior before relying on it in production designs.

Business skills connect closely to the Dataverse MCP server, which is the discovery path agents use to find them. The M365.FM episode list also pairs the topic with "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]", "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" and "Dataverse - Simply Explained", which cover the integration layer, the security model and the platform basics that surround the feature. Data model design is a related concern, covered in episodes such as "Design Scalable Dataverse Data Models for Business Apps", since instructions written in natural language still operate on the tables, relationships and permissions defined in Dataverse.

dataverse-business-units.desc: Dataverse business units are tree-structured security boundaries under a root unit that, with security roles, decide which rows a user can reach in an environment.

faq.a: They are security boundaries in a Dataverse environment, arranged as a tree under a root unit. Together with security roles they determine which rows a user can access.
faq.q: What are Dataverse business units?

faq.a: Every Dataverse database has exactly one root business unit. Child business units are created beneath it to divide users and data into smaller boundaries.
faq.q: How many business units does a Dataverse database have at the top level?

faq.a: No. Permissions are cumulative, so the broadest permission that applies is the one in effect, and one role cannot restrict another.
faq.q: Can a security role limit another role's access in a business unit setup?

dataverse-business-units.long:
Dataverse business units are security boundaries within a Dataverse environment. They are arranged as a tree beneath a single root unit, and together with security roles they determine what a user can access. Administrators use them to manage users and data by dividing a database into smaller units, each with its own set of users and records.

Every Dataverse database has exactly one root business unit. Child business units are created below it to split users and data into further boundaries, and each user belongs to one business unit. The structure may mirror the organization chart, but it does not have to; it can be designed around whatever separation of access is needed. Business units apply only to environments that have a Dataverse database and are managed separately in each environment.

Business units work together with security roles rather than replacing them. A security role defines which privileges a user holds, and the business unit structure defines the scope at which those privileges reach rows. Access can be granted at the business unit level, and it can be controlled so that data from child business units is either included or excluded. Permissions are cumulative: the broadest permission that applies to a user is the one that takes effect, and one security role cannot restrict another.

Ownership is part of the model. Each record carries an owning business unit, which by default is the business unit of the user who created it. That value can be changed only when the feature for record ownership across business units is enabled. Dataverse also creates a default team for every business unit, and this team always contains all users of that unit. Teams belong to a business unit, and a business unit can be linked to a Microsoft Entra security group through a group team, which connects directory groups to the Dataverse security structure.

Typical decisions around business units involve how deep the tree should be, whether it should follow the organizational hierarchy or a different logic, and at which scope privileges should be granted so that users see only the rows intended for them. Because permissions accumulate, the role design and the business unit layout need to be planned together, since a broad grant cannot be narrowed by adding another role.

The M365.FM episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" discusses business units in the context of tenant isolation. The episode says that Power Pages uses Dataverse business units to keep tenant data separate, that business units create a security hierarchy, and that privileges can be granted at the business unit level. It also notes that each user belongs to one business unit and that access can be set to include or exclude data from child business units. According to the episode, this structure supports a strong tenant isolation model and helps enforce tenant-aware security, with partition-aware routing described as an additional layer.

dataverse-mcp-server.desc: The Dataverse MCP server is a Microsoft tool that lets AI agents query and update Dataverse and Dynamics 365 data through the Model Context Protocol, as an alternative to connectors.

faq.a: It is an MCP server from Microsoft that lets agents query and update Dataverse and Dynamics 365 data through the Model Context Protocol. It is part of Dataverse and serves as an alternative to connectors.
faq.q: What is the Dataverse MCP server?

faq.a: A connector is the established way to reach data, while the MCP server gives agents a standardized protocol-based path to Dataverse. A knowledge source mainly grounds an agent's answers on content, whereas the MCP server also allows updating data.
faq.q: How does the Dataverse MCP server differ from a connector or a knowledge source?

faq.a: "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]" and "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" discuss it directly. "Dataverse - Simply Explained" provides background on Dataverse itself.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover the Dataverse MCP server?

dataverse-mcp-server.long:
The Dataverse MCP server is an MCP server developed by Microsoft that lets agents query and update data stored in Dataverse and Dynamics 365 through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It is classed as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool, and it is part of Dataverse. It is positioned as an alternative to connectors: instead of building a custom integration for each data source, an agent talks to Dataverse through a standardized protocol.

The purpose of the server is to give AI agents a consistent way to work with business data. Dataverse is the cloud data platform behind Power Apps, Power Automate and Dynamics 365, so the tables and records that these applications use are the same ones an agent can reach through the MCP server. Because the server supports both reading and updating, an agent is not limited to looking up information. It can also take actions on the data, which distinguishes it from a knowledge source, where content is mainly used to ground an agent's answers.

The Model Context Protocol is the technical basis of the server. MCP defines how an agent discovers and calls the capabilities that a server exposes. The Dataverse MCP server applies this approach to Dataverse, so that an agent built in a tool such as Copilot Studio can connect to Dataverse data without a one-off integration. Connectors remain the established way of reaching data in the Microsoft ecosystem, and the MCP server offers a different path for agent scenarios, which is why the two are often compared when teams decide how an agent should access business data.

Typical decisions around the Dataverse MCP server concern how an agent should reach data, what it should be allowed to change, and how this fits into existing Dynamics 365 and Power Platform solutions. Since the server can update data as well as query it, questions about security and governance in Dataverse become part of any design. The M365.FM catalog also covers this angle in the episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained", which is listed alongside the MCP episodes as related listening.

The M365.FM episodes discuss the Dataverse MCP server together with Microsoft MVP Nathan Rose. The episode "Dataverse MCP Integration with Nathan Rose [MVP]" starts from the point that custom integrations have long been one of the biggest bottlenecks in enterprise applications and explores how Dataverse MCP changes that. According to the episode description, the discussion looks at why traditional APIs, custom connectors and one-off integrations struggle to scale in an AI-first setting, and how MCP and Dataverse change the way AI agents connect with business data.

The episode "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]" looks at how Copilot Studio, Dataverse and MCP shape agentic AI in Microsoft 365. The episode describes a move beyond simple chatbots toward agents that understand intent, access business data and take meaningful actions, evolving from simple assistants into digital coworkers that understand context and work with business data.

For a broader foundation, the episode "Dataverse - Simply Explained" covers the key concepts behind Dataverse and how it fits into the wider Microsoft technology ecosystem. Related episodes on the protocol side include "MCP (Model Context Protocol) - Simply Explained", "MCP Architecture for Microsoft Copilot and AI Agents", "Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server - Simply Explained" and "Fix an MCP Server That Is Invisible to Copilot Studio". Together they place the Dataverse MCP server within the larger set of MCP servers and agent tooling around Microsoft products.

dataverse-plug-in.desc: A Dataverse plug-in is custom server-side code registered in the Dataverse event pipeline that runs during data operations, for example validation or calculations.

faq.a: A Dataverse plug-in is a custom event handler, written as a class in a .NET Framework assembly and registered in Dataverse, that runs in response to a specific event during a data operation. Each class implements the IPlugin interface with a single Execute method.
faq.q: What is a Dataverse plug-in?

faq.a: Yes. Plug-ins can run synchronously, so the operation waits for them, or asynchronously after the operation completes. Microsoft Learn notes that synchronous plug-ins need to run quickly and that there is a hard time limit on execution.
faq.q: Can a Dataverse plug-in run synchronously and asynchronously?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn advises checking declarative options first, such as custom actions, calculated and rollup columns, webhooks and Power Automate. The episode "Customize Dataverse for Complex Business Apps" suggests a plug-in or Dataflow for heavy compute or complex joins.
faq.q: When should a Dataverse plug-in be used instead of other options?

dataverse-plug-in.long:
A Dataverse plug-in is a custom event handler that responds to a specific event during the processing of a data operation in Microsoft Dataverse. It is written as a class in a .NET Framework assembly, and that assembly is then registered in Dataverse. One assembly can hold several classes, each registered to a different step of the event framework. In Dynamics 365, plug-ins are used for server-side logic such as transactional validation and calculations that must run when data is created, updated or otherwise processed.

Each plug-in class implements the IPlugin interface, which defines a single Execute method. When the registered event occurs, Dataverse calls that method and passes context data about the operation being processed. From there, the code can cancel the running pipeline operation, change the business data being processed, call further data operations, contact external systems, or pass information on to later plug-ins in the same pipeline. Plug-ins can run synchronously, in which case the operation waits for them to finish, or asynchronously after the operation completes.

The choice between these modes matters in practice. Logic that has to prevent bad data from being saved belongs in the synchronous part of the pipeline, while work that can happen after the save can run asynchronously. Microsoft Learn notes that synchronous plug-ins need to run quickly, and that execution is subject to a hard time limit. Poorly written code can also hurt performance, and building plug-ins requires developer skills, so they carry a cost that declarative options do not.

Because of these drawbacks, the Microsoft documentation advises checking declarative options first. Alternatives it lists include custom actions, calculated and rollup columns, webhooks and Power Automate. A plug-in becomes the appropriate tool when those options do not cover the requirement, for example when logic must be enforced inside the transaction itself.

The M365.FM episode "Customize Dataverse for Complex Business Apps" places the Dataverse plug-in inside a decision matrix for business rules. According to the episode, the questions run roughly as follows: if a rule must block bad data, use synchronous server logic; if it can run after the save, use asynchronous server logic; for cross-app messaging or approvals, use Flow or Teams; and for heavy compute or complex joins, use a Dataverse plug-in or a Dataflow. The episode also recommends keeping a rule catalog that records the table, trigger, condition, action and owner of each rule, and advises using calculated and rollup fields for deterministic math and sums over related records instead of reaching for code.

The episode "Why Power Platform Is Your Real Automation Layer — Not Custom Code" looks at the same topic from the customization-history angle. It describes the traditional Dynamics model, in which every difference between the standard application and the business process becomes another customization: a Dataverse plug-in, JavaScript attached to a form, a custom workflow activity, a scheduled job or another integration service. The episode says that each feature may work correctly on its own, but the complete process gradually becomes distributed across assemblies, scripts, workflows, APIs, configuration values and specialist knowledge. As a result, the process owner understands the policy but cannot inspect how it is implemented. This is the main argument for treating plug-ins as a deliberate choice rather than a default response to every process change.

dataverse-prompt-columns.desc: Dataverse prompt columns are a column type whose value an AI prompt generates from other columns of the same record, with the result stored for apps, flows and reports.

faq.a: It is a Dataverse column type whose value is generated by an AI model from a natural-language prompt that references other columns of the same record. The result is stored on the record and can be used in apps, flows and reports.
faq.q: What is a Dataverse prompt column?

faq.a: It runs when a record is created or when a referenced column changes, and a filter condition can restrict when it runs. Processing is asynchronous, and existing records can be handled in bulk as a background job.
faq.q: When does a prompt column run?

faq.a: Formula columns, file columns, image columns and other prompt columns cannot serve as inputs. Prompt columns also cannot be re-run on demand and are not covered by auditing.
faq.q: Which columns cannot be used as inputs to a prompt column?

dataverse-prompt-columns.long:
Dataverse prompt columns are a column type in Microsoft Dataverse whose value is generated by an AI prompt. The prompt is written in natural language and refers to other columns of the same table. The AI model reads those input columns, produces a response, and the response is stored permanently in the prompt column. Because the result is saved on the record, it can be used later in apps, workflows and reports like any other column value.

The purpose is to bring AI reasoning directly into the data layer. Instead of calling a model from each app or flow, a table owner defines the prompt once on the column, and every record of that table receives a generated value. Typical situations include deriving a summary, a classification or another piece of text from fields that already exist on the record. The episode "Automate Power Platform Data Entry with AI Tools" describes Dataverse Prompt Columns as enabling reasoning within Dataverse records and places them among four capabilities introduced in 2025, alongside AI Form Filler / Form Assist, Generative Pages and Copilot Agents. The episode frames these as a new build model in which the maker describes the intent and the platform constructs the logic.

According to the official documentation, a prompt column runs when a record is created or when one of the referenced columns changes. A filter condition can be set to restrict when the prompt runs. Processing is asynchronous, so the value does not appear instantly. Status and details columns are created automatically and show whether a run completed, was skipped or failed. Existing records can be processed in bulk as a background job, which is relevant when a prompt column is added to a table that already holds data.

There are several documented constraints that influence design decisions. Formula columns, file columns and image columns cannot be used as inputs, and neither can other prompt columns, so chains of prompt columns are not possible. The number of prompt columns per table is capped. A run cannot be triggered on demand, and auditing is not available for these columns. If the feature is disabled, or if the filter condition is not met, the prompt is skipped silently, which makes the automatically created status column an important place to check when a value is missing.

On the administration side, licensing follows the AI Builder prompt model, and the Copilot and AI prompts features must be enabled in the environment before prompt columns work. Teams evaluating the feature therefore need to confirm both the capacity and the environment settings, and decide whether a stored, generated value on the record is preferable to generating text at the moment of use in an app or flow.

In practice, prompt columns suit cases where a generated value should be consistent, stored and reusable across Power Apps, Power Automate and reporting, and where the inputs are plain data columns on the same record. They fit less well where a re-run on demand, audit history or inputs from file, image or formula columns are required. Reading the status and details columns, and testing the filter condition, are the practical ways to understand why a given record did or did not receive a generated value.

dataverse-security-roles.desc: Dataverse security roles are sets of per-table privileges such as create, read and write, each with an access level, that decide what users can see and change.

faq.a: A Dataverse security role is a set of privileges, such as create, read, write, delete, append, append to, assign and share, defined per table with an access level or depth. It determines what a user can do with data in Dataverse.
faq.q: What is a Dataverse security role?

faq.a: When a user is assigned more than one role, the permissions from all roles combine. One role does not remove privileges granted by another.
faq.q: What does it mean that security roles are additive?

faq.a: The episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" lists Organization, Parent: Child Business Unit, Business Unit and User. They range from access to all records in the organization down to records the user owns or that are shared with them or their team.
faq.q: Which access levels exist for Dataverse security roles?

dataverse-security-roles.long:
Dataverse security roles are sets of privileges that control what users can do with data stored in Dataverse. Each role defines privileges per table, such as create, read, write, delete, append, append to, assign and share, and each privilege is paired with an access level, also called depth. Roles are additive, which means that when a user holds several roles, the permissions from all of them combine rather than cancel each other out. The official Microsoft Learn documentation on database security describes this model in detail.

The episode "Dataverse Security Roles - Simply Explained" frames the topic by saying that Dataverse does not protect business data with a password or a firewall, but with a security role. According to the episode, this can sound like a small administrative setting, yet it determines what every person in a company can see, change and even print. That framing explains why roles sit at the center of any Dataverse design: they are the primary mechanism that links a person to the data they are allowed to work with.

The access level is what turns a simple privilege into a scoped permission. The episode "Dataverse Security - Simply Explained" lists the levels in a table. Organization lets users access all records in the organization regardless of business unit. Parent: Child Business Unit lets users access records in their own business unit and all subordinate business units. Business Unit limits access to records in the user's own business unit. User gives access to records the user owns and those shared with them or their team. The episode gives an example: a Sales Manager may view records from their own Business Unit but not from others, depending on how the security role is configured.

In practice, working with security roles means deciding which tables a group of people needs, which actions they need on each table, and how far that access should reach across the business unit structure. Because roles are additive, a common approach is to keep roles focused and assign several of them where a person has several responsibilities, instead of building one very broad role. Permissions should also be refreshed as team responsibilities change.

Security roles appear in several related scenarios covered by M365.FM. In "Build Your First Power App: Beginner Step-by-Step Guide", the episode recommends using Dataverse security roles to set limits on who can see or change data, alongside multi-factor authentication for all users and checks with the App Checker in Power Apps Studio. In "Modernize Legacy Power Apps Portals and Power Pages", the episode says Power Pages brings together web roles and Dataverse security roles, which it describes as making user management simple and clear, and it mentions a security agent that can help set up complex roles and permissions during website authoring.

Security roles also influence analytics. The episode "Embed Power BI and Fabric Analytics in Dynamics 365" states that embedded Power BI reports in model-driven apps inherit the security context of the app, and that row-level security in Power BI aligns with Dataverse security roles so users see only data that matches their permissions. The same episode points to integration with Microsoft Entra ID, where security groups and user attributes update automatically as the organization changes.

Taken together, the sources present Dataverse security roles as a foundational concept: a per-table, privilege-and-depth model that is additive and that other parts of the Microsoft ecosystem, including model-driven apps, Power Pages and embedded Power BI reports, build on when deciding who can see and change which records.

date-table.desc: A date table is a dedicated calendar dimension in a Power BI semantic model, with one row per date, used for filtering, grouping and time intelligence.

faq.a: A date table is a dedicated calendar dimension in a Power BI semantic model with one row per date over a continuous range. It is used for filtering, grouping and time intelligence calculations.
faq.q: What is a date table in Power BI?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports", marking a proper date table unlocks built-in time intelligence and ensures correct behavior for CALCULATE filters and many visuals. An unmarked date table can lead to subtle, incorrect results.
faq.q: Why should a date table be marked as a date table?

faq.a: The episode "Fix Power BI Models That Fail to Deliver Results" says custom date tables are better because they offer more control and flexibility, and it recommends disabling auto date/time to save space and improve performance.
faq.q: Should a custom date table or auto date/time be used?

date-table.long:
A date table is a dedicated calendar dimension in a Power BI semantic model. It holds one row per date over a continuous range and serves as the basis for filtering, grouping and time intelligence calculations. Instead of relying on date columns scattered across fact tables, a model uses a single date table that other tables relate to, so that every measure and visual works from the same calendar.

The date table fits naturally into a star schema, where fact tables sit at the center and dimension tables surround them. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" describes how marking a proper date table unlocks built-in time intelligence and ensures correct behavior for CALCULATE filters and many visuals. According to that episode, an unmarked date table can lead to subtle, incorrect results. The same episode also points to performance concerns in relationships, noting that replacing high-cardinality text keys with surrogate integer keys in the star schema usually helps.

A recurring decision is whether to use automatic date/time or custom date tables. The episode "Fix Power BI Models That Fail to Deliver Results" says custom date tables are better because they give more control and flexibility for time-based analysis. It recommends disabling auto date/time to save space and improve performance, and it advises marking the custom date table as a date table in Power BI so that calculations are accurate. This reflects the guidance linked to the topic in Microsoft documentation on date tables in Power BI models.

Correct setup matters most when time intelligence functions are used. The episode "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" warns that time intelligence functions may produce misleading results if the date table is not set up correctly. It places this within a wider point about filter context: measures can yield different results depending on the context in which they are used, so their behavior should be checked in each visual, and writing measures without considering context can give incorrect results when slicers are used.

In the context of reusable models, the episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" lists implementing and testing time intelligence functions and the date table as part of the measures and calculations work. It also mentions natural hierarchies for drill-down, with date given as one example alongside geography and product, as well as default formats and sort orders as part of the user experience of a semantic layer.

Practical usage is shown in the episode "Link Microsoft 365 Usage to Real Business Results". Its modeling checklist calls for a star schema with single-direction relationships, hidden surrogate keys, a marked date table and time intelligence enabled. Timestamps from audit extracts are converted to UTC before modeling, and the date table then supports views such as rolling windows and lagged comparisons that the episode suggests adding to usage reports.

Taken together, the episodes treat the date table as a basic part of model design rather than an optional extra. The common points are to build a continuous calendar with one row per date, relate it to the fact tables in a star schema, mark it as the date table, and prefer a custom table over automatic date/time handling.

dax-user-defined-functions.desc: DAX user-defined functions (UDFs) package DAX logic once so it can be reused like a built-in function in measures, calculated columns, visual calculations and other functions.

faq.a: They package DAX logic once so it can be reused like a built-in function in measures, calculated columns, visual calculations and other functions. This helps centralize business rules and change calculations more safely over time.
faq.q: What are DAX user-defined functions used for?

faq.a: A compatibility level of 1702 or higher is required. Microsoft Learn lists limitations including no recursion, no overloading, no explicit return type, no hiding in the model, and limited IntelliSense in some tools.
faq.q: What is required to use DAX UDFs, and what are their limits?
