The same source stresses that the full potential appears only when these technologies work together, not when they are used in isolation.

Before starting, organizations are advised to assess their digital maturity and to consider how new technology fits into existing systems. The challenges named are integrating legacy equipment, skill gaps in data science, AI and security, a larger attack surface caused by connectivity, and heavy demands on storage and compute. Because factories typically combine information technology with operational technology, the topic is closely related to Operational technology (OT), Industrial IoT and Digital twin, and it sits within the wider field of Manufacturing.

Two M365.FM episodes touch on the topic. The episode "Your Factory Cloud Bill Is Much Higher Than You Think" carries Industry 4.0 among its topics, alongside MQTT, OPC UA, data egress, cloud costs, FinOps, IT/OT integration, predictive maintenance and vibration monitoring. It is aimed at manufacturing IT leaders, OT engineers, cloud architects, IoT architects, data engineers and plant managers who design or operate connected factory environments, and it questions architectures that show a simple arrow from factory to cloud. This points to a practical decision in Industry 4.0 projects: how much factory data is sent to the cloud, and what that costs.

The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" mentions Industry 4.0 in a regional market context. According to the episode, Germany is a prominent market for Infrastructure as Code in Europe, and manufacturing organizations involved in Industry 4.0 use it to manage cloud-connected operations effectively. In that framing, Industry 4.0 is a driver for managing cloud infrastructure in a repeatable, code-based way.

Taken together, the sources describe Industry 4.0 less as a single product and more as a set of practices and technologies. Typical situations include connecting sensors on existing machines, deciding what to process at the edge versus in the cloud, building digital twins of assets, and bringing IT and OT teams together under shared security and data practices.

infinite-capacity-planning.desc: Infinite capacity planning is a rough-cut approach that loads demand into time buckets without limiting it to resource capacity; useful for load, not a shop-floor schedule.

faq.a: It is a rough-cut planning approach that loads demand into time buckets without limiting it to the actual capacity of resources. It shows how load builds up but does not produce an executable shop-floor schedule.
faq.q: What is infinite capacity planning?

faq.a: Under infinite loading, work is loaded onto resources regardless of spare capacity, so resources can be overbooked and delivery dates are not pushed out. Finite scheduling considers resource limits and can move a job to when capacity exists, which may push the delivery date out.
faq.q: How does infinite loading differ from finite capacity scheduling?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Learn states that outside the configurable time fence, scheduling behaves as infinite, even when finite capacity is enabled in master planning parameters, the master plan and on the resource.
faq.q: Does infinite capacity planning still apply in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management?

infinite-capacity-planning.long:
Infinite capacity planning is a rough-cut planning approach that loads demand into time buckets without limiting that demand to the actual capacity of the available resources. It is used to see how load builds up across a planning horizon, but the result is not an executable shop-floor schedule. The method answers the question of how much work is coming and when it is due, rather than whether the factory can physically perform that work at that time.

The approach is closely tied to ERP and MRP planning. According to the M365.FM episode "How Finite Capacity Scheduling Actually Works in Manufacturing", infinite capacity planning has an important purpose: ERP and MRP systems can quickly calculate demand, material requirements, planned orders and dates across thousands of products and long planning horizons. That speed and breadth are what make the approach valuable at the planning level. The episode also stresses the limit of the method, noting that a planned date does not prove that the factory has enough usable capacity to execute the work.

The contrast with finite capacity scheduling is where the concept is usually explained. The episode describes finite scheduling as the step that accounts for the physical constraints of machines, people, tools, materials, quality gates, maintenance and time. Finite scheduling asks the harder question of whether a specific operation can actually run at a given time on a given resource. Infinite capacity planning does not ask that question, so it tends to show demand as if resources could absorb any amount of it.

Microsoft Learn documentation for Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management explains finite capacity planning mainly by contrasting it with infinite loading. Infinite loading is not formally defined there, but its example shows that work is loaded onto resources regardless of whether spare capacity exists. As a result, resources can be overbooked, the schedule is less realistic, and delivery dates are not pushed out because of capacity. In the finite case, by contrast, the system considers resource limits within a configurable time fence. Planned production orders are backward-scheduled from the requirement date, and if capacity is unavailable the job is scheduled when capacity exists, which can push the delivery date out. The system may also request components earlier. Outside the time fence, scheduling behaves as infinite.

This means infinite loading is not only a separate method but also the default behavior beyond the fence in a finite setup. In Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, finite capacity must be enabled in master planning parameters, in the master plan and on each resource. The documentation walks through three examples with welding and assembling operations that show how a new sales order lands under infinite loading, a one-day time fence and a two-day time fence. The comparison makes visible how the same demand produces different dates depending on whether capacity limits are applied.

In practice, the choice is not between a correct and an incorrect method but between levels of detail. Infinite capacity planning suits long horizons, early load visibility and quick calculation across many products. Finite scheduling suits the near term, where a schedule has to be executable on the shop floor. The documentation adds cautions for the finite side, such as that finite scheduling considers only reserved capacity and is not suited to capacity that changes with requirements, and that a one-day fence is probably too short for most manufacturers. Reading both sources together, infinite capacity planning serves as the rough-cut view that shows where load accumulates, while finite capacity scheduling turns the relevant part of that plan into something the factory can run.

infopath.desc: InfoPath is a legacy Microsoft tool for designing electronic forms, often used with SharePoint; Power Apps is commonly seen as its successor.

faq.a: InfoPath is a legacy Microsoft tool for designing electronic forms, often used with SharePoint. Power Apps is commonly seen as its successor.
faq.q: What is InfoPath?

faq.a: The episode "Replace SharePoint 2013 Workflows Before Retirement" names Power Apps as the target for migrating legacy forms such as InfoPath, combined with Power Automate for workflows and approval processes.
faq.q: What replaces InfoPath forms?

faq.a: According to the episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained", the Enterprise CAL ($90) adds features including InfoPath Services, together with Access Services, business intelligence tools and Power View.
faq.q: How is InfoPath connected to SharePoint Server licensing?

infopath.long:
InfoPath is a legacy Microsoft product for designing electronic forms. It was widely used together with SharePoint, where forms built in InfoPath supported business processes such as approvals, document routing and notifications. Today, Power Apps is commonly seen as its successor, and much of the material about InfoPath now concerns how to move away from it.

In practice, InfoPath belonged to the classic SharePoint toolset. The M365.FM episode "Classic vs Modern SharePoint: Which Should You Use?" describes how classic SharePoint supported complex workflows, and that organizations could automate business processes using tools like SharePoint Designer and InfoPath. According to the episode, these legacy workflows helped manage approvals, document routing and notifications. The episode also notes that Microsoft has shifted its focus to newer workflow solutions: modern SharePoint integrates with Power Automate, which it describes as a more flexible and user-friendly way to build workflows. Organizations that still rely on classic workflows may therefore need to plan a migration.

InfoPath also appears in SharePoint Server licensing. The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" lists an Enterprise CAL priced at $90 that adds advanced features such as business intelligence tools, Access Services, InfoPath Services and Power View. This shows that InfoPath Services was a capability tied to the higher licensing tier of SharePoint Server, alongside other server-side services.

The most practical guidance in the available episodes concerns migration. "Replace SharePoint 2013 Workflows Before Retirement" presents Power Apps as the way to create custom, mobile-friendly applications tailored to specific needs, and treats moving from legacy forms such as InfoPath to Power Apps as a multi-step effort. The steps listed in the episode are: design the data architecture and application components; integrate with Power Automate for seamless workflows; implement approval processes using Power Automate Approval actions; create custom connectors for external web service calls; manage security and permissions effectively; plan for application lifecycle management (ALM); and identify reusable components. These steps suggest that replacing an InfoPath form is closer to rebuilding a small application than to a simple conversion, because the data model, the workflow logic, external calls and security all have to be considered.

InfoPath also features in career stories from the Microsoft ecosystem. In the episode "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]", Microsoft MVP and Microsoft Certified Trainer Nathalie Leenders describes a path that led from IT service management and support roles into SharePoint, InfoPath, Power BI and eventually Power Platform consulting. The episode uses her story to make the point that technology careers are rarely linear and often grow through curiosity, experimentation and hands-on problem solving. For many practitioners, experience with InfoPath forms was an early step toward the Power Platform skills now in demand.

Typical decisions around InfoPath center on inventory and replacement. Teams that still run InfoPath forms or related SharePoint workflows need to identify where they are used, decide whether the process is still needed, and choose a successor. The episodes point to Power Apps for the form and application layer and Power Automate for the workflow layer, with attention to approvals, connectors, permissions and lifecycle management during the move.

information-architecture.desc: Information architecture is the deliberate structuring of sites, content, metadata and navigation so information can be found and managed in Microsoft 365.

faq.a: It is the deliberate structuring of sites, content, metadata and navigation so that information can be found and managed. The M365.FM episodes break it into elements such as global navigation, hub navigation, local navigation, metadata, search and personalization.
faq.q: What is information architecture in SharePoint?

faq.a: The episodes argue that Copilot can only work with what the SharePoint structure lets it find and what permissions let it see. According to "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Accuracy with Information Architecture", wrong or inaccurate answers stem from broken site structure and weak metadata rather than from prompts or models.
faq.q: How does information architecture affect Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: Per "Fixing the SharePoint Metadata Gap for AI and Governance", AI services depend on context to retrieve information, and poorly structured content can lead to inaccurate responses. The episode suggests standardized classification, automated metadata capture and tools such as SharePoint Premium to enrich content.
faq.q: Why does metadata matter for information architecture?

information-architecture.long:
Information architecture is the deliberate structuring of sites, content, metadata and navigation so that information can be found and managed. In the Microsoft 365 context, the term most often comes up in connection with SharePoint Online, where it shapes how sites are organized, how documents are classified, how users move between areas of an intranet, and how search returns results. One M365.FM episode describes it as the biggest pain point in SharePoint implementations.

The episodes treat information architecture as a set of connected parts rather than a single setting. In "Make SharePoint Search Show the Right Files First", the foundations are broken into six core elements: global navigation, hub navigation, local navigation, metadata, search and personalization. The episode explains how each element supports the others, and argues that when a file's exact title can be pasted into intranet search and nothing comes back, the cause is an information architecture problem rather than a user problem. It also describes a flat site architecture combined with hubs as preferable to older, deeply nested structures.

Information architecture has become a recurring theme in discussions about Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Accuracy with Information Architecture" presents, in a noir-style narrative, the idea that Copilot, search and other enterprise AI tools can hallucinate or surface the wrong answers even when the data exists. The episode attributes this not to prompts or models but to broken site structure and weak metadata. Its practical advice includes giving Copilot context in requests and using relevant keywords in queries, while the underlying argument is that the structure of the content environment determines the quality of what AI can retrieve.

"SharePoint Information Architecture That Survives Copilot" frames the same point in terms of access: Copilot can only work with what the SharePoint structure lets it find and what permissions let it see. The episode covers information architecture for SharePoint Online in the Copilot era, including sites, hubs, content types, metadata, navigation and permissions. The stated goal is to structure content so that it stays findable, governable and safe to surface, which links information architecture directly to governance and security rather than treating it only as a usability topic.

Metadata is a central component in these discussions. "Fixing the SharePoint Metadata Gap for AI and Governance" explains that Copilot and other AI services depend on context to understand and retrieve information, and that poorly structured content can lead to inaccurate responses, reduced productivity and missed business insights. The episode covers strategies such as improving information architecture, standardizing content classification, automating metadata capture and building governance models that scale across large SharePoint environments. It also mentions SharePoint Premium, intelligent document processing and AI-powered classification as tools that can enrich content without relying entirely on manual input from users.

Information architecture also appears in the context of how people access files. "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync" notes that organizations organize content and streamline access by applying information architecture, which shapes global navigation, hub structure, metadata and search experiences. The episode contrasts mapped drives with OneDrive sync and presents a sound information architecture as helping both IT staff and business users work more effectively.

Taken together, the episodes position information architecture as the groundwork that search, navigation, governance and Copilot all depend on. Typical decisions around it include how to structure sites and hubs, which content types and metadata to standardize, how navigation should be layered, and how permissions interact with what can be surfaced. The common message across the episodes is that these structural choices should be made deliberately and early, because retrieval quality for both people and AI follows from them.

infrastructure-as-code.desc: Infrastructure as code (IaC) manages cloud infrastructure through versioned code and automated deployment instead of manual portal clicks, as covered in M365.FM episodes.

faq.a: Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the practice of managing and deploying cloud infrastructure through versioned code and automated deployment instead of manual configuration in a portal. Because the desired state is written in files, it can be reviewed, repeated and rebuilt.
faq.q: What is infrastructure as code?

faq.a: Bicep and Terraform are the two tools named in the topic's relations as common ways to describe resources as code. GitHub Actions can run such deployments automatically, and the Azure landing zone is usually deployed through code.
faq.q: Which tools are associated with infrastructure as code on Azure?

faq.a: Three episodes focus on it: "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained", "Azure Bicep at Scale: Modular Infrastructure as Code" and "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]". Other episodes, such as the one on Azure Local and landing zones, touch on it as part of a wider platform discussion.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover infrastructure as code?

infrastructure-as-code.long:
Infrastructure as code, often shortened to IaC and sometimes called Infrastruktur als Code, is the practice of managing and deploying cloud infrastructure through code instead of configuring resources by hand in a portal. The desired state of an environment is written down in files, which means it can be reviewed, stored in version control, repeated for other environments and rebuilt after a failure. It is generally treated as a part of DevOps, the broader practice it falls under.

The core idea is that infrastructure is handled the way application code is handled. Instead of a series of manual clicks that exist only in someone's memory, the configuration lives in a repository and changes to it follow the same review and automation steps as software changes. The M365.FM episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" presents it as a foundational practice for Azure, DevOps and cloud engineering. According to the episode, it covers concepts such as declarative versus imperative deployments, idempotency, version control and automation, and it explains why treating infrastructure like application code improves reliability and reduces operational risk.

In the Azure ecosystem, IaC is closely tied to two tools for describing resources as code: Bicep and Terraform. Teams choosing between approaches typically weigh how a tool fits their platform, their existing skills and the way deployments are run. The topic also relates to the Azure landing zone, which is usually deployed through code, and to GitHub Actions, which can run such deployments automatically as part of a pipeline. Together these pieces make a deployment repeatable: code defines the environment, version control records every change, and an automated workflow applies it.

The episode "Azure Bicep at Scale: Modular Infrastructure as Code" looks at Bicep as more than a cleaner replacement for ARM templates. The episode describes it as an architectural approach to managing cloud infrastructure at enterprise scale, focused on modular, reusable and maintainable code that supports long-term growth instead of creating technical debt. It says this approach supports collaboration between teams, reduces deployment errors and improves consistency across environments, and that it integrates with Azure Policy, CI/CD pipelines and governance frameworks.

The human and organizational side appears in "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", a conversation between host Mirko Peters and a Microsoft Azure MVP. It discusses the future of Azure and how Infrastructure as Code and DevOps are changing the way organizations build and manage cloud solutions, with a focus on modern cloud engineering and automation. The episode "Azure Local and Landing Zones: How to Build Hybrid Cloud the Right Way with Christoffer Klarskov Jakobsen [MVP]" places Infrastructure as Code alongside platform services, automated deployment pipelines and Azure Landing Zones, in a hybrid scenario where some workloads must stay close to factories, offices, regulated environments or latency-sensitive systems.

The practice also carries costs and trade-offs. The episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" notes that developers have been expected to become experts in Kubernetes, cloud networking, Infrastructure as Code, observability, security, compliance, cost optimization and CI/CD while still building business features. In that framing, the breadth of tooling can leave teams spending more time managing infrastructure than delivering customer value, which is one reason the episode examines how the DevOps model struggles at enterprise scale.

For readers deciding where to start, the sources point to a sequence: understand the concepts such as declarative deployment and idempotency, choose a tool such as Bicep or Terraform, keep the code in version control, and run it through an automated pipeline such as GitHub Actions. Landing zones and policy guardrails then become code that is deployed and maintained in the same way.

insider-risk-management.desc: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management correlates activity signals to detect, investigate and act on potentially risky behavior inside an organization.

faq.a: It is a compliance solution within Microsoft Purview that correlates activity signals to detect, investigate and act on potentially risky behavior inside an organization. It combines policy-based controls and investigation workflows with privacy safeguards.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Data Loss Prevention identifies and protects sensitive data across Microsoft 365 services, while Insider Risk Management detects and mitigates internal risks such as data leakage and IP theft. Insider Risk Management is described as the investigation and privacy-aware risk-management layer.
faq.q: How does Insider Risk Management differ from Data Loss Prevention?

faq.a: The episode "Purview Insider Risk Management: Setting It Up Without Alienating Employees" recommends starting with a narrow, well-explained scope and addressing policies, privacy settings, roles and communication with HR and legal, since the rollout needs trust as much as configuration.
faq.q: How should an organization roll out Insider Risk Management?

insider-risk-management.long:
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management is a compliance solution within Microsoft Purview that correlates activity signals to detect, investigate and act on potentially risky behavior inside an organization. It is aimed at risks that originate from people who already have legitimate access, which can arise from both malicious and negligent behavior. The solution is used by security, compliance and HR teams that need a structured way to reduce data-loss risk without treating every employee action as a security incident.

As described in the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management - Simply Explained", the product identifies potentially risky user activity while applying privacy safeguards, investigation workflows and policy-based controls. The episode cites reports indicating that approximately 22% of all data breaches stem from insider threats, which is given as the reason a dedicated approach to internal risk is needed. The emphasis is on policy-based detection and a defined investigation process rather than on blanket monitoring of all activity.

Insider Risk Management is part of Microsoft Purview and sits alongside other Purview capabilities. In the episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust", it is listed together with Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention, with the description that Insider Risk Management detects and mitigates internal risks such as data leakage and IP theft, while Data Loss Prevention identifies and protects sensitive data across Microsoft 365 services. The episode "Microsoft Purview Information Protection - Simply Explained" similarly points to Insider Risk Management as the investigation and privacy-aware risk-management layer that complements labeling and policy enforcement.

A recurring theme in the episodes is the use of the solution in the context of AI. The episode "Control Rogue AI Data Risks with Microsoft Purview" describes how employees may use AI tools in ways that put organizational data at risk, and presents Insider Risk Management as a way to spot and respond to such threats before they cause harm. According to the episode, this includes tracking how users interact with AI applications and setting up policies to identify and respond to risky AI usage.

Because the tooling concerns people rather than only systems, rollout design is treated as a central decision. The episode "Purview Insider Risk Management: Setting It Up Without Alienating Employees" states that the rollout needs trust as much as configuration. It covers setting up the product responsibly through scope, policies, privacy settings, roles, and communication with HR and legal, and it recommends starting with a narrow, well-explained scope. Typical decisions therefore include which risks to address first, which roles may see and act on findings, how privacy settings are applied, and how employees are informed.

In practice, the product is relevant for organizations that want to combine detection with governance: signals are correlated into potentially risky behavior, policies define what is in scope, and investigation workflows define how cases are handled and by whom. Its place within Microsoft Purview means it is usually evaluated together with Data Loss Prevention and Information Protection rather than in isolation. Official documentation for the product is published on Microsoft Learn under the Insider Risk Management section of the Purview documentation.

instance-metadata-service.desc: Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) is a REST endpoint at 169.254.169.254, reachable only from inside Azure resources, that returns VM metadata and managed identity tokens.

faq.a: It is a REST endpoint at the non-routable address 169.254.169.254. It can only be reached from inside the Azure resource, and the traffic never leaves the host.
faq.q: What is the address of Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS)?

faq.a: Requests must include a specific metadata header and an API version parameter, run over the primary network interface and bypass any proxy. Only GET over plain HTTP is supported, and a per-VM rate limit applies.
faq.q: What requirements apply to requests sent to IMDS?

faq.a: After enabling a managed identity and assigning permissions, a script on the Azure resource can request an access token from the IMDS identity endpoint. The episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" shows this with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: How is IMDS used with managed identities?

instance-metadata-service.long:
Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) is a REST API that provides information about running virtual machines and virtual machine scale set instances in Microsoft Azure. It listens on the non-routable address 169.254.169.254 and can only be reached from inside the resource itself; the traffic never leaves the host. The service supports Linux and Windows VMs as well as flexible scale sets, and it is part of Microsoft Azure.

The main purpose of Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) is to help with managing and configuring instances. The documentation describes several endpoint categories. Instance metadata covers compute, network and storage details such as SKU and network configuration, plus tags and user data. Attested data provides signed documents that prove a VM runs in Azure. Another category issues tokens for managed identities. Further categories cover load balancer metadata, scheduled events such as upcoming maintenance, and a list of supported API versions. Typical uses named in the documentation include retrieving a unique VM identifier, reading fault and update domains for replica placement, reading tags, determining the Azure environment, and obtaining signed attestation documents.

A request to Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) has to follow a few rules. It must carry a specific metadata header and include an API version parameter. It has to run over the primary network interface and must bypass any proxy. Only GET requests over plain HTTP are supported. A rate limit applies per VM, and an error is returned when it is exceeded.

Security is an important consideration. According to the documentation, the API is unauthenticated and open to every process running inside the VM. For this reason, sensitive data does not belong in the metadata or user data that the service exposes. Because any process in the VM can call it, the identity token endpoint in particular is something to keep in mind when deciding which workloads run on a given machine.

One common scenario is acquiring access tokens for a managed identity. The M365.FM episode "Use Managed Identity with PowerShell for Microsoft Graph" (2025-12-08) describes this flow. The steps are to enable a managed identity on the Azure resource, assign the required Microsoft Graph API permissions to that identity, and then use PowerShell to request a token from the local Azure Instance Metadata Service. The example in the episode builds a token URI on the 169.254.169.254 address with the identity OAuth2 token path, an API version and the target resource, here the Microsoft Graph address. It sends the request with a header named Metadata set to "true" using Invoke-RestMethod and reads the access token from the response. This shows how the metadata header and API version requirement look in practice, and how a script running on an Azure resource can authenticate without storing credentials.

In summary, Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) serves two roles inside Azure: it exposes descriptive data about the VM or scale set instance for management and configuration, and it acts as the local endpoint from which managed identity tokens are obtained. The official documentation lists no license requirements for the service itself.

integration-runtime.desc: Integration runtime is the compute infrastructure in Azure Data Factory that runs activities and connects them to linked services; types are Azure, self-hosted and Azure-SSIS.

faq.a: There are three types: Azure, self-hosted and Azure-SSIS. Each is chosen according to where the data sits and what kind of workload needs to run.
faq.q: What are the types of integration runtime in Azure Data Factory?

faq.a: It is the compute infrastructure that runs activities in Azure Data Factory and acts as the bridge between an activity and a linked service.
faq.q: What does an integration runtime do?

faq.a: The episode "How to Fix Azure at Scale Without Buying More Tools" describes a case where all pipelines were triggered simultaneously and overwhelmed the integration runtime, which caused a missed SLA until triggers were staggered manually.
faq.q: Why can an integration runtime become a bottleneck?

integration-runtime.long:
Integration runtime is the compute infrastructure in Azure Data Factory that executes activities. It acts as the bridge between an activity and a linked service: an activity describes the work to be done, a linked service describes the data store or compute resource involved, and the integration runtime is the engine that connects the two and performs the work. Without an integration runtime, a pipeline in Azure Data Factory has nothing to run on.

There are three types of integration runtime: Azure, self-hosted and Azure-SSIS. The choice of type depends on where the data or the target systems are located and what kind of workload has to run. The Azure type is managed within Azure. The self-hosted type runs on infrastructure that the organisation operates itself, which is relevant when sources sit outside the cloud boundary or inside a controlled network. The Azure-SSIS type is the variant used for SQL Server Integration Services packages. Because the facts available here describe each type only by name, detailed capabilities and sizing options should be checked in the official Microsoft documentation.

In practice, the integration runtime matters most when pipelines run in volume. The episode "How to Fix Azure at Scale Without Buying More Tools" lists several Azure Data Factory problems that illustrate how a lack of understanding of the fundamentals can cause inefficiency and extra cost. One example is an integration runtime that became overwhelmed when all pipelines were triggered at the same time. According to the episode, this led to a missed SLA and required manual staggering of triggers. The same list mentions a limitation on nested ForEach loops, which had to be simulated with parent-child pipelines, and a failure when field types changed. The episode uses these cases as part of a broader argument that ignoring architectural fundamentals increases risk.

The integration runtime also appears in hybrid and governance scenarios. The episode "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" names Integration Runtime together with the on-premises data gateway as a way to give cloud automation secure access to on-premises systems. This is described as one of the benefits for enterprise scenarios, alongside reusable components such as child workflows and templates.

The episode "Microsoft Purview Data Governance for Information Architects" refers to the self-hosted type in the context of private networking. Its recommendations include using self-hosted integration runtime VMs in both a primary and a secondary region so that Data Map scan traffic stays within the governance domain. This is combined with a governance portal private endpoint in the primary region, account and ingestion private endpoints in both regions so that data sources can be scanned locally, and DNS configuration for multiple accounts using private endpoints.

Typical decisions around an integration runtime therefore include which of the three types fits the data source, where the compute should run relative to the data, and how many pipelines may run in parallel against the same runtime. The episodes suggest treating trigger scheduling and capacity as design questions rather than leaving them to chance, since simultaneous triggers were the cause of the overload described in "How to Fix Azure at Scale Without Buying More Tools". For scanning scenarios in Microsoft Purview, the self-hosted type is presented as a means of keeping traffic inside a defined network boundary.

integration-testing.desc: Integration testing is a software testing practice that checks whether components work together with the real services they rely on, such as databases, queues and authentication.

faq.a: Unit testing checks whether a single part of the code, such as one function, works by itself. Integration testing checks that different parts work together, including the real services they depend on.
faq.q: What is the difference between unit testing and integration testing?

faq.a: According to the episode on automated testing for Power Apps and Dataverse, it validates how Dataverse, connectors and external systems work together and helps spot problems with data flow and end-to-end flows.
faq.q: What does integration testing cover in Power Apps and Dataverse solutions?

faq.a: The Dev Tunnels episode describes exposing a local service through a public URL so a Microsoft 365 App can be tested, including for integration testing, with a persistent tunnel keeping the URL stable for OAuth redirect URIs.
faq.q: How do Dev Tunnels relate to integration testing?

integration-testing.long:
Integration testing is a software testing practice that verifies that components of an application work together with the real services they depend on. Those dependencies typically include queues, databases, authentication and configuration. Where a unit test examines one piece of code in isolation, an integration test checks the connections between pieces, so that problems in data flow, communication or setup surface before a release.

The M365.FM episode "Unit vs Integration vs Frontend Testing" places integration testing between two other levels. Unit testing checks whether a single part of the code works by itself, for example a login function in a .NET app. Integration testing makes sure different parts of an app work together, for example testing user profile updates against a real dependency. Frontend testing looks at the whole application from the user's point of view. The episode frames these as complementary levels that together help a team improve quality and ship with more confidence, with each level answering a different question about the software.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept shows up in several settings. The episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" describes integration testing as checking how different parts of a solution work together, and it names the validation of integrations between Dataverse, connectors and external systems as a typical use. According to that episode, this type of test helps spot problems with data flow and end-to-end flows. Unit tests, by contrast, cover small pieces of logic such as formulas or functions, and UI and end-to-end tests focus on the user experience of screens and forms.

The episode "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" applies the same layering to agents built with an agent framework. It describes unit tests for each skill and function of an agent, followed by integration tests that verify that the different parts of the agent interact as intended. The episode recommends developing test suites that cover both routine and edge cases, so that issues are caught before deployment and agents perform as expected in real-world scenarios.

Integration testing also appears in data migration work. In "The Death of the Chatbot: Why Your Dataverse Strategy Is Broken", the testing and rehearsal phase of a Dynamics 365 migration includes entity and integration testing. That phase involves unit and integration tests across linked entities and full-scale rehearsals with production data volumes. The episode connects this to careful management of entity relationships, which is where integration problems tend to arise when data moves between structures.

A further, more practical angle comes from "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels". The episode shows how the devtunnel command can expose a locally running service, for example on port 5000, through a public URL that can be shared with a team or used for integration testing of a Microsoft 365 App. It notes that a persistent, named tunnel keeps the same URL across sessions, which matters for OAuth redirect URIs and consistent testing. This illustrates how integration tests often depend on reachable endpoints and stable authentication settings.

Taken together, the episodes treat integration testing as one layer in a broader test strategy rather than a replacement for unit or frontend testing. The decisions around it usually concern what to test against real services, which dependencies such as authentication or configuration must be present, and how integration checks fit into migration rehearsals or pre-deployment validation.

intelligent-recap.desc: Intelligent recap is a Microsoft Teams Premium feature that creates AI notes, suggested tasks, chapters and highlights from transcribed meetings and calls.

faq.a: It requires a Microsoft 365 subscription with Teams plus a Teams Premium or Microsoft Copilot license. Transcription must be enabled, and recording is needed for the full experience; the audio recap requires Copilot.
faq.q: What does Intelligent recap require?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it offers AI notes and recommended tasks, personalized timeline markers, speaker markers, chapters and topics, an audio recap and a video recap.
faq.q: What does the Recap tab contain after a meeting?

faq.a: The episode "Cultural Nuance in Global Meetings Beyond Translation" warns against overtrusting AI-generated summaries, because clean outputs can create a false sense of clarity and do not interpret intent.
faq.q: Can AI-generated recaps be fully trusted?

intelligent-recap.long:
Intelligent recap is a feature in Microsoft Teams that uses AI to reduce note-taking and follow-up after meetings, events and calls. It is part of Teams Premium, and an intelligent call recap is also available with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license. After a transcribed meeting, the feature generates AI notes, suggested tasks, chapters and personalized highlights, so participants and people who missed the session can review what happened without replaying the whole recording.

According to Microsoft Learn, the Recap tab in Teams offers several elements. These include AI notes and recommended tasks, personalized timeline markers for mentions, screen shares and joins, speaker markers, chapters and topics, an audio recap and a video recap. For events, recap is available only to organizers, co-organizers and presenters. For PSTN and peer-to-peer VoIP calls, a Recap button offers AI notes and tasks instead of the full meeting layout.

Several prerequisites apply. Intelligent recap requires a Microsoft 365 subscription with Teams plus either a Teams Premium or a Microsoft Copilot license. The audio recap requires Copilot, and PSTN calls additionally need Teams Phone and a calling plan. Transcription must be enabled in the meeting. Recording is needed for the full experience; without it, the recap lacks the recording, speakers, topics and chapters. The video recap needs a meeting of at least 10 minutes that is both recorded and transcribed, and it can hold up to 100 highlights.

Two parts of the feature are described as public preview. The audio recap combines up to eight scheduled meetings and is stored for 60 days. Multilingual recap translates recaps into the languages of the participants. Recaps can also be shared with external attendees through Outlook, which matters for follow-up with customers or partners who are not part of the organization.

In practice, the feature supports decisions about licensing and meeting setup. Teams that want recap output need to confirm that transcription is switched on and decide whether to record meetings, because the quality and completeness of the recap depends on both. Organizations also need to separate the Teams Premium path from the Copilot path, since some outputs, such as the audio recap, depend on Copilot.

The M365.FM episode "Cultural Nuance in Global Meetings Beyond Translation" discusses Intelligent Recap together with live translation as enablers within Microsoft Teams Premium rather than complete solutions. The episode says these features improve accessibility and post-meeting analysis but do not interpret intent. Their value, as described there, lies in helping teams revisit conversations, identify ambiguity, and look for signals such as weak commitments or unclear ownership after the meeting. The episode also warns against overtrusting AI-generated summaries, noting that clean, well-structured outputs can create a false sense of clarity.

The episode "Copilot Cowork with Vesa "Vesku" Nopanen [MVP]" mentions Intelligent Recap among AI-powered Teams tools. It describes the feature as summarizing key points and action items to help manage tasks efficiently, alongside live captions for accessibility and real-time translation for global collaboration.

internet-of-things.desc: Internet of Things (IoT) is the network of physical devices such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data.

faq.a: IoT is the network of physical devices such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data.
faq.q: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained", Azure Sphere is Microsoft's end-to-end security platform for IoT devices, combining certified secure hardware, a custom Linux-based operating system and a cloud security service that authenticates devices and delivers automatic security updates.
faq.q: How does Azure Sphere relate to IoT?

faq.a: The episodes describe Azure Event Hubs for real-time ingestion of telemetry from devices and sensors, and Event Grid for routing telemetry data for real-time processing and alerts.
faq.q: Which Azure services handle IoT telemetry according to the episodes?

internet-of-things.long:
Internet of Things (IoT) describes the network of physical devices, such as sensors, appliances and industrial controllers, that connect to the internet to collect and exchange data. Instead of being isolated machines, these devices send information to other systems and can receive instructions or updates in return. The term covers a wide range of equipment, from small sensors that report measurements to controllers that run industrial processes.

In practice, IoT matters because connected devices produce data that organizations can monitor, analyze and act on. The M365.FM episodes touch on this from several angles: how devices are secured, how their data is ingested at scale, how events from them are routed to other services, and how they feed automation. Taken together, they show that IoT is less a single product than a pattern that spans hardware, networking, cloud services and security.

Security is one central concern. The episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained" describes Azure Sphere as Microsoft's end-to-end security platform for IoT devices. According to the episode, it protects connected devices from the silicon chip all the way to the cloud rather than focusing only on software security. The platform combines three core components: certified secure hardware, a custom Linux-based operating system, and a cloud security service that continuously authenticates devices and delivers automatic security updates throughout their lifetime. This illustrates one typical decision around IoT: because devices stay deployed for a long time and are exposed to a network, security and update delivery have to be considered across the whole device lifecycle.

Data ingestion is another recurring theme. The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" describes Azure Event Hubs as scalable and reliable in the IoT sector. According to the episode, it supports real-time ingestion of telemetry data from devices and sensors, which allows organizations to monitor, analyze and alert based on the data received. The episode also says it supports processing of large data volumes, which helps data-driven decision-making. Telemetry in this context means the continuous stream of readings and status information that devices send to a central service.

Event routing and automation form a third area. The episode "Event Grid - Simply Explained" lists IoT among the use cases for Event Grid, where telemetry data can be routed for real-time processing and alerts. It places this next to other scenarios such as triggering Azure Functions for tasks like image processing, notifying teams about builds and deployments, and implementing monitoring for security alerts. The episode presents serverless architectures built on Event Grid as offering dynamic scaling and reduced operational overhead compared with automation approaches that rely on fixed infrastructure.

IoT also appears in the discussion of automation governance. In "High-Performance Automation Control Plane for Power Automate", IoT is named alongside artificial intelligence, machine learning and service-as-software as a technology that will shape how automation is managed. The episode describes IoT as connecting various devices and systems and providing data and context for automation processes. In that framing, device data becomes an input that makes automated workflows more informed and responsive.

For people searching for the term, the main takeaways from these episodes are that an IoT solution usually involves several layers: secured devices, a way to ingest large streams of telemetry, a mechanism to route events to the right consumers, and automation or analytics that act on the results. The sources do not prescribe a single architecture, and the episodes discuss each layer through specific Azure services rather than as one unified product.

intranet.desc: An intranet is a private company website or network for internal news, policies and tools; M365.FM covers it through SharePoint, Viva Connections and AI-driven design.

faq.a: An intranet is a private company website or network for internal information such as news, policies and tools. Classic static versions are described as having suffered from low engagement and poor mobile access.
faq.q: What is an intranet?

faq.a: The episodes treat SharePoint as the platform for building intranets, covering navigation, metadata, search and pages. One episode says modern SharePoint sites and pages can act as lightweight knowledge hubs that replace many traditional intranet portal needs.
faq.q: How does SharePoint relate to the intranet in the M365.FM episodes?

faq.a: According to the episode "Viva Connections - Simply Explained", Viva Connections integrates with Microsoft Teams and SharePoint to give access to the company's intranet, with a personalized dashboard and a News Reader that tailors updates to a person's role.
faq.q: What role does Viva Connections play for an intranet?

intranet.long:
An intranet is a private company website or network that gives employees access to internal information such as news, policies and tools. It is separate from the public internet and is meant for the people inside an organization. Classic static intranets are described as having suffered from low engagement and poor mobile access, which is one reason the topic keeps returning in discussions about modern workplace design.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the intranet is most often built on SharePoint. The M365.FM episode "Make SharePoint Search Show the Right Files First" frames intranet quality as an Information Architecture (IA) question. It breaks IA into six core elements: global navigation, hub navigation, local navigation, metadata, search and personalization. According to the episode, each element supports the others, and a user who pastes the exact title of a file into intranet search and gets nothing back has an IA problem rather than a user problem. The episode also mentions Viva Connections as a way to deliver the right content to the right roles without manual tinkering.

Navigation is a recurring theme. The episode "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync" describes site maps as a way to give an overview of a SharePoint environment, showing how sites connect and where important content sits. It says top navigation helps employees move around the intranet quickly and that custom navigation options go beyond the default settings, supporting branding and user experience goals. It also lists common navigation bar types, including an informative navigation bar with a logo, Quick Links, real-time updates and a clean design.

Knowledge management is another angle. In "Fix SharePoint Knowledge Management", the episode argues that metadata-driven content delivery often outperforms folder structures, because properly applied metadata enables dynamic views, rollups and targeted content without moving files. It also says SharePoint pages and modern sites can act as lightweight knowledge hubs, replacing many traditional intranet portal needs with less custom code. On search, the episode states that relevance can be improved considerably by tuning managed properties, synonyms and result sources, so that search becomes more of a configuration task than a development one. It further mentions that Viva Topics can build topic pages and curate experts by analyzing documents and communications, reducing manual taxonomy work.

The intranet is also discussed as something that is changing in form. "AI-Powered SharePoint Intranets: Beyond Static Design" says the traditional SharePoint intranet is reaching the end of its lifecycle, because manually designed sites, static navigation structures and curated content pages quickly become outdated. The episode explores how artificial intelligence can shift intranet design from a static publishing model to a dynamic, adaptive experience, where intranets become intelligent knowledge experiences rather than static websites. Topics named include personalization, knowledge discovery and content recommendation.

On the employee-facing side, "Viva Connections - Simply Explained" describes how Viva Connections integrates with Microsoft Teams and SharePoint to provide access to a company's intranet. The episode says it offers a personalized dashboard for organizing essential resources and a News Reader feature that tailors updates to a person's role. It presents resource centralization as a one-stop platform for emails, documents and meetings, with the stated aim of higher engagement and less time spent searching for information.

Taken together, the episodes treat the intranet less as a single product and more as a combination of structure, content and delivery: navigation and metadata decide how content is organized, search decides how it is found, and personalization and AI decide who sees what. Typical decisions around an intranet include how to structure navigation across hubs and sites, whether to rely on metadata instead of folders, how much to tune search, and whether to surface intranet content inside Teams through Viva Connections.

intrusion-detection-and-prevention-syste.desc: Intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS): signature-based monitoring of network traffic that alerts on or blocks malicious activity, offered in Azure Firewall Premium.

faq.a: In Azure, the intrusion detection and prevention system is a feature of the Azure Firewall Premium SKU. The episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" also lists it alongside TLS inspection as a Premium tier capability.
faq.q: Where is IDPS available in Azure?

faq.a: Each signature can run in one of three modes: disabled, alert, or alert and deny. The effective mode depends on the policy, a parent policy, an override or the system default.
faq.q: What modes can an IDPS signature use?

faq.a: Encrypted HTTPS traffic is only inspected in content when TLS inspection is enabled. Without it, the payload of encrypted sessions is not matched against signatures.
faq.q: Does IDPS inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic?

intrusion-detection-and-prevention-syste.long:
An intrusion detection and prevention system (IDPS) is a security capability that monitors a network for malicious activity, logs and reports what it finds, and can optionally block that activity. In the Azure ecosystem, this capability is delivered as a feature of the Azure Firewall Premium SKU rather than as a separate product. It is used to add inspection of traffic patterns on top of ordinary firewall rules, so that known attack techniques can be recognized even when the traffic would otherwise be allowed by address, port or protocol.

The approach in Azure Firewall Premium is signature based. A signature describes a specific pattern, such as a byte sequence in network traffic or a command sequence known from malware, and the firewall compares passing traffic against these patterns. According to the Microsoft Learn implementation guide, the signatures cover the application layer and the network layer, are fully managed, and are updated continuously. Because the signature set is maintained and refreshed by the platform, administrators do not need to author or distribute detection patterns themselves for the managed set.

The inspection applies to several traffic paths: inbound traffic, spoke-to-spoke traffic and outbound traffic, including traffic to and from on-premises networks. This makes the capability relevant in hub-and-spoke network designs, where the firewall sits between workloads, and in hybrid scenarios where traffic crosses into or out of a private network.

Behavior is controlled per signature. Each signature can run in one of three modes: disabled, alert, or alert and deny. The effective mode depends on the firewall policy, a parent policy, an override, or the system default. Signatures also carry a severity and a traffic direction. Private IP ranges follow RFC 1918 by default and can be adjusted to match the actual address space of an environment. A bypass list allows certain addresses or subnets to be excluded from filtering, which is a typical decision point when a known, trusted source produces traffic that would otherwise trigger detections. Alerts can be found in the network rule logs, so reviewing those logs is part of operating the feature. The number of custom IDPS rules is capped, which matters when planning policy beyond the managed signatures.

One limitation concerns encryption. Encrypted HTTPS traffic is only inspected in content when TLS inspection is enabled. Without TLS inspection, the firewall cannot match signatures against the payload of encrypted sessions, so the two Premium features are closely linked in practice.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Firewall - Simply Explained" places the IDPS within the Premium tier. The episode says that with the Premium tier, users gain access to features like TLS inspection and an Intrusion Detection and Prevention System (IDPS), and describes this tier as suited to enterprises that demand the highest level of network security. It also gives a pricing breakdown for Azure Firewall Premium: a deployment hour rate of $1.75, data processing at $0.065 per GB, and extra cost for capacity units if enabled. As an example, the episode states that processing 50 TB of data monthly would cost around £2,880. Because the IDPS is part of Premium, these figures are relevant when deciding whether the added inspection capabilities justify the tier.

intune.desc: Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps, enforcing policies on Windows, macOS, iOS and Android and informing Conditional Access.

faq.a: Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps. It enforces configuration and compliance policies on Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, deploys applications and helps protect company data.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Intune used for?

faq.a: Microsoft Intune feeds device status into Conditional Access, so access to company data can depend on device compliance. Microsoft Entra ID holds the identities of the users who own the managed devices.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Intune relate to Conditional Access and Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" presents Intune as Microsoft's cloud-first approach and SCCM as the long-standing enterprise standard. It notes that many organizations use both together during their transition to the cloud.
faq.q: Does Microsoft Intune replace SCCM?

intune.long:
Microsoft Intune is Microsoft's cloud-based endpoint management solution. It is used to manage devices, applications and users across Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Linux from a single cloud platform. Microsoft develops it, and it is a paid product. On M365.FM it is classified as a Microsoft tool and as an identity and security tool, and it is closely related to Microsoft Entra ID.

In practice, Microsoft Intune lets IT teams deploy applications, enforce security policies, protect company data and manage endpoints centrally. It enforces configuration and compliance policies on managed devices, so that settings and security requirements are applied consistently rather than device by device. The M365.FM overview episode "Microsoft Intune - Simply Explained" describes it as a cornerstone of modern workplace management. Related material in the show notes also mentions remote support, where administrators can resolve problems and offer assistance remotely, and security enforcement that checks devices against organizational standards.

A key part of how Microsoft Intune works is the link to identity. Microsoft Entra ID holds the identities of the users who own the devices, while Intune reports the status of those devices. That device status is fed into Conditional Access, which means access to company data can depend on whether a device is compliant. This is why Intune sits at the boundary between endpoint management and identity protection, and why it is listed as an identity and security tool as well as a management tool.

A common decision around Microsoft Intune is how it relates to System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM). The episode "SCCM vs Intune: Key Differences | Simply Explained" presents SCCM as the long-standing enterprise standard and Intune as Microsoft's cloud-first approach to managing modern devices. The episode notes that the choice is not always one or the other: many organizations use both together while they transition to the cloud.

Licensing and security architecture are another recurring theme. In "Licensing, Security & Management: Making Microsoft 365 Defender and Intune Work Together with Videsh Chavan", the discussion frames Microsoft 365 licensing as an architecture decision rather than purely procurement. The episode says that licensing choices directly influence security architecture, endpoint management, identity protection and operational costs, and it explores how licensing, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Defender, identity and endpoint security can work together instead of operating as separate silos.

Managed service providers also appear in the episodes. "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" features a Microsoft Intune MVP and discusses how an MSP can build a scalable, Microsoft-first security practice using Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Entra ID. The episode argues that customers now expect proactive security, cloud expertise and modern identity protection from day one, and that identity has become the new security perimeter.

Looking ahead, "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision with Christiaan Brinkhoff [Nerdio]" explores where Windows 365 and Microsoft Intune can support more autonomous IT operations and Cloud PC management. It places Intune alongside Agent 365, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Entra, with governed workflows, observability, identity and human oversight as part of the picture. Taken together, the episodes position Microsoft Intune as the device and app management layer that connects endpoint operations, identity and security in the Microsoft ecosystem.

inventory-dimensions.desc: Inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365 are the product, storage and tracking attributes that distinguish stock records, such as site, warehouse, location, batch and serial number.

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn training unit names three: product dimensions (configuration, size, style, color, version), storage dimensions that control how items are stored and removed, and tracking dimensions (batch and serial numbers).
faq.q: What are the main categories of inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365?

faq.a: They let companies trace products and support quality assurance and warranty handling, according to the Microsoft Learn training unit.
faq.q: Why are batch and serial numbers treated as tracking dimensions?

faq.a: The Learn unit advises planning how inventory should work before creating dimensions, so that they reflect how the company actually categorizes and handles each item.
faq.q: How should inventory dimensions be planned?

inventory-dimensions.long:
Inventory dimensions in Dynamics 365 are the labels that distinguish one stock record from another. Instead of holding a single quantity per item, the system records stock against combinations of dimensions, so that the same product can be tracked separately by where it is, what it looks like and how it can be traced. They are a core part of how Dynamics 365 Inventory Management answers questions about quantities, locations, availability, ownership and movements.

According to the Microsoft Learn training unit on Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, inventory dimensions fall into three categories. Product dimensions describe the physical characteristics of an item: configuration, size, style, color and version. Storage dimensions control how items are stored and removed from inventory, for example site, warehouse and location. Tracking dimensions are batch and serial numbers, which let companies trace products and support quality assurance and warranty handling. The version dimension, which tracks multiple versions of a product, must be enabled through a configuration key.

The Learn unit advises planning how inventory should work before creating dimensions. The dimensions that are set up should reflect how the company actually categorizes and handles each item, rather than being added without a clear purpose. This planning step matters because the choice of dimensions determines at what level stock is recorded, reserved, moved and counted.

A packaging product dimensions feature adds three physical dimension types. Storage is used together with location volumetrics to decide how many items fit in warehouse locations, and it is the default. Packing is used for containerization and manual packing. Nested packing is used for multilevel packing. Volume is calculated from depth, height, width, weight and the units entered on the released product. If a product is placed where it will not fit, the system returns an error. The unit does not explain dimension groups.

In the M365.FM episode "Dynamics 365 Inventory Management - Simply Explained", Mirko Peters walks through how Dynamics 365 Inventory Management works from supplier receipt to customer shipment. The episode lists inventory dimensions among the topics covered, alongside reservations, transfers, costing, cycle counting, safety stock, consignment inventory and the connection between inventory and finance. It frames inventory management as a shared stock record across the business that connects quantities, locations, availability, ownership, movements and financial value, with dimensions being one of the mechanisms that make that record specific enough to answer where stock is and whether it can be used.

Typical decisions around inventory dimensions include which items need batch or serial tracking for traceability or warranty reasons, how detailed the site, warehouse and location structure should be, and which product attributes such as size or color must be tracked as separate stock. Because these choices shape how stock is stored, reserved and counted, they are usually settled early in an implementation and aligned with real warehouse and product handling practice.

iops.desc: IOPS (input/output operations per second) measures how many read or write requests a storage system handles each second; it is a core Azure storage metric.

faq.a: IOPS stands for input/output operations per second. It describes how many individual read or write operations a storage system can perform each second.
faq.q: What does IOPS mean?

faq.a: IOPS counts individual storage operations per second, while throughput describes how much data can move during a period. Per the Elastic SAN episode, databases often issue many small reads and writes, which makes IOPS especially important for them.
faq.q: What is the difference between IOPS and throughput?

faq.a: They appear as specifications of storage options. The Azure Managed Disks episode lists Ultra Disks with a maximum of 400,000 IOPS and a maximum throughput of 10,000 MB/s.
faq.q: Where do IOPS limits appear in Azure storage?

iops.long:
IOPS stands for input/output operations per second. It is a measure of storage performance that describes how many individual read or write requests a storage system can handle in one second. In the M365.FM episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained", the term is defined as the number of individual storage operations that can be performed each second, and it is discussed next to throughput as one of the two central concepts when talking about storage performance.

IOPS and throughput describe different things. IOPS counts operations, while throughput describes how much data can move during a given period. The Elastic SAN episode points out that databases frequently generate large numbers of small reads and writes, which makes IOPS particularly important for database-style workloads. A workload that moves large files in a few big transfers is mostly a throughput question, whereas a workload that issues many small requests is mostly an IOPS question. When sizing storage, both values are therefore looked at together.

In the Azure context, IOPS appears as a published specification of storage options. The episode "Azure Managed Disks - Simply Explained" lists Ultra Disks with a maximum of 400,000 IOPS and a maximum throughput of 10,000 MB/s, alongside a maximum disk size of 65,536 GiB. According to the episode, Ultra Disks suit data-intensive applications such as SAP HANA and Oracle Database and transaction-heavy workloads that need consistent performance and low latency, and they cannot be used as an OS disk. The episode "Azure Disk Storage - Simply Explained" explains that disk performance is measured through IOPS and throughput, and it places this alongside OS disks, data disks, temporary disks, snapshots, backups, encryption, redundancy and resizing as part of choosing the right disk type for a scenario such as a production database or an enterprise application.

IOPS also plays a role in cost and capacity planning. The Elastic SAN episode notes that when every workload is sized individually for its own peak, organizations can end up paying for performance that remains unused for much of the time, because some systems consume significant storage bandwidth overnight while others stay almost idle. Understanding IOPS requirements per workload is therefore a prerequisite for deciding whether performance should be provisioned per disk or pooled and shared.

IOPS is equally relevant for diagnosing problems. The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" includes a checklist for Azure VM performance issues that starts with confirming baseline metrics per VM, including CPU, memory, disk IOPS, throughput and network, over expected workloads. It recommends enabling Azure Monitor metrics with a Log Analytics workspace, checking collection frequency and retention, and creating alerts for sustained high CPU, memory pressure, disk queue length or network saturation. Baselines of disk IOPS make it possible to tell whether a slowdown stems from storage limits or from another resource.

The episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" connects IOPS to the location of data. It argues that managed storage adds network hops, caps IOPS and adds latency to every read and write, and that proximity is the fix rather than adding more nodes. Azure Container Storage v2 is described as placing hot data on local NVMe inside AKS nodes through a CSI-based, ephemeral driver that stripes across all NVMe disks, with multi-GB/s throughput and roughly a million IOPS, as the episode puts it. Taken together, the episodes treat IOPS as a figure that must be matched to the access pattern of the workload, checked against the limits of the chosen storage service, and monitored over time.

isa-95.desc: ISA-95 is an international standard that defines how enterprise systems and manufacturing control systems exchange information, using a common hierarchy and object models.

faq.a: ISA-95, or ANSI/ISA-95, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation that describes how enterprise systems and control systems exchange information through an automated interface. It covers batch, continuous and repetitive manufacturing.
faq.q: What is ISA-95?

faq.a: Part 1 defines terminology and object models, Part 2 gives object attributes, Part 3 covers manufacturing operations management at level 3, Part 4 covers operations management objects and attributes, and Part 5 covers business-to-manufacturing transactions. Further parts address messaging, alias services and information exchange profiles.
faq.q: What do the parts of ISA-95 cover?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode on MQTT and OPC UA describes the ISA-95 enterprise-to-cell hierarchy as a naming contract for locating assets consistently. It also says a Unified Namespace is a common event space for publishing facts, not a new master database.
faq.q: How does ISA-95 relate to a Unified Namespace?

isa-95.long:
ISA-95, formally ANSI/ISA-95, is an international standard from the International Society of Automation. It describes how enterprise systems and control systems should exchange information through an automated interface. The standard applies to batch, continuous and repetitive manufacturing. Its stated goals are consistent terminology, shared information models and shared operations models between suppliers and manufacturers, so that responsibilities and interfaces can be placed in a predictable way.

The standard is organised in several parts. Part 1 defines terminology and object models, including a hierarchy model based on the Purdue model, an equipment hierarchy, functional data-flow models and operations activity models. Part 2 gives the attributes of each object. Part 3 covers manufacturing operations management activities at level 3, the production and MES layer. Part 4 covers objects and attributes for operations management, and Part 5 covers business-to-manufacturing transactions. Further parts address messaging, alias services and information exchange profiles. The standard also supplies reference models for production, quality, maintenance and inventory activities and for the information passed between them.

In practice, ISA-95 is used as a map. The levels run from the physical process and its control, through manufacturing operations management, up to enterprise planning. This makes it possible to say which system owns which data, where an interface belongs, and how a plant-floor event relates to business-level processes. Teams use it when they need to decide where a piece of logic should live, for example whether a function belongs in a control system, in a manufacturing execution layer or in enterprise planning.

The M365.FM episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" discusses ISA-95 in the context of Microsoft-based manufacturing data architectures. According to the episode, the enterprise-to-cell hierarchy of ISA-95 can serve as a naming contract: a stable map used to locate assets consistently before changing business context such as work orders and products is applied. The idea is that asset identity stays fixed while context around it changes. The same episode argues for normalizing data once near the source, at the edge, rather than mapping it several times in different downstream systems, and notes that a raw state code means little without context from the machine.

The episode also places ISA-95 next to the Unified Namespace (UNS) discussion. It describes UNS as a common event space where IT and OT publish facts, and cautions that it is not a new master database and not a shortcut to a shared operating model without effort. In that framing, an ISA-95-style hierarchy gives the namespace a consistent structure for naming and locating assets, while the work of agreeing on meaning and ownership still has to be done.

A caveat applies to the available sources: the public description of the standard does not detail each individual level, and edition dates are reported inconsistently, so anyone adopting it for a project should consult the standard itself for exact definitions of the levels and object attributes.

iscsi.desc: iSCSI (Internet Small Computer Systems Interface) carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, giving servers network access to block storage.

faq.a: iSCSI (Internet Small Computer Systems Interface) is a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, giving servers network access to block storage.
faq.q: What is iSCSI?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" states that Azure Elastic SAN volumes connect to workloads using iSCSI, which carries storage commands between the server and the Elastic SAN across the network.
faq.q: How does iSCSI relate to Azure Elastic SAN?

faq.a: The episode "Speed Fabric and AKS Workloads with Local NVMe Storage" mentions setting the MTU to 9000 at both the cluster and virtual machine levels to reduce packet fragmentation, and keeping the Layer 2 network on the same fabric interconnects for low latency.
faq.q: Which network setting does an M365.FM episode mention for iSCSI performance?

iscsi.long:
iSCSI stands for Internet Small Computer Systems Interface. It is a protocol that carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, which gives servers network access to block storage. Instead of attaching a disk directly to a machine, the server sends its storage requests across an ordinary network connection, and the storage system on the other end answers them as if the disk were local.

The main purpose of iSCSI is to provide a disk-like, block-storage model through a network. Workloads that need large numbers of controlled reads and writes, such as database files, transaction logs and indexes, work with block storage rather than with ordinary files. With iSCSI, a virtual machine or server requests a particular block of data or sends a write operation, and the protocol transports that command between the server and the storage system across the network.

The episode "Azure Elastic SAN — Simply Explained" uses iSCSI as the connection method for Azure Elastic SAN. According to the episode, Azure Elastic SAN volumes connect to workloads using iSCSI. The episode describes the terminology as sounding complicated while the basic concept is straightforward: iSCSI carries storage commands between the server and the Elastic SAN. In that model, a VM asks for a block of data or issues a write, and the request travels over the network to the volume that holds the data.

iSCSI also appears in planning discussions around Kubernetes and fast storage.
