In practice, the admin center serves as a central starting point for administration across the services in a subscription. Typical tasks include handling user accounts and assigning licences, but the portal also leads to the settings of individual services. Because many Microsoft 365 workloads are configured from the admin center or from portals reachable through it, the same entry point shows up in episodes on very different topics, from email security to app governance and AI rollout.

The episode "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?" describes the admin center as part of a Copilot deployment. According to that episode, a typical deployment overview includes confirming eligibility and licensing, planning access to Copilot through the Microsoft 365 admin center, preparing enterprise data and security controls, configuring network requirements, testing with pilot groups, and installing the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on devices. It names Microsoft Configuration Manager, the Microsoft 365 apps admin center and Microsoft Store strategies as installation routes. Licence assignment and access planning are therefore two points where the admin center enters the rollout.

The episode "Microsoft AppSource - Simply Explained" covers app management. It states that installed apps can be controlled through the Microsoft 365 admin center and the Teams admin center. The methods it lists include blocking AppSource for all users through settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center, restricting AppSource for specific users by modifying user licences in the admin center, and controlling app availability in Teams. This shows how licence and settings management in the portal can limit which marketplace apps users can reach.

The episode "Exchange Online Protection (EOP) - Simply Explained" mentions the admin center in the context of email filtering. It says protection is applied automatically without setup, and that administrators can view filtering reports and adjust settings via the Microsoft 365 admin center. It also notes that Exchange Online Protection works with Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services, and that Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds features such as Safe Links and Safe Attachments.

The episode "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps - Simply Explained" notes that setting up Microsoft Defender involves accessing the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and following a setup wizard. It also points to flexible subscription plans, so organisations can choose the level of protection that fits their needs.

The episode "Microsoft Agent 365 Admin Center - Simply Explained" deals with a related but separate topic, the Agent 365 admin centre. It addresses the question of AI agents that accumulate inside a company and who owns them, and describes the place where that ownership is recorded as a page most people never open. Together with the general admin center, it illustrates how administration in Microsoft 365 is split across several portals, each focused on a particular area. Anyone planning licensing, security settings or app access in a Microsoft 365 tenant will usually begin in the Microsoft 365 admin center and then move into the service-specific portals the work requires.

microsoft-365-agents-sdk.desc: Microsoft 365 Agents SDK is a developer toolkit within Microsoft 365 for building agents, covering channels and conversation management, and orchestration alongside other agents.

faq.a: It is a developer toolkit that is part of Microsoft 365. The M365.FM episodes describe it as a way to extend agents with code, with a focus on channels and conversation management.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained", Microsoft 365 agents can use the Microsoft Agent Framework as the orchestration layer while relying on the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK for channels and conversation management.
faq.q: How does the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK relate to the Microsoft Agent Framework?

faq.a: The episode "Build Multi-Channel Agents with the Microsoft 365 Agent SDK" says durable conversation management lets agents remember previous messages and context. It adds that this avoids stateless bot problems and supports multi-turn interactions, including across multiple nodes.
faq.q: Why does conversation management matter in the SDK?

microsoft-365-agents-sdk.long:
Microsoft 365 Agents SDK is a software development kit that is part of Microsoft 365. Based on how it is described in M365.FM episodes, it is the code-first option for building agents and extending what agents can do with code. Its most frequently mentioned roles are handling channels and conversation management, and allowing agents to be orchestrated together with other Microsoft agents.

One area the SDK addresses is conversation management. The episode "Build Multi-Channel Agents with the Microsoft 365 Agent SDK" explains that durable conversation management prevents the issues of stateless bots. With it, an agent can remember previous messages and context, which makes multi-turn interactions feel more natural. The episode also describes conversation resumption as a way to avoid common stateless problems, and says that agents can be scaled across multiple nodes while still retaining context. The title of that episode also points to the multi-channel use case, where one agent is made available through more than one channel.

A second theme is the SDK's place in a larger agent landscape. The episode "Microsoft Agent Framework - Simply Explained" describes Microsoft 365 agents that use the Microsoft Agent Framework as the orchestration layer while relying on the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK for channels and conversation management. In that description the two have different jobs: the framework coordinates the agent's work, and the SDK supplies the channel connection and the conversation handling. The episode presents this combination as a way to make use of existing Microsoft tools.

The SDK also appears in discussions of multi-agent setups. In "Agentic AI with Copilot Studio and Dataverse MCP with Nathan Rose [MVP]", the speaker describes using the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK to orchestrate Copilot Studio agents alongside existing Microsoft 365 agents. The stated benefits are less duplication and the reuse of existing capabilities. The same episode describes agents that communicate and delegate tasks to each other through an open protocol, which it connects to interoperability across different platforms.

"Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]" makes a similar point. The episode describes a platform that integrates with the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK so that existing capabilities can be reused and workflows composed more efficiently. It frames multi-agent orchestration as a way to connect different systems and teams, so that agents work across channels and knowledge sources instead of staying isolated experiences within a single product.

The episode "How I Built a JARVIS-Like Microsoft Copilot Assistant" mentions the SDK in a smaller way, noting that developers can expand what agents can do with code using the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK. In that context it sits next to low-code agent features such as voice capabilities and analytics for generative systems, which positions the SDK as the route for developers who need behavior beyond what configuration alone provides.

For teams evaluating it, the episodes suggest a few decision points: whether an agent needs to keep context across multi-turn conversations and across several nodes, whether it must be reachable through more than one channel, and whether it has to cooperate with agents built in Copilot Studio or with other orchestration layers. The sources provided here do not give version numbers, supported languages, pricing or a full feature list, so those details should be checked in official Microsoft documentation.

microsoft-365-apps.desc: Microsoft 365 Apps are the installable, subscription-delivered Office applications such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote, part of Microsoft 365.

faq.a: They are the installable Office applications of Microsoft 365, such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote, delivered and updated through a subscription.
faq.q: What are Microsoft 365 Apps?

faq.a: The episode "Customize Microsoft 365 Apps Deployment with ODT XML" describes using one Office Deployment Tool configuration file to control included apps, update channel and languages, with the XML versions documented per department.
faq.q: How are Microsoft 365 Apps deployed and configured in an organization?

faq.a: Microsoft 365 Copilot works inside these applications. The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" says that enabling it raises privacy, DLP and audit workloads, so governance should be planned.
faq.q: How do Microsoft 365 Apps relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

microsoft-365-apps.long:
Microsoft 365 Apps are the installable Office applications of Microsoft 365, including Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote. They are delivered and updated through a subscription, so users receive new features and security updates over time rather than purchasing a fixed version. The product is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365, and is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Older or alternative names include Office apps, Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise and Office 365 ProPlus.

In practice, the term matters most to IT departments. Because the apps are installed on many devices, deployment and update management are central topics: administrators decide which applications are included, which update channel a group of users follows, and which languages are installed. The episode "Customize Microsoft 365 Apps Deployment with ODT XML" covers this area. It describes how a single configuration file for the Office Deployment Tool controls included apps, update channel and languages. Its notes recommend documenting XML versions per department in a repository such as Git together with a change log.

The same episode lists several troubleshooting situations. An "Unlicensed product" message on shared PCs points to the SharedComputerLicensing property, which should be set to TRUE. Missing features such as Power Query or Solver should prompt a check that the installed SKU is Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise rather than a legacy MSI installation. Updates that interrupt meetings can be addressed by moving a user group to the Monthly Enterprise channel, setting the display level to none, scheduling a maintenance window and considering the FORCEAPPSHUTDOWN=FALSE setting. If the wrong apps appear, the ExcludeApp IDs should be confirmed and any older MSI-based Office installation removed, for example with OffScrub.

Microsoft 365 Apps are also the surface on which Microsoft 365 Copilot appears. The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" looks at how Copilot works inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote, where it saves time, and why privacy, data loss prevention (DLP) and audit workloads increase once it is switched on. The episode states that faster workflows do not come with free compliance, which makes governance a prerequisite rather than an afterthought. A further episode, "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]", discusses using Copilot across Microsoft 365 apps and recommends multi-part prompts for larger projects. According to the episode, Copilot connects Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams into one system. Another episode, "How Do You Successfully Deploy Microsoft 365 Copilot Across an Enterprise?", touches on managed Windows Cloud PCs that work with Microsoft Intune for device control and Microsoft Entra ID for identity, and that connect the Microsoft 365 Copilot app to devices running Microsoft 365 apps within company boundaries.

Developers meet Microsoft 365 Apps from a different angle. The episode "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels" explains how Dev Tunnels in Visual Studio can expose local Teams, SharePoint or Power Platform services to the internet for testing, without an Azure deployment. A named, persistent tunnel with private, authenticated access tied to Microsoft Entra ID keeps tests secure and OAuth redirect URIs stable. The episode names leaving a tunnel public or anonymous as the biggest risk and advises locking tunnels down, logging them and shutting them off when testing ends.

Typical decisions around Microsoft 365 Apps therefore fall into three groups: how to package and deploy the installation, how to set the update cadence so that users are not disrupted, and how to govern AI features that operate inside the applications. Official documentation for the product is available through Microsoft Learn, and the product overview is on the Microsoft website.

microsoft-365-business-premium.desc: Microsoft 365 Business Premium is a Microsoft 365 plan for small businesses that bundles Office apps with Defender for Business, device management and identity and data protection tools.

faq.a: According to the episode, it includes Defender for Business along with email protection, device management, identity protection and data protection tools, alongside Office apps and cloud services.
faq.q: What does Microsoft 365 Business Premium include?

faq.a: The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" lists Business Standard at $12.50 per user per month and Business Premium at $22.00 per user per month.
faq.q: How does Business Premium differ from Business Standard in cost?

faq.a: The episodes say Microsoft Entra IAM integrates with Business Premium and that Azure Information Protection can be used with it for classification and sensitivity labels, though some advanced Entra features may require additional licenses.
faq.q: Can Microsoft Entra and Azure Information Protection be used with Business Premium?

microsoft-365-business-premium.long:
Microsoft 365 Business Premium is a plan within Microsoft 365 aimed at small businesses. According to the M365.FM episodes, it combines productivity apps and cloud services with security and management capabilities, including Defender for Business, email protection, device management, identity protection and data protection tools. It is part of the wider Microsoft 365 family of subscriptions.

The plan is often explained by contrast with Office 365 plans. The episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System" says that Office 365 Business plans focus on Office apps and cloud services, while the Microsoft 365 Business tier bundles Office 365 with Windows licensing, device management and security features, which is where Business Premium sits. The same episode notes that Office 365 Business Premium, now generally part of Microsoft 365 Business Premium, provided apps and services but less device management and security than the full Microsoft 365 Business Premium package. That distinction matters when an organization is deciding whether it needs only apps and mail or also managed devices and protection against threats.

Pricing follows the per-user subscription model that the episode describes for Microsoft 365 generally, where licenses are billed per user per month. The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" gives a cost comparison in which Microsoft 365 Business Standard is listed at $12.50 per user per month and Microsoft 365 Business Premium at $22.00 per user per month. For 50 users the episode lists annual costs of $7,500 for Business Standard and $13,200 for Business Premium, and for 200 users $30,000 and $52,800 respectively. These figures are quoted from the episode and illustrate how the additional security and management features are reflected in the price difference. The same episode describes SharePoint Premium as a separate pay-per-use add-on rather than something included in either plan.

Several episodes connect Business Premium to information protection and identity. In "Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection" and "What Is Microsoft Intune Used For?", the show notes state that Azure Information Protection can be used with Microsoft 365 Business Premium to classify data and control who can access it. Sensitivity labels play a central role: they can be applied to documents and emails, and can encrypt files, add visual markings and set sharing rules. Azure Information Protection connects with Microsoft Purview Information Protection, so labels can be created and published from one place and work across Microsoft 365 apps. The Intune-related episode places device management in the same ecosystem of tools that a Business Premium subscription touches.

Identity is the other recurring theme. The episode "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform" answers whether Microsoft Entra IAM can be used with Microsoft 365 E3 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium: yes, it integrates tightly with both to provide unified identity and secure access to applications across Microsoft services. It also cautions that some advanced features, such as certain risk-based conditional access policies or Entra ID P2 functionality, may require specific licenses beyond the standard plan. Organizations evaluating Business Premium should therefore check which identity-protection capabilities are included and which need an upgrade.

In practice, the decision around Microsoft 365 Business Premium typically involves comparing it with Business Standard on cost, with the enterprise E3 and E5 tiers on feature depth, and with add-ons such as SharePoint Premium on specialised needs. The episodes present it as the small-business option that brings Office apps together with device, identity, email and data protection in one subscription.

microsoft-365-e3.desc: Microsoft 365 E3 is Microsoft's enterprise subscription plan that bundles Microsoft 365 apps and services with core security, compliance and device management.

faq.a: Microsoft 365 E3 is an enterprise subscription plan in Microsoft 365 that bundles the Microsoft 365 apps and services with core security, compliance and device management. E5 adds more advanced security and compliance features.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 E3?

faq.a: According to the episode "The Copilot Tax: Hidden Costs of Enterprise AI Strategy", Copilot requires an existing Microsoft 365 E3 or E5 subscription, or Business Standard or Business Premium. Users on lower-tier licenses may need upgrades.
faq.q: Does Microsoft Copilot require Microsoft 365 E3?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" states that Defender for Endpoint P1, which offers basic features, is included with Microsoft 365 E3 and E5. P2 adds advanced features such as threat hunting and longer data retention.
faq.q: Which Microsoft Defender for Endpoint plan is included with Microsoft 365 E3?

microsoft-365-e3.long:
Microsoft 365 E3 is an enterprise subscription plan within Microsoft 365. It bundles the Microsoft 365 apps and services with core security, compliance and device management capabilities. Together with Microsoft 365 E5, it forms the enterprise tier of the Microsoft 365 plan family. Compared with E3, the E5 plan adds more advanced security and compliance features.

Within the wider Microsoft 365 lineup, E3 sits alongside several other plan groups. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System" describes consumer plans such as Microsoft 365 Personal and the family plans, and business plans such as Business Basic, Business Standard and Business Premium, which focus on core productivity apps and simpler management for small and medium businesses. The enterprise plans, E3 and E5, add broader compliance, advanced security and analytics tools. For an organization, the choice between these groups usually comes down to company size, the depth of compliance and security requirements, and the management model in use.

Licensing questions around Microsoft 365 E3 also appear in connection with Microsoft Copilot. The episode "The Copilot Tax: Hidden Costs of Enterprise AI Strategy" states that Copilot requires an existing Microsoft 365 E3 or E5 subscription, or Business Standard or Business Premium. It adds that users on lower-tier licenses may need upgrades, which increases overall cost. The episode lists further cost factors such as configuration, end-user training, ongoing management overhead and usage-based charges for AI APIs and premium models. It cites a 15-20% rise in Microsoft spending with AI integration and recommends aligning subscription plans with business needs, monitoring usage, and applying governance and prompt discipline to avoid unnecessary spending.

Identity is another area where E3 comes up. In "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform", the answer to whether Microsoft Entra IAM can be used with Microsoft 365 E3 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium is yes: the episode says Entra integrates tightly with these plans to provide unified identity and secure access to applications across Microsoft services. It also notes that some advanced features, such as certain risk-based conditional access policies or Entra ID P2 functionality, may require specific licenses beyond the base plan. Organizations therefore compare P1 and P2 capabilities against their identity security needs.

Update and device management form a further connection. The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" lists Office 365 E3, Office 365 E5, Microsoft 365 E3 and Microsoft 365 E5 among the enterprise plans that support the update management features it discusses, alongside education plans (A3, A5) and business plans (Business Standard, Business Premium). It also names further prerequisites: Microsoft Intune Plan 1 and a Windows license that includes the Autopatch entitlement. The episode advises making sure the IT team has admin permissions for all relevant services to avoid delays in update deployment.

Endpoint security licensing is covered in "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained". Its feature comparison states that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint P1 offers basic features and is included with Microsoft 365 E3 and E5, generally at lower cost. Defender for Endpoint P2 adds advanced capabilities such as threat hunting and longer data retention at higher cost, while Microsoft Defender for Business targets small and medium organizations and includes email protection. The episode suggests that the choice should reflect device management needs.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft 365 E3 as a baseline enterprise license: it is a prerequisite or integration point for Copilot, Entra, Intune-based update management and Defender for Endpoint, while more advanced capabilities in each area may depend on E5 or additional licenses.

microsoft-365-e5.desc: Microsoft 365 E5 is an enterprise licensing tier above E3 that adds advanced security, compliance and analytics capabilities within Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Microsoft 365 E5 is an enterprise licensing tier of Microsoft 365 above E3. The episodes describe it as adding broader compliance, advanced security and analytics tools, including additional Defender and identity security capabilities.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 E5?

faq.a: The episodes link it to extended auditing in Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Security Copilot setup, and Microsoft Security Exposure Management. They also list it among the plans that support certain update-management features.
faq.q: Which features do the episodes link to Microsoft 365 E5?

faq.a: No. The episode on Microsoft Security Exposure Management says the features are available with Microsoft 365 E5, certain E3 setups with add-ons, or Defender suite licenses.
faq.q: Is Microsoft 365 E5 the only license for Security Exposure Management?

microsoft-365-e5.long:
Microsoft 365 E5 is an enterprise subscription tier within Microsoft 365. It sits above Microsoft 365 E3 and is positioned for organizations that need broader compliance, advanced security and analytics tools. In the M365.FM material it appears mainly as the license level that unlocks additional Defender and identity security capabilities, as well as extended auditing and compliance features.

The episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System" places Microsoft 365 E5 in the wider plan structure. It describes consumer plans such as Microsoft 365 Personal and family plans, business plans such as Business Basic, Business Standard and Business Premium, and enterprise subscriptions such as E3 and E5. According to the episode, the enterprise plans add broader compliance, advanced security and analytics tools, while the business plans focus on core productivity apps and simpler management. Microsoft 365 E5 is therefore one of the top-end enterprise options in that lineup, and it is a licensing decision as much as a technical one.

In the area of auditing and compliance, the episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview" explains that Microsoft Purview centralizes auditing across services such as SharePoint Online, Exchange Online and Microsoft Teams. The episode says the audit experience gains added capabilities when the tenant holds an appropriate license, such as Microsoft 365 E5 or Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance. The practical guidance given there is to open the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, check that audit is enabled, and configure policies to retain audit records. The episode notes that auditing is enabled by default in many tenants but should still be verified.

Security tooling is the other recurring theme. In "Microsoft Security Copilot - Simply Explained", the episode says that setting up Microsoft Security Copilot is straightforward for organizations that already use Microsoft 365 E5, because only minimal configuration is needed to start using it. The episode also describes how the tool filters and prioritizes alerts by risk level so that teams can concentrate on high-priority threats and reduce alert fatigue. The connection to Microsoft 365 E5 here is the existing security foundation the license provides.

The episode "Microsoft Security Exposure Management with Uros Babic [MVP-MCT]" covers licensing requirements for Microsoft Security Exposure Management. It states that the features are available with Microsoft 365 E5, with certain E3 setups that include add-ons, or with Defender suite licenses. It also lists prerequisites such as a minimum version of the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint agent and the permissions needed, either a dedicated Exposure Management role or traditional roles like Security Admin or Global Admin. The episode advises checking these licensing and permission requirements before starting, to avoid delays.

Microsoft 365 E5 also appears in update management. The episode "Manage Microsoft 365 Update Overload" lists plans that support certain update-control features, naming Office 365 E3, Office 365 E5, Microsoft 365 E3 and Microsoft 365 E5 on the enterprise side. It adds that Microsoft Intune Plan 1 and a Windows license that includes the Autopatch entitlement are also required, so the plan alone does not cover every prerequisite.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft 365 E5 as a license that is part of Microsoft 365 and that determines which security, compliance and auditing features an organization can use. Typical decisions around it involve comparing E3 with E5, checking whether add-ons or separate suites could cover a specific need, and confirming that supporting licenses and admin permissions are in place before rolling out features.

microsoft-365-e7.desc: Microsoft 365 E7 is an enterprise plan within Microsoft 365 that bundles Microsoft 365 E5, Copilot, Agent 365 and the Microsoft Entra Suite on one platform.

faq.a: According to Microsoft, it bundles Microsoft 365 E5, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Agent 365 and the Microsoft Entra Suite. It also covers Office apps, Exchange, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams Phone, Windows 11 Enterprise, Intune and Windows 365 Cloud PCs.
faq.q: What does Microsoft 365 E7 include?

faq.a: It is billed per user per month with an annual commitment and is available in a variant with Teams and one without. Purchase goes through sales.
faq.q: How is Microsoft 365 E7 licensed and purchased?

faq.a: Agents require an Azure subscription billed by usage, and some Teams-integrated features need a Teams license. Availability can vary by market and license.
faq.q: Are there extra costs or requirements with Microsoft 365 E7?

microsoft-365-e7.long:
Microsoft 365 E7 is an enterprise licensing tier that is part of Microsoft 365. According to Microsoft's product information, it combines Microsoft 365 E5, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Agent 365 and the Microsoft Entra Suite on a single platform. The stated aim is to protect employees and their AI agents while an organization scales AI across its workforce, without weakening security or compliance. One episode describes it more generally as a tier that adds AI capabilities on top of the lower tiers at a notably higher price.

The plan covers a broad set of workloads. On the productivity side it includes the Office apps, Exchange, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams Phone, together with Windows 11 Enterprise, Intune and Windows 365 Cloud PCs. On the AI side it includes Copilot in apps, AI chat, agents and agent building with Copilot Studio. The security and compliance stack named for the plan includes Defender, Purview and Security Copilot. Two components are specific to the E7 positioning: Agent 365, which acts as a control plane for managing and securing agents across Microsoft 365 and third-party services, and the Microsoft Entra Suite, which unifies identity, security and network access.

In practice, the tier is relevant to organizations that treat AI agents as part of the workforce and want one licensing vehicle that pairs agent capabilities with identity, security and compliance controls. The choice is largely about whether Copilot, agent management and the Entra Suite are needed alongside the E5 feature set, since these are all included in the bundle rather than purchased separately. Microsoft lists the plan in two variants, one with Teams and one without, both billed per user per month with an annual commitment. Purchase goes through sales rather than self-service.

Several conditions apply according to the documentation. Agents require an Azure subscription, which is billed by usage, so agent consumption is not simply covered by the per-user fee. Some Teams-integrated features need a Teams license, which matters when selecting the variant without Teams. Availability can also vary by market and by license, so planning should include a check of what is offered in a given region.

The M365.FM episode "Replace Reactive Dashboards with Proactive Notifications" (2026-05-03) mentions Microsoft 365 E7 in the context of proactive notifications. The episode presents a comparison table in which Microsoft 365 E7 is described as offering AI-driven orchestration for proactive notifications, AI agents that act on intent as a workflow enhancement, unified communications with AI, and intelligent, productivity-enhancing tools for employees. The same table contrasts these with other enterprise solutions that it characterizes as using traditional notifications, manual processes, basic integration without AI and standard tools. These comparisons are the episode's own framing and are presented there as a way to show how AI-driven notification and orchestration could replace reactive dashboard checking.

Microsoft 365 E7 relates most directly to its parent, Microsoft 365, and to the lower enterprise tiers it builds on, particularly E5, which it explicitly includes. Anyone evaluating it typically weighs the added cost against the value of the bundled AI, agent governance and identity components, and confirms licensing details such as Teams inclusion, Azure billing for agents and regional availability with Microsoft sales.

microsoft-365-f3.desc: Microsoft 365 F3 is a frontline worker license plan in Microsoft 365 with core communication and collaboration tools at lower cost than E3 and E5.

faq.a: Microsoft 365 F3 is a Microsoft 365 license plan for frontline workers. It provides core communication and collaboration capabilities at a lower cost than the E3 and E5 enterprise plans.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 F3?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]", Microsoft 365 F3 is among the licenses that include Azure Virtual Desktop access. The episode notes that infrastructure costs such as compute, storage and networking are typically the largest expense.
faq.q: Does Microsoft 365 F3 include Azure Virtual Desktop access?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" lists Microsoft 365 F3 as a prerequisite license for Microsoft Teams Phone Standard, Microsoft Teams Phone Standard for Frontline Workers and Microsoft Teams Phone with Calling Plan.
faq.q: Can Microsoft 365 F3 be used with Teams Phone?

microsoft-365-f3.long:
Microsoft 365 F3 is a license plan within Microsoft 365 designed for frontline workers. It provides core communication and collaboration capabilities and is positioned at a lower cost than the Microsoft 365 E3 and E5 enterprise plans. Because it is part of Microsoft 365, it is assigned to individual users in the same way as other Microsoft 365 licenses and acts as a prerequisite license for a range of additional services and add-ons.

The plan is intended for users whose work is not primarily desk-based, such as people who rely on shared devices or mobile access rather than a full office setup. The facts available on this topic do not describe the full feature list of Microsoft 365 F3 in detail. What the M365.FM episodes show instead is how the plan is treated as a qualifying license when other Microsoft products and features are added, which is a common decision point for administrators planning licensing.

One recurring context is Microsoft Teams Phone. The episode "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" lists the prerequisite licenses for the different Teams Phone license types. According to the episode, Microsoft 365 F3 appears among the prerequisite licenses for Microsoft Teams Phone Standard, alongside Microsoft 365 Business Basic, Business Standard, Business Premium, F1 and E3, and several Office 365 and Teams plans. It also appears for Microsoft Teams Phone Standard for Frontline Workers, where the episode names Microsoft 365 F1 and F3 as well as Office 365 F3. For Microsoft Teams Phone with Calling Plan, Microsoft 365 F3 is again listed among the qualifying base licenses. The episode additionally notes that further licenses should be considered for shared devices.

A second context is virtual desktops. The episode "Azure Virtual Desktop vs Windows 365 with Dieter Kempeneers [MVP] & Dominiek Verham [MVP]" includes a table of licenses that include Azure Virtual Desktop access. According to the episode, Microsoft 365 F3 is one of these, together with Microsoft 365 E3 and E5, Microsoft 365 Business Premium, Windows 11/10 Enterprise E3 and E5 per user, and Windows 11/10 VDA per user. The episode points out that licensing is only one part of Azure Virtual Desktop pricing; infrastructure costs, including compute, storage and networking, typically represent the largest expense. Having a qualifying license such as Microsoft 365 F3 therefore covers access rights but does not remove the infrastructure cost question.

A third context is Viva Connections. The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" lists the license types under which the feature is available. Microsoft 365 F3 is named in that list next to F1, E3, A3, E5 and A5, with Office 365 F3 also appearing among the Office 365 options. The episode adds that a Teams license is required to access the Viva Connections app and that SharePoint admin permissions are needed to set up Viva Connections and manage the dashboard.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft 365 F3 mainly as a base license that unlocks eligibility for other capabilities rather than as a standalone feature set. Typical planning decisions around it include whether frontline users should receive Microsoft 365 F3 or a higher plan such as E3, which add-on or service the user group actually needs, and whether the prerequisite license rules for that service are met. Because the same plan name sits in the prerequisite tables of several products, checking the license requirements of each service before assigning licenses is a practical step. Microsoft 365 F3 belongs to the broader Microsoft 365 family and shares its administration model, so license assignment, service access and add-on eligibility are managed together with the other plans in the tenant.

microsoft-365-groups.desc: Microsoft 365 Groups is the membership object behind every team, provisioning a SharePoint site, shared mailbox, calendar and plan under one membership list.

faq.a: A Microsoft 365 Group provisions a SharePoint site, a shared mailbox and calendar, a plan and other connected resources, all governed by one membership list.
faq.q: What does a Microsoft 365 Group provision?

faq.a: The episodes treat provisioning, lifecycle, ownership and guest access of groups as elements of a governance plan, together with retention, classification and monitoring.
faq.q: Why do the M365.FM episodes discuss Microsoft 365 Groups in a governance context?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance" describes audits for external users, attestation requests to group owners, recurring review schedules and timeouts for inactive users.
faq.q: How can group membership be kept under control according to the episodes?

microsoft-365-groups.long:
Microsoft 365 Groups is the membership object that sits behind every team in Microsoft 365. A single group defines who belongs to a collaboration space, and from that one membership list it provisions a set of connected resources: a SharePoint site, a shared mailbox and calendar, a plan, and other related services. The product is part of Microsoft 365 and works as the common identity layer that ties these separate workloads together, so that access to the site, the mailbox and the plan follows the same list of members.

Because one membership list controls several resources, the way groups are created, named, owned and retired has a direct effect on how data is organized and who can reach it. In the M365.FM material, Microsoft 365 Groups appear mainly in discussions of governance rather than as a feature walkthrough. The episodes repeatedly treat group management as one of the areas that an organization has to define clearly when it builds a governance framework for Microsoft 365.

The episode "Why Microsoft 365 Governance Strategies Fail" lists provisioning and lifecycle for 365 groups and Microsoft 365 groups among the core components of an M365 governance plan. In the same list it places scope and objectives, roles and responsibilities, policies for data retention and the data lifecycle, security controls, compliance mapping, monitoring and reporting, and adoption and training. The episode says such a plan should align with the collaboration features of Microsoft 365 and use governance tools to automate enforcement where possible.

The episode "Leadership and Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Central Control" describes what a governance plan should contain and again names the provisioning of 365 Groups and Microsoft 365 Group management as one element. Alongside it, the episode lists roles and responsibilities including data stewards, lifecycle rules for data and retention, naming and classification standards, monitoring and reporting, and escalation paths. The group is therefore treated as an object that needs rules from creation to deletion, not only at the moment a team is set up.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Structural Debt from Default Governance" focuses on remediation. It describes running audits to find external users in Microsoft 365 groups and removing anyone who does not need access. It also describes sending attestation requests to group owners so they can confirm or update group membership, and setting these actions to repeat weekly, monthly or yearly. The same episode mentions timeouts for inactive users, such as 60 or 90 days, alerts to managers about users who have not signed in, and removal of guest users who no longer need access.

In "Cloud Governance as Architecture, Not Feature Management", group handling is placed under identity and access management. The checklist in that episode includes defining group and guest access policies for Microsoft 365 Groups and Teams and enforcing identity lifecycle processes for joiners, movers and leavers. It pairs this with information protection topics such as a data classification taxonomy, sensitivity labels, and retention, deletion and records management policies.

The episode "Microsoft 365 Governance as Code Beyond Written Policies" places clear policies and procedures for Microsoft 365 groups, SharePoint and Microsoft Teams alongside identity management in Microsoft Entra, data protection and retention policies in Microsoft Purview, classification, monitoring, incident response and lifecycle management. Across these episodes the common point is that Microsoft 365 Groups are a governance object: membership, ownership, external access and lifecycle all need defined rules and recurring review.

microsoft-365-lighthouse.desc: Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is an admin portal that helps managed service providers onboard, monitor and manage Microsoft 365 customer tenants at scale.

faq.a: It is a portal that lets managed service providers onboard, monitor and manage Microsoft 365 customer tenants at scale. It offers cross-tenant views, a default security baseline and risk detection.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 Lighthouse?

faq.a: No. Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is for managing Microsoft 365 customer tenants, while Azure Lighthouse is a different offering for Azure services.
faq.q: Is Microsoft 365 Lighthouse the same as Azure Lighthouse?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, managing Microsoft 365 services and connected devices through it carries no additional cost. It is available to Cloud Solution Provider partners, both direct-bill and indirect resellers, provided the provider and customer tenants meet the listed requirements.
faq.q: Does Microsoft 365 Lighthouse cost extra and who can use it?

microsoft-365-lighthouse.long:
Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is a portal that lets managed service providers (MSPs) manage Microsoft 365 customer tenants and deliver their services at scale. It is part of the Microsoft 365 ecosystem and is aimed at IT providers who look after many small and medium-sized businesses at once. Microsoft Learn describes its stated aims as standardizing configurations, managing risk and surfacing AI-supported sales opportunities. It is separate from Azure Lighthouse, which is a different offering for Azure services.

The core idea is a single place from which one provider can see and act on many customer tenants instead of signing in to each tenant individually. According to the documentation, service engineers can onboard tenants with recommended security configurations for small and medium-sized businesses, work with cross-tenant views, and detect and act on risks. Account managers, in turn, receive AI-based insights intended to help win and retain customers and to add premium offerings. The portal therefore serves both a technical and a commercial role within an MSP.

The capabilities described in the documentation include tenant deployment workflows and a default security baseline that can be applied to customer tenants. Device compliance insights are available across tenants, and the portal supports setting up multifactor authentication (MFA) and self-service password reset. It can detect risky sign-ins and show threat details from Microsoft Defender XDR for Windows 10 devices. It also shows service incidents and advisories that affect the managed tenants, so a provider can see which customers are impacted by a given issue.

On cost and eligibility, the documentation states that managing Microsoft 365 services and connected devices through the portal carries no additional cost. It is available to Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partners, both direct-bill partners and indirect resellers. Both the provider tenant and the customer tenants must meet separately listed requirements, so checking those prerequisites is a practical first step before planning an onboarding.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 Lighthouse - Simply Explained" presents the product in accessible terms. The episode says Microsoft 365 Lighthouse is free and that almost nobody outside the IT world talks about it, and it describes it as one screen that lets a single IT provider look after Microsoft 365 for dozens of small businesses at the same time. It is framed as an introduction to what the tool is and who it is relevant for.

The episode "Building a Secure Microsoft-First MSP: Intune, Defender & Entra ID at Scale with Albin Klinaku [MVP]" places Microsoft 365 Lighthouse in the context of an MSP security practice. The episode says that Lighthouse can be used to manage multiple clients' Defender solutions from a single interface, which it links to centralized monitoring, streamlined remediation and consistent reporting. In that discussion, bundling Microsoft Defender into security offerings is also described as a way to generate revenue, for example by upselling clients to higher-value Microsoft 365 plans and monetizing ongoing security management services.

Taken together, the sources position Microsoft 365 Lighthouse as a multi-tenant management layer for MSPs working with Microsoft 365, closely tied to security topics such as MFA, device compliance and Defender, and distinct from Azure Lighthouse, which addresses Azure services.

microsoft-365-local.desc: Microsoft 365 Local runs Exchange Server, SharePoint Server and Skype for Business Server on customer-controlled Azure Local infrastructure for sovereignty and data residency.

faq.a: Microsoft 365 Local is a deployment model that runs Exchange Server, SharePoint Server and Skype for Business Server on Azure Local infrastructure that the customer owns and manages. It is intended to support sovereignty and data residency requirements.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 Local?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Learn describes two operating modes: a connected mode, where Azure acts as a cloud-based control plane, and a fully disconnected mode with a local control plane.
faq.q: Can Microsoft 365 Local run without a cloud connection?

faq.a: It must be deployed on an Azure Local Premier Solution from a hardware partner that meets the stated requirements. Deployment goes through a Microsoft-certified Microsoft 365 Local partner in phases such as assessment, planning, acquisition and deployment, with customer-specific sizing.
faq.q: How is Microsoft 365 Local deployed?

microsoft-365-local.long:
Microsoft 365 Local is a deployment model within the Microsoft 365 family that runs Exchange Server, SharePoint Server and Skype for Business Server on Azure Local infrastructure. The infrastructure is owned and managed by the customer. The model is aimed at organizations with sovereignty and data residency requirements that want more control over where their collaboration and messaging workloads run, who can access them, and how compliance is handled.

According to Microsoft Learn, the purpose of Microsoft 365 Local is to support sovereignty requirements through greater control over data residency, access and compliance. It has two further uses described in the documentation. First, it can modernize existing on-premises deployments of Exchange Server, SharePoint Server and Skype for Business Server by moving them into what Microsoft calls a sovereign private cloud. Second, it can serve as a fallback or business continuity environment that continues to run locally in a crisis.

The technical foundation is a validated reference architecture that covers networking, storage, compute and identity integration. Management follows the same approach as Azure, with a unified control plane. Two operating modes are available. In connected mode, Azure acts as a cloud-based control plane for monitoring, updates and policy. In fully disconnected mode, a local control plane is used, so the environment can operate without a connection to the cloud.

Deployment has specific prerequisites. Microsoft 365 Local must be deployed on an Azure Local Premier Solution from a hardware partner that meets the stated requirements. Deployment goes through a Microsoft-certified Microsoft 365 Local partner and proceeds in phases such as assessment, planning, acquisition and deployment. Sizing is customer specific and has to be worked out together with a Microsoft partner. The overview page gives no licensing details or pricing, so those points need to be clarified separately.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" places Microsoft 365 Local in the wider discussion of sovereignty. The episode describes the goals as storing and processing data within the EU or other specified jurisdictions, avoiding exposure to foreign cloud legal frameworks such as the CLOUD Act, and retaining control of data and key management. It says that Microsoft 365 Local options and in-country data processing can help keep Microsoft 365 data and certain services within a geographic boundary, and that such sovereign cloud configurations can limit where data is stored and processed.

The episode "How to Design Sovereign Cloud Architecture for Microsoft Azure" looks at the offline side. It describes Azure Local disconnected operations as a way to run important systems with governance and policy control without cloud access. In that context, the episode says Microsoft 365 Local lets key productivity tasks keep working within the customer's controlled area even when offline. It mentions this alongside Foundry Local, which it describes as supporting large AI models in fully offline settings, and stresses building a strong governance system so that data access rules are met.

For planning, the main decisions are the choice between connected and disconnected operation, the selection of a qualifying Azure Local Premier Solution hardware partner, and the engagement of a certified Microsoft 365 Local partner for assessment and sizing. Microsoft 365 Local is part of Microsoft 365 and relates closely to Azure Local, since the workloads run on that platform.

microsoft-365-sprawl.desc: Microsoft 365 sprawl is the unmanaged buildup of workspaces, permissions, guest access and other assets in a tenant, which Copilot can make more visible.

faq.a: It is the unmanaged accumulation of workspaces, sharing links, permissions, guest access, connectors and other assets in a Microsoft 365 tenant that outpaces governance.
faq.q: What is Microsoft 365 sprawl?

faq.a: No. According to the episode with Richard Harbridge, sprawl is multidimensional and also covers permission and access sprawl, ownership problems, inactive resources, lifecycle problems, administrative complexity and conditional access.
faq.q: Is Microsoft 365 sprawl only about too many Teams or SharePoint sites?

faq.a: The episode says Copilot operates on top of the existing environment, so stale workspaces, permanent permissions and unclear ownership become part of what Copilot works with, which amplifies the effect of sprawl.
faq.q: How does Copilot relate to Microsoft 365 sprawl?

microsoft-365-sprawl.long:
Microsoft 365 sprawl describes the unmanaged accumulation of workspaces, sharing links, permissions, guest access, connectors and other assets in a Microsoft 365 tenant. It develops when the volume and variety of content and access grows faster than governance can keep up. The concept sits under the broader topic of Microsoft 365 and is relevant to any organization that lets employees create and share content on their own.

The term is often reduced to "too many Teams or SharePoint sites," but the episode "Copilot Inherits Your Mess: Modernizing Microsoft 365 for AI with Richard Harbridge [MVP]" argues that sprawl is multidimensional. According to the episode, it can show up as workspace sprawl, permission and access sprawl, ownership problems, inactive resources, lifecycle problems, administrative complexity and conditional access issues. Counting sites or teams therefore captures only one part of the picture.

The same episode describes how sprawl usually comes about over time rather than through a single event. Permissions become permanent, old collaboration spaces remain accessible, ownership changes, business structures evolve, and content stays online long after its original purpose has disappeared. Each of these is a small, ordinary outcome of day-to-day work, but together they leave a tenant full of content and access paths that nobody actively reviews.

This matters more once AI is involved. The episode's central point is that Copilot operates on top of the existing environment. If a tenant already contains stale workspaces, broad permissions and unclear ownership, Copilot works with that content as it stands. In that sense sprawl is amplified by AI: what was previously hidden in forgotten sites and loosely scoped access becomes relevant to what an AI assistant can draw on. Modernizing the environment is therefore presented as a precondition for adopting Copilot, not an afterthought.

A typical reaction to sprawl is to restrict who can create Teams and other workspaces. The episode "From Garage Band to Symphony Orchestra- How Microsoft 365 Governance Creates Harmony at Scale — with Heiko Brenn" describes a more nuanced approach. Instead of blocking self-service, organizations can introduce naming conventions, predefined templates, ownership requirements, guest policies, lifecycle controls and other guardrails while still allowing employees to create what they need. The episode uses a musical comparison: governance is like agreeing on the key and rhythm before everybody starts playing, and freedom works better when everyone understands the basic framework.

Taken together, the two episodes frame sprawl as a governance problem rather than a purely technical one. The practical decisions revolve around who owns each workspace, how long it should exist, who may be invited from outside the organization, how permissions are reviewed, and which templates and conventions apply at creation time. Because sprawl spans workspaces, permissions, guests and lifecycle, the measures that address it also span several areas instead of one setting or tool.

For teams planning a Copilot rollout, the episodes together suggest reviewing the existing tenant first and establishing guardrails that keep new content manageable, so that growth in collaboration does not outpace oversight.

microsoft-ai-cloud-partner-program.desc: The Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program is Microsoft's partner program, formerly the Microsoft Partner Network, offering benefits, designations, specializations and incentives.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's partner program, formerly the Microsoft Partner Network and the Microsoft Cloud Partner Program. Partners use it to obtain benefits, offers, designations, specializations and incentives.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, a partner needs program membership, a verified Partner Center account and the partner admin role. Benefits are then redeemed in a benefits workspace in Partner Center.
faq.q: What is needed to use the program's offers?

faq.a: No. Microsoft Learn states that legacy Silver, Gold, MAPS and LAPS offers are no longer sold, although existing purchases run until their end date.
faq.q: Are the Silver and Gold offers still available?

microsoft-ai-cloud-partner-program.long:
The Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program is Microsoft's partner program. It was formerly known as the Microsoft Partner Network and later as the Microsoft Cloud Partner Program. Through it, partners receive benefits, offers and incentives, and they can earn designations and specializations that signal capability in particular areas of the Microsoft portfolio. Membership and the associated offers are managed in Partner Center.

According to Microsoft Learn, the program gives partners access to benefits such as Azure credits, cloud services, product licenses, technical consultations, developer tools and marketing assets such as badges. These benefits are redeemed in a benefits workspace within Partner Center. The membership workspace is where the overall partnership is administered. To use the program, a partner needs program membership, a verified Partner Center account and the partner admin role.

Offers in the program differ by partner type. Services partners can buy packages such as Partner Launch Benefits, Success Core and Expanded Benefits, as well as the Solutions Partner designation. ISV partners have ISV Success and Marketplace Rewards, and training services partners have their own program. Specializations and Azure Expert MSP carry no added cost, but they require the Solutions Partner designation. The older Silver, Gold, MAPS and LAPS offers are no longer sold, although purchases made earlier remain valid until their end date.

Several purchasing rules apply. Each offer can be purchased only once, and upgrades and proration are not supported. Renewal does not redeem benefits automatically, so benefits must be redeemed deliberately. Terms generally run one year plus a 30-day grace period, and refunds apply only when benefits are unused. These conditions matter when planning which offer to buy and when to activate it.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" places the program at the start of the partner path. It describes joining the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program as one of the milestones every Microsoft partner encounters, alongside building technical capabilities, earning certifications, publishing solutions, developing managed services and aligning with Microsoft's strategic solution areas. The episode says that creating value comes from combining technical expertise, customer success and recurring services rather than simply selling Microsoft licenses, and that competencies alone are no longer enough. In its account, partners differentiate themselves through specialization, measurable customer outcomes and deep expertise in areas such as Microsoft 365 and Azure.

The episode "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready" focuses on change within the program. It describes the FY26 designation restructuring as the program's biggest transformation in years and says many partners are not prepared. The episode explains why Microsoft is simplifying its partner ecosystem and what the new designation model means for Solution Partners, MSPs, ISVs and consulting organizations. For partners, the practical consequence is that designation strategy, specialization choices and benefit planning should be reviewed against the current structure rather than the legacy competency model.

In short, the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program is the framework that links a partner's Partner Center account to Microsoft's benefits, designations and incentives. Decisions around it typically involve which partner type applies, which offer package to purchase, whether to pursue the Solutions Partner designation and any specializations that build on it, and how to keep the terms and renewals aligned with business plans.

microsoft-applied-skills.desc: Microsoft Applied Skills are scenario-based credentials that validate specific hands-on technical skills through lab tasks, complementing role-based Microsoft certifications.

faq.a: Microsoft Applied Skills are credentials that validate specific, hands-on technical skills. They are earned by completing interactive, lab-based tasks that mirror real work, rather than by taking a multiple-choice exam.
faq.q: What are Microsoft Applied Skills?

faq.a: Applied Skills are scenario-based and focus on a specific practical capability, while role-based Microsoft certifications are aligned to a broader job role. Microsoft describes them as complementary and provides guidance on choosing between the two.
faq.q: How do Applied Skills differ from Microsoft certifications?

faq.a: The program targets IT professionals, business professionals, developers, students, educators and career changers. People use the credentials to demonstrate practical skills for job applications or project assignments.
faq.q: Who are Microsoft Applied Skills intended for?

microsoft-applied-skills.long:
Microsoft Applied Skills are scenario-based credentials that validate specific, practical technical skills. They show that a person can use Microsoft technologies in realistic AI and cloud scenarios, and they are positioned as a complement to role-based Microsoft certifications rather than a replacement for them.

The central idea is that the assessment is hands-on. Instead of answering multiple-choice questions, learners complete interactive, lab-based tasks that mirror real work. The program is framed around three steps: prepare, earn and share. Learners can work at their own pace and on their own schedule, which makes the format usable alongside a job or other studies.

Applied Skills credentials are grouped by role. Examples named in the program overview include AI engineer, Azure administrator, security engineer, data engineer and Power Platform functional consultant. Newer credentials cover the business use of Microsoft 365 Copilot as well as technical topics such as Copilot Studio and Foundry. Because each credential targets a defined scenario, it describes a narrower, task-oriented capability than a certification aligned to an entire job role.

The intended audience is broad: IT professionals, business professionals, developers, students, educators and career changers. People typically use the credentials to prove practical skills when applying for jobs or when being considered for project assignments. A common decision is whether to pursue an Applied Skills credential, a Microsoft Certification, or both, and the official program page points to guidance on choosing between the two. The overview page is a marketing summary and does not state fees, passing scores or how long a credential stays valid, so those details need to be checked in the official documentation for the specific credential.

The topic appears in the M365.FM episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals". There, Microsoft Applied Skills are mentioned as an option for people who prefer hands-on learning while preparing for Microsoft Fabric. The episode describes the assessments as a way to practice real-world challenges and build confidence, and it lists them alongside other preparation steps: live sessions with Microsoft Fabric experts, preparation for the DP-600 exam toward the Fabric Analytics Engineer certification, and a structured learning path on Microsoft Learn that spans beginner to advanced topics for roles such as Data Analyst, Data Engineer and Data Scientist.

In that context, Applied Skills sit next to the exam-based route rather than replacing it. A learner working toward a role-based certification such as the Fabric Analytics Engineer credential can use lab-style assessments to rehearse practical tasks, while the certification exam addresses the broader role. Which path fits depends on the goal: demonstrating a specific, verifiable skill, or earning a role-based certification that covers a wider scope.

microsoft-appsource.desc: Microsoft AppSource is Microsoft's marketplace for business applications and add-ins that extend Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and the Power Platform.

faq.a: Microsoft AppSource is a marketplace for business applications and add-ins that extend Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and the Power Platform. It is developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: What is Microsoft AppSource?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained", Azure Marketplace mainly serves technical buyers looking for items like virtual machines, containers and security appliances. AppSource is oriented toward business applications for Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and the Power Platform, although Microsoft now presents a unified Marketplace experience.
faq.q: How does AppSource differ from Azure Marketplace?

faq.a: The episode "Your AppSource Listing Is Costing You Deals" says it is not. It argues that a poorly optimized listing can reduce discoverability, credibility and conversion rates.
faq.q: Is publishing a solution on AppSource enough to win customers?

microsoft-appsource.long:
Microsoft AppSource is an online marketplace, developed by Microsoft, for business applications and add-ins. It is used to find and acquire solutions that extend Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and the Power Platform. Microsoft documents it in an overview page on Microsoft Learn, and it is classed here as a Microsoft tool related to those three product families. It is also described as similar to Azure Marketplace, the other storefront in Microsoft's marketplace platform.

The core idea is reuse. Instead of every organization building the same functionality on its own, a software vendor packages a solution once and offers it to many customers. The episode "Dynamics 365 Business Central Extensions - Simply Explained" gives an example from Dynamics 365 Business Central: when many companies need to connect the product to the same bank or shipping company, an ISV can create one reusable application that several organizations purchase or subscribe to. The episode says many third-party Business Central applications can be found through Microsoft AppSource, and that this is particularly useful when the business requirement is common across customers.

The relationship to Azure Marketplace is a recurring theme. The episode "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained" notes that Microsoft now presents one unified Marketplace experience, but the platform still serves two different audiences. According to the episode, Azure Marketplace is aimed mainly at technical buyers such as cloud architects, developers, infrastructure engineers and Azure administrators, who look there for items like virtual machines, managed applications, containers and security appliances. AppSource is the storefront oriented toward business applications for Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and the Power Platform. The episode also points out that customers working within their Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365 tenants can spend less time managing vendors and more time deploying technology that addresses business problems.

The episode "Microsoft AppSource - Simply Explained" presents AppSource as a platform for improving productivity through a wide range of solutions that integrate with Microsoft products. It frames the topic for administrators, architects and business stakeholders, covering what AppSource does, where it fits in the Microsoft ecosystem, and the considerations that matter for technical decisions and safe implementation. For customers, typical decisions revolve around whether a common requirement is already covered by a published solution before commissioning custom development.

For publishers, the picture is more demanding. The episode "Your AppSource Listing Is Costing You Deals" argues that simply publishing a solution is not enough to generate business. According to the episode, a poorly optimized listing can reduce discoverability, weaken credibility and lower conversion rates, and it describes common mistakes that Microsoft partners and ISVs make when creating listings. A related episode, "The Hard Way to Get Listed on Microsoft Marketplace", states that getting approved is only the beginning. It covers the differences between Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource, when each is appropriate, marketplace eligibility, how Microsoft evaluates submissions, and topics such as co-sell opportunities, private offers and transactable listings. The episode addresses ISVs, MSPs, Microsoft partners and other software vendors who want to grow through Microsoft's ecosystem.

Taken together, the episodes treat AppSource from two sides: as a discovery channel for organizations that want to extend Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 or the Power Platform with ready-made solutions, and as a distribution channel for vendors whose results depend on listing quality and an understanding of the marketplace process. Anyone evaluating or publishing through AppSource can use the Microsoft Learn overview page as the official starting point.

microsoft-authenticator.desc: Microsoft Authenticator is Microsoft's phone app for authentication, used with Microsoft Entra ID for passwordless sign-in, device-bound passkeys and verified credentials.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's authentication app for phones and is one of the authentication methods supported by Microsoft Entra ID. The episodes describe it for passwordless sign-in, as a second factor and for step-up authentication, and it can hold device-bound passkeys for work accounts.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Authenticator used for in Microsoft Entra ID?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained", digitally signed credentials issued by trusted organizations are stored securely in the Microsoft Authenticator app. The user decides whether to share the requested information with a verifier.
faq.q: Does Microsoft Authenticator store verified credentials?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation" describes retrieving the Microsoft Authenticator configuration through Microsoft Graph, mentioned in connection with preventing MFA fatigue.
faq.q: Can Microsoft Authenticator settings be managed by administrators?

microsoft-authenticator.long:
Microsoft Authenticator is Microsoft's authentication app for phones. In the context of Microsoft Entra ID, it serves as one of the methods organizations can use to verify who is signing in to a work account. It can hold device-bound passkeys for work accounts, which makes it a practical building block for moving away from passwords. The app appears in several M365.FM episodes, always as one piece of a wider identity and access picture rather than as a standalone topic.

The main use described in the episodes is passwordless authentication. The episode "Passkeys vs Passwords in Microsoft Entra ID" explains how organizations are shifting away from passwords and walks through how FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello and the Microsoft Authenticator app work. It opens with data on credential theft and then covers case studies the episode associates with lower breach risk, faster onboarding and cost savings. It also offers a playbook for piloting passwordless authentication, including common pitfalls, quick wins and the security trade-offs that come with removing passwords.

The episode "ENTRA PIM EXPLAINED: Securing Privileged Access with Mark Orr [MVP]" places the app in a recommendation for privileged and general accounts. The guest, who the episode says has run passwordless authentication for many years, recommends moving organizations toward Windows Hello for Business, passkeys, Microsoft Authenticator passwordless sign-in and hardware security keys such as YubiKeys. According to the episode, passwordless authentication improves security and also the user experience, because forgotten passwords disappear and users are better protected against phishing and credential theft.

Microsoft Authenticator also appears in the list of authentication methods supported by Microsoft Entra ID. The episode "Graph API - Simply Explained" names password, phone (SMS and voice calls), FIDO2 security keys and the Microsoft Authenticator app as methods that can serve as primary authentication, second-factor authentication and step-up authentication, and that also support self-service password resets. The same episode notes that authentication methods such as phone numbers and email addresses can be managed through APIs, so they can be added, updated or deleted programmatically.

Administrators can also manage the app's behavior through Microsoft Graph. The episode "Microsoft Graph and PowerShell for Enterprise Automation" lists a call that retrieves the Microsoft Authenticator configuration within the authentication methods policy, described there as a way to prevent MFA fatigue. It places this alongside other automation topics such as updating a user's MFA state, conditional access policies, admin consent policy and directory settings, and notes that automated policies reduce manual work and help meet compliance standards.

A further role is covered in "Microsoft Entra Verified ID - Simply Explained". There, trusted organizations issue digitally signed credentials based on open standards for decentralized identity, and individuals store them securely inside the Microsoft Authenticator app. These credentials carry verified claims such as employee status, completed training, professional licenses, student enrollment or supplier relationships. When another organization requests proof, the user decides whether to share the required information, and the verifier can check the credential's authenticity, issuer, expiration date and revocation status.

Taken together, the episodes treat Microsoft Authenticator as an app that connects three areas: sign-in with passkeys and passwordless methods, policy-based management of authentication methods through Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Graph, and storage of verifiable digital credentials. Typical decisions around it include whether to pilot passwordless sign-in, which combination of Authenticator, Windows Hello for Business and hardware keys to offer, and how to configure the app's settings centrally.

microsoft-bookings.desc: Microsoft Bookings is a Microsoft 365 scheduling tool with a public booking page that checks Outlook calendars and sends appointment confirmations.

faq.a: Microsoft Bookings is used to schedule appointments through a public booking page. It checks Outlook calendars for free times and sends confirmations, which suits consultations, service appointments and interviews.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Bookings used for?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Bookings is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365 and is included in the license. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Bookings part of Microsoft 365?

faq.a: Outlook calendars determine which times are available on the booking page, so offered slots reflect the real schedule. Microsoft Teams can be used for online appointments.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Bookings relate to Outlook and Teams?

microsoft-bookings.long:
Microsoft Bookings is an appointment scheduling tool developed by Microsoft and included in Microsoft 365. It provides a public booking page on which customers or colleagues can choose an appointment time. The tool checks Outlook calendars for free times and sends confirmations, which removes the back-and-forth emails that scheduling often involves. In Microsoft's product landscape it is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool.

The core purpose of Bookings is to let people book time with others without manual coordination. Typical uses are consultations, service appointments and interviews. The person or team offering appointments publishes a booking page, and the visitor picks from the times that are actually open. Because availability is read from Outlook calendars, a time that is already taken by another meeting is not offered, and confirmations are sent once a booking is made.

Bookings sits within the wider Microsoft 365 environment and is related to two other products. Microsoft Outlook matters because its calendars determine availability, so the booking page reflects the real schedule of the people involved. Microsoft Teams is relevant because it can be used for online appointments, which suits situations where the consultation or interview takes place remotely instead of at a physical location. Official documentation for the tool is available through Microsoft Support.

Several decisions typically come up when Bookings is considered. One is whether a public booking page fits the use case, for example when external customers need to arrange appointments without access to internal calendars. Another is whether the appointment is held in person or online, which links the tool to Teams. A third is which calendars should be consulted, since the accuracy of the offered times depends on how current the Outlook calendars are.

Bookings also appears in discussions about managing many Microsoft 365 work tools. The episode "Unify Microsoft 365 Tasks Across To Do, Planner, Lists, and Loop" lists Microsoft Bookings together with Microsoft To Do, Planner, tasks in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Lists as part of a mix of apps that can feel confusing. The episode presents the goal as bringing this mix into one coherent system and suggests simplifying the approach, for instance by creating separate lists for work and personal tasks.

Other M365.FM episodes touch on scheduling and booking concepts in neighbouring products, but none of them is specifically about Microsoft Bookings. "Dynamics 365 Field Service - Simply Explained" describes work orders and bookings that move through statuses such as waiting for scheduling, booked, the technician's visit and completion or follow-up. "Dynamics 365 Project Operations - Simply Explained" explains resource bookings as a way of reserving part of someone's working capacity for project work. "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" mentions managing meetings and workspace bookings alongside other tasks. "Microsoft Teams Premium - Simply Explained" includes a section titled "Appointments and Bookings" among the Teams Premium topics it covers. These uses of the word booking refer to separate features and products, so they should not be confused with the Bookings tool described here.

In summary, Microsoft Bookings is a focused tool for self-service appointment scheduling. Its value rests on its connection to Outlook calendars for availability, its confirmations, and its fit with Teams for online appointments, all within a Microsoft 365 subscription.

microsoft-bot-framework.desc: Microsoft Bot Framework is a set of SDKs and services for building conversational bots, including bots that run in Microsoft Teams.

faq.a: It is a set of SDKs and services for building conversational bots. In Microsoft Teams, bots and action-based message extensions typically run behind a Bot Framework endpoint that receives user requests and returns cards.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Bot Framework?

faq.a: According to the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", bots use the Microsoft Bot Framework and connect to Teams through secure messaging. The bot is created as a capability in the Teams Developer Portal and configured with a unique ID and password.
faq.q: How do Teams bots connect to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: The episode "Build Actionable Teams Notifications with Adaptive Cards" says the Bot Framework REST API can send Adaptive Cards to users or channels. Card actions such as Action.Submit and Action.Execute can send data to a flow or trigger context-aware bot actions.
