According to the Microsoft Learn getting-started page for incentives in Partner Center, the process follows a clear path. A partner reviews the available programs under Microsoft investments and incentives, enrolls in a program, and checks eligibility where the program requires it. The eligibility check applies only to some programs. The page works as an entry point rather than a catalog: it does not list specific programs, payout amounts or eligibility criteria, and further detail sits in linked articles on enrollment, eligibility, profiles and engagements.

Payment depends on administrative groundwork in Partner Center. Partners set up payout and tax profiles, which hold the bank and tax details Microsoft needs to make payments. They can also review Microsoft Commerce Incentives engagements and their own eligibility status. Membership in the partner program is required, and the user working on this needs the Incentives admin or Incentives user role. Program details, payout profile and eligibility information must all be in place before a payout can happen, so a missing profile or role can delay or block a payment even when the underlying activity qualifies.

In practice, the decisions around partner incentives are partly organizational and partly strategic. On the organizational side, a partner has to decide who holds the incentives roles, who maintains the payout and tax profiles, and who monitors eligibility status. On the strategic side, incentives are one of several factors that shape how a partner positions its business. The funds can be reinvested in pre-sales, co-marketing and events, which links incentives directly to how a partner generates and develops customer demand.

The M365.FM episode "How to Build a Winning Microsoft Partner Strategy" (2026-07-15) places partner incentives alongside other building blocks of a partner business. According to the episode, a strong approach combines high-value service offerings with a specialization strategy around areas such as Microsoft 365, Azure, Security, Business Applications, Data & AI or Modern Work. It also explains the importance of recurring managed services, customer success, partner incentives, solution designations and Marketplace listings, and it stresses building long-term customer relationships instead of focusing solely on licensing revenue. In that framing, incentives are one element of a wider strategy and not a goal in themselves.

The episode "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained" (2026-07-22) connects incentives to the Marketplace. The episode says that for many software companies, Marketplace has moved from an optional distribution channel to a fundamental part of their go-to-market strategy. It adds that Microsoft continues to invest in partner incentives and Marketplace Rewards, which is making the platform increasingly relevant for software vendors building on Azure and Microsoft 365. Incentives therefore appear in two contexts in the episodes: as a driver of service-partner growth and as part of the commercial case for listing solutions in Marketplace.

Because the available sources do not name specific programs, amounts or eligibility rules, partners need to consult the current program pages in Partner Center for those details. What the sources establish is the general structure: incentives reward eligible activities and sales, require program membership and defined roles, depend on completed payout and tax profiles, and can be reinvested in pre-sales, co-marketing and events.

microsoft-places.desc: Microsoft Places is a Microsoft 365 workplace app for hybrid work that shows where colleagues plan to work and handles desk and room booking.

faq.a: Microsoft Places is used in hybrid work to see where colleagues plan to work, book desks and rooms, and coordinate in-office days. It brings these tasks into Microsoft 365 instead of separate booking systems.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Places used for?

faq.a: According to the episode "Coordinate Hybrid Work with Microsoft Places", Places integrates directly into Microsoft 365 tools employees already use, especially Outlook and Teams. Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Outlook are listed as related topics.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Places relate to Outlook and Teams?

faq.a: The episodes "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" and "Coordinate Hybrid Work with Microsoft Places" cover it directly. The episode "Designing an Inclusive Hybrid Workplace with Onyinye Madubuko [MVP]" discusses hybrid work practices more generally.
faq.q: Which M365.FM episodes cover Microsoft Places?

microsoft-places.long:
Microsoft Places is a workplace app in Microsoft 365 built for hybrid work. It shows where colleagues plan to work, lets people book desks and rooms, and helps teams coordinate their in-office days. Microsoft develops it, and it is part of Microsoft 365. It sits alongside the Microsoft tools that employees already use for collaboration, in particular Microsoft Outlook and Microsoft Teams.

The core problem Microsoft Places addresses is coordination. In a hybrid setup, people split their time between home and the office, and it is often unclear who will be on site on a given day. Without a shared view, employees tend to guess, or they move between separate booking systems for desks and meeting rooms. Microsoft Places brings these tasks into one place: users can see their team's in-office plans, reserve a desk or room, and arrange face-to-face time with colleagues.

The episode "Coordinate Hybrid Work with Microsoft Places" describes Places as turning scattered office coordination into a connected, AI-driven experience. It says Places weaves itself directly into the Microsoft 365 tools employees already rely on, especially Outlook and Teams. In practice, this means that planning where to work and booking a space does not require leaving the apps used for email, calendar and chat. The episode highlights that users can see where their team members plan to be, reserve desks and rooms in seconds, and organize in-person collaboration.

The episode "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" approaches the topic with a practical focus on what Microsoft Places is, how it works, and which decisions matter for architecture, adoption, security, governance and day-to-day operations. It presents Places as a solution meant to improve the experience in a hybrid work environment by simplifying workspace management and encouraging collaboration among teams. The episode also cites a statistic that 51% of hybrid employees are likely to go fully remote, using it to frame why coordinating office presence has become a concern for organizations; this figure is attributed to the episode and is not independently verified here.

Typical situations where Microsoft Places is relevant include planning which days a team meets in the office, finding an available desk when arriving on site, and reserving a room for an in-person meeting. For administrators and decision makers, the topics named in the episode are architecture, adoption, security, governance and operations. These indicate that introducing Places involves more than switching on an app: it calls for decisions on how the service fits into the existing Microsoft 365 environment, how employees are brought on board, and how access and data are governed.

Microsoft Places is related to several other topics on this site. Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Outlook are the main places where the experience surfaces for users, so familiarity with those tools supports adoption. It is also classed as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool, and it belongs to the wider Microsoft 365 offering. The episode "Designing an Inclusive Hybrid Workplace with Onyinye Madubuko [MVP]" covers hybrid work more broadly, recommending that technology make teamwork easier, that organizations collect feedback often, and that managers be trained to lead teams working in different locations. That discussion is about hybrid work practices in general rather than Places specifically, but it provides context for why a tool that coordinates presence and space can be useful.

For current details on capabilities and setup, Microsoft's official documentation for Places on Microsoft Learn is the reference point.

microsoft-planner.desc: Microsoft Planner is a task and project planning tool in Microsoft 365 with boards, buckets, schedules and goals, available as an app in Microsoft Teams.

faq.a: Microsoft Planner is used to plan and share team work with boards, buckets, schedules and goals. Tasks can be assigned and followed so that progress is visible to the whole team.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Planner used for?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop", To Do is meant for personal focus, while Planner is meant for team visibility and coordination.
faq.q: How does Planner differ from Microsoft To Do?

faq.a: Yes. Planner is integrated in Microsoft Teams as the Planner app, so teams can work with their plans from within Teams.
faq.q: Can Planner be used inside Microsoft Teams?

microsoft-planner.long:
Microsoft Planner is a task and project planning tool developed by Microsoft and included in Microsoft 365. It organizes work on boards with buckets, and it offers schedules and goals for tracking progress. In Microsoft Teams it appears as the Planner app, so teams can reach their plans without leaving the collaboration workspace. The product is also referred to as Planner, and in some contexts under the combined name "Tasks by Planner and To Do". It is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool.

Planner is used to make shared work visible. Tasks are created, assigned to people and grouped into buckets on a board, so that a team can see who is responsible for what and how far the work has progressed. The same structure supports simple task boards as well as more structured planning with schedules and goals. Because Planner is part of Microsoft 365, it sits alongside the other tools of the suite and is available as an app inside Teams channels and tabs.

Planner is closely related to several other Microsoft products. Microsoft To Do covers personal task lists, while Planner addresses team coordination. Microsoft Project is a related product, and its cloud scheduling capabilities continue in the Planner family. Microsoft Teams is the main place where many users meet Planner day to day, since the app can be added to a channel. A recurring decision in organizations is which task tool fits which context, and the episodes on this topic treat that question directly.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop" states that the task tools in Microsoft 365 are not the problem, but using them all at once is. It proposes a simple operating model: To Do for personal focus, Planner for team visibility, Lists for structured and recurring workflows, and Loop for real-time capture that flows into the others. The episode offers a practical playbook and a one-page decision map for choosing between them. A companion episode, "Unify Microsoft 365 Tasks Across To Do, Planner, Lists, and Loop", makes a similar argument: Microsoft 365 does not suffer from too many task apps but from unclear roles. According to the episode, chaos appears when teams mix those roles, duplicate tasks across tools and have to update each of them by hand. In that framing Planner is assigned to team coordination, and the episode describes automation and Copilot patterns that turn several apps into one coherent system.

Automation is the subject of "Automate Microsoft Planner Tasks with Copilot Studio". The episode shows how to build a "Task Planner" Copilot agent so that tasks can be created from natural-language requests instead of by dragging cards around a board. It describes how the pieces fit together: Planner keeps the board tidy, Copilot Studio reasons over the request, and Power Automate runs the rules in the background. The agent is built step by step in Copilot Studio with tight instructions and fixed Group and Plan IDs, so that it knows exactly where to create each task.

The direction in which Planner is developing is covered in "Microsoft Planner for Enterprise PPM with Erik van Hurck [MVP]". In this episode, host Mirko Peters talks with Microsoft MVP Erik van Hurck about how Planner is evolving from a simple task management tool into an enterprise Project and Portfolio Management platform. The discussion concerns moving beyond personal to-do lists and team task boards towards managing complex projects, portfolios, resources and strategic initiatives within the Microsoft ecosystem.

Planner also comes up in "Microsoft Teams Hidden Features with Josh Blalock [MVP]", which lists Planner among project management apps that can be added to a Teams channel. The episode notes that such apps let users check tasks, update files and receive reminders without leaving Teams, and that some send updates to the activity feed. It also suggests adding a project management app to a frequently used channel as a way to see how the integration works.

microsoft-pluton.desc: Microsoft Pluton is a security processor built into the CPU or system-on-chip, providing a hardware root of trust, secure identity, attestation and cryptographic services.

faq.a: Microsoft Pluton is a cryptographic security processor integrated into the CPU or system-on-chip, made up of a secure hardware subsystem and Microsoft-owned software. It provides a hardware root of trust, secure identity, attestation and cryptographic services.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Pluton?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn states that Pluton is meant to cover the functions of a Trusted Platform Module and to add capabilities beyond the TPM 2.0 specification. It can act as the system TPM, and device-based conditional access in Intune applies only when Pluton is configured as the TPM.
faq.q: Does Pluton replace the TPM?

faq.a: Pluton is the security subsystem of the Azure Sphere MCU. The episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained" says one core of the multi-core MCU is dedicated to the Pluton runtime, with firewalls between cores to isolate resources.
faq.q: How does Pluton relate to Azure Sphere?

microsoft-pluton.long:
Microsoft Pluton is a cryptographic security processor integrated directly into the CPU or system-on-chip. It consists of a secure hardware subsystem and Microsoft-owned software that runs on it. Microsoft designed Pluton, and silicon partners build it into their processors. It is also the security subsystem of the Azure Sphere microcontroller unit (MCU).

The purpose of Pluton is to provide a hardware-based root of trust, secure identity, secure attestation and cryptographic services. In practice this means protecting credentials, identities, personal data and encryption keys. According to Microsoft Learn, it is meant to cover the functions of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and to add capabilities beyond the TPM 2.0 specification. Because the processor sits inside the chip rather than being a separate component, the security functions are part of the silicon itself.

On the hardware side, Pluton includes a secure element with a trusted execution environment. Firmware authorized by Microsoft is stored in the motherboard's SPI flash and loaded at boot, and Windows uses the newest available version. Updates are delivered through Windows Update or through classic UEFI capsule updates. Pluton is documented for Windows 11 on supported editions such as Pro, Enterprise and Education, with listed AMD, Intel and Qualcomm processors.

A typical use is Pluton acting as the system TPM. In that configuration it can support device-based conditional access in Intune, where device health is confirmed through tamper-resistant, cryptographically verifiable logs. The documentation notes that this conditional access benefit applies only when Pluton is configured as the TPM. For administrators, the practical decision is therefore whether a device's TPM role is handled by Pluton and whether the processor is among the supported ones for the Windows 11 edition in use.

Pluton also appears outside the Windows PC context. In the M365.FM episode "Azure Sphere - Simply Explained", Pluton is described as part of the secured MCUs used in Azure Sphere devices. The episode explains that these MCUs incorporate security features such as the Pluton security subsystem and silicon-based attestation. Unlike standard MCUs, Azure Sphere MCUs use a multi-core architecture in which one core is dedicated to the Pluton runtime, which improves security through isolation. The design includes firewalls between cores so that resources remain accessible only to designated cores, which the episode says significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access.

Taken together, the sources show Pluton as one security design used in two settings: as a TPM-capable security processor in supported Windows 11 devices, and as the security subsystem of the Azure Sphere MCU. In both cases the common idea is to anchor trust in hardware, so that identity, attestation and key protection do not depend solely on software running on the main processor.

microsoft-product-terms.desc: Microsoft Product Terms are Microsoft's published licensing terms, incorporated into customer agreements, that govern use of its software and online services, including Copilot.

faq.a: They are Microsoft's published licensing terms that are incorporated into customer agreements and govern the use of Microsoft software and online services.
faq.q: What are the Microsoft Product Terms?

faq.a: The episodes describe both as part of the contractual baseline for Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episodes say customer data and training data usage are governed by the privacy statement and terms, the Data Protection Addendum and the Product Terms together.
faq.q: How do the Product Terms relate to the Data Protection Addendum?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Copilot Rollout: DPA and Product Terms Checklist", the contracts set the legal wiring for a rollout, covering topics such as data residency, the processor role, IP ownership and no training on tenant data, before licenses and permissions are applied.
faq.q: Why do the Product Terms matter for a Copilot rollout?

microsoft-product-terms.long:
The Microsoft Product Terms are Microsoft's published licensing terms. They are incorporated into customer agreements and govern how Microsoft software and online services may be used. In discussions of Microsoft 365 Copilot, they are described as part of the contractual baseline for an organization's deployment, sitting alongside the Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

The main purpose of the Microsoft Product Terms is to define the legal framework in which licensed products are used. Because they are incorporated into customer agreements, they are not an optional reference document. They form part of the contractual wiring that determines what a customer may do with a service and what commitments apply to the data processed in it. For administrators, compliance teams and legal reviewers, the Product Terms are therefore one of the documents to read before enabling a new service across a tenant.

The episode "Microsoft Copilot Rollout: DPA and Product Terms Checklist" treats the Product Terms and the DPA together as the contractual layer of a Copilot rollout. The episode says that turning on Microsoft Copilot is not a single switch but governance in motion: the toggle activates a chain of contractual, technical and organizational controls that either align or fail. In that framing, contracts set the legal wiring. The episode lists data residency, the processor role, intellectual property ownership and a commitment that tenant data is not used for training as the topics the contractual documents establish. Licenses then unlock features, while roles and permissions decide what Copilot can actually reach.

The Product Terms are also referenced in the episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Copilot Data Quality and Leak Risks". There, the point is that data used by Copilot, including content reachable through Microsoft Graph or connectors when permissions are granted, is governed by several documents rather than one. According to the episode, Microsoft states that customer data and training data usage are governed by the privacy statement and terms, the data protection addendum and the Microsoft Product Terms. The episode advises checking the privacy statement, the terms of use and the data protection addendum for details. This places the Product Terms within a set of related documents, each covering a different part of how data and services are handled.

In practice, the Product Terms come into play at the start of a rollout and during governance reviews. A typical sequence described in the episodes is to confirm the contractual position first, then address licensing, then configure permissions and protective controls. The later episode "Secure a Microsoft Copilot Rollout with Microsoft Purview" lists the checklist episode among its related reading, linking the contractual review to technical safeguards such as Purview, data loss prevention and insider risk controls. The contractual documents do not replace those controls; they define the legal baseline on which the technical and organizational measures are built.

For readers searching for the term, the key points are limited. The Microsoft Product Terms are a published, regularly consulted document set. They are incorporated into customer agreements. They govern use of Microsoft software and online services. They are read together with the Data Protection Addendum when assessing a Microsoft 365 Copilot deployment. The sources provided here do not detail the internal structure of the Product Terms or specific clauses, so anyone assessing a particular obligation should consult the published terms directly and involve legal or compliance staff.

microsoft-purview-audit.desc: Microsoft Purview Audit records user and administrator activity across Microsoft 365 in a searchable unified audit log, offered as Audit (Standard) and Audit (Premium).

faq.a: Microsoft Purview Audit records user and administrator activity from Microsoft 365 services in a searchable unified audit log. It is part of Microsoft Purview and is available as Audit (Standard) and Audit (Premium).
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Audit?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Purview Audit - Simply Explained", it helps answer what happened, who performed the action and when it took place, for example during a security incident, compliance investigation or legal request.
faq.q: What questions can the audit log help answer?

faq.a: The episodes describe it as complementary to services such as Records Management, Communication Compliance, Content Search, eDiscovery and Data Loss Prevention. Purview Audit supplies the activity history, for instance showing when retention labels were applied or when disposition approvals were completed.
faq.q: How does Purview Audit relate to other Microsoft Purview services?

microsoft-purview-audit.long:
Microsoft Purview Audit is the auditing capability of Microsoft Purview that records user and administrator activity from Microsoft 365 services in a searchable unified audit log. It is offered in two tiers, Audit (Standard) and Audit (Premium). The capability is part of Microsoft Purview, the compliance and governance portfolio, and is documented by Microsoft in its audit solutions overview.

The purpose of Purview Audit is to give organizations a factual record of what happened, who performed an action, and when it took place. The episode "Microsoft Purview Audit - Simply Explained" describes the everyday context: employees open files, share documents, send emails, change Microsoft Teams settings, update compliance policies and perform many other actions across Microsoft 365. When a security incident, a compliance investigation or a legal request occurs, the audit log is the place where those questions can be answered.

The episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview" approaches the topic as a step-by-step walkthrough. It frames auditing user activity as important for maintaining security and ensuring compliance, since it helps identify suspicious behavior and protect sensitive information. According to the episode, Microsoft Purview makes tracking easier by allowing teams to monitor a large number of audit events and gain insight into user behavior and compliance status. Typical scenarios named in the episode are investigating suspicious behavior, preparing for a compliance review and strengthening the overall security posture, with the aim of turning audit data into actionable insight.

Audit readiness is a second recurring theme. The episode "Microsoft 365 Audit Readiness and Governance Debt" defines Microsoft 365 audit readiness as having the people, processes and technical configuration in place to capture, retain, search and produce audit records across Microsoft services when required. It explains that this matters because organizations must demonstrate compliance and investigate incidents, and it points to Purview audit log retention policies as part of that picture. The episode also recommends reviewing and updating an audit readiness checklist regularly to reflect platform changes and regulatory requirements, so that controls remain evidence-based and interactions with auditors stay efficient.

Purview Audit also works alongside other Microsoft Purview services. In "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained", the episode says Purview Audit complements records management by maintaining an activity history that shows when retention labels were applied, when record declarations occurred, when disposition approvals were completed and when other lifecycle events took place. These records provide the evidence organizations need to demonstrate regulatory compliance and defend records management decisions.

The episode "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" places Purview Audit within the wider Purview landscape in a similar way. It describes Purview Audit as the service that records user activities and administrative actions across Microsoft 365, next to Content Search, which locates emails, documents and messages relevant to investigations, and Microsoft Purview eDiscovery, which manages legal cases, preserves evidence and supports litigation workflows. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and Communication Compliance are named as further complementary services.

In practice, decisions around Purview Audit usually concern which tier fits the organization's needs, how long audit records need to be retained, and how the log is used during investigations, compliance reviews and audits. The M365.FM episodes treat the audit log as a source of evidence that supports security teams, compliance officers and legal teams, rather than as a standalone control.

microsoft-purview-data-lifecycle-managem.desc: Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management governs how long Microsoft 365 content is retained and whether it is deleted or reviewed, using retention policies and labels.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft Purview solution that helps organizations decide how long Microsoft 365 content is kept and whether it is deleted or reviewed at the end of its lifespan. It does this mainly through retention policies and retention labels.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management?

faq.a: The episode "Data Lifecycle Management - Simply Explained" names emails, Teams chats, SharePoint documents, OneDrive files, and other Microsoft 365 content as examples that would otherwise accumulate indefinitely.
faq.q: Which content does Data Lifecycle Management apply to?

faq.a: It is part of Microsoft Purview. Episodes mention it together with retention labels, records management, review workflows, auditing, eDiscovery, and Compliance Manager.
faq.q: How is Data Lifecycle Management related to Microsoft Purview?

microsoft-purview-data-lifecycle-managem.long:
Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management is a solution within Microsoft Purview that helps organizations decide how long Microsoft 365 content is kept and what happens to it when its retention period ends. The end-of-lifespan outcome can be deletion or a review step. The main mechanisms are retention policies and retention labels, which let administrators apply defined retention behavior to content instead of leaving it to accumulate without limits.

The purpose of the solution is to bring information under a defined business, legal, or regulatory process. Without such controls, emails, Teams chats, SharePoint documents, OneDrive files, and other Microsoft 365 content can pile up indefinitely. Data Lifecycle Management addresses this by establishing how long information should be kept, when it should be reviewed, and when it should be securely deleted. Retaining what is needed and removing what is not is the idea at the center of the product.

In practice, the work starts with defining retention requirements and then expressing them as retention policies and retention labels. A retention policy applies retention settings to content in the Microsoft 365 locations it covers, while a retention label can be applied to individual items. These two building blocks are the ones named in the product description, and the available documentation entry point for the solution is the Microsoft Learn page on data lifecycle management. Decisions that typically arise include how long different content types must be retained, which content should be deleted at the end of that period, and where a review is more appropriate than automatic deletion.

Data Lifecycle Management is part of Microsoft Purview and sits alongside other Purview capabilities. The episode "Microsoft Purview vs Azure Information Protection" lists, in a deployment checklist, integrating with records management and retention labels as needed, configuring supervised and automatic content review where necessary through review workflows, and deploying content scanning and labeling for repositories using Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management and the scanner. The same checklist also covers centralized logging and auditing of label and protection activities, and enabling and testing eDiscovery and legal hold capabilities for protected content. The same excerpt appears in the episode "What Is Microsoft Intune Used For?".

The topic also appears in the context of AI governance. The episode "Control Rogue AI Data Risks with Microsoft Purview" describes Purview Data Lifecycle Management as retaining necessary content and deleting non-essential data. In that episode it is one element in a wider list of compliance measures, which includes logging and retaining AI interactions, using eDiscovery tools to investigate AI interactions, running privacy impact assessments, and building assessments in Purview Compliance Manager. In this framing, retention and deletion rules apply to the data generated by AI use in the same way as to other Microsoft 365 content.

The most direct treatment is the episode "Data Lifecycle Management - Simply Explained". It describes the solution as a way to control how long information should be kept, when it should be reviewed, and when it should be securely deleted, and it names emails, Teams chats, SharePoint documents, and OneDrive files as examples of content that would otherwise accumulate. Taken together, the episodes position Data Lifecycle Management as a retention and deletion layer that works together with labeling, review workflows, auditing, and eDiscovery rather than as a standalone control.

microsoft-purview-records-management.desc: Microsoft Purview Records Management manages official records in Microsoft 365 with retention labels, record declaration, disposition review and audit history.

faq.a: A locked record blocks editing and deletion in SharePoint and OneDrive. A regulatory record is stricter: its label cannot be removed or changed, even by a global administrator, and retention can only be extended. Regulatory records must first be enabled with PowerShell and cannot come from auto-labeling policies.
faq.q: What is the difference between a record and a regulatory record in Microsoft Purview Records Management?

faq.a: Retention labels mark items as a record or a regulatory record. They can be applied manually or automatically based on sensitive information, keywords or content types.
faq.q: How are items marked as records?

faq.a: Disposition reviews allow content to be checked before deletion. Proof of deletion and the export of deleted items support the end of the lifecycle.
faq.q: What happens at the end of a retention period?

microsoft-purview-records-management.long:
Microsoft Purview Records Management is a solution within Microsoft Purview for handling content that has regulatory, legal or business-critical importance. It is used to meet legal obligations, to demonstrate compliance and to dispose of content that no longer needs to be kept. Organizations create contracts, financial reports, employee records, policies and many other business documents across SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Microsoft Teams and Exchange Online. Records management provides the rules that define which of these items become official records, how long they must be preserved and when they can safely be deleted.

The central building block is the retention label. A retention label can mark an item as a record or as a regulatory record. Labels can be applied manually, or automatically based on sensitive information, keywords or content types. Organizations can import or build a file plan, which structures their retention requirements, and they can define retention periods based on the creation date or the modification date of an item. Event-based retention is also supported, where the retention period starts only when a defined trigger occurs.

The documentation distinguishes two levels of protection. A locked record blocks editing and deletion in SharePoint and OneDrive. A regulatory record is stricter: the label cannot be removed or changed, not even by a global administrator, and the retention period can only be extended. Regulatory records have to be enabled with PowerShell first, and they cannot come from auto-labeling policies. For Exchange, only the behavior of locked records applies. Because of these differences, choosing between a record and a regulatory record is a decision that depends on how strict the legal or regulatory requirement is.

The end of the lifecycle is covered as well. Disposition reviews allow content to be checked before it is deleted, and proof of deletion and the export of deleted items support traceability. Audit history records what happened to items over their lifecycle. Specific roles control who can access records manager functions, so that responsibility for records can be separated from general administration. The documentation also describes how migrated files can be verified by comparing hash values, which is relevant when records are moved into Microsoft 365 from other systems.

In practice, a typical approach is to define a file plan, create retention labels that reflect the required retention periods, decide which labels declare records or regulatory records, and then publish or automatically apply those labels to content in Microsoft 365 locations. Disposition review is then configured for the end of the retention period so that deletion is deliberate and documented. Licensing is covered in a separate part of the Microsoft documentation and is not described here.

Microsoft Purview Records Management is part of Microsoft Purview and sits alongside other information governance capabilities in that portfolio. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Purview Records Management - Simply Explained" introduces the topic in an accessible way. It starts from the observation that organizations must retain contracts, financial reports, employee records and policies for legal, regulatory and operational reasons, and that modern work spans SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Microsoft Teams and Exchange Online while clear rules are still needed for what counts as an official record, how long it is preserved and when it can be deleted.

microsoft-scout.desc: Microsoft Scout is an always-on desktop AI agent for Windows 11 and macOS that works proactively across Microsoft 365, local files and the web.

faq.a: Microsoft Scout is an always-on desktop AI agent for Windows 11 and macOS that Microsoft describes as its first Autopilot. It works proactively across Microsoft 365, local files and the web under its own identity.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Scout?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Scout - Simply Explained" says Scout moves beyond chatbots to autonomous agents that actively complete work on a user's behalf. It can execute multi-step tasks across files, Microsoft 365 data, the browser and the local computer, rather than only answering prompts.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Scout differ from Microsoft 365 Copilot?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Agent Builder — Simply Explained", the Scout Agent autonomously operates a browser to achieve user-defined goals such as research. It pulls data from web pages and interacts with SaaS applications without human input.
faq.q: What can the Scout Agent do in a browser?

microsoft-scout.long:
Microsoft Scout is an always-on desktop AI agent for Windows 11 and macOS. Microsoft describes it as its first Autopilot. It works proactively across Microsoft 365 data, local files and the web, and it operates under its own identity rather than only reacting to a single prompt. The product reflects a move from chat-style assistants toward agents that act on a user's behalf.

The central idea behind Microsoft Scout is autonomy. A conventional chatbot answers questions or drafts text when asked. According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Scout - Simply Explained", Scout is positioned as the next generation of AI assistants, meant to actively complete work instead of only responding to prompts. The episode describes it as a major shift in Microsoft's AI strategy and discusses how it differs from Microsoft 365 Copilot. Where Copilot is typically associated with assisting inside applications, Scout is described as an agent that can carry out multi-step tasks on its own.

The working scope named in the sources covers several areas. Scout can work across a user's files, Microsoft 365 data, the browser and the local computer. The episode gives examples such as organizing documents, managing emails and running workflows, and says it can interact with business systems. Because it runs on the desktop and not only in the cloud, it can reach local files and local applications, which is part of what distinguishes it from assistants that live inside a single app. The fact that it works under its own identity is relevant for administrators, since an agent with an identity can be treated as a distinct actor when thinking about access, permissions and accountability.

Scout also appears in the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Agent Builder — Simply Explained". There it is listed as a Scout Agent: an AI agent that autonomously operates a browser to achieve user-defined goals, such as research. The episode says this agent pulls data from web pages and interacts with SaaS applications without human input, and that it integrates with Microsoft 365. This points to browser operation as one of the ways Scout acts, alongside file and Microsoft 365 work. The same episode places Scout among other building blocks in the agent tooling, including MAI models that support structured output generation and tool-calling, and long-context handling suited to tasks like contract analysis.

Typical decisions around a product like Microsoft Scout follow from its autonomy. Organizations considering it would weigh which tasks to hand over, how much access an always-on agent should have to local files and Microsoft 365 content, and how its actions are reviewed. The sources do not give details on configuration, licensing, pricing or administrative controls, so those points are not covered here. What the episodes do establish is the conceptual framing: Scout acts, rather than only advising, and it spans the desktop, Microsoft 365 and the web.

In relation to the wider Microsoft ecosystem, Scout sits alongside Microsoft 365 Copilot and the agent-building tooling discussed in the M365.FM coverage. The episode "Microsoft Scout - Simply Explained" is the main source for the product's definition and its contrast with Copilot, while "Microsoft Agent Builder — Simply Explained" shows where the Scout Agent fits within a broader set of agent capabilities. Readers looking for the product's role in Microsoft's direction toward autonomous agents will find it described in those two episodes.

microsoft-search.desc: Microsoft Search is enterprise search in Microsoft 365 that finds people, files, sites and answers across Microsoft 365 apps, Bing and connected data sources.

faq.a: Microsoft Search is enterprise search in Microsoft 365 that finds people, files, sites and answers across Microsoft 365 apps, Bing and connected data sources. It is developed by Microsoft and is part of Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Search?

faq.a: Copilot connectors are a related topic because connected data sources extend what Microsoft Search can find beyond content stored in Microsoft 365. This allows information held in other systems to appear in search results.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Search relate to Copilot connectors?

faq.a: No. Microsoft Search is the search experience within Microsoft 365, while Azure AI Search is a separate Microsoft service for building search experiences and AI-powered applications, as covered in the M365.FM episode "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained".
faq.q: Is Microsoft Search the same as Azure AI Search?

microsoft-search.long:
Microsoft Search is the enterprise search capability built into Microsoft 365. It is designed to find people, files, sites and answers across Microsoft 365 apps, Bing and connected data sources. Developed by Microsoft, it is classified as a Microsoft tool and is part of Microsoft 365 rather than a separate stand-alone product. Official documentation for it is published in the Microsoft Learn library under the Microsoft Search section.

In practice, Microsoft Search serves as a single entry point for locating information that would otherwise be spread across many applications and repositories. Instead of opening each app and searching separately, a user can query for a colleague, a document, a SharePoint site or a direct answer from one search experience. Because it also reaches Bing and connected data sources, the scope is not limited to content stored inside Microsoft 365 itself. Content that lives in other systems can be brought into search results through Copilot connectors, which is a related topic in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem.

The relationship to Copilot connectors is relevant for organizations that keep important knowledge outside Microsoft 365. Connecting external data sources extends what the search can surface, so that results are not restricted to files and sites inside the tenant. Decisions around this typically involve which sources are worth connecting, who should be able to see their content, and how the results fit into the daily work of different user groups.

The episodes in the M365.FM knowledge base do not describe Microsoft Search feature by feature, but they cover the wider theme of how enterprise search and retrieval work, which shapes how search quality is judged. The episode "Microsoft Graph API Discovery for Enterprise Semantic Search" argues that enterprise search is no longer limited by storage capacity or indexing speed. According to the episode, the real challenge is the growing gap between when information is created and when it becomes discoverable. It describes a shift from traditional crawl-and-index models to a relationship-driven, real-time discovery architecture built on Microsoft Graph.

Several other episodes look at retrieval from the angle of Azure AI Search, which is a separate Microsoft service for building search experiences and AI-powered applications. "Azure AI Search – Simply Explained" describes that service as combining traditional keyword search with vector search, semantic ranking and AI enrichment, and as a core component for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), AI agents and enterprise search solutions. "Azure AI Search Hybrid Retrieval - Simply Explained" explains why a single method falls short: keyword search reads the exact words typed, which suits a policy code but fails when someone asks about time off and the document says vacation. "HNSW vs DiskANN for Vector Search in Azure AI Search" compares two vector search algorithms, noting that HNSW delivers strong performance and high recall but needs significant RAM as datasets grow, while DiskANN, originally developed by Microsoft Research, uses SSD storage to reduce memory requirements.

A further episode, "Improve Microsoft Copilot Accuracy Beyond Vector Search", makes a point that applies to any search-backed system. The episode says vector search alone is not a complete or reliable strategy, because it finds content that is mathematically similar rather than necessarily correct, and that poor answers often come from retrieving wrong or low-quality data rather than from the language model itself. Taken together, these episodes frame search quality as a question of how information is retrieved, ranked and kept discoverable, which is the same concern that applies when evaluating Microsoft Search inside a Microsoft 365 environment.

microsoft-security-copilot.desc: Microsoft Security Copilot is Microsoft's generative AI security assistant that works with Defender, Entra and Intune to help security teams triage and investigate threats.

faq.a: Microsoft Security Copilot is Microsoft's generative AI security assistant. It integrates with products such as Defender, Entra and Intune and aims to help security teams detect, investigate and respond to threats faster.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Security Copilot?

faq.a: No. According to the episode "Microsoft Security Copilot - Simply Explained", it automates repetitive work like alert analysis, event correlation and incident summaries so that experts can focus on higher-value decisions.
faq.q: Does Security Copilot replace security analysts?

faq.a: No. One episode describes it as the Copilot used for Intune and as separate from Microsoft 365 Copilot.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Security Copilot the same as Microsoft 365 Copilot?

microsoft-security-copilot.long:
Microsoft Security Copilot is Microsoft's generative AI security assistant. It is designed to help security teams detect, investigate and respond to threats more quickly, and it integrates with Microsoft security products such as Defender, Entra and Intune. In one M365.FM episode it is described as the Copilot used for Intune, and as a product separate from Microsoft 365 Copilot. The official documentation for the product is published on Microsoft Learn.

The core idea described in the episodes is support rather than replacement. According to the episode "Microsoft Security Copilot - Simply Explained", the assistant does not replace security analysts. Instead, it automates repetitive work such as analyzing alerts, correlating events, summarizing incidents and generating remediation recommendations. This is meant to leave experts more time for higher-value decisions. The same episode frames Security Copilot as an AI-powered cybersecurity assistant for security teams, with the emphasis on speeding up the detect, investigate and respond cycle.

A recurring theme in the episodes is the workload of a Security Operations Center (SOC). The episode "Security Copilot for SOC Operations: Reduce Alert Fatigue" recounts a discussion with security analyst Mirko Peters about the challenges security teams face. The episode says analysts often handle more than 200 alerts a day and work with fragmented cybersecurity tools, which makes effective response to threats harder. It argues that on a normal day analysts are always behind, reacting to threats instead of proactively hunting and improving security posture. The proposed remedy is a combination of integrated tools, automation and AI assistance, and Security Copilot is presented as part of that answer.

The episode "Reduce Defender False Positives with Security Copilot Analysts" takes a more agent-oriented view. It describes autonomous, synthetic analysts built into Defender, Entra, Intune and related products, and presents them as a way for SOCs to cope with alert volume, phishing noise and Patch Tuesday workload. The framing there is that traditional Security Operations Centers are moving toward AI-driven defense. The episode also lists AI literacy among the skills involved, meaning a basic understanding of AI and cybersecurity so that tasks can be automated and threats analyzed. As with any show-notes summary, these points reflect the episode's own characterization rather than product documentation.

Security Copilot also appears in identity and zero trust discussions. The episode "Copilot in Microsoft Entra ID - Simply Explained" says that AI tools like Microsoft Security Copilot can automate the initial triage of identity protection alerts, particularly sign-in anomalies, reducing manual workloads. It connects this to proactive decision-making and to higher efficiency in SOCs, and it notes that organizations can build workflows that fit their own needs. In "Zero Trust AI Security with Microsoft Copilot and Azure – Mourtaza Fazlehoussen [MVP]", the product is named alongside Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Sentinel and Azure security services. The episode covers how these work together to detect threats, automate investigations and reduce risk, and places that in the context of least privilege, Conditional Access, identity protection, privileged access management and security monitoring in an AI-first world.

In practice, the decisions around Security Copilot concern where it fits among existing security tooling and which tasks to hand to automation. The episodes point to alert triage, incident summarization, event correlation and remediation recommendations as typical uses, and to Defender, Entra and Intune as the connected products. Because the show notes describe the assistant as supporting analysts, human judgment remains part of the process. Readers who need exact capabilities, requirements or licensing details should consult the official documentation, since the episode material summarized here is descriptive and does not specify them.

microsoft-security-exposure-management.desc: Microsoft Security Exposure Management is a Defender portal solution giving security teams a unified view of exposure and posture across Microsoft security products and connected data sources.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft security solution in the Defender portal that gives security teams a unified view of exposure and security posture across Microsoft security products and connected data sources.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Security Exposure Management?

faq.a: According to the Defender EASM episode, Security Exposure Management can bring information from different Microsoft security products into one exposure picture. For example, Defender EASM may identify a public-facing server while Defender for Cloud provides information about its configuration.
faq.q: How does it relate to Microsoft Defender EASM and Defender for Cloud?

faq.a: The episode with Uros Babic describes attackers looking for weak identities, excessive permissions, exposed cloud resources, forgotten devices and misconfigurations that can be combined into an attack, rather than focusing only on vulnerability counts, alerts and compliance dashboards.
faq.q: What attacker-oriented problems does the topic address?

microsoft-security-exposure-management.long:
Microsoft Security Exposure Management is a Microsoft security solution in the Defender portal. It gives security teams a unified view of exposure and security posture across Microsoft security products and connected data sources. Rather than treating each product's findings in isolation, it is intended to bring information from different tools into a broader exposure picture that teams can review in one place.

The underlying idea, as discussed in the M365.FM episodes, is to look at security from an attacker's perspective. The episode "Microsoft Security Exposure Management with Uros Babic [MVP-MCT]" notes that traditional cybersecurity often concentrates on vulnerability counts, alerts and compliance dashboards, while attackers look for weak identities, excessive permissions, exposed cloud resources, forgotten devices and misconfigurations that can be combined into a successful attack. In that episode, host Mirko Peters speaks with Microsoft Security MVP and MCT Uros Babic about approaching cybersecurity from this angle. A single finding may look minor on its own, but several findings together can form a path to a valuable asset, which is why a combined view of exposure matters.

Microsoft Security Exposure Management is used to understand how different parts of an environment relate to one another. The episode "Microsoft Defender EASM - Simply Explained" gives an example: Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management might identify a public-facing server, while Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides information about how that server is configured. Combining these perspectives can help security teams understand relationships between assets and weaknesses. In the same discussion, Defender for Cloud is described as addressing security across cloud workloads, Microsoft Entra ID as providing identity and access controls, and Defender EASM as showing what is publicly discoverable before an attacker reaches internal systems. Security Exposure Management sits above these tools and draws their information together.

Typical situations in which this kind of view is relevant include reviewing security posture across several Microsoft security products, identifying where identity, device, cloud and externally visible risks overlap, and deciding which exposures deserve attention first. The decision for an organization is largely about how its existing Microsoft security products and other data sources feed into one exposure picture, and how the findings are used by the teams that own identities, devices and cloud resources.

The topic connects to several other areas covered by M365.FM. Related episodes listed alongside it include "Privileged Identity Management (PIM) - Simply Explained", which touches on privileged access, and episodes on Microsoft Entra Permissions Management and Microsoft Entra Agent ID, which relate to permissions and identity. These themes correspond to the weak identities and excessive permissions that the Uros Babic episode names as things attackers look for.

M365.FM also offers a general explainer, "Microsoft Security Exposure Management: Simply Explained", for listeners who want an accessible introduction to the product. Official documentation for the solution is available from Microsoft Learn. This page summarizes only what is stated in those sources and episodes, and does not cover licensing, availability or configuration details.

microsoft-sentinel.desc: Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native SIEM and SOAR platform that gathers security data into a Log Analytics workspace to detect, investigate and respond to threats.

faq.a: Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native SIEM and SOAR platform. It collects security data from users, devices, applications, cloud services and on-premises infrastructure into a Log Analytics workspace to detect, investigate and respond to threats.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Sentinel?

faq.a: It uses analytics rules over the data collected in a Log Analytics workspace to raise alerts, and security teams can additionally hunt for threats with KQL.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Sentinel detect threats?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Defender vs Sentinel: When You Need Both", Defender focuses on real-time protection at the endpoint, in Microsoft 365 and across cloud workloads, while Sentinel plays a different role in the Azure security landscape. The episode discusses when both are needed.
faq.q: What is the difference between Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel?

microsoft-sentinel.long:
Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platform. It is designed to help organizations detect, investigate and respond to cyber threats across their entire IT environment. Instead of monitoring individual systems in isolation, Microsoft Sentinel collects security data from users, devices, applications, cloud services and on-premises infrastructure, giving security teams a single view of potential attacks.

Technically, the platform collects security data into a Log Analytics workspace. Detection is handled through analytics rules, which evaluate the collected data and raise alerts when suspicious activity is found. Security teams can also hunt for threats proactively with KQL, the query language used against the workspace data. This combination of central data collection, rule-based detection and query-driven investigation is what the product documentation describes as the core of a security operations platform.

In practice, Microsoft Sentinel is used by security analysts and security operations teams who need visibility beyond a single product. Signals from many sources end up in one place, so that an incident can be examined in context rather than as isolated alerts. Because it covers both SIEM and SOAR functions, it supports not only detection and investigation but also automated response to threats.

A frequent point of confusion is how Microsoft Sentinel relates to the Microsoft Defender products. The episode "Microsoft Defender vs Sentinel: When You Need Both" addresses this directly. It describes Defender as focused on real-time protection at the endpoint, in Microsoft 365 and across cloud workloads, acting like an automated guard, while Sentinel plays a different role in the Azure security landscape. The two sound similar but serve different purposes, and the episode discusses when an organization needs both. The episode "Microsoft Defender XDR - Simply Explained" adds that Defender XDR correlates events across identities, devices, email, cloud apps and Microsoft Teams, and that it integrates with Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Security Copilot, Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Entra to support a Zero Trust security strategy. Similarly, "Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - Simply Explained" notes that Defender for Endpoint works alongside Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel as part of a broader defense.

The episode "Detect Microsoft 365 Attack Chains with Entra and Sentinel" shows a typical detection scenario. It walks through a breach of a Microsoft 365 tenant in which a phishing click, an adversary-in-the-middle proxy and an OAuth app are used to steal session cookies, hijack mailboxes and pull data from SharePoint. The episode argues that MFA alone is not a sufficient shield in such cases, and it frames Entra and Sentinel as the pairing used to detect the chain of events across identity and Microsoft 365 activity rather than any single step.

The introductory episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" presents the platform in the format of Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets and covers the SIEM and SOAR definition and the idea of one view across users, devices, applications, cloud services and on-premises systems. Together, the episodes position Microsoft Sentinel as the central place where security data is collected, analyzed and acted on, with the Defender products and Microsoft Entra supplying signals and context around it.

microsoft-stream.desc: Microsoft Stream, also called Stream on SharePoint, is the Microsoft 365 video service that stores recordings in OneDrive and SharePoint and plays them in Teams.

faq.a: Microsoft Stream, also called Stream on SharePoint, is the video service of Microsoft 365. Recordings and clips are stored in OneDrive and SharePoint and played back in Teams and other places.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Stream?

faq.a: Videos are stored in OneDrive and SharePoint, so the permissions that apply to those locations also govern who can access the recordings.
faq.q: Where are Stream videos stored?

faq.a: No. Episodes such as "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" and "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service" cover Azure data streaming, not the Microsoft Stream video service.
faq.q: Are the M365.FM episodes about event streaming related to Microsoft Stream?

microsoft-stream.long:
Microsoft Stream, also referred to as Stream on SharePoint or simply Stream, is the video service of Microsoft 365. It covers the storage, management and playback of video content such as meeting recordings, training videos and internal communication clips. Rather than keeping video files in a separate silo, the service relies on the file storage already present in Microsoft 365: recordings and clips are stored in OneDrive and SharePoint, and they are played back in Microsoft Teams and other places. Stream is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365, and is included in the Microsoft 365 license.

In practice, Stream is used wherever an organization produces video that needs to be shared with colleagues. Typical situations are the recording of a Teams meeting, a recorded training session for new employees, or a short clip used in internal communication. Because the underlying files live in OneDrive and SharePoint, the same storage locations and permission settings that govern other documents also apply to the videos. This ties Stream closely to those two services, and it means that questions about who can watch a recording are answered in the place where the file is stored.

The relationships to neighbouring products are central to understanding Stream. Microsoft Teams is where many recordings originate and where they are played back, SharePoint holds video files in team and site libraries, and OneDrive holds files that belong to individual users. Stream sits across these three as the video layer of Microsoft 365. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool, which reflects its role in helping people share spoken and visual information instead of written documents alone. Administrators and content owners who plan a video strategy therefore usually have to consider Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive together rather than treating Stream as an isolated application.

A decision that follows from this design is where videos should be kept. Because storage is handled by OneDrive and SharePoint, a recording can sit in a personal location or in a shared site, and that choice shapes who can find, open and manage it. Organizations that want training or communication videos to remain available independently of a single person's account will typically think about shared SharePoint locations, while personal recordings naturally follow the OneDrive model. Official documentation for the service is published by Microsoft on its Learn platform under the Stream section.

The M365.FM episodes assigned to this topic share the word stream rather than the product itself, and it is worth being clear about that. "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" describes Event Hubs as a high-throughput event streaming platform for IoT and real-time analytics, and covers concepts such as namespaces, partitions, consumer groups, offsets and event retention. "IoT Hub vs Event Hubs — Why Most Manufacturers Pick the Wrong Service" compares two Azure services for factory telemetry and stresses separating device control, configuration state, commands and stream processing. "Can Value Stream Mapping Become a Live Data Model?" asks whether lean value stream maps can stay in sync with a changing factory. Two further episodes, "Reduce Fabric Dataflows Gen2 Compute Costs" and "Automate Real-Time Actions with Fabric Data Activator", discuss stream processing and real-time event handling in Microsoft Fabric. None of these episodes is about Microsoft Stream the video service, so they should not be read as guidance on recordings, clips or playback in Teams.

For readers searching for the video product, the useful takeaway is the distinction itself: Microsoft Stream is the Microsoft 365 video service tied to OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams, whereas the data streaming topics in the episodes belong to Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Keeping the two apart avoids confusion when the same word appears in very different parts of the Microsoft ecosystem.

microsoft-to-do.desc: Microsoft To Do is a personal task list app in Microsoft 365 with My Day, lists and reminders, synced with Outlook tasks and Planner.

faq.a: Microsoft To Do is a personal task list app with My Day, lists and reminders. It is used to keep an individual list of things to do, plan the day and set reminders.
faq.q: What is Microsoft To Do used for?

faq.a: It syncs with Outlook tasks and with Planner, so tasks from those apps can appear in the personal list. Planner remains the place for shared team boards, while To Do shows an individual's own work.
faq.q: How does Microsoft To Do relate to Outlook and Planner?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop", To Do fits personal focus, Planner fits team visibility, Lists fits structured or recurring workflows and Loop fits real-time capture.
faq.q: When should To Do be used instead of Planner, Lists or Loop?

microsoft-to-do.long:
Microsoft To Do is a personal task list app developed by Microsoft. It is included in Microsoft 365 and is described as the successor of Wunderlist. The app is built around a small set of concepts: My Day for planning what to work on today, lists for grouping tasks, and reminders for timing. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool, although its core purpose is an individual list of things to do.

In practice, Microsoft To Do is used to capture tasks quickly, organize them into lists and decide which items belong in the current day. It syncs with Outlook tasks, so tasks that live in Microsoft Outlook appear in the same personal view. It also connects to Microsoft Planner: tasks assigned to a person in a Planner plan can show up in their personal list, while the shared board and team coordination stay in Planner. This makes To Do a single place for an individual to see their own work, even when parts of it originate in other Microsoft 365 apps.

A recurring decision around Microsoft To Do is where a task should live. Microsoft 365 contains several task-related tools, and the episodes on this topic argue that the difficulty lies in unclear roles rather than in having too many apps. According to "Microsoft To Do vs Planner vs Lists vs Loop", a simple operating model is to use To Do for personal focus, Planner for team visibility, Lists for structured or recurring workflows and Loop for real-time capture that flows into the others. The episode presents this as a practical playbook with a one-page decision map, and its key takeaways stress choosing the right tool, centralizing tasks to reduce chaos and avoid missed deadlines, and matching the workflow to the tool.

The episode "Unify Microsoft 365 Tasks Across To Do, Planner, Lists, and Loop" makes a closely related point. It says that To Do, Planner, Lists, Outlook and Loop each serve a different context: personal focus, team coordination, structured tracking, communication-driven follow-ups and freeform co-creation. According to the episode, problems appear when teams mix these roles, duplicate the same task across several tools and then have to maintain every copy by hand. The episode also covers automation and Copilot patterns intended to make the separate apps work as one coherent system.

In this framing, Microsoft To Do is the personal layer. A task that matters to a team belongs where the team can see it, such as in Planner, and To Do reflects the individual's share of that work rather than replacing the shared plan. A follow-up that starts in an email belongs to Outlook, which To Do then displays alongside other personal items. Keeping one authoritative location for each task, and using To Do as the personal view across them, is the approach the episodes describe for reducing duplication.

Other M365.FM episodes touch on adjacent themes rather than To Do itself. "Reduce Microsoft 365 Notification Overload and Protect Focus" addresses the distraction caused by constant alerts in the workplace, a concern relevant to anyone who relies on reminders and wants to protect focused work time. "The Human Side of CRM with Thomas Sandsør [MVP]" is about the people-centered side of customer relationship management and is a separate topic from task management.

For readers evaluating Microsoft To Do, the main points are its role as a personal task manager inside Microsoft 365, its sync with Outlook tasks and Planner, and the guidance from the episodes to define clearly which tool owns which kind of work. Official documentation is available through Microsoft Support for the product.

microsoft-trust-center.desc: The Microsoft Trust Center is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information on its cloud services, used for audits and assessments.

faq.a: It is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information about its cloud services. It hosts documentation and resources that customers can use for audits and assessments.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Trust Center?

faq.a: The overview page is organized into tabs for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform and additional products and services. Examples include Azure AI, Azure OpenAI Service, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Power Apps and Power BI.
faq.q: Which products does the Microsoft Trust Center cover?

faq.a: The overview page itself lists no concrete certifications or audit results. Those details sit on the linked pages, which the overview reaches through its product tabs and its navigation to audit reports and related topics.
faq.q: Where do concrete certifications and audit results appear?

microsoft-trust-center.long:
The Microsoft Trust Center is Microsoft's public site for security, privacy and compliance information about its cloud services. It brings together documentation and resources that customers can use when they carry out audits and assessments, and it presents Microsoft products and services in terms of security, privacy, compliance and transparency. A short statement on the overview page says that data is handled securely and in line with privacy and legal requirements.

The Microsoft Trust Center Overview page is organized around product tabs. These cover Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform and additional products and services. Example entries include Azure AI, Azure OpenAI Service, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Power Apps and Power BI. For each product, the page links to topics such as security, privacy, GDPR, data location and compliance. For Azure AI, the links also include responsible AI, a transparency note and limited access.

Beyond the product tabs, the wider navigation covers data management, data access and data location. It also lists regulations such as DORA, the EU AI Act and NIS2, and it points to the Secure Future Initiative, Zero Trust, audit reports and Compliance Score. In practice the Trust Center works as a starting point: a reader chooses a product, then follows the links to the detailed security, privacy and compliance documents. The overview page itself names no licenses or prerequisites and contains no concrete certifications or audit results, because those details sit on the linked pages.

Typical situations in which people consult the Trust Center are compliance reviews, vendor assessments and preparations for audits. A security or compliance team can use it to find out where data is located, how data access is handled, which regulations Microsoft addresses for a given service, and which audit reports are available. Because the content is organized per product, the same site serves teams that work with Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 or the Power Platform.

The M365.FM episodes mention the Trust Center in two contexts. In "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]", the discussion of protecting sensitive data as agents interact with different systems includes data loss prevention policies and monitoring through audit logs in the Power Platform admin center. The episode adds a tip to always follow Microsoft Trust Center guidelines to stay compliant with GDPR, HIPAA and other industry standards.

In "Prepare Microsoft 365 for German KRITIS Requirements", the Trust Center appears in connection with certifications. The episode says that certifications show Microsoft 365 following strict rules for data protection and backup, that Microsoft updates its certifications regularly to match new regulations, and that readers can check the Trust Center for the latest information. It lists ISO 27001, BSI C5 and GDPR in a table as supporting KRITIS, and says that certifications help show auditors that systems meet legal and industry standards.

Taken together, the Trust Center serves as a reference point rather than a configuration tool. It documents how Microsoft describes its services in terms of security, privacy and compliance, while decisions about policies, data residency and retention remain with the organization using the services. Anyone preparing evidence for an auditor would typically use the Trust Center to locate the relevant product page and the linked documents, then combine that information with the organization's own settings and processes.

microsoft-whiteboard.desc: Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming, used in Teams meetings and on devices as part of Microsoft 365.

faq.a: Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming. It is used for workshops, planning sessions and visual collaboration, including in hybrid meetings.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Whiteboard used for?

faq.a: Whiteboard is available in Teams meetings as a shared canvas, so participants can draw and add notes together during a meeting. It is also used on devices outside of Teams.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Whiteboard relate to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: Yes. Microsoft Whiteboard is developed by Microsoft, is part of Microsoft 365, and is included in the license.
faq.q: Is Microsoft Whiteboard part of Microsoft 365?

microsoft-whiteboard.long:
Microsoft Whiteboard is a digital canvas for sketching, sticky notes and brainstorming. It is developed by Microsoft, is included in Microsoft 365, and is used in Teams meetings and on devices. In short, it gives participants a shared surface on which ideas can be drawn, noted and arranged together, instead of relying only on spoken discussion or slides.

The tool is classified as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. Its typical uses are workshops, planning sessions and visual collaboration, including hybrid meetings in which some participants are in a room and others join remotely. Because the canvas is shared, everyone taking part can contribute at the same time, which suits activities such as collecting ideas, grouping sticky notes or sketching a rough structure before it is formalised elsewhere.

The main connection of Microsoft Whiteboard is to Microsoft Teams, where it is available during meetings as a shared canvas. This makes it one of the collaboration options inside a meeting, next to chat, files and other apps. The same canvas can also be used on devices, so the experience is not limited to a single meeting window. Detailed feature descriptions are maintained in Microsoft's official support documentation for Whiteboard.

In practice, teams often have to decide whether a whiteboard is the right place for a given piece of work. A digital canvas is well suited to early, loosely structured thinking: brainstorming, mapping options, sketching a process or drafting a diagram together. Content that needs to be tracked, assigned or stored long term usually belongs in other tools. This question of where information should live is a recurring theme in discussions of the Microsoft 365 collaboration landscape.

Whiteboard appears in the M365.FM episodes mainly as one tool among several rather than as the central subject. The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Meeting Apps and Bots" describes Teams meetings as a live work hub and mentions that built-in and custom apps can enhance collaboration, giving examples such as running polls or brainstorming on a whiteboard. It also notes that bots can capture meeting notes, send reminders and act as virtual assistants, and it advises staying aware of security and compliance when using apps and bots.

The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" places Whiteboard in a list of places where employees can store ideas, tasks, meeting notes, project updates and collaborative content, alongside OneNote, Loop, Teams, Copilot, Planner, Outlook and SharePoint. The episode frames the resulting spread of locations as information chaos and discusses how organisations can decide where information should actually live and keep it organised, searchable and actionable.

In the episode "Customize Dataverse for Complex Business Apps", a whiteboard is mentioned as the first step of an implementation plan: sketching an entity relationship diagram covering entities, keys, relationships and ownership before building tables. This illustrates a common use of a shared canvas, namely drafting a design collaboratively before it is turned into a working solution. The episodes do not go into feature-level detail about Whiteboard itself.

migration-cutover.desc: Migration cutover is the point in a migration when users stop working in the old system or tenant and switch to the new one, usually in a planned quiet window.

faq.a: It is the moment when users stop working in the old system or tenant and switch to the new one, typically scheduled for a quiet window such as a weekend.
faq.q: What is a migration cutover?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, the network identity of the source computer moves to the destination. The destination takes over the source's name, IP addresses and Active Directory computer account, while the source keeps its files but is no longer available to users.
faq.q: What happens during a cutover in Storage Migration Service?

faq.a: The episode "Shared Data Reservoirs for Multi-Tenant Microsoft 365" recommends testing migration tooling before each cutover, scheduling windows during low-usage periods, validating data afterwards and documenting lessons learned after each phase.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode recommend for cutovers?

migration-cutover.long:
Migration cutover is the moment in a migration when users stop working in the old system or tenant and begin working in the new one. It is usually scheduled for a quiet window such as a weekend, so that the switch affects as few people as possible. Before the cutover, the source environment remains the working system; after it, the destination takes over.
