faq.q: How can Azure manage resources in a multi-cloud setup?

multi-cloud.long:
Multi-cloud is a strategy in which an organization runs workloads across more than one public cloud provider, for example Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The usual motivation is portability and reduced vendor lock-in: if no single provider holds every workload, the dependence on any one platform is lower. The cost of this approach is added operational complexity, because each provider brings its own identity model, networking, monitoring and tooling that must be run side by side.

In the M365.FM episode "Public vs Hybrid vs Multi-Cloud Azure Architecture", the central argument is that organizations rarely choose public cloud, hybrid or multi-cloud on purpose. According to the episode, these architectures emerge over time: one exception, one acquisition, one regulatory constraint, one latency issue at a time. The episode says those accumulated decisions later determine who can ship, who can comply and who gets blamed when something breaks. It frames the result as configuration rather than intent, and says that when intent is not enforced through a coherent control plane, entropy fills the gap. In that reading, multi-cloud is less a strategy someone drafted and more the visible outcome of many separate decisions that were never governed together.

The cost side is covered in the episode "Reduce the Multi-Cloud Network Tax Across Azure, AWS, and GCP". It describes multi-cloud as sounding like freedom until physics and billing collide. Connecting Azure, AWS and GCP, according to the episode, creates a toll road: egress fees to leave one cloud, port and cross-connect fees at a colocation meet-me point, and the operational overhead of running three of everything, including IAM, gateways, monitors and DNS. Latency adds a further hidden cost, even when private interconnects are used. The episode calls this combination the multi-cloud network tax.

The design advice in that episode is disciplined rather than product-driven. It recommends picking a primary cloud, meaning the place where the data lives, and treating the other clouds as satellites. It also recommends preferring shared services and APIs over bulk data copies, and placing compute near storage instead of moving large datasets between providers. The point is to avoid designs that move data back and forth in circles and generate repeated charges.

Multi-cloud also shows up in Azure management tooling. The episode "Azure Arc - Simply Explained" describes Azure Arc as a way to project on-premises or multi-cloud servers into Azure and manage them similarly to native Azure virtual machines. Once a server is connected as an Arc-enabled server, it is integrated into the Azure control plane, so consistent policies and governance can be applied across environments. The episode says this central approach improves operational consistency and reduces configuration drift, and that Azure Arc extends the same idea to Kubernetes clusters, which can be managed alongside other resources.

The episode "Azure Resource Manager - Simply Explained" touches on the same theme from the governance side. It describes Azure Resource Manager (ARM) as the central control plane for managing Azure resources and suggests exploring multi-cloud strategies with ARM to keep a unified governance model across different cloud environments. By contrast, "PowerShell vs Bicep for Azure Infrastructure Automation" notes that Bicep is specifically designed for Azure, which makes it unsuitable for multi-cloud environments. Tooling choices therefore matter: a language or service built for one provider limits how far automation can be reused across several.

Taken together, the episodes present multi-cloud as a decision with trade-offs rather than a default. Portability and reduced lock-in are the stated benefits, while network charges, duplicated operational work, latency and fragmented governance are the stated costs. The recurring recommendation is to make the architecture intentional: define a primary platform, limit cross-cloud data movement, and use a unifying control plane where multiple environments must be managed together.

multimodal-ai.desc: Multimodal AI covers models and applications that process more than one input type, such as text, images, voice and video, in one system or workflow.

faq.a: Multimodal AI refers to models and applications that process more than one input type, such as text, images, voice and video. The underlying research field is called multimodal learning, which combines several kinds of data, called modalities, to give a fuller picture than a single type.
faq.q: What is multimodal AI?

faq.a: Common approaches include early fusion, where embeddings are merged before prediction, intermediate fusion of separately processed representations, and cross-attention. Many multimodal LLMs convert an encoder's output into tokens interleaved with text tokens.
faq.q: How do multimodal models combine different data types?

faq.a: According to an M365.FM episode, computer vision supports tasks such as OCR for serial numbers, barcode and QR scanning to retrieve records, and photo-based checks like verifying a window installation, although advanced visual checks require significant effort.
faq.q: How does multimodal AI apply to frontline work?

multimodal-ai.long:
Multimodal AI refers to models and applications that process more than one type of input, such as text, images, voice and video. In the research literature the underlying field is called multimodal learning, a branch of deep learning that combines several kinds of data, known as modalities. These can include text, images, audio, video and, in robotics, proprioception. The central idea is that combining modalities gives a fuller picture than any single data type can provide.

Multimodal approaches are used for tasks such as visual question answering, cross-modal retrieval, text-to-image generation and image captioning. Beyond these, applications named in the sources range from search and recommendation to healthcare diagnostics, robotics, emotion recognition and code search. In enterprise settings, the same principle shows up when a system accepts a photo, a spoken request or a document alongside written text and uses all of it to complete a task.

Technically, a multimodal model has to represent the information from each modality jointly. Several approaches exist. In early fusion, the embeddings of the different modalities are merged before a prediction is made. In intermediate fusion, each modality is first processed separately and the resulting representations are then combined. Cross-attention is another mechanism for relating one modality to another. A common recipe for multimodal large language models converts the output of an encoder into tokens that are interleaved with text tokens, often using a frozen image encoder. Examples named in the sources include CLIP for joint image-text representations, LLaVA, Whisper for audio and DALL-E for generation. The field was proposed in 2011, and large multimodal models such as Google Gemini and GPT-4o have become popular since 2023.

The M365.FM episode "Beyond Copilot: Building AI That Works in the Real World with Azure AI Foundry and Agentic AI for Frontline Workers with Fergus Kidd [MVP]" places multimodal AI in the context of frontline work. The episode describes computer vision as having immediate practical value in the field. OCR can capture long serial numbers without a technician having to read them aloud, and barcode and QR scanning can quickly identify equipment and retrieve the right records. More advanced visual quality checks, such as verifying a window installation from a photo, are described as possible but requiring significant additional effort. The episode frames this as the point where enterprise AI becomes operational: it does not merely generate text, it connects people with the right data and helps them complete real tasks, moving between knowledge retrieval, notes and reporting within the same session.

The episode "How Microsoft Built an Enterprise AI Architecture Advantage" lists multimodal AI among the areas of AI innovation it discusses. It describes advances in AI generation that combine text, audio and images for richer user experiences, alongside other areas such as AI copilots integrated into business applications and machine learning for energy management.

Several open challenges are associated with multimodal systems according to the source material. Aligning the modalities with each other is one. Deciding how and when to fuse them is another, as is handling situations in which one modality is missing. Choosing data sources that complement each other also matters. Privacy is a further concern, because combining several data sources can make it possible to re-identify people. These points are relevant when evaluating whether a multimodal capability fits a given scenario, particularly where images, audio or video of people or equipment are captured as part of everyday workflows.

nested-groups.desc: Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups, so a user's effective access can arrive indirectly through several layers of group membership.

faq.a: Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups. A user's effective access can therefore come indirectly, through several layers of group membership, rather than through a single direct assignment.
faq.q: What are nested groups?

faq.a: They can create access paths that are hard to see. The episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" describes a tool that finds users who have access through groups inside other groups, alongside direct and inherited permissions, so hidden access paths are not missed.
faq.q: Why do nested groups matter for permission audits?

faq.a: The episodes give two angles. "Design Around Microsoft 365 Service Limits" recommends preferring direct members over deep nested groups for Teams at scale, while "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures" suggests composing separate dynamic group rules via nested groups to keep licensing automation easier to change.
faq.q: Should nested groups be used in Teams and licensing setups?

nested-groups.long:
Nested groups are groups that are members of other groups. Instead of adding every person directly to every group that grants access, an administrator can place one group inside another, so that the members of the inner group inherit whatever the outer group has been granted. As a result, a user's effective access can come indirectly, through several layers of group membership, rather than from a single, visible assignment.

The concept matters mainly because of what it does to visibility. When permissions are assigned to a group, and that group itself contains other groups, the list of people who actually have access is no longer obvious from looking at the top-level group alone. Someone can reach a site, list or item through a chain of memberships that is easy to overlook. This is why auditing work in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem treats nested groups as a category of their own, next to direct permissions and inherited permissions.

The M365.FM episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" addresses this directly. It describes a permissions audit that needs to show all types of access, including the ones that are hard to find. According to the episode, the tool it discusses checks nested groups, direct permissions and inherited permissions, with the aim of giving a complete picture of the access structure. For nested groups specifically, the system finds users who have access through groups inside other groups, so that hidden access paths are not missed. The episode contrasts this with direct permissions, where users and groups have access to sites, lists or items explicitly, and with inherited permissions, which come from a parent object.

Nested groups also appear as a design choice in the episode "Design Around Microsoft 365 Service Limits". In its guidance on running Teams at scale and avoiding silent failures, the episode recommends tracking member and channel counts with alerts at 70, 85 and 95 percent thresholds. It also advises preferring direct members over deep nested groups, and auditing guests regularly. The reasoning implied in that advice is that deep nesting makes membership harder to reason about and to monitor, while the episode places it alongside other practices such as splitting mega-teams into functional teams and archiving unused channels.

A third perspective comes from the episode "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures". There, nested groups are used constructively as a way to make automation easier to change. The episode suggests splitting dynamic group rules by concern, for example role (title or job code) versus region versus business unit, and then composing the results via nested groups. It pairs this with other practices for change-ready automation, such as adopting name prefixes so that a startsWith rule survives renames, reviewing rules quarterly, treating the HR system as the source of truth for synchronization into Entra, and keeping a living catalog of groups, rules, attributes and license intent.

Taken together, the episodes show nested groups as a trade-off. They can organize access and licensing logic into smaller, reusable building blocks, but each additional layer makes the effective membership of a user less transparent. Typical decisions therefore include how many layers to allow, when to use direct members instead, and how to document group structures so that reviewers can follow them. For audits, the practical takeaway from the episodes is that a permissions review which ignores nested groups risks missing real access paths, and that tooling able to resolve membership through multiple levels gives a more accurate view than inspecting only the groups named in a permission assignment.

network-security-group.desc: A network security group (NSG) is an Azure control that filters inbound and outbound traffic between resources in a virtual network using prioritized security rules.

faq.a: A network security group filters inbound and outbound traffic between Azure resources in an Azure virtual network by applying security rules that allow or deny traffic. Rules are evaluated by priority, and the first matching rule is applied.
faq.q: What does a network security group do in Azure?

faq.a: According to the episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained", an NSG is a logical firewall service that filters at the network layer (Layer 4) and operates on individual resources. Azure Firewall is described as a managed service with stateful packet inspection, application-level protection and centralized management.
faq.q: How is an NSG different from Azure Firewall?

faq.a: An NSG is associated with a subnet or with a network interface. Default rules allow traffic within the virtual network and deny other inbound traffic, and they can be overridden with higher-priority rules.
faq.q: Where is a network security group applied?

network-security-group.long:
A network security group (NSG) is an Azure networking control that filters network traffic between Azure resources in an Azure virtual network. It does this with security rules that allow or deny inbound or outbound traffic. The NSG is a basic building block for segmenting and protecting workloads that run in a virtual network, such as virtual machines, and it is often the first layer of traffic control that administrators configure.

Each security rule in an NSG has a name, a priority, a source and destination, a protocol, a direction, a port range and an action. The priority is a number between 100 and 4096. Rules are processed in priority order, with lower numbers evaluated first, and processing stops at the first matching rule. Evaluation is based on the five-tuple of source, source port, destination, destination port and protocol. Flows are tracked statefully, so reply traffic for an allowed connection does not need a separate rule in the opposite direction.

Every NSG also contains default rules. These allow traffic within the virtual network and from the Azure load balancer, and they deny other inbound traffic. The default rules cannot be deleted, but they can be overridden by creating rules with a higher priority, meaning a lower number. This makes it possible to open specific ports or sources while keeping the restrictive baseline in place.

To keep rule sets manageable, NSGs support several grouping constructs. Service tags group the IP address prefixes of an Azure service, so a rule can refer to a service by name instead of by a list of addresses. Application security groups group virtual machines, so that policy follows the workload and does not depend on manually maintained IP lists. Augmented rules allow multiple IP addresses and ports to be placed in a single rule, which reduces the number of rules needed. An NSG takes effect once it is associated with a subnet or with a network interface.

NSGs are not the only place where traffic rules can be applied. Security admin rules from Azure Virtual Network Manager are evaluated before NSG rules, which gives central network teams a way to set guardrails that individual NSGs do not override. A further platform behavior documented by Microsoft is that outbound SMTP traffic on port 25 is blocked for several subscription types, which is relevant when mail-related workloads are planned.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Network Security Groups - Simply Explained" places NSGs next to Azure Firewall. According to the episode, the two serve different purposes. It describes Azure Firewall as a managed, cloud-based network security service with stateful packet inspection, application-level protection and centralized management for resources in a virtual network. It describes an NSG as a logical firewall service that filters at the network layer (Layer 4) and operates on individual resources. The episode frames this comparison as a way to choose the right tool for a given security need.

NSGs also appear as a prerequisite in other Azure scenarios. The episode "Azure Chaos Studio - Simply Explained" lists setting up a Network Security Group to allow inbound and outbound traffic for Chaos Studio among the setup requirements, together with a managed identity and a virtual network with subnets for the target resources. In that context the NSG is part of the network preparation needed before the service can be deployed.

nist-ai-risk-management-framework.desc: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary US framework for managing AI risks, organized around governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk.

faq.a: It is a voluntary framework from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology for managing AI risks. It is organized around governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk.
faq.q: What is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?

faq.a: No. The episodes describe it as voluntary and note that, although it includes provisions such as decommissioning, it lacks regulatory enforcement.
faq.q: Is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework mandatory?

faq.a: The episode with Peter Rising says Microsoft Purview supports responsible AI enablement by aligning with global standards like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, which guides the AI lifecycle from governance to risk mapping, measurement and management.
faq.q: How does the NIST AI Risk Management Framework relate to Microsoft Purview?

nist-ai-risk-management-framework.long:
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. It helps organizations manage risks that come with building, deploying and operating artificial intelligence. It is organized around four activities: governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk. Because it is voluntary, it works as guidance that organizations can adopt to structure their own policies and practices, not as a law that carries enforcement.

In practice, the framework serves as a reference point for AI governance. Organizations use it to define policies, assess risks and support transparency. The M365.FM episodes describe it as one of several frameworks that organizations commonly draw on, alongside the OECD Principles on AI and the EU AI Act. One episode lists it under the United States as a voluntary framework for managing AI risks, with an emphasis on trustworthiness, safety and fairness. That description places it among other responsible-AI guidance, some of it non-binding but influential in shaping policy.

The four activities give the framework its structure. Governing covers the policies, roles and accountability that surround AI use. Mapping establishes the context in which an AI system operates and identifies where risk can arise. Measuring assesses and tracks those risks. Managing addresses them through action. The episode with Peter Rising describes this as guidance that runs through the AI lifecycle, from governance to risk mapping, measurement and management. The same episode says Microsoft Purview supports responsible AI enablement by aligning with global standards such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and it mentions the Microsoft Responsible AI Council as a body that puts responsible AI policies into action.

Typical decisions around the framework concern how to anchor an organization's AI governance. The episode "Grounding Microsoft Copilot for Trusted Enterprise AI" recommends a cross-functional AI governance board with clear roles and responsibilities to oversee AI strategy and accountability. It suggests using the NIST AI Risk Management Framework together with the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications to address core risks and to validate controls throughout the AI lifecycle. The same episode advises testing and updating policies regularly and notes that ongoing validation and oversight keep an AI platform aligned with business goals.

The framework also appears in discussions of AI agents. The episode "Enterprise AI Agents with Sailaja Mantripragada [MVP-MCT]" says organizations building agents with Microsoft Copilot Studio and the Power Platform often follow governance frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD Principles on AI and the EU AI Act. It adds that AI governance is not a one-time task and that agents need to be monitored, audited and improved on an ongoing basis.

The episode "Microsoft Entra Agent ID: Secure Identity for AI Agents" looks at the framework's limits. It says the framework includes provisions for decommissioning AI agents but lacks regulatory enforcement. It contrasts this with the EU AI Act, which the episode says has no mandatory sunset clauses or specific decommissioning procedures for orphaned agents, and with ISO/IEC 42001:2023, which defines a retirement phase for AI agents but relies on voluntary compliance. According to the episode, none of these require automatic termination of orphaned agents after a set period, emergency shutdown mechanisms, or standardized handover when an agent's creator ceases operations.

Taken together, the episodes treat the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a structured, voluntary reference for organizations that want to align AI governance with an established model. They also make clear that using it is a choice made by the organization, and that its provisions, for example on decommissioning, are not backed by enforcement.

non-human-identity.desc: A non-human identity is a digital identity used by software, such as a service principal, managed identity or AI agent, that needs its own owner, scoped permissions and revocation.

faq.a: It is a digital identity used by software instead of a person. Examples named in the episodes are service principals, managed identities, app registrations, workload identities, service accounts and AI agent identities.
faq.q: What counts as a non-human identity?

faq.a: The episodes say user-based automation breaks when the person leaves and leaves no clear evidence of who acted under what control. They recommend an app registration or workload identity with scoped, revocable permissions instead.
faq.q: Why not run automation under a personal account?

faq.a: It needs its own ownership, permissions limited to the task, and a revocation path. The episodes also suggest tagging each identity with Owner, System and Data Class and alerting on expiring secrets.
faq.q: What does a non-human identity need to be governed properly?

non-human-identity.long:
A non-human identity is a digital identity that is used by software rather than by a person. Typical examples are a service principal, a managed identity or the identity of an AI agent. Like a user account, it authenticates and acts on resources, which means it can read data, send mail or change configuration. Because of that, it needs the same kind of control as a human identity: a named owner, permissions limited to what the task requires, and a way to revoke access when the workload is retired or compromised.

The concept matters because many organizations still treat automation as if it were a person. The M365.FM episode "Service Accounts vs App Registrations for Power Automate Email" describes the root problem as pretending a robot is a person. It argues that applications should have their own non-human identity with machine-grade authentication and precise, inspectable, revocable permissions. Its example is an app registration in Entra with Mail.Send at the application scope rather than a delegated permission, so that the app acts as itself. The episode also warns that Mail.Send left unrestricted could allow the app to send as any mailbox in the tenant, so the scope has to be narrowed deliberately.

The episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" covers the failure modes of user-based automation: workflow breakage when the person behind a flow leaves, service accounts operating as unsecured ghost users, and rot across Power Automate and Logic Apps. It explains that Microsoft 365 security policies are designed for humans, while enterprise automation requires a non-human identity architecture. According to the episode, Microsoft is pushing in this direction by retiring legacy SharePoint 2013 workflows, deprecating Azure AD Graph and making app-only modern authentication mandatory.

A practical side of the topic is the move away from shared service accounts. The episode "Replace Service Accounts with Entra Workload Identities" lists patterns to avoid, such as embedding passwords in scripts or web.config, storing secrets in Key Vault with no rotation policy, granting Global Admin or Owner just in case, and keeping temporary Conditional Access exceptions that never expire. Its suggested quick wins include tagging every non-human identity with Owner, System and Data Class, switching one high-risk job to federated credentials (GitHub OIDC to Entra), replacing a shared service account in Power Automate with a workload identity, and reporting on service principals with expiring or expired secrets, with alerts scheduled. The same episode states that workload identities do not have to break legacy on-premises jobs, which can be bridged with app-only authentication and certificates.

AI agents add a further category. The episode "AI Agent Identity Security: Beyond Service Accounts" says traditional IAM systems recognize only users and service accounts, which leaves a gap for agents that act autonomously, make decisions and interact with sensitive data. It argues that treating them as service accounts creates security and compliance risk, and that agent identity needs its own blueprint, governance and lifecycle. The episode cites that almost half of organizations still use static API keys or shared usernames and passwords for agent authentication, and that only 18% feel confident in their current IAM for agent identities.

Governance ties these points together. The episode "Secure Microsoft Copilot with Entra ID and Zero Trust" discusses non-human identity governance for AI agents and automation bots, naming Microsoft Entra privileged identity management as a tool for managing these identities. The stated goals are greater visibility and ownership across service accounts, less risk from excessive access, and accountability through lifecycle management. Taken together, the episodes treat a non-human identity as something to be inventoried, owned, scoped and revoked, not as an anonymous background account.

nonconformance.desc: A nonconformance is a documented failure to meet a stated requirement in quality management, handled through containment, correction and corrective action.

faq.a: A nonconformance is a failure to meet a stated requirement. It is documented against an identifiable requirement and handled through containment, correction and corrective action.
faq.q: What is a nonconformance in quality management?

faq.a: Microsoft Learn lists six standard types: customer, service request, vendor, production, internal and co-product production. Each type needs its own source information, such as a sales order, purchase order or production order.
faq.q: What types of nonconformance exist in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management?

faq.a: A new record starts with the status New. It can then be approved, refused, closed or reopened.
faq.q: What statuses can a nonconformance record have in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management?

nonconformance.long:
A nonconformance, in quality management, is a failure to meet a stated requirement. The key point is that it is documented against an identifiable requirement: a specification, an order, a standard or another defined expectation. A defect or problem is only recorded as a nonconformance once it can be tied to what was supposed to be met. The record then becomes the starting point for handling the issue in a structured way, through containment, correction and corrective action.

The three handling steps have different purposes. Containment limits the impact of the problem, for example by keeping affected material from moving on. Correction deals with the specific item or situation that failed. Corrective action looks at the cause so that the same problem does not return. Keeping these apart helps teams avoid treating a quick fix as a lasting solution.

In Microsoft's ecosystem, the concept is built into Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management. According to Microsoft Learn, a nonconformance there describes an item that has a quality problem. The process creates a nonconformance order that records the quantity of nonconforming material, the source of the problem, the problem type and explanatory notes. Six standard types exist: customer, service request, vendor, production, internal and co-product production. Each type needs its own source information, such as a sales order, a purchase order or a production order.

A new nonconformance record starts with the status New. It can then be approved, refused, closed or reopened. Tags and reports carry the nonconformance number, the item and the problem type. The tag can also show a quarantine zone and a disposition, such as unusable or restricted usage. Approved records can carry operations with costs, and a quality order can be created from a nonconformance. A corrections page tracks required fixes with an owner, a due date and a completion status. The documentation states that the calculated costs are reference data used only within quality management, and that the feature has to be enabled before use.

The documentation names three goals: handling problems quickly regardless of where they originate, linking diagnostic findings to corrective tasks to avoid repeats, and analyzing nonconformances by problem type. In practice, decisions around the concept include which problem types to use, who owns each correction, how approval is handled, and what disposition applies to the affected material.

Two M365.FM episodes touch the topic from different angles. "Quality Nonconformance Workflows With Power Platform: From Defect to Corrective Action" is part of the iFAKT series. It starts from the idea that a defect becomes expensive when the workflow from detection to corrective action is slow or unclear. The episode shows how Power Platform can support nonconformance workflows, covering capture, triage, approvals, corrective and preventive actions, and reporting, along with how to model the process.

"Can Value Stream Mapping Become a Live Data Model?" mentions nonconformance as one signal among several operational data sources. According to the excerpt, a quality system can place material on hold after an inspection, and a nonconformance could trigger rework. The episode also notes that a quality release may happen hours after the physical inspection has finished. In that context, nonconformance events are one of the signals that influence the real production situation alongside test results, maintenance and machine availability.

ntlm.desc: NTLM (NT LAN Manager) is a suite of Microsoft authentication protocols for Windows networks, still needed by some legacy apps and supported by Microsoft Entra Domain Services.

faq.a: NTLM (NT LAN Manager) is a suite of Microsoft security protocols for authentication in Windows networks. Some legacy applications still require it.
faq.q: What is NTLM?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Entra Domain Services - Simply Explained", legacy Windows applications often still depend on LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM, domain join, DNS and Group Policy. Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides these capabilities without requiring self-operated domain controllers.
faq.q: Why does NTLM still matter when moving applications to Azure?

faq.a: The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" names continued use of outdated protocols like NTLM as a legacy protocol risk that enables relay and replay attacks. The episode on Defender for Identity also lists NTLM abuse among the behaviors it can detect.
faq.q: What security concerns are associated with NTLM?

ntlm.long:
NTLM, short for NT LAN Manager, is a suite of Microsoft security protocols used for authentication in Windows networks. It predates modern cloud identity standards and is still required by some legacy applications. For this reason it remains relevant in hybrid and migration scenarios, even though newer protocols are available for most current workloads.

NTLM is typically discussed alongside Kerberos. Both are traditional protocols from the on-premises Active Directory world, and the M365.FM episodes list them together when contrasting Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID. In the comparison described in the episodes "Move Active Directory Groups to Microsoft Entra ID" and "Microsoft Entra as a Complete IAM Platform", Active Directory is associated with Kerberos and NTLM, while Microsoft Entra ID is associated with OAuth2, SAML and OpenID Connect. The first of these episodes also notes that single sign-on in the traditional model is limited to domain-joined devices, whereas Microsoft Entra ID offers broader single sign-on, including federation for hybrid and cloud apps.

The practical question around NTLM usually appears when an application is moved to the cloud. The episode "Microsoft Entra Domain Services - Simply Explained" makes the point that moving an application to an Azure virtual machine does not automatically make it cloud-native. Many established Windows applications were designed around Active Directory and still depend on LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM, domain join, DNS and Group Policy. Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides these capabilities as a managed service, so organizations do not have to operate their own domain controllers. In that context, NTLM support is one of the reasons a legacy application can keep working after it has been lifted into Azure.

NTLM also has a security side. The episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches" lists legacy protocol risks as one element of the attack surface in hybrid Active Directory environments. It states that continued use of outdated protocols like NTLM enables relay and replay attacks. The episode treats this as one of several hybrid risks, alongside weak service account passwords and synchronization vulnerabilities, and recommends prevention-focused measures such as multi-factor authentication and least privilege access.

Monitoring is a second angle. The episode "Conditional Access with Defender for Identity Signals" describes Defender for Identity together with Microsoft 365 Defender as a watcher that looks for lateral movement, abnormal resource access, Kerberoasting and NTLM abuse, and privilege hunting. In the mental model of that episode, Conditional Access acts as the gatekeeper at sign-in, while these detections can raise user risk or session risk, which in turn lets Conditional Access tighten controls such as step-up MFA, blocking or restricting the session.

Taken together, the episodes frame NTLM as a legacy dependency that has to be understood rather than ignored. Some applications still need it, and Microsoft Entra Domain Services is one way to support those applications without self-managed domain controllers. At the same time, continued use of NTLM is described as a risk factor in hybrid environments, and abuse of it is a detection scenario in Defender for Identity. Decisions about NTLM therefore usually involve identifying which applications depend on it, deciding whether they can move to modern protocols such as OAuth2, SAML or OpenID Connect, and applying monitoring and access controls to the remainder.

number-matching.desc: Number matching is an MFA safeguard in which a number shown at sign-in must be typed into Microsoft Authenticator to approve a push notification.

faq.a: It is a safeguard for MFA push notifications in which the sign-in screen displays a number that the user must type into the Authenticator app to approve the sign-in, rather than just tapping approve or deny.
faq.q: What is number matching in Microsoft Authenticator?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Learn, number matching is enabled for all Authenticator push notifications and users cannot opt out.
faq.q: Can users turn number matching off?

faq.a: AD FS is covered through the adapter but needs specific Windows Server updates, otherwise it keeps showing approve or deny. The NPS extension asks for a one-time passcode instead, and the server must use PAP because MSCHAPv2 does not support TOTP.
faq.q: Does number matching work with AD FS and NPS?

number-matching.long:
Number matching is a security safeguard for multifactor authentication push notifications. During sign-in, the screen shows a number, and the user must type that number into the Microsoft Authenticator prompt to approve the request. This replaces the older pattern in which a user could simply tap approve or deny. Microsoft enforces number matching for Microsoft Authenticator push notifications, and users cannot opt out.

The purpose of the control is to make sure that the person approving a sign-in is actually looking at the sign-in screen that triggered the request. Because the number appears only on the screen where the sign-in takes place, an approval cannot be given blindly in response to an unexpected prompt. The documentation describes it as a security improvement for Authenticator push notifications.

According to Microsoft Learn, number matching is enabled for all Authenticator push notifications. It applies to multifactor authentication, to self-service password reset when Authenticator is used, and to combined registration. It also reaches some related sign-in paths: AD FS is covered through the adapter, and NPS is covered through a different mechanism. Administrators do not need to configure number matching for the standard cases, and the documentation page lists no license requirements.

There is one exception to typing the number. With same-device sign-in, users who sign in through Microsoft apps such as Teams or Outlook can choose approve or deny without entering the number. Sign-ins in a browser still require the number. This behavior needs no administrator configuration, but users need the current version of the Authenticator app. Older Authenticator versions that lack number matching cannot be used to sign in.

Several environments need extra attention. AD FS needs specific Windows Server updates; without them it keeps showing the approve or deny prompt instead of number matching. The NPS extension works differently: it asks for a one-time passcode instead of a number, and the server must use PAP, because MSCHAPv2 does not support TOTP. Push notifications on Apple Watch and Android wearables are not supported, so approval has to happen on the phone. The retired Azure Multifactor Authentication Server does not offer number matching.

In practice, the topic matters to administrators who maintain Authenticator-based MFA, hybrid sign-in with AD FS or NPS, and user guidance. Typical points to check are that users have a current Authenticator version, that AD FS servers have the required Windows Server updates, that NPS setups use PAP with one-time passcodes, and that users know approvals on wearables are not supported. No M365.FM episodes are linked to this concept in the available facts, so the description here rests on the Microsoft Learn documentation.

oauth-2-0.desc: OAuth 2.0 is an open authorization standard that lets apps reach data on a user's behalf through scoped access tokens, without handing over a password.

faq.a: OAuth 2.0 is an open authorization standard that determines what an app can reach on a user's behalf by using scoped access tokens. It lets users sign into new apps, for example with a Microsoft account, without giving the app their password.
faq.q: What is OAuth 2.0 used for?

faq.a: No. OAuth 2.0 handles authorization and is not a login system on its own. OpenID Connect adds sign-in on top of it.
faq.q: Is OAuth 2.0 the same as signing in?

faq.a: According to the episode "Stop OAuth Consent Attacks in Microsoft Entra ID", a malicious app approved by a user or admin can obtain tokens with scopes like mail or files read and offline_access. That access can persist through password resets and new MFA devices, so the grants must be removed explicitly.
faq.q: Why are OAuth consent grants a security risk?

oauth-2-0.long:
OAuth 2.0 is an open authorization standard that decides what an app may reach on a user's behalf. Instead of asking for a password, an app receives access tokens that carry defined scopes, so the access it holds is limited to what was approved. The standard is an authorization mechanism, not a login system on its own. Sign-in is added on top by OpenID Connect, which is why the two are often mentioned together in the Microsoft identity context. Microsoft documents the protocol in its identity platform documentation, and OAuth is also used as a short name for the standard.

The M365.FM episode "OAuth 2.0 - Simply Explained" uses an analogy to describe the idea: a password is the master key to an account, and OAuth 2.0 is the valet key. This explains why a person can sign into a new app with a Microsoft account without ever giving that app the password. The episode covers why apps no longer ask for passwords, the four players involved in every OAuth handshake, and what happens when a user clicks "Sign in with Microsoft". It also addresses why the standard by itself is not an authentication system.

In practice, OAuth 2.0 shows up wherever one service needs limited access to another. Scopes describe the access, such as reading mail or files, and the resulting tokens are what the app presents when it calls a service. The episode "API Gateway - Simply Explained" lists token-based authentication, with OAuth 2.0 and JWT named as examples, among the methods a gateway uses to validate who may call an API, alongside role-based access control for permissions. The episode "Dynamics 365 ERP MCP Server - Simply Explained" mentions OAuth 2.0 as a security measure for interactions between AI systems and enterprise tools.

Because OAuth grants access through consent rather than through credentials, the consent step is also a security concern. The episode "Stop OAuth Consent Attacks in Microsoft Entra ID" explains how attackers can bypass MFA by abusing OAuth consent instead of stealing passwords. When a user or admin approves a malicious "productivity" app, the app obtains tokens with scopes such as mail or files read and offline_access. According to the episode, this allows quiet access to email, files and chats for months, even after password resets and new MFA devices, because normal identity events do not revoke these grants. The episode states that such grants have to be removed deliberately, which makes consent review and governance a recurring decision for administrators.

The topic also connects to monitoring tools. The episode "Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps - Simply Explained" lists OAuth app protection and app governance among the capabilities of that platform, next to Cloud Discovery, SaaS Security Posture Management, threat detection, adaptive access controls and data loss prevention. It describes integration with Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft 365, which places OAuth app oversight within a wider view of identities, applications and data.

For anyone evaluating OAuth 2.0 in a Microsoft environment, the points raised across these episodes are consistent. The standard limits what an app can do through scopes and tokens, avoids sharing passwords, and is distinct from sign-in, which OpenID Connect provides. At the same time, granted consent is a durable form of access, so approvals, granted scopes and persistent permissions such as offline_access deserve the same attention as passwords and MFA.

object-level-security.desc: Object-level security (OLS) secures specific tables or columns in a Power BI semantic model so they do not exist for users without permission.

faq.a: Object-level security (OLS) secures specific tables or columns in a semantic model so that they do not exist for users without permission. It controls whether an object is visible at all, rather than filtering rows.
faq.q: What is object-level security (OLS) in Power BI?

faq.a: RLS restricts data visibility at a granular level so users see only the rows relevant to their roles, while OLS hides whole tables or columns. The episode "Create Role-Based Dashboards in Power Platform" describes combining both, with OLS hiding sensitive columns such as salary.
faq.q: How does OLS differ from row-level security (RLS)?

faq.a: The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" recommends testing RLS and OLS rules to confirm users only see the data they should, for example by logging in as different users to check that the security works as planned.
faq.q: How should OLS rules be tested?

object-level-security.long:
Object-level security (OLS) is a security feature for semantic models in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric. It secures specific tables or columns so that they do not exist for users who lack permission. Instead of filtering the rows a user can see, OLS controls whether a user can see an object at all, which makes it suited to hiding sensitive structures such as a salary column from audiences that should not know the data is there.

OLS is usually discussed next to Row-Level Security (RLS), and the two address different questions. RLS restricts data visibility at a granular level, so users see only the rows relevant to their role. This matters for confidentiality and compliance, particularly in sensitive industries such as finance and healthcare, according to the episode "DP-600 Training 4/4: Incremental Refresh, RLS, and OLS". OLS adds a further layer on top of that by removing whole tables or columns from view. The episode "Create Role-Based Dashboards in Power Platform" describes this combination as a cell-level privacy pattern: RLS limits which rows a user receives, and OLS hides sensitive columns such as salary.

In practice, OLS appears in role-based reporting designs. A typical situation is one shared semantic model serving several audiences, for example executives and analysts. The same model can support audience-specific navigation while OLS keeps certain columns or tables out of reach of roles that are not meant to use them. The same episode lists other RLS patterns that are often paired with OLS, including a manager-of tree built from a flattened org table for "my team" views, and a many-to-many bridge table between users and regions for multi-region analysts.

OLS also belongs to the broader governance practices that the episode "Make Power BI Dashboards Drive Better Decisions" lists for keeping data trustworthy. It recommends controlling who can access data with RLS and OLS, standardizing data sources and datasets through certified datasets and dataflows, setting up data validation and error handling, and creating a report certification and approval process. The episode also names user education on data literacy and governance rules as part of the same set of practices.

Testing is a recurring theme. The episode "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" treats security as a key part of validating a model before it is shared. It advises testing the RLS and OLS rules to make sure users only see the data they should, and suggests logging in as different users to check that the security works as planned. This kind of role-based testing is a practical way to confirm that a hidden table or column is truly absent for the intended audiences.

The official documentation for OLS is part of the Power BI enterprise administration guidance on Microsoft Learn. For anyone preparing for the DP-600 exam, OLS is covered together with RLS and incremental refresh, as in the four-part training episode mentioned above, which emphasizes how these security features support data trust and better decision-making across large organizations.

observability.desc: Observability is the ability to understand what happens inside a system or integration from its outputs, using tracing, correlation IDs, dashboards and alerts.

faq.a: Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system or integration from its outputs. It uses tracing, correlation IDs, dashboards, alerts and replay capabilities rather than plain logs alone.
faq.q: What is observability?

faq.a: The episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability" says automation can use telemetry such as logs, metrics and traces to understand system state in real time. This allows problems to be detected and fixed without waiting for manual intervention.
faq.q: How does observability relate to self-healing automation?

faq.a: M365.FM episodes on AI agents list observability as part of supervisory layers, governance and runtime design. It supports monitoring of agent activity and helps keep enterprise AI systems transparent and auditable.
faq.q: Where does observability appear in AI agent architectures?

observability.long:
Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system or integration by examining what it produces. Instead of relying on plain logs alone, observability combines several kinds of signals and tooling: tracing, correlation IDs, dashboards, alerts and replay capabilities. Together these make it possible to follow a request or workflow through its steps, see where something went wrong, and reconstruct the situation afterwards.

The concept matters most where work is spread across several components. In an integration, a single business event may pass through multiple services, queues and connectors. A log line from one component says little about the whole path. Correlation IDs tie the separate records of one transaction together, tracing shows the sequence of steps, dashboards give a running view of health, and alerts draw attention to deviations. Replay capabilities allow a failed or questionable event to be run again so that the cause can be examined rather than guessed at.

The M365.FM episode "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability" places observability in the context of automation that is moving from simple scripts to systems that monitor themselves. According to the episode, modern automation uses telemetry data such as logs, metrics and traces to understand what is happening inside systems in real time. This supports the idea of self-healing automation, in which problems are detected and addressed without waiting for human intervention. The episode contrasts this with the traditional approach, where engineers respond to alerts and troubleshoot manually, which it describes as slow and hard to scale.

Observability also appears as one building block in several other M365.FM episodes about Microsoft-centred architectures. "API Gateway - Simply Explained" lists observability next to routing, security, authentication and throttling as something an API gateway handles when it provides a single managed entry point for APIs. In that setting, observability helps teams see how internal and external consumers use an API and supports the governance choices the episode discusses.

In the AI and agent episodes, observability is treated as part of keeping systems transparent and manageable. "From Data to Intelligent Agents: Building Trusted Enterprise AI with Microsoft AI Foundry with Shubhangi Goyal [MVP]" names observability alongside agentic AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, governance, responsible AI and model evaluation, with the aim of building enterprise solutions that remain transparent, auditable and aligned with business goals. "Graph-Powered AI Agents: An Enterprise Architecture Guide" describes supervisory layers that monitor agent activity and enforce guardrails, and says these layers provide oversight, conflict resolution and observability, together with task routing engines, memory and state layers, and monitoring tools. "Microsoft AI Agent Runtimes: Beyond Enterprise Chatbots" lists observability among topics such as agent communication, orchestration, long-term memory, security, governance and human-in-the-loop approval for agents built on technologies like Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft Graph and Dataverse.

A recurring decision around observability is how much to build in from the start. Because the signals come from the system's outputs, the useful questions are which traces, identifiers and alerts exist before a problem occurs, and whether failed events can be replayed. Treating logs as the only source tends to leave gaps once a process crosses several systems or involves autonomous agents. The episodes frame observability as a supporting capability for reliability, governance and automation rather than as a standalone product.

oee.desc: Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) is a manufacturing metric that combines availability, performance and quality to show how well equipment is used.

faq.a: OEE measures how well equipment is used relative to its planned production time by combining three factors: availability, performance and quality.
faq.q: What does OEE measure?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, no. OEE helps explain equipment performance, but it does not calculate a feasible schedule or decide whether a specific customer order will ship on time.
faq.q: Can OEE be used to build a production schedule?

faq.a: The episode "OEE Done Right: Measuring Overall Equipment Effectiveness You Can Actually Trust" says OEE is only useful when everyone trusts how it is calculated, so inconsistent definitions and data pitfalls can lead to misleading comparisons.
faq.q: Why do OEE numbers sometimes fail to be comparable?

oee.long:
Overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) is a manufacturing metric that combines availability, performance and quality to show how well equipment is used relative to its planned production time. Rather than looking at a single figure such as output or uptime, OEE brings three perspectives together: how much of the planned time a machine was actually available, how close its speed came to the expected rate, and how much of what it produced met quality requirements.

In practice, OEE is used by production managers, continuous improvement teams and data analysts to understand where equipment loses productive time. The three components point to different kinds of loss. Availability relates to stops and downtime, performance relates to running slower than the standard, and quality relates to output that does not meet the specification. Breaking a single number into these parts helps teams decide where to focus improvement work and whether a change on the shop floor has had the intended effect.

The M365.FM episode "OEE Done Right: Measuring Overall Equipment Effectiveness You Can Actually Trust", part of the iFAKT series, stresses that OEE numbers are only useful when everyone trusts how they are calculated. The episode covers availability, performance, quality and data pitfalls, and discusses how to define OEE consistently so that comparisons are not misleading. The recurring point is that the definition and the underlying data matter as much as the formula. If different lines, plants or teams count planned time, stops or good output in different ways, their OEE values cannot be compared with each other.

OEE also has limits, and two other M365.FM episodes address them directly. "Why Your Critical Path Changes When Production Changes" says that OEE remains useful for understanding equipment performance, but that OEE alone does not calculate a feasible production schedule or determine whether a specific customer order will ship on time. "Why Your Production Schedule Is Wrong Before It Even Starts" makes a similar argument: OEE helps organizations understand equipment availability, performance and quality, but OEE and production scheduling solve different problems. According to that episode, a machine can show strong OEE while production still misses an important customer delivery because the wrong work was placed in front of the bottleneck. The episode also says that poor OEE does not by itself explain a schedule problem. In other words, OEE describes how well equipment is used, while scheduling decides what should run next and whether an order is still feasible.

OEE also appears in discussions of AI and automation. The episode "Computer-Using Agents: How CUA Could Transform SaaS" includes a table of reported improvement ranges for manufacturing and supply chain use cases, in which an improvement in overall equipment effectiveness of 15-25% is listed alongside figures such as reduced unplanned downtime and lower maintenance costs. These are figures reported in that episode and are not a general benchmark for OEE.

Typical decisions around OEE include how to define planned production time, which stops count against availability, which standard rate is used for the performance measure, and how defects and rework are classified for the quality measure. Teams also have to decide how OEE is used alongside other planning and scheduling information, since the episodes treat it as one input among several rather than as a complete picture of production health. Used with a consistent definition and trustworthy data, OEE gives a shared reference for discussing equipment losses; used without those safeguards, it risks producing numbers that look precise but cannot support decisions.

office-365-management-activity-api.desc: The Office 365 Management Activity API delivers user, admin, system and policy events from Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra audit logs as content blobs by record type.

faq.a: It delivers user, admin, system and policy events from Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra audit logs as content blobs organized by record type, so the data can be streamed into a store the organization controls.
faq.q: What does the Office 365 Management Activity API provide?

faq.a: According to the episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview", audit search in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal and a call to the Office 365 Management Activity API are two ways to search for specific activities, filterable by user, activity type, date range or service.
faq.q: How does the API relate to audit search in Microsoft Purview?

faq.a: Yes. The episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" says PowerShell scripts can call the Office 365 Management Activity API to retrieve audit data, filter it by date range and event types, and export it to CSV for analysis or reporting.
faq.q: Can the API be used in scripts?

office-365-management-activity-api.long:
The Office 365 Management Activity API is a Microsoft API that delivers user, admin, system and policy events from Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra audit logs. The events are provided as content blobs organized by record type. The API is part of Microsoft 365 and is used to stream unified audit log data into a store that the organization controls, such as a SIEM, a data lake or another analysis platform.

In practice, the API serves as the programmatic route to audit data. Where an administrator can search the audit log interactively in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, the Office 365 Management Activity API allows the same kind of activity information to be pulled by code. This supports automated data collection and analysis, repeatable reporting, and long-term storage under the organization's own retention rules. Because the data is grouped into content blobs by record type, a consuming application can retrieve the categories of events it is interested in, such as SharePoint Online or Microsoft Teams activity, and process them separately.

The episode "Audit Microsoft 365 User Activity with Purview" describes two ways to search for specific activities: the audit search functionality in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, or a call to the Office 365 Management Activity API. According to the episode, audited activities can be filtered by user, activity type, date range or service, for example SharePoint Online or Microsoft Teams. This makes it possible to find actions performed by a particular user or administrator. The same episode also raises the question of audit retention, which matters when deciding how long event data stays available and whether it should be copied into separate storage.

The episode "Fix Microsoft 365 Compliance Drift Beyond Green Dashboards" places the API within the wider set of Office 365 Management APIs, which it describes as a platform for management tasks, including security and compliance monitoring. In that discussion, the Office 365 Management Activity API is the part that offers detailed information about user, admin, system and policy actions to enhance security. The episode says that APIs enable automated data collection and analysis, making compliance efforts more efficient and accurate, and that they help detect malware activity, unauthorized data access and policy violations in near real time. The framing is that dashboards showing a healthy status do not replace deeper visibility into what users and systems actually did.

The episode "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" shows a typical scripting scenario. According to the episode, PowerShell scripts can query the Microsoft 365 audit logs, call the Office 365 Management Activity API, or use SharePoint Online cmdlets to enumerate site collections, unique permissions and permission changes. Such scripts usually filter by date range and event types, then export audit log data to CSV for analysis, or feed the results into automation workflows for repeatable reporting. The episode also advises making sure that audit settings align with the retention period and with whether the audit log is trimmed automatically.

When deciding whether to use the API, the main considerations are scale, automation and where the data should live. Manual searches in the compliance portal suit occasional investigations, while the Office 365 Management Activity API suits continuous ingestion into a store the organization manages, for example for correlation with other security data or for retention beyond what the portal provides. The API is documented by Microsoft in its Office 365 Management APIs reference, which describes the available record types and how content is retrieved.

on-premises-data-gateway.desc: The on-premises data gateway is a Windows application that carries data between on-premises sources and Microsoft cloud services such as Power BI, Power Apps and Fabric.

faq.a: It carries data between on-premises sources, such as local SQL servers and file shares, and cloud services like Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Microsoft Fabric. It uses outbound connections only, so the data stays behind the firewall until it is requested.
faq.q: What is the on-premises data gateway used for?

faq.a: It runs in standard mode or personal mode. The facts available only state that these two modes exist.
faq.q: What modes does the on-premises data gateway run in?

faq.a: The episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" says that issues between the gateway and the Power BI service can cause subtle failures. It also notes that auto-updates may be disabled by default in some environments, which can lead to "gateway not working" errors.
faq.q: Why might a gateway stop working?

on-premises-data-gateway.long:
The on-premises data gateway, often called the Power BI gateway, is a Windows application installed inside a private network. It carries data between on-premises data sources and Microsoft cloud services such as Power BI, Power Apps, Power Automate and Microsoft Fabric. It does this using outbound connections only, so the cloud service does not need to open an inbound path into the corporate network. The gateway runs in one of two modes, standard or personal.

The main purpose of the gateway is to let cloud services use data that stays behind a firewall. In the Power BI context, the M365.FM episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" describes it as the component that brings secure, on-premises data into the cloud capabilities of Power BI without moving that data outside the firewall. Typical sources named there are local SQL servers and file shares, which the gateway connects to the Power BI service.

The same gateway concept appears across several Microsoft products, not only Power BI. The episode "Secure Microsoft Fabric Data Pipelines" explains that secure ingestion of on-premises data into Microsoft Fabric typically uses an on-premises data gateway or a virtual network data gateway to bridge on-premises sources and cloud services. The episode recommends combining gateways with firewall-enabled Azure Data Lake Storage, VNet integration and role-based secure access, so that data is encrypted in transit and at rest and leakage is limited during ETL and ingestion workflows.

In automation scenarios the gateway provides hybrid connectivity. The episode "Power Automate vs Azure Logic Apps for Enterprise Integration" states that Azure Logic Apps can reach legacy systems behind corporate firewalls through the on-premises data gateway, which supports automating processes and exchanging data securely. The episode "Build Enterprise Automation with Azure Logic Apps" adds that, together with Hybrid Connections, the gateway lets Logic Apps securely access legacy databases, file shares and APIs, so that business processes can span cloud and on-premises environments.

The gateway also matters for Power Apps and custom connectors. In "Build Secure Custom Connectors for Power Apps", the on-premises data gateway is listed as the option for reaching internal APIs from a custom connector. That episode places this advice alongside other practices, such as storing secrets in Azure Key Vault or environment variables, limiting who can create connections and applying data loss prevention policies to the connector.

Operationally, the gateway is a component that needs attention, because it is installed and maintained on a machine inside the network. The troubleshooting episode points out that problems between the gateway and the Power BI service can cause subtle failures. It also notes that auto-updates are available but disabled by default in some environments, which can lead to unexpected "gateway not working" errors. Keeping the gateway current and checking its connection to the cloud service are therefore part of a stable setup.

When choosing between the modes and related gateway types, the decision depends on who uses the connection and where the data lives. The standard mode is the shared gateway for multiple users and services, while the personal mode is intended for individual use. For sources inside an Azure virtual network, the Fabric episode mentions the virtual network data gateway as an alternative to the on-premises variant. Official Microsoft documentation describes the gateway in more detail.

onecopy.desc: The OneCopy principle in Microsoft Fabric means data is stored once in OneLake and read directly by Spark, SQL and Power BI instead of being duplicated.

faq.a: It means data is stored once in OneLake and read directly by multiple engines such as Spark, SQL and Power BI, rather than being copied between tools.
faq.q: What does the OneCopy principle mean in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. The principle describes a logical copy, and physical redundancy still exists. Database mirroring creates a copy, and shortcuts depend on the availability of their source.
faq.q: Does OneCopy mean there is never any duplicated data?

faq.a: Shortcuts act as references to data stored elsewhere, such as other workspaces, Azure storage, Amazon S3 or Dataverse, so teams can share data without duplicating it.
faq.q: How do shortcuts relate to the OneCopy principle?

onecopy.long:
The OneCopy principle is a design idea in Microsoft Fabric. Data is stored once in OneLake, and the different analytics engines work directly on that single copy instead of each tool keeping its own duplicate. Engines such as Spark, SQL and Power BI read the same stored data, so there is no need to move it between tools before it can be used somewhere else.

The principle rests on OneLake, the unified data lake that comes automatically with every Microsoft Fabric tenant. One OneLake exists per tenant. It builds on Azure Data Lake Storage and stores tables in open formats such as Delta Parquet or Iceberg. Because the format is open and shared, all Fabric analytics engines can operate on the same files. According to Microsoft Learn, a table created with T-SQL can be read by Spark without special connectors or exports, and Power BI reports can read the data directly through Direct Lake.

In practice, the principle is meant to remove a common source of friction in analytics projects: copying data from one system to another so that a different team or engine can use it. Each copy adds storage cost, needs a pipeline to keep it current, and can drift out of sync with the original. With OneCopy, a data engineer working in Spark, an analyst writing T-SQL and a report author in Power BI all point at the same data. The episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained" lists this among its key takeaways: use the OneCopy principle to access data without unnecessary duplication, which the episode links to saving storage costs. It also presents OneLake as a way to centralize analytics data and reduce duplication, which it says improves collaboration among teams.

Shortcuts are the mechanism for data that does not live in the same place. A shortcut acts as a reference to data stored elsewhere, for example in another workspace, in Azure storage, in Amazon S3 or in Dataverse. Teams can then share and use that data without creating a duplicate inside their own workspace. Security is meant to follow the data as well: according to the documentation notes, security roles apply consistently at folder, table, row and column level across SQL, Spark and Power BI, so access rules do not have to be rebuilt for each engine. The episode similarly points to OneLake's governance features for data security and compliance.

There are limits to how literally the principle should be read. A shortcut depends on the availability of its source, so if the referenced system is unavailable, the data behind the shortcut is as well. Database mirroring does create a copy, which means it is an exception to the one-copy idea in the strict sense. The documentation also describes OneCopy as a logical copy: physical redundancy still exists underneath, so the principle is about having one logical version of the data to work with, not about the absence of any replication in the storage layer.

Typical decisions around the principle involve choosing between reading data in place through a shortcut, mirroring it into OneLake, or ingesting it as a new table. Teams weigh the benefit of avoiding duplicate pipelines and storage against the dependency on the source system and the fact that mirroring produces a copy. Integration with other Microsoft tools, such as Power BI and Teams, is described in the episode as a way to streamline workflows and improve decision-making, and it also mentions performance benefits such as faster data queries and reduced operational overhead.

onedrive.desc: OneDrive is Microsoft's cloud storage for personal work files, syncing folders across devices and integrating with SharePoint, sharing controls and Microsoft 365 apps.

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft OneDrive - Simply Explained", they are two separate accounts that only look alike, even though they share the OneDrive name.
faq.q: Is the OneDrive on a home computer the same as OneDrive at work?

faq.a: Files shared in Teams chats are stored in OneDrive, while team files live in SharePoint.
faq.q: Where are files stored when they are shared in a Teams chat?

faq.a: The episodes say full library sync causes storage use, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks, and recommend shortcuts to the source instead.
faq.q: Why do the episodes advise against syncing entire SharePoint libraries?

onedrive.long:
OneDrive, also referred to as Microsoft OneDrive, is Microsoft's cloud storage service for personal work files. It keeps folders available across devices, connects to File Explorer through sync, and works together with sharing controls and the Microsoft 365 apps. It is developed by Microsoft, is included with Microsoft 365, and is classified on M365.FM as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. The service dates back to 2007-08.

OneDrive is used to store and access a person's own working files from different devices, to share those files with colleagues or external recipients, and to protect work through version history and folder backup. It relates closely to Microsoft Word, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft PowerPoint and Microsoft OneNote, since documents created in these applications can be saved to and opened from OneDrive. It also relates to Microsoft Teams and SharePoint: files that people share in Teams chats are stored in OneDrive, while team files live in SharePoint. This split between personal storage and team storage is a recurring theme when organizations decide where a given file should be kept.

The episode "Microsoft OneDrive - Simply Explained" points out that the name OneDrive covers two different products. The OneDrive on a home laptop and the OneDrive provided by an employer are separate accounts that only look alike. The episode also walks through how files get onto a computer, how sharing and permissions work, the folder backup that users did not explicitly ask for, and the undo options provided by version history.

Sync is the area where most practical questions arise. The episode "OneDrive Sync: Setup and Troubleshooting | Simply Explained" describes OneDrive Sync as the mechanism that connects SharePoint and OneDrive files to File Explorer, so people can work with familiar folders while Microsoft 365 keeps collaboration and cloud storage connected. The episode covers how sync works, why common problems occur, and how teams can use it safely at scale.

Several episodes discuss the limits of syncing everything. "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" says that syncing entire SharePoint libraries to local devices creates unnecessary storage usage, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks. According to the episode, large synced libraries increase metadata overhead and network traffic and raise the likelihood of duplicate or outdated files across devices. It also argues that locally copied files can bypass SharePoint retention policies, version history and sensitivity labels, weakening compliance. The proposed alternative is to use shortcuts rather than full library sync. "Stop OneDrive Sync Conflicts with SharePoint Shortcuts" makes a similar case, describing OneDrive shortcuts as a way to turn a slow, overloaded laptop into a curated workspace by pointing to the source instead of copying it.

A related decision is covered in "SharePoint Network Drive vs OneDrive Sync". That episode examines mapping SharePoint or SharePoint Online as a network drive, explains how SharePoint document libraries work behind the scenes and how mapped drives behave in Windows, and notes that treating SharePoint like a traditional file share can lead to slow performance, sync problems and missing features. Taken together, the episodes frame OneDrive as one part of a wider Microsoft 365 file architecture in which SharePoint, Teams and local sync each have a distinct role.

onedrive-files-on-demand.desc: OneDrive Files On-Demand is a OneDrive sync feature that lists all cloud files in File Explorer as online-only placeholders and downloads them only when opened.

faq.a: According to Microsoft Support, a blue cloud marks an online-only file. It is downloaded when opened and cannot be opened while the device is offline.
faq.q: What does the blue cloud icon mean in OneDrive Files On-Demand?

faq.a: The documentation says it works with OneDrive, SharePoint in Microsoft 365, and SharePoint Server 2019 team sites. It needs a supported Windows 10 or Windows Server version and a signed-in OneDrive account.
faq.q: Which services does OneDrive Files On-Demand work with?

faq.a: The episode "Fix OneDrive Files On-Demand Sync Issues" explains four core components (filter driver, sync engine, cache database, cloud module), where each can break, and a step-by-step playbook for diagnosing red Xs, "file not available" messages, and ghosted folders.
faq.q: What does the M365.FM episode on Files On-Demand sync issues cover?

onedrive-files-on-demand.long:
OneDrive Files On-Demand is a feature of the OneDrive sync client that gives access to every file in OneDrive cloud storage without downloading all of them and without using local disk space for each one. Files appear in File Explorer as placeholders. The actual content is fetched only when a user opens a file, which keeps the local disk free of data that is rarely needed.

File Explorer shows the state of each item with a status icon. According to Microsoft Support documentation, a blue cloud marks an online-only file that is downloaded when opened and cannot be opened while offline. A green check marks a file that was opened and is now locally available. A green circle with a white check marks a file that has been set to always stay on the device.
