Right-click commands let users keep items on the device or free up space again, and Storage Sense can return unused files to online-only status after a period the user chooses. New files appear as online-only by default, unless they are created inside a folder that is marked to always keep files on the device.

The feature works with OneDrive, with SharePoint in Microsoft 365, and with SharePoint Server 2019 team sites. It requires a supported Windows 10 or Windows Server version and a signed-in OneDrive account. The documentation lists several limits. Desktop search finds online-only files by name only, not by their content. The feature is not supported when Windows Information Protection is enabled, and some third-party antivirus products are incompatible with it. Deleting an online-only file removes it from OneDrive on all devices, although the recycle bin can restore it. These points matter when planning a rollout, because users who expect a placeholder to behave like a local file may be surprised by offline access or search behavior.

The M365.FM episode "Fix OneDrive Files On-Demand Sync Issues" (2025-08-05) looks at the feature from a troubleshooting angle. It describes common symptoms such as files that spin forever, red Xs, "file not available" messages, and ghosted folders. The episode explains the problems through four core components: a filter driver, a sync engine, a cache database, and a cloud module. It discusses where each component can fail and says that small factors, such as path length or a bloated cache, can stall sync. The episode also presents a step-by-step playbook for diagnosing these problems before a team loses working time.

Files On-Demand also appears in discussions about how to organize shared content. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" (2026-05-26) is aimed at administrators, architects, developers, security professionals, and business leaders who need a practical foundation before making implementation decisions. It lists the Files On-Demand troubleshooting episode among related listening, alongside episodes on stopping OneDrive sync conflicts with SharePoint shortcuts and on comparing a SharePoint network drive with OneDrive sync. Together these episodes place Files On-Demand in the wider question of how SharePoint libraries and OneDrive content reach the desktop and how reliably that works.

In practice, decisions around the feature usually concern which folders should always stay available offline, how aggressively Storage Sense should free up space, and how to handle sync problems when they appear. The documentation and the episodes together suggest that understanding the online-only, locally available, and always-keep states, and the components behind them, makes it easier to explain unexpected behavior and to troubleshoot it in a structured way.

onedrive-shortcuts.desc: Add shortcut to OneDrive places a cloud-managed link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in a user's OneDrive instead of syncing a separate copy.

faq.a: It adds a link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in the user's OneDrive, so the content appears in My files without a separate replica being synced. The content stays with its owner.
faq.q: What does Add shortcut to OneDrive do?

faq.a: No. According to Microsoft Support, a shortcut uses no storage of its own, because the content counts against the owner of the shared folder.
faq.q: Does a shortcut use the user's OneDrive storage?

faq.a: The episode warns that deleting or renaming a shortcut can affect the shared source. Microsoft Support states that removing a shortcut deletes only the link, and that a rename is visible only to the person who set it.
faq.q: What happens if a shortcut is deleted or renamed?

onedrive-shortcuts.long:
Add shortcut to OneDrive is a OneDrive feature that places a link to a shared SharePoint library or folder in a user's OneDrive, instead of syncing a replica of that content to the device. The shortcut is managed in the cloud and points to the shared source. The user reaches the shared content from their own My files area while the data stays in its original location. Microsoft Support describes the same idea for shared folders: a shortcut is a link that puts a shared folder in My files, using the Add shortcut to My files command.

The feature exists to make shared folders easier to reach and edit. It is available from the Shared view: the user selects a folder and uses the circle on its tile or the right-click menu. On a PC or Mac where the OneDrive app syncs the shortcut, the content can also be opened locally. A shortcut can be renamed, and the new name is visible only to the person who set it. Because a shortcut is only a link, it uses no storage of its own. The content counts against the owner of the shared folder.

The feature comes up mostly in comparison with traditional library syncing. The episode "SharePoint Sync vs Add Shortcut to OneDrive" describes syncing entire SharePoint libraries to local devices as a growing problem for modern enterprises. According to the episode, it creates unnecessary storage usage, performance slowdowns, sync conflicts and governance risks. Large synced libraries increase metadata overhead and network traffic, and they raise the likelihood of duplicate or outdated files across devices. The episode also says that files copied locally can bypass SharePoint retention policies, version history and sensitivity labels, which weakens compliance. A shortcut avoids a full local replica of the library and keeps the content under the source's controls.

The episode "Stop OneDrive Sync Conflicts with SharePoint Shortcuts" covers the move away from syncing. Its guidance includes stopping the sync before deleting any synced folders, and disabling the sync button in the SharePoint admin settings to prevent new syncs. It also advises promoting the "Add shortcut to OneDrive" feature to users and monitoring usage while providing support during the transition. One tip from that episode is not to disable offline client availability, because shortcuts need it to function properly.

Handling the shortcut needs some care. The short description of the feature, based on the episode, warns that deleting or renaming a shortcut can affect the shared source. The Microsoft Support page describes a narrower behavior: removing a shortcut deletes only the link, so the folder stays with its owner, and a rename is visible only to the person who made it. Removing a shortcut also removes it from synced computers. Anyone planning a rollout should weigh the episode's caution against this documented behavior and check how the shortcut behaves in their own tenant.

The documentation lists several requirements and limits. Users need to be signed in with a Microsoft account and need edit rights on the shared folder. Only folders are supported, not single shared files. The page states limits of 100 folder shortcuts per person and 1,000 shortcuts overall for files and folders. If the owner stops sharing the folder, it disappears from OneDrive. These points matter when deciding whether shortcuts can replace library syncing for a team, since access follows the sharing permissions of the source.

In practice, the choice is between syncing a library to each device and linking to it from OneDrive. Shortcuts suit shared content that people want in their own OneDrive without copying it. The two episodes frame this as a way to reduce sync conflicts, storage use and governance gaps, while keeping files under the policies applied in SharePoint.

onelake.desc: OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake in Microsoft Fabric, which lets workloads share data and use shortcuts instead of duplicate copies.

faq.a: OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake that comes with Microsoft Fabric. It gives all Fabric workloads one shared place for analytics data.
faq.q: What is OneLake?

faq.a: Shortcuts let workloads reference data stored in other locations without importing a duplicate copy of it. This helps avoid the multiplying copies and refresh jobs described in the episodes.
faq.q: What are shortcuts in OneLake?

faq.a: The episode "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" says Power BI can query lakehouse tables directly through Direct Lake with performance similar to Import mode, without duplicate copies or complex refresh cycles.
faq.q: How does OneLake relate to Power BI and Direct Lake?

onelake.long:
OneLake is the single, organization-wide logical data lake that comes with Microsoft Fabric. It serves as the central location for an organization's analytics data, so that the different Fabric workloads can work against the same storage rather than each keeping its own separate copy. Shortcuts are a key mechanism in this design: they let a workload reference data that lives in another location without importing a duplicate of it.

The problem OneLake addresses is data duplication. The episode "OneLake - Simply Explained" describes a familiar scenario in which one sales table exists in a warehouse, a lakehouse, a Power BI import model and several team folders. Each copy begins as a convenience, but over time the numbers diverge, reports become stale, and someone inherits yet another refresh job. The episode presents OneLake as the answer to this mess, aimed at stopping the cost of copying data across systems.

According to the episode "Microsoft Fabric OneLake - Simply Explained", OneLake is the unified data lake at the heart of Microsoft Fabric and provides one centralized place for all of an organization's analytics data. Every Fabric workload, from Power BI and Data Engineering to Data Science and Data Warehouse, can access the same data. The stated effects are less duplication and fewer data silos. The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" places OneLake alongside common Fabric capacity and the Delta format as shared foundations, so that lakehouses, warehouses, Power BI and other Fabric experiences operate as parts of one platform rather than isolated services. In that episode, Amit Chandak compares OneLake conceptually to OneDrive: instead of every analytics workload creating independent storage, workloads share a common foundation.

OneLake also plays a role in the way Power BI handles data. The episode "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" explains that, with OneLake and Direct Lake, Power BI can query lakehouse tables directly with performance similar to Import mode, without creating duplicate copies or maintaining complex refresh cycles. The pattern described there runs from Dataflows Gen2 into a Lakehouse, through Pipelines and a Semantic Model, to a Direct Lake report, with OneLake as the storage layer underneath.

In the episode "Eliminate Data Silos with Microsoft Fabric and OneLake", OneLake is described as one storage plane within Fabric's wider approach to fragmentation, alongside one identity through Entra. The episode argues that a stack made of Power BI, ad hoc pipelines, shadow CSVs and several conflicting dashboards amounts to entropy rather than a coherent platform, and it frames Fabric as a response to that fragmentation. Related themes raised there include data silos, lack of governance, scalability, and security and compliance.

For decisions about adopting OneLake, the episodes point to a few recurring considerations. Teams weighing whether to copy data into each workload can instead consider referencing it through shortcuts. Teams building Power BI models can consider Direct Lake over lakehouse tables as an alternative to import refresh cycles. Teams planning a broader platform can look at how shared foundations such as OneLake, Fabric capacity and the Delta format reduce the number of separate services and storage technologies to manage. Further technical detail is available in the official Microsoft Learn overview of OneLake.

onelake-security.desc: OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data in OneLake, with row-level and object-level rules defined once and applied across Fabric engines.

faq.a: OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data stored in OneLake. Administrators define roles that grant access to folders or tables in a Fabric item and assign them to users or groups, and the permissions apply across Fabric engines.
faq.q: What is OneLake security?

faq.a: New SQL analytics endpoints start in delegated identity mode and are not protected by OneLake security. The access mode must be switched to the user's identity mode for the roles to take effect.
faq.q: Why do SQL analytics endpoints need a configuration change?

faq.a: DefaultReader is a role that new items come with, and its membership is virtualized, so anyone with a permission such as ReadAll is automatically a member. Since it grants full access, users should be removed from it once they are placed in a more restrictive role.
faq.q: What is the DefaultReader role?

onelake-security.long:
OneLake security is a role-based access control model for data stored in OneLake, the unified storage layer of Microsoft Fabric. It lets administrators define access rules once, directly on the data, so the same rules apply across Fabric engines and endpoints instead of being rebuilt separately in each tool. Row-level and object-level restrictions are part of the model, which allows access to be narrowed to specific folders, tables, rows or columns.

In practice, an administrator creates security roles that grant access to specific folders or tables inside a Fabric item and then assigns those roles to users or groups. Row-level and column-level security can narrow table access further. A ReadWrite permission, available only for lakehouses, allows writing through Spark notebooks, the OneLake file explorer or OneLake APIs without granting rights to manage Fabric items. Creating roles requires write and reshare permission, which workspace admins and members usually hold. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, lakehouses and mirrored items are listed as supported.

New items come with a DefaultReader role. Its membership is virtualized, so anyone who holds the needed permission, such as ReadAll, is automatically a member. Because this role grants full access, the documentation notes that users should be removed from it once they are placed in a more restrictive role; otherwise the broader access remains in effect. Users who have no data access role at all see no data in the item.

SQL analytics endpoints need specific attention. New endpoints start in delegated identity mode and are not protected by OneLake security until the access mode is switched to the user's identity mode. This is a typical decision point when rolling out OneLake security, since the protection only reaches that endpoint once the mode is changed.

OneLake security is one layer in a wider security picture. The episode "Microsoft Fabric End-to-End: From Raw Data to Business Decisions with Amit Chandak [MVP]" describes security across multiple layers, starting with Fabric workspace roles and continuing through item-level access, OneLake security and semantic-model security. In that discussion, Amit Chandak recommends using security groups rather than managing individual users wherever possible. Microsoft Entra provides the identity and group foundation, while Fabric applies those identities and groups to workspaces, items and data access. Assigning OneLake security roles to groups fits this approach.

The episode "Microsoft Fabric 2025 Updates Explained" mentions OneLake Security improvements alongside new governance tools, describing them together as part of an enterprise-grade foundation for secure data operations. The episode frames these changes in the context of real-time intelligence and the wider set of Fabric updates it covers.

Taken together, the sources present OneLake security as a way to centralize data-level access control in Fabric: roles are defined on the data in OneLake, assigned to Entra identities and groups, and enforced consistently by the engines that read the data, provided the endpoint is configured to use the user's identity.

onelake-shortcuts.desc: OneLake shortcuts are pointers in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that reference data stored elsewhere, so the data is reachable in a lakehouse without being copied.

faq.a: A OneLake shortcut is a pointer in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that references data stored elsewhere, inside Fabric or in external storage. The data stays at its target path while the shortcut appears in a lakehouse or other item.
faq.q: What is a OneLake shortcut?

faq.a: Shortcuts avoid physical data movement. The episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" says this reduces both storage and compute costs, since redundant ingestion pipelines and repeated copies are not needed.
faq.q: Why are OneLake shortcuts used instead of copying data?

faq.a: The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" names OneLake Shortcuts as the way to share high-quality data as a product between domain teams. The episode "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric" lists shortcuts as an engineering output, separate from governance policies such as sensitivity labels.
faq.q: How do OneLake shortcuts relate to data mesh and governance?

onelake-shortcuts.long:
OneLake shortcuts are pointers in Microsoft Fabric's OneLake that reference data stored in another location, either inside Fabric or in external storage, without copying that data. The data stays at its target path, while the shortcut appears as an entry in a lakehouse or another Fabric item. Because only a reference is created, users and workloads can read the data as if it were part of the item they are working in, while the original location remains the single place where the data actually lives.

The main purpose of OneLake shortcuts is to avoid physical data movement. Without shortcuts, making the same data available in several places typically means building ingestion pipelines and storing duplicate copies. With a shortcut, one team can expose data to another team or workspace by reference. This is why shortcuts come up in discussions of data architecture in Fabric: they change the question from how to move data to where the data should live and who should be able to reach it.

The M365.FM episode "Build ETL with Microsoft Fabric Dataflows Gen2" covers shortcuts from a cost and capacity angle. It lists factors that raise compute usage, such as cross-region access with higher latency, repeated transformations and redundant ingestion pipelines, and contrasts them with OneLake shortcuts, which the episode says reduce physical data movement and therefore lower storage and compute costs. In that context, shortcuts are presented as one way to keep ETL operations efficient and predictable, alongside managing compute resources carefully and using managed staging.

Shortcuts also appear in the governance and data mesh discussion. The episode "Use Microsoft Fabric Domains for Data Mesh Governance" maps data mesh principles to Fabric features. Under the principle of data as a product, it names shared access to high-quality data through OneLake Shortcuts. In that model, domain teams own and manage their own data and workspaces, and shortcuts are one mechanism for letting other teams consume that data without taking over ownership or duplicating it. The episode pairs this with semantic models, metadata-rich catalogs, role-based access and cataloging for compliance.

A third episode, "Build a Trusted Semantic Layer in Microsoft Fabric", places OneLake shortcuts on the technical side of a split between governance and engineering. According to the episode, the governance side produces policies, sensitivity labels and data ownership definitions, while the engineering side, owned by data engineers, Fabric administrators and developers, produces validated datasets, automated workflows and OneLake shortcuts. The episode argues that separating these concerns lets an organization address governance and security effectively, with shortcuts belonging to integration and data availability rather than to policy setting.

In practice, decisions around OneLake shortcuts concern where data should be stored, which team owns the target location, and how access is controlled when the same data is surfaced in several lakehouses or items. Since a shortcut is only a reference, the target path remains the authoritative copy, and ownership, quality and access rules defined there continue to matter for every place the shortcut appears. Shortcuts therefore connect naturally to topics such as lakehouses, domains, data products and ETL design in Microsoft Fabric.

onenote.desc: Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings, organised in notebooks, sections and pages and synced through OneDrive.

faq.a: Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings. It is typically used for meeting notes, research collections, project documentation and personal knowledge management.
faq.q: What is Microsoft OneNote used for?

faq.a: Notebooks are organised into sections and pages and are synced through OneDrive, so the same notes are available across devices. OneNote is included in the Microsoft 365 licence as part of Microsoft 365 Apps.
faq.q: How does OneNote store and sync notes?

faq.a: "Build a OneNote System for Notes and Follow-Ups" describes a workflow built on tags, linked pages and templates. "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" compares OneNote with Loop and Copilot, and "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" covers governance when Copilot works with notes through Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about OneNote?

onenote.long:
Microsoft OneNote is a digital notebook for typed notes, ink, images and web clippings. Content is organised in a hierarchy of notebooks, sections and pages, and notebooks are synced through OneDrive, so the same notes are available across devices. It was developed by Microsoft, first released in 2003, and is included in the Microsoft 365 licence as part of Microsoft 365 Apps. In the M365.FM knowledge base it is classified both as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool.

OneNote is typically used for meeting notes, research collections, project documentation and personal knowledge management. Because a page can hold typed text, handwritten ink, images and clipped web content side by side, it suits situations where information arrives in mixed formats and needs to be kept in one place. The notebook, section and page structure gives a familiar way to group related material, for example one notebook per project or topic, with sections for areas of work and pages for individual notes.

Storage and sync work through OneDrive. Notebooks live there, which is how notes stay consistent when opened on different devices. This link to OneDrive also shapes decisions about where notebooks are kept and who can reach them. OneNote is also closely related to Microsoft Teams, where notebooks are commonly shared with a team and used alongside meetings and channels. An episode on organising projects in Teams lists native access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, SharePoint and Outlook among the benefits of the Microsoft 365 integration, since it supports document collaboration and version control in one workspace.

The M365.FM episode "Build a OneNote System for Notes and Follow-Ups" argues that most people use only about ten percent of OneNote and end up with a digital junk drawer that hides decisions and weakens follow-ups. It describes turning OneNote into a working system built on action-ready tags, linked pages, smart templates and a workflow-first notebook structure, so that less time goes into searching and more into acting on notes. The emphasis is on how the notebook is organised rather than on adding more features.

A second line of discussion concerns where OneNote fits among other Microsoft tools for notes. The episode "OneNote vs Loop vs Copilot with Karinne Diamond Bessette [MVP]" compares OneNote, Microsoft Loop and Copilot for notes. It approaches the topic from the problem of information chaos in the modern workplace and focuses on how each option works, where it fits, and the architecture, security, governance and operational choices that matter in real Microsoft environments.

Copilot is the third theme. The episode "Copilot in Office Apps: The Governance Checklist" notes that Copilot is presented as available across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and OneNote. It explains that Copilot draws on emails, files, meetings and notes through Microsoft Graph, and that privacy, data loss prevention and audit workloads increase once it is switched on. For OneNote this means notes can become part of the data Copilot works with, which makes governance of where notes are stored and who can access them a practical concern. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Prompts That Deliver Better Results" also mentions organising notes in OneNote as one of the daily routines in which clear, contextual prompts help Copilot deliver useful results.

Taken together, the sources describe OneNote as a flexible notebook whose value depends on how it is structured, how it is shared through OneDrive and Microsoft Teams, and how it is governed once AI features such as Copilot are involved.

ontology.desc: An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions that names the types of things in a domain and the relationships between them, so people and systems read data alike.

faq.a: An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions for a domain that specifies the types of things and the relationships that may connect them. Its aim is that people and systems interpret data the same way.
faq.q: What is an ontology?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions", a schema defines the shape of a record, an ontology defines the shared meaning of concepts and relationships, and a graph stores and queries the connected entities.
faq.q: How does an ontology differ from a schema and a graph?

faq.a: The episodes describe an ontology as a layer that can describe relationships across several semantic models and give AI systems a structure for navigating enterprise information. It also gives a chatbot or agent a formal model of the business domain to reason with.
faq.q: How does an ontology relate to semantic models and AI agents?

ontology.long:
An ontology is a formal set of shared definitions for a domain. It specifies the types of things that exist in that domain and the relationships that may connect them, so that people and systems interpret data in the same way. In practice it acts as a common vocabulary with rules: instead of each team or system describing a customer, a machine, or an order in its own terms, the ontology states what those concepts mean and how they relate to one another.

The main purpose is to keep meaning consistent across teams, tools, and AI systems. The episode "Fabric IQ - Simply Explained" illustrates the problem with a familiar situation: two teams call the same customer two different things. The episode describes this as data that is fine, while the meaning behind it has quietly drifted apart. An ontology addresses that drift by fixing shared definitions rather than only storing records. That episode covers the ontology as one part of Fabric IQ, alongside how it connects to semantic models and how it grounds AI agents.

An ontology is often discussed next to two related ideas, a schema and a graph, and the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions" separates them clearly. A schema defines the shape of a record, for example by requiring fields such as asset ID, event timestamp, fault code, work-order ID, or engineering unit. An ontology defines the shared meaning of the concepts and relationships used across the factory. A graph provides a practical way to store and query those connected entities. According to the episode, once those relationships exist, the same machine event becomes more useful for planning and decision-making, because it can be read with context such as whether output is released, restricted, or held, and which relationships were valid when the event happened.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, the concept appears in the context of digital twins. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Digital Twin Builder Explained" describes the ontology in the digital twin builder as a semantic model that defines entities, relationships, and properties. According to the episode, this lets teams structure data into an ontology and create comprehensive digital replicas, and it allows disparate data, including OT data, to be mapped into a consistent schema, which simplifies digital twin creation.

The concept also relates to AI. The episode "Codify Business Logic into a Digital Twin for AI Agents" states that ontology and semantics shape how a chatbot reasons and interacts. In that framing, the ontology gives a formal model of the business domain, defining relationships and business logic, and creates a structured framework for the AI system. The episode describes this as a shift from unstructured data to structured, semantic reasoning, and says it improves consistency and reliability. It also mentions combining tools such as Databricks for storage and Stardog for knowledge graphs to model relationships within data.

The episode "Everyone Wants Copilot—but Is Your Data Ready: Microsoft Fabric Architecture with Walter Calcagno [MVP-MCT]" adds an architectural view. Large organizations often have many semantic models across departments and domains, and the episode notes that solving this by building one enormous semantic model is not necessarily the answer. Walter Calcagno highlights the ontology as another layer: rather than forcing everything into a single semantic model, an ontology can describe relationships across models and provide a structure through which AI systems can navigate enterprise information. In his view, semantic models combined with ontology models are an increasingly important foundation for connecting enterprise data with large language models.

Taken together, the episodes treat an ontology as a layer of meaning that sits above raw data and records. Typical decisions around it include whether a schema alone is sufficient, whether relationships need to be modeled explicitly, how an ontology relates to existing semantic models, and how its definitions can be used to ground AI agents in business terms.

opc-ua.desc: OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture) is an industrial communication standard that exchanges machine data in a structured information model with typed values and status codes.

faq.a: OPC UA (OPC Unified Architecture) is an industrial communication standard that exchanges data in a structured information model. It uses typed values, status codes, client-server subscriptions and certificate-based application security.
faq.q: What is OPC UA?

faq.a: The episodes describe them as complementary: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Microsoft Fabric can ingest and analyze the stream. One episode rejects the idea of a winner-takes-all battle between the two.
faq.q: How does OPC UA relate to MQTT in a Microsoft manufacturing setup?

faq.a: According to the episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration", it does not. A fault event can reach a dashboard immediately, but questions such as which shipment is at risk still require MES, ERP, maintenance and quality data.
faq.q: Does OPC UA connectivity alone answer operational questions?

opc-ua.long:
OPC UA, short for OPC Unified Architecture, is an industrial communication standard for exchanging data between machines, controllers and higher-level systems. Instead of passing around loose, unlabeled values, it exposes data in a structured information model. Values are typed, they carry status codes, and clients can subscribe to changes. Application security is based on certificates, so that the applications taking part in an exchange can be identified and trusted.

In practice, OPC UA is the layer that makes a machine signal available in the first place. The episode "How Machine Data Reaches Microsoft Fabric - From OPC UA to Real-Time Analytics" describes the typical chain: OPC UA exposes the machine signal, an edge layer collects it, MQTT can distribute it locally, and Microsoft Fabric can ingest and analyze the resulting stream. Machine alarms, sensor values, production counters and fault events are examples of the kind of data that travels along this path. The same episode stresses that the hard part begins after the data arrives, because raw telemetry still has to be turned into enough production context to support an actual decision.

The client-server pattern with subscriptions is one of the defining traits of the standard. A client connects to a server that represents a device or a control system and subscribes to the nodes it cares about, receiving updates when values change. The typed values and status codes matter because a reading such as a temperature is only useful together with its data type and an indication of whether the value can be trusted. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" points to the same idea from the PLC side: a raw tag value comes with a timestamp and a quality state, and older plants often run several generations of equipment that use proprietary protocols or OPC UA.

OPC UA is often discussed together with MQTT, but the episodes treat them as complementary rather than competing. The episode "MQTT and OPC UA in Microsoft Manufacturing: Azure IoT Operations + Fabric Architecture" rejects the framing of industrial connectivity as a winner-takes-all battle and instead places the discussion in the context of a broader problem, a lack of trust in manufacturing data. According to the episode, factories can have ERP, MES and Azure systems in place and still rely on manual exports and guesswork. Because PLCs rarely speak cloud MQTT directly, the pipeline episode describes an industrial gateway on the operational technology (OT) network that bridges the gap by normalizing data into a common message shape, managing collection frequency and forwarding state changes immediately.

An information model also raises the question of how machine-level structures relate to the rest of the business. The episode "What Is an Industrial Data Model" gives an example: a single machine may appear as a work center in ERP, an asset number in maintenance, a resource in MES, a group of OPC UA nodes in the control system, and a different friendly name on the shop floor. According to the episode, an industrial model does not force all of these systems to share one identifier. It records how the different references relate to the same physical or logical object, which gives the factory a stable identity layer without destroying the local structures each source system needs. In this view, OPC UA nodes are one of several representations of an asset, not the complete picture.

The episode "Connectivity Is Not Integration — Why Your Connected Factory Still Can't Answer the Right Questions" makes the limits of connectivity explicit. A packaging machine stops, the PLC reports the fault, OPC UA exposes the event, MQTT distributes it and a dashboard updates immediately, yet a planner asking which customer shipment is now at risk still needs MES data, ERP records, maintenance history, quality status, production quantities and delivery commitments, often combined in a spreadsheet. The takeaway from the episodes is that OPC UA solves the problem of getting a well-described machine signal out of the plant, while contextualization, shared identity and integration with business data remain separate design decisions.

Typical decisions around OPC UA therefore concern where the signal is collected (an edge or gateway layer), how it is distributed (for example via MQTT), how it reaches analytics (for example Microsoft Fabric) and how it is tied to production context so that the data can answer operational questions.

openapi.desc: OpenAPI is an open specification for machine-readable descriptions of web APIs, used by Semantic Kernel and Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe plugin and extension capabilities.

faq.a: OpenAPI is an open specification for machine-readable descriptions of web APIs. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used by Semantic Kernel and Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe what plugins and extensions can do.
faq.q: What is OpenAPI?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, an OpenAPI or Swagger file is used to build custom connectors in Power Apps, and importing an openapi.json file is part of creating an MCP custom connector for Copilot Studio.
faq.q: Where is OpenAPI used with Power Apps and Copilot Studio?

faq.a: The episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists API plugins based on OpenAPI as a way to connect external systems so Copilot can retrieve data and invoke business processes.
faq.q: How does OpenAPI relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins?

openapi.long:
OpenAPI is an open specification for describing web APIs in a machine-readable form. An OpenAPI document states what an API offers and how it can be called, so that other tools and services can understand it without custom documentation or guesswork. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used by Semantic Kernel and by Microsoft 365 Copilot to describe what plugins and extensions can do.

The core purpose is a standard, shared way of describing an API. When an API is described in this format, tools that consume it can learn how to call it, which makes integration easier and more reliable. The M365.FM episode "Build Microsoft Copilot Plugins with Azure Functions" makes this point directly: OpenAPI describes an API in a standard way so that other tools and services can understand how to call the underlying functions. That episode presents OpenAPI as one of the integration patterns for connecting Azure Functions to external systems, and it includes a table to help decide when to use certain integration patterns and when not to.

OpenAPI appears in several places across Copilot and Power Platform work. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, the episode "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists API plugins based on OpenAPI as one way to connect external systems, alongside Microsoft Graph connectors and custom connectors built in Azure. According to the episode, these approaches let Copilot retrieve data, invoke business processes and integrate with systems such as ERP, CRM or proprietary databases, so that Copilot chat and actions become more conversational and context-aware. In this role the OpenAPI description tells Copilot what an API plugin can do.

In Power Apps, OpenAPI files, also referred to as Swagger files, are used to define custom connectors. The episode "Build Fusion Apps with Power Apps and Azure Functions" describes a pattern in which an Azure Function is protected with API Management, a new API is created for the function, and a custom connector is then built in Power Apps from an OpenAPI or Swagger file that shows what the function does and adds security. Once the connector exists, the app calls the API through it as a data source. The episode "Build Secure Custom Connectors for Power Apps" covers a related path, walking through creating a secure custom connector for an API, including authentication, OpenAPI, error handling and throttling, so that apps can work with live business data rather than CSV exports or copy-paste.

OpenAPI also features in connecting Model Context Protocol servers to Copilot Studio. The episode "MCP Custom Connector in Copilot Studio: The Complete Integration Guide" outlines a procedure that starts in the Copilot Studio Tools area, adds a new tool of the custom connector type, and then, in Power Apps, creates a new custom connector by importing an OpenAPI file. The steps include naming the connector, uploading an openapi.json file, reviewing the configuration settings, creating the connector and then refreshing the Tools tab in Copilot Studio to see the new connector.

In practice, the decisions around OpenAPI usually concern which surface consumes the description. For a Copilot plugin, the OpenAPI document describes the plugin's capabilities. For a Power Apps custom connector, it defines the operations the connector exposes, with security added separately. For an MCP connector in Copilot Studio, an openapi.json file serves as the import for the connector definition. Across these scenarios the shared benefit named in the episodes is that a single, standard description lets different Microsoft tools understand and call an API consistently.

openid-connect.desc: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication layer on OAuth 2.0 that signs users in with signed ID tokens and, via federation, removes stored secrets from pipelines.

faq.a: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, and OpenID Connect extends it with authentication. OIDC adds the ID token, a signed JWT that lets a client verify the user and read claims about them.
faq.q: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?

faq.a: It needs an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID, a matching registered redirect URI and ID token issuance enabled. The sign-in request must include the client ID, the id_token response type, the openid scope and a nonce.
faq.q: What does an app need to sign users in with OIDC on the Microsoft identity platform?

faq.a: The M365.FM episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" describes OIDC and Federated Credentials replacing long-lived secrets in GitHub Actions and other pipelines. The pipeline exchanges tokens with Entra ID instead of storing credentials.
faq.q: How is OIDC used in CI/CD pipelines?

openid-connect.long:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an authentication protocol built on top of OAuth 2.0. OAuth 2.0 describes how an application obtains authorization, while OpenID Connect adds a standard way to establish who the user is. This extension makes single sign-on possible between OAuth-enabled applications. According to the material behind this page, Microsoft recommends OIDC as the default for new cloud apps, and it relies on compact JSON-based tokens to handle sign-in.

The central element is the ID token. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed with public-key cryptography, and a client can use it to verify the user and read claims about that user. On the Microsoft identity platform, OIDC is supported by several endpoints: a discovery document published on a well-known path, a key endpoint used to verify token signatures, an authorize endpoint and a token endpoint, a logout endpoint, and a UserInfo endpoint. The UserInfo endpoint returns claims according to the openid, profile and email scopes.

To use OIDC with Microsoft Entra ID, an application needs an app registration, a matching registered redirect URI, and ID token issuance enabled. A sign-in request must include the client ID, the id_token response type, the openid scope and a nonce. Apps that rely on ID tokens are expected to validate both the signature and the claims, ideally with a token validation library rather than custom code. The documentation notes that native apps and single-page apps gain little from such validation. It also states that tokens issued for other Microsoft APIs should not be read or validated by the client.

Some practical details affect implementation. Sign-out needs two parts: the redirect to the end-session endpoint and clearing the application's own session. Because responses delivered in the URL fragment are limited in length, the form_post response mode is recommended.

Beyond interactive user sign-in, OIDC also appears in automation and DevOps scenarios. The M365.FM episode "Service Principal Security: Stop Using Personal Accounts" describes Federated Credentials and OpenID Connect as replacements for long-lived secrets in GitHub Actions, CI/CD pipelines and multi-cloud integrations. The episode presents static secrets as one of the largest liabilities in enterprise automation. It covers how OIDC token exchange works with Entra ID, why workload federation removes the need for stored credentials, and why temporary trust is described as stronger than permanent passwords.

The episode "GitHub vs Azure DevOps for Microsoft Fabric CI/CD" mentions OIDC in a similar deployment context. It says GitHub supports OpenID Connect for secure deployments to cloud platforms, alongside features such as reusable workflows, artifact attestations, deployment rules that control who can deploy and when, and a deployment history useful for audits and compliance checks.

In practice, the choice to use OIDC usually comes up in two situations: adding sign-in to a new app registered in Microsoft Entra ID, and replacing client secrets in pipelines with federated trust. In both, the protocol exchanges short-lived signed tokens instead of relying on passwords or static secrets kept by the application or the pipeline.

openrewrite.desc: OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring that applies recipes to migrate frameworks, fix security issues and reduce technical debt.

faq.a: OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring. It runs recipes that perform framework migrations, security fixes and stylistic consistency changes, with the goal of eliminating technical debt.
faq.q: What is OpenRewrite?

faq.a: It modifies Lossless Semantic Trees that represent the source code and then prints the changed trees back as source. This keeps changes minimally invasive and preserves the original formatting, so the result can be reviewed as a diff.
faq.q: How does OpenRewrite change code without disrupting formatting?

faq.a: In the episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents", a modernization agent auto-applies OpenRewrite recipes, which drive the migration of Java APIs during the upgrade. Changes stay traceable in Git.
faq.q: What role does OpenRewrite play in the Java 8 to Java 21 episode?

openrewrite.long:
OpenRewrite is an open-source ecosystem for automated source-code refactoring. Its stated goal is to help developers eliminate technical debt in their repositories by running prepackaged, open-source recipes for framework migrations, security fixes and stylistic consistency. The aim is to reduce work that would otherwise take hours or days to a matter of minutes. OpenRewrite was originally focused on Java, and the community is widening its language and framework coverage.

The central concept is the recipe. Recipes are the units that users run, and they are built from visitors, which make the actual modifications to the code. The OpenRewrite documentation gives one example: a visitor that turns assertTrue calls into static imports consistently across all test files. Because recipes are composed from such visitors, a larger migration can be expressed as a set of smaller, repeatable code changes that run in the same way every time.

Technically, OpenRewrite does not edit source files as plain text. It modifies Lossless Semantic Trees, which represent the source code, and then prints the changed trees back out as source. Because of this design, changes are minimally invasive and preserve the original formatting of the code. The practical result is a clean diff that a developer can review and commit like any other change. Recipes are run on one repository at a time through Gradle and Maven plugins. For running the recipe catalogue across many repositories, with mass commits and impact analysis, the documentation describes Moderne as a commercial platform. Moderne offers a free public service for open-source projects, and a multi-repo command-line interface is also available. The documentation further notes that recipes are moving from Maven Central to the Code Genome Project.

Typical situations for using OpenRewrite include upgrading the Java version of an application, moving from one framework version to another, and applying security fixes in bulk. In each case, the value lies in applying a known, reviewable transformation instead of hand-editing many files, with each modification visible in version control.

OpenRewrite appears in the M365.FM episode "Upgrade Java 8 Apps to Java 21 with AI Agents" (2025-11-28). In that episode, a co-pilot-style modernization agent takes over much of the repetitive work of moving a Java 8 application to Java 21 on Azure. According to the episode description, the agent inventories the entire stack, ranks CVEs by real reachability, auto-applies OpenRewrite recipes, aligns BOMs, fixes illegal reflective access and keeps every change traceable in Git. In this workflow, OpenRewrite recipes drive the migration of Java APIs during the upgrade, while the agent coordinates the surrounding steps. The same episode extends the scenario beyond the code upgrade to platform decisions such as Azure App Service versus Azure Spring Apps, migration to Azure SQL Database, Dockerfile generation, GitHub Actions CI/CD and secrets handling with Key Vault and managed identities.

The combination described in the episode reflects a common pattern: deterministic, recipe-based refactoring handles well-understood API migrations, while an AI agent handles inventory, prioritization and orchestration. Keeping the changes as reviewable diffs in Git is what makes the result auditable.

opentelemetry.desc: OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications to emit traces, metrics and logs.

faq.a: OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications so they emit traces, metrics and logs.
faq.q: What is OpenTelemetry?

faq.a: According to the episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery", it supports distributed tracing, which follows a request across services and helps reveal where delays and bottlenecks occur.
faq.q: How does OpenTelemetry help with microservices?

faq.a: The episodes describe using it, for example with Azure AI Foundry, to visualize how agents run, which tools they call and how they make decisions, and to monitor pilot agent deployments.
faq.q: How is OpenTelemetry used with AI agents in the Microsoft ecosystem?

opentelemetry.long:
OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open-source observability standard and framework for instrumenting applications so that they emit traces, metrics and logs. It gives teams a common way to describe what a running system is doing, independent of the monitoring product that eventually stores or visualizes the data. Because the approach is not tied to a single vendor, the same instrumentation can in principle feed different backends, which is why it appears in discussions of cloud, microservice and AI workloads alike.

The three signal types named in its definition each answer a different question. Traces follow a single request as it moves through the components of a system. Metrics capture aggregated measurements over time, such as latency or request counts. Logs record individual events and decisions. OpenTelemetry is used to produce all three in a consistent form, so that data coming from different services, languages and frameworks can be correlated rather than analyzed in isolation.

One of the clearest use cases in the M365.FM material is distributed tracing in microservice architectures. The episode "Why Microservice Architecture Slows Software Delivery" explains that distributed tracing lets teams follow a request across many services, with each service adding its own processing time and network delay. It lists OpenTelemetry alongside Jaeger and Zipkin as tracing tools that connect the dots and show the full path of a request. According to the episode, this makes it easier to spot where delays happen, exposes bottlenecks and accelerates debugging, so teams can identify latency sources and improve reliability.

OpenTelemetry also comes up in the context of AI agents. The episode "Secure AI Agents and Shadow IT in Microsoft 365" describes framework fragmentation as a governance problem: different AI frameworks use different metrics and logging styles, which complicates observability and integration. The episode suggests that tools such as Datadog and OpenTelemetry can give better visibility into AI workflows, helping teams track decision paths and identify issues before they escalate, and it stresses continuous monitoring to detect misuse, policy violations and changes in AI behavior early.

The same theme appears in two further episodes about building agents on Microsoft's cloud. "How to Build Low-Cost AI Agents in Microsoft Cloud" addresses debugging opacity, where agents make decisions that are hard to trace. It recommends structured reasoning logs and using Azure AI Foundry with OpenTelemetry to visualize how agents run, which tools they call and how they make decisions. "Production AI Agents with Microsoft Foundry and Edgar McOchieng [MVP]" advises starting with a low- or medium-risk pilot project and monitoring everything with tools like OpenTelemetry, alongside least-privilege access for agent actions and a human in the loop for important decisions.

Cost is another angle. In "Azure Monitor — Simply Explained", OpenTelemetry appears in a list of ways to tune the amount of telemetry collected and keep Azure monitoring costs under control. The episode mentions using OpenTelemetry metric instruments and aggregating metrics to reduce data volume, next to limiting reported data and disabling unneeded instrumentation. The underlying idea is to collect only the signals that are necessary while keeping visibility into the environment.

Taken together, the episodes treat OpenTelemetry as an instrumentation layer rather than a monitoring product in itself. It produces traces, metrics and logs; tools such as Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog or Azure Monitor are the places where such data is examined. Typical decisions around it include which signals to collect, how much data to send in order to manage cost, and how to apply it to both classic microservices and AI agent workflows where decision paths need to be traceable.

operational-technology.desc: Operational technology (OT) is the hardware, software and work used to monitor and control physical production processes and equipment, distinct from IT.

faq.a: OT monitors and controls physical production processes and equipment, while IT covers business, computing and data services. OT stresses availability and real-time control, whereas IT security centers on confidentiality, integrity and availability.
faq.q: What is the difference between OT and IT?

faq.a: OT includes industrial control systems such as SCADA, distributed control systems, remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers, as well as IoT and industrial IoT devices and building automation.
faq.q: Which systems count as operational technology?

faq.a: According to the episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub", an industrial gateway on the OT network translates data into a common message shape, manages collection frequency and buffers data locally during network outages.
faq.q: How does OT data reach cloud services like Azure IoT Hub?

operational-technology.long:
Operational technology (OT) refers to the hardware and software that detects or causes change by directly monitoring and controlling industrial equipment, assets, processes and events. It is usually defined in contrast to information technology (IT), which covers business computing and data services. A common shorthand describes OT as IT in the non-carpeted areas of a facility, meaning the plant floor, the field and the physical infrastructure rather than the office.

OT environments include industrial control systems such as SCADA, distributed control systems, remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers (PLCs). They also cover IoT and industrial IoT devices and building automation. These systems regulate physical values such as temperature, pressure and flow, which means they need real-time or near-real-time processing and high reliability. They typically communicate through specialized protocols such as Modbus, DNP3, Profibus, BACnet and OPC-UA rather than the general-purpose protocols common in office networks. The term was introduced by Gartner in 2006, first in connection with power utility control systems.

The priorities of OT and IT differ. OT stresses availability and real-time control of a physical process, while IT security is usually framed around confidentiality, integrity and availability. Security in OT was long based on isolation and obscurity. Since at least 2005, OT has been connected to IT systems, which created new risks. Stuxnet is cited as an illustration. Typical weaknesses include weak segmentation, plaintext protocols and legacy devices without authentication. Recommended responses include layered defenses, continuous anomaly monitoring and the ISA/IEC 62443 series of standards.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, OT mostly appears where plant data meets cloud services. The episode "From Sensor to Dashboard: The MQTT Pipeline Through Azure IoT Hub" describes the situation in older plants, which often run several generations of equipment with proprietary protocols or OPC UA. PLCs therefore rarely speak cloud MQTT directly. According to the episode, an industrial gateway deployed on the OT network bridges this gap. It normalizes data by translating disparate formats, scales and engineering tags into a common message shape. It manages collection frequency by aggregating high-frequency scans into meaningful intervals while forwarding state changes immediately. It also buffers data locally during network outages and replays it once connectivity returns.

The second angle is data governance. In "Microsoft Purview for Copilot Security with Peter Rising [Microsoft]", the guidance includes segmenting OT and IT data and sharing only aggregated insights with the cloud. The episode pairs this with multi-factor authentication for supervisors, contractors and suppliers, keeping Copilot from indexing outdated or risky shared files, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies that monitor and block sensitive files from leaving secure channels. The stated aim is to protect intellectual property and control who can access it. The episode's tip is to review the data segmentation strategy and make sure only necessary information moves to the cloud.

Taken together, the sources show OT as a distinct domain with its own protocols, reliability needs and risk profile. Decisions around it usually concern where the boundary between OT and IT lies, which data crosses that boundary, in what form, and how that crossing is secured and governed.

outcome-based-pricing.desc: Outcome-based pricing is a model in which clients pay for measurable business results rather than billable hours, often via build fees plus retainers or licences.

faq.a: It is a pricing model for consulting and IT services in which clients pay for measurable business results rather than billable hours. It is often delivered as build fees plus recurring retainers or licences.
faq.q: What is outcome-based pricing?

faq.a: Time-and-materials contracts pay for inputs such as man-hours, while outcome-based contracts pay for results the business wants. The CIO article reports that time-and-materials is still the most common model and that outcome-based contracts are at most about 15 percent of new deals.
faq.q: How does outcome-based pricing differ from time-and-materials contracts?

faq.a: The CIO article names difficulty agreeing on outcomes between executives, limited vendor control over external factors, the risk of gaming metrics and uneven results. The M365.FM episode on computer-using agents adds that agent and outcome must be clearly defined.
faq.q: What challenges come with outcome-based pricing?

outcome-based-pricing.long:
Outcome-based pricing is a pricing model for consulting and IT services in which the client pays for measurable business results instead of billable hours. In practice it is often structured as a build fee combined with recurring retainers or licences, so that the price is tied to the value delivered rather than to the time a provider spends on the work. The term is used both in outsourcing contracts and in discussions about how Microsoft ecosystem partners package their services.

The idea is easiest to understand by contrast with input-based contracts. A CIO article on outsourcing describes task-based, or input, contracts as agreements that pay for resources such as servers, hardware or man-hours, while outcome-based contracts pay for results the business actually wants. A consultant quoted in that article notes that clients generally want business results rather than infrastructure. The article also reports that time-and-materials contracts remain the most common model, followed by fixed price, and that outcome-based contracts make up at most about 15 percent of new deals and may cover only part of the work.

The same source lists several challenges. Agreeing on the outcome can be difficult when the CEO, CFO and CIO want different things. The vendor has limited control over factors such as marketing and economic conditions that influence results. Metrics such as customer satisfaction can be gamed, and results may be uneven. Forrester's listed advantages include more cohesive delivery, less monitoring of individual staff, stronger incentives to innovate and potential long-term savings. The drawbacks it names are less transparency into how work is done, limited cost visibility and extra effort for root-cause analysis. Both sides can resist the model: clients give up day-to-day control and need trust, while vendors absorb more risk the higher the outcome sits on the value chain.

In the M365.FM episode "5 High-Margin Microsoft 365 Business Models", the shift from hourly billing to outcome-based pricing is presented as part of a broader change in how Microsoft 365 services are sold. The episode says that as complexity in the Microsoft ecosystem increases, organizations struggle with governance, which creates demand for specialists who design and operate control systems rather than deliver one-time projects. In that framing, value is tied to measurable business impact such as risk reduction, automation and efficiency gains, and the episode links this to recurring revenue streams rather than traditional consulting engagements.

The episode "Computer-Using Agents: How CUA Could Transform SaaS" approaches the topic from the software side. It says organizations redefine value in contracts and shift to outcome-based pricing as agent-driven systems become more common. According to the episode, pricing models evolve and require clear definitions of what counts as an agent and what counts as an outcome. It also states that advanced instrumentation and real-time data observability become essential for compliance, and that SaaS companies need to adapt to avoid obsolescence.

Taken together, the sources point to the same practical decisions. A provider and client need a shared, measurable definition of the outcome before any price is set. Both need a way to observe results, which is why instrumentation and observability come up in the episode on computer-using agents. They also need to decide how risk is split, how the build work is charged, and whether ongoing value is billed as a retainer or a licence. The CIO article adds that the model may cover only part of a contract and is not yet the dominant form of engagement, so it is often used alongside other pricing methods rather than as a full replacement.

outlook.desc: Microsoft Outlook is the email, calendar, contacts and tasks client of Microsoft 365, connecting to Exchange Online and other mail accounts.

faq.a: Microsoft Outlook is the Microsoft 365 client for email, calendar, contacts and tasks. It connects to Exchange Online and other mail accounts and is used to organize communication and schedules.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Outlook used for?

faq.a: Exchange Online hosts the mailboxes that Outlook connects to, while Outlook on the web is the browser version of the same environment. Together they give access to the same mail and calendar data from different clients.
faq.q: How does Outlook relate to Exchange Online and Outlook on the web?

faq.a: "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" describes an internal newsletter pipeline using Dynamic Distribution Groups, a shared mailbox and a reusable template. "Use Microsoft Loop Components Across Teams and Outlook" covers Loop components that update in several places at once, and "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]" covers Copilot across Microsoft 365 apps including Outlook.
faq.q: What do the M365.FM episodes say about Outlook?

outlook.long:
Microsoft Outlook is the email, calendar, contacts and tasks client of Microsoft 365. It connects to Exchange Online as well as to other mail accounts and is used to organize communication and schedules in one place. The catalog lists its release as 1997-01-16 and describes it as included with Microsoft 365 licensing. The product is also referred to as Outlook, as the new Outlook, or as Outlook for Windows.

Outlook is developed by Microsoft and is classed as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. It is part of Microsoft 365 Apps. Its closest technical relationship is with Exchange Online, which hosts the mailboxes that the client reads and writes. Outlook on the web is the browser-based counterpart, so the same mailbox and calendar can be reached either through the desktop client or through a web browser.

In day-to-day use, Outlook covers four connected areas: email for sending and receiving messages, a calendar for appointments and meetings, contacts for people and addresses, and tasks for to-do items. Because it can connect to accounts beyond Exchange Online, it can serve as a single client for several mailboxes. Its calendar is tightly connected to Microsoft Teams, which matters for scheduling and joining meetings. Microsoft 365 Copilot is also related to Outlook, since it can assist with drafting and summarizing within the mail environment.

The M365.FM episodes show how Outlook fits into wider Microsoft 365 workflows. The episode "Build Internal Outlook Newsletters with Dynamic Groups" argues that many internal updates get lost in Teams noise and that the fix is wiring together tools an organization already owns rather than adopting a new platform. It describes a repeatable newsletter pipeline: targeting audiences with Dynamic Distribution Groups that rely on Entra ID attributes, sending from a shared mailbox for branding and continuity, composing with a reusable Outlook template, and then scaling the same pattern to other departments. According to the episode, the aim is that updates are no longer buried, audiences only see what matters to them, and leaders can measure engagement without extra licenses.

The episode "Use Microsoft Loop Components Across Teams and Outlook" looks at Loop components as living, embeddable data that updates everywhere at once. It contrasts this with copy-paste and scheduled syncs between systems such as CRM, Power BI and Teams, and describes how a single canonical object can appear in several places, including Outlook, without the numbers drifting apart. The episode also points to gotchas to watch when adopting this approach.

Copilot in Outlook is addressed in "Beyond the Prompt: Mastering Microsoft Copilot for Real Productivity with Jess Stratton [MVP]". The episode notes describe Microsoft Copilot as working inside Microsoft 365 apps and connecting Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams into one system. Guest Jess Stratton recommends multi-part prompts that divide larger projects into small steps, and follow-up prompts to adjust writing style, correct errors and add missing context to AI drafts.

Outlook also appears as an integration point in other episodes. "Microsoft Places - Simply Explained" notes that Microsoft Places features are embedded in Teams and Outlook so they can be used in the flow of work, such as for desk booking in hybrid work. "Dynamics 365 Customer Service - Simply Explained" lists Outlook among the products the service platform integrates with, alongside Teams, Microsoft 365, Power Platform, Copilot and Azure, so that support agents have the information they need to resolve issues.

For decisions around Outlook, the relevant questions are usually which mailbox platform it connects to, whether the new Outlook or another variant is deployed, how groups and shared mailboxes are structured for communication, and how adjacent services such as Teams and Copilot are combined with it.

outlook-web.desc: Outlook on the web (OWA) is the browser version of Outlook for mail, calendar and contacts, hosted by Exchange Online and developed by Microsoft.

faq.a: Outlook on the web is the browser version of Outlook for mail, calendar and contacts. It is hosted by Exchange Online and is also known as Outlook Web App or OWA.
faq.q: What is Outlook on the web?

faq.a: No. It is used through a browser from any computer with an internet connection, so no desktop application has to be installed.
faq.q: Does Outlook on the web require installing software?

faq.a: Exchange Online provides the mailbox service behind both. Mailbox data stays there, so the same mail and calendar appear in the browser and in the installed Microsoft Outlook client.
faq.q: How does Outlook on the web relate to Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online?

outlook-web.long:
Outlook on the web is the browser version of Outlook. It provides mail, calendar and contacts without installing a desktop application and is hosted by Exchange Online. It is also known as Outlook Web App or OWA, and it is reached through a browser from any computer with an internet connection. According to the catalog data, it is included with the relevant Microsoft 365 licensing, so no separate purchase is described for it.

The product is developed by Microsoft and is part of Office on the web, the set of browser versions of Office applications. It is classed as a Microsoft tool and as a collaboration tool. It is closely related to Microsoft Outlook, the full client, and to Exchange Online, which provides the mailbox service behind both. Because mailbox data stays in Exchange Online, the same mail and calendar content appears in the browser and in the installed client.

According to Microsoft Support, Outlook on the web is a browser-based way to keep email, calendar and contacts close at hand and to work together with other people. Messages can be sent and files shared, and the page mentions suggested replies and a like button as ways to save time. A focused inbox prioritizes important messages. A search function covers mail, appointments and contacts, which helps when looking for a specific message or person.

The calendar is another central part. A meeting can be started by clicking a time slot, with further settings available under more options. Smart time suggestions point to slots when all attendees are free. An appointment can be turned into a Teams meeting, and suggested locations are offered. A Microsoft 365 account can also be connected to LinkedIn to exchange messages and files with contacts. Typical uses named in the documentation are collaboration through email and file sharing, scheduling, and organizing meetings. The Microsoft page is an overview without step-by-step instructions and names no licenses, system requirements, plans or limitations.

In practice, typical scenarios include accessing mail from a shared or unmanaged device, using email on a computer where Office is not installed, and administering shared mailboxes or calendar settings from a browser. For administrators, it can also be a quick way to check how a user's mailbox looks without the influence of a local client profile, since the view comes directly from the service rather than from a locally configured application.

The decision between the browser version and the installed Microsoft Outlook usually depends on the device and the working situation. The browser version needs no installation and works wherever a browser is available, while the full client is the related desktop option for the same Exchange Online mailbox. No M365.FM episode is currently linked to Outlook on the web in the catalog, so there are no episode statements to summarize here. Related topics for further reading are Microsoft Outlook, Exchange Online and Office on the web.

parameter-sniffing.desc: Parameter sniffing is SQL Server-style query-plan behavior: a plan is compiled for the parameter values seen at compile time, then reused for later executions.

faq.a: It is the behavior of SQL Server-style engines that compile a query plan for the parameter values seen at compile time and reuse the cached plan. This can perform poorly when later parameter values differ greatly. It is also called parameter sensitivity.
faq.q: What is parameter sniffing?

faq.a: According to Microsoft's query processing guide, the hint makes the optimizer treat parameters and local variables as compile-time constants that can be folded into literals, which can help with highly variable or skewed data. The query is recompiled on every execution, which can be expensive, so the effect on the whole workload should be measured first.
faq.q: How can OPTION (RECOMPILE) affect parameter sniffing problems?

faq.a: No. The documentation states that values of local variables are not sniffed at compile time. The optimizer instead estimates from density information or, without statistics, uses fixed percentage guesses for equality and range comparisons.
faq.q: Are local variables sniffed in the same way as parameters?

parameter-sniffing.long:
Parameter sniffing is a behavior of SQL Server-style database engines in which a query plan is compiled for the parameter values seen at compile time and the cached plan is then reused. It is also called parameter sensitivity. The behavior is not a defect in itself: the engine inspects the current parameter values while compiling or recompiling a query and passes them to the query optimizer, which can then produce a more efficient execution plan for those values. The difficulty appears when the cached plan is later used for parameter values that look very different from the original ones, because a plan that suits one value can perform poorly for another.

Microsoft's query processing architecture guide for SQL Server describes parameter sniffing in a section on parameter sensitivity. According to that guide, the process applies to stored procedures, queries run through sp_executesql, and prepared queries. It interacts directly with plan reuse, because compiled plans are stored in the plan cache and can be picked up again by later executions. The first set of values that triggers a compilation therefore shapes the plan that subsequent calls receive, which is why results can vary depending on which call happened to compile the plan.

The guide names one remedy: the OPTION (RECOMPILE) query hint. With this hint, the optimizer treats parameters and local variables as compile-time constants, which can be folded into literals. The values used are those in effect right before the statement runs, which are not necessarily the values originally passed in. This can help when input data is highly variable or skewed. The guide also warns that the hint recompiles the query on every execution, which can be expensive, and advises measuring the effect on the whole workload before adopting it. The guide also points to a separate article on the Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization for further reading.

A related detail from the same documentation concerns local variables. Their values are not sniffed at compile time. Instead, the optimizer estimates from density information, or, when no statistics are available, uses fixed percentage guesses for equality and range comparisons. This distinction matters when diagnosing a slow query, since a parameter and a local variable can lead to different estimates and therefore different plans.

In practice, parameter sniffing shows up as queries that run fast for some inputs and slowly for others, or as performance that changes after a plan is evicted and recompiled. The M365.FM episode "Fix Bad Data Upstream with T-SQL Contracts" lists parameter sniffing among common enterprise failures, describing it as something that can masquerade as randomness. The episode also frames plan shapes as a governance matter, saying that if plan shapes change, spend and reliability change with them, so that plan behavior translates into cost stability and operational risk.

The episode "Design Reliable and Resilient Azure Architectures" places parameter sniffing in a troubleshooting workflow for Azure SQL Database. It suggests enabling Intelligent Insights and Query Performance Insight, capturing long-running queries, reviewing execution plans, and identifying missing indexes or parameter sniffing. It further mentions Azure SQL's automatic tuning recommendations and index suggestions via Azure Advisor, along with query optimization, appropriate indexing, and considering scaling DTUs or vCores or moving to Hyperscale.

Taken together, the sources treat parameter sniffing as a plan-caching trade-off: reusing a compiled plan saves compilation work, while a plan tuned to one parameter value may not suit others. Typical decisions around it involve examining execution plans, checking whether data distribution is skewed, and weighing the compile cost of options such as OPTION (RECOMPILE) against the benefit of more suitable plans.

pass-the-hash.desc: Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique that reuses a captured NTLM password hash to authenticate to other systems without the clear-text password.

faq.a: Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique in which a captured NTLM password hash is reused to authenticate to other systems without knowing the clear-text password.
faq.q: What is pass-the-hash?

faq.a: The episodes mention blocking credential theft from LSASS, using privileged access workstations for privileged tasks, tiering and least privilege, and detecting the technique with Defender for Identity alerts combined with blocking, password reset and device isolation.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes suggest defending against pass-the-hash?

faq.a: According to the episode "Harden Azure AD Connect Against Hybrid Identity Breaches", it follows an initial phished user as lateral movement, before privilege escalation such as DCSync or a Golden Ticket leads to domain-wide control.
faq.q: Where does pass-the-hash fit in an attack chain?

pass-the-hash.long:
Pass-the-hash is a lateral movement technique in which an attacker takes a captured NTLM password hash and reuses it to authenticate to other systems, without ever learning the clear-text password. Because the hash itself acts as the credential, an attacker who obtains it from one machine can try it against further machines and services. This makes the technique a common step once an initial foothold has been gained inside a Windows or hybrid environment.
