faq.a: The episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" describes the DevOps Tax as the hidden productivity cost of developers spending most of their time on infrastructure problems. It presents platform engineering, Golden Paths, Infrastructure as Code and Policy as Code as a practical way forward.
faq.q: How does platform engineering relate to the DevOps Tax?

platform-engineering.long:
Platform engineering is a software engineering discipline focused on building standardized, self-service toolchains, services and processes that development teams can use without depending on a central team. The result is often delivered as an internal developer platform. Instead of every team managing its own infrastructure, a shared internal platform offers secure access to the things teams need to build and run software.

The core idea described across the M365.FM episodes is a shift in operating model. Cloud infrastructure is no longer treated as a collection of individual projects. A platform team provides a common foundation that gives development teams self-service access to standardized infrastructure, deployment pipelines, monitoring and governance. Developers consume these capabilities on demand, while the organization keeps control over security and compliance through the platform itself.

The episode "Platform Engineering: The New Operating Model for Azure" describes how this applies to Azure environments. It names several building blocks: Infrastructure as Code, reusable templates, platform APIs and self-service provisioning. It also stresses developer experience and the importance of treating the platform itself as a product that continuously evolves to meet customer needs. In this framing, the internal teams that use the platform are its customers, and the platform team is responsible for keeping it useful and current. The episode "Platform Engineering - Simply Explained", from Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets, covers the same ground at an introductory level and describes how platform engineering changes the way organizations build and operate cloud environments.

Platform engineering is also presented as a response to a problem in the DevOps model. The episode "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" defines the DevOps Tax not as a licensing cost or a cloud bill, but as the hidden productivity cost created when developers spend most of their time solving infrastructure problems instead of building products. According to the episode, many teams ended up spending more time managing infrastructure than delivering customer value, and the DevOps model struggles at enterprise scale. As a practical path forward, the episode points to Platform Engineering together with Golden Paths, Infrastructure as Code, Policy as Code and AI-ready governance.

Governance is a recurring theme. In the conversation with Microsoft MVP Jev Suchoi, titled "Azure Platform Engineering, Azure Landing Zones, Cloud Adoption Framework & Building Enterprise Cloud Platforms", the starting point is that moving workloads into Microsoft Azure is only the beginning of a cloud journey. Building a platform that is secure, scalable, automated and developer-friendly is described as requiring a different mindset. The episode connects platform engineering with Azure Landing Zones and the Cloud Adoption Framework, and says proactive governance replaces traditional reactive operations through policy enforcement, remediation, monitoring and standardized deployment practices. It also covers building self-service capabilities and reducing operational risk.

The discipline is also applied to AI workloads. The episode "Azure Copilot Agents: Building a Synthetic Platform Team" proposes treating AI agents not as isolated applications but through a platform engineering approach, where reusable infrastructure, governance, observability and automation become the foundation for every agent. Platform teams can standardize identity, security, model access, prompt management, deployment pipelines, monitoring and cost optimization, while development teams keep the freedom to build their own AI solutions.

Taken together, the episodes describe platform engineering as a way to balance two needs: giving development teams autonomy through self-service, and giving the organization consistency through standardized, governed building blocks. Typical decisions around it include what the platform should offer, how to encode policies and templates as code, and how to treat the platform as a product with its own users and roadmap.

pnp-powershell.desc: PnP PowerShell is a free, community-maintained PowerShell module for managing SharePoint, Teams and Microsoft 365 through Microsoft Graph and CSOM.

faq.a: PnP PowerShell is an open-source, community-maintained PowerShell module for managing SharePoint, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 through Microsoft Graph and CSOM. It is free and counts as a developer tool rather than a Microsoft product.
faq.q: What is PnP PowerShell?

faq.a: According to the episode "PnP PowerShell vs PnP Framework", PnP PowerShell suits surgical fixes and speed, while PnP Framework provisioning is better for repeatable, audited, at-scale site builds.
faq.q: When should PnP PowerShell be used instead of PnP Framework?

faq.a: The episode "Automate SharePoint Sites with Site Scripts and PnP Templates" says Site Scripts handle predictable structure, while PnP PowerShell covers advanced needs such as unique permissions and custom web parts that Microsoft does not support natively.
faq.q: How does PnP PowerShell relate to Site Scripts?

pnp-powershell.long:
PnP PowerShell, also written PnP.PowerShell and sometimes spelled out as Patterns and Practices PowerShell, is an open-source PowerShell module maintained by the community. It is used to manage SharePoint, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 through Microsoft Graph and CSOM, the client-side object model. The module is free to use and is classified as a developer tool. It is not a Microsoft product in itself, although it works against Microsoft services.

The module is mainly used to automate administration work that would be slow or error-prone in a browser. Typical areas are site creation, user permissions, document libraries, content migration and configuration changes that have to be applied to many sites. Because it exposes these actions as PowerShell commands, administrators can run them in scripts, schedule them and keep them under source control. An episode on Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility describes it as a tool that suits both IT administrators and developers, and says that simple scripts are enough to get results without writing complex code.

Technically, PnP PowerShell sits on top of two interfaces: Microsoft Graph and CSOM. This ties it closely to SharePoint, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Graph, the topics it is most often related to. It is also commonly combined with SharePoint Advanced Management when administrators script governance and cleanup tasks across a tenant. The official documentation for the module is published by the PnP community on its documentation site.

A recurring decision is whether PowerShell is the right tool for the job at all. The episode "PnP PowerShell vs PnP Framework" frames the choice this way: PnP PowerShell is suited to surgical fixes and speed, while PnP Framework provisioning fits repeatable, audited, at-scale site builds. The episode also covers versioning tips and a migration plan so that templates apply correctly the first time and on later runs. The distinction matters for teams that start with ad hoc scripts and later need consistent, auditable provisioning.

The episode "Automate SharePoint Sites with Site Scripts and PnP Templates" places PnP PowerShell alongside native automation. According to the episode, Site Scripts handle predictable site structure, while PnP PowerShell fills the gaps when needs go deeper, for example unique permissions, custom web part deployment, or scenarios Microsoft does not support natively. Used together, the two cover both the standard layout and the advanced configuration that keeps sites secure and usable at scale. The episode also warns about real-world pitfalls of automation such as version drift and silent failures, and stresses source control, sandbox testing and logging.

Auditing is another use case. In "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale", PnP PowerShell is combined with Microsoft Graph and Azure Automation to enumerate every site, expand nested, group and inherited permissions, and produce a daily report. The episode points to app-only authentication, throttling-safe queries and diff alerts as the elements that turn a manual review into an automated pipeline.

Module installation and versioning also come up in practice. The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" notes that warnings about module versions being in use can appear when installing modules. It suggests checking the module path in the PSModulePath environment variable to find where a conflicting module is installed, uninstalling all versions of PnP.PowerShell with Uninstall-Module and the AllVersions and Force options, and then reinstalling the desired version with Install-Module. This is a typical maintenance step when several versions of the module exist on one machine.

In short, PnP PowerShell is a free scripting layer over SharePoint, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 that covers administration, provisioning support, migration and permission auditing. The M365.FM episodes treat it as one tool in a wider automation toolbox, to be chosen deliberately next to Site Scripts, PnP Framework and Microsoft Graph depending on scale, repeatability and audit needs.

pnpjs.desc: PnPjs is an open-source community JavaScript library that wraps the SharePoint and Microsoft Graph REST APIs, handling requests and authentication to reduce boilerplate.

faq.a: PnPjs is used to call the SharePoint and Microsoft Graph REST APIs from JavaScript or TypeScript with less boilerplate. It builds requests with a fluent, type-safe syntax and handles request and authentication details.
faq.q: What is PnPjs used for?

faq.a: According to the project documentation, it runs inside SharePoint Framework solutions, in Node.js, and in ordinary JavaScript or browser projects. Authentication is documented separately for SPFx, browser and Node.js.
faq.q: Where can PnPjs run?

faq.a: It is split into packages under the @pnp scope, such as sp for SharePoint REST, graph for Microsoft Graph and sp-admin for tenant admin methods. Supporting packages include core, queryable, logging, nodejs, msaljsclient and azidjsclient.
faq.q: How is PnPjs organized?

pnpjs.long:
PnPjs is an open-source set of client-side JavaScript libraries from the Microsoft 365 and Power Platform Community (PnP). The project describes it as a collection of fluent libraries for consuming SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and Office 365 REST APIs in a type-safe way. Its purpose is to let developers work with these services without hand-writing repetitive request code, since the library takes care of building requests and handling authentication.

Calls in PnPjs are composed with a chainable, fluent syntax. Because the library ships with typings, editors can offer IntelliSense help while a query is being written, which makes it easier to discover available methods and properties. The library can run inside SharePoint Framework (SPFx) solutions, in Node.js, and in ordinary JavaScript or browser projects, so the same approach applies across several kinds of Microsoft 365 development.

The code is divided into packages published under the @pnp scope, and these packages depend on each other. The sp package covers SharePoint REST, graph covers Microsoft Graph, and sp-admin provides tenant administration methods. Supporting packages include core, queryable, logging and nodejs, along with client wrappers for MSAL (msaljsclient) and Azure Identity (azidjsclient). Developers can pick the packages they need rather than loading everything.

The documentation addresses topics that come up in real projects. Authentication is explained separately for SPFx, browser and Node.js scenarios. Further sections cover batching and caching, async paging, error handling, and selective imports that help keep bundles smaller. Behaviors can be used to customize how requests are processed. A transition guide supports users who are moving from version 2. Bugs and ideas are managed as GitHub issues, under the Microsoft Open Source Code of Conduct.

Typical decisions around PnPjs involve whether to use a library abstraction or write raw REST or Graph calls directly, and which packages to import for a given solution. In SPFx work, it is commonly one part of a wider stack. The M365.FM episode "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" describes a modern SPFx project as bringing together TypeScript, React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls rather than relying on a single framework. In that episode's breakdown, PnPjs simplifies interaction with SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and other Microsoft 365 services by replacing repetitive REST request code with reusable abstractions, while TypeScript adds stronger typing and compile-time checks and Fluent UI helps custom solutions keep the familiar Microsoft user experience.

PnPjs also appears in the episode "Building Modern Microsoft 365 Solutions with SharePoint Framework, Microsoft Graph, PnPjs & Great User Experiences with Julie Turner [MVP]". The episode frames modern Microsoft 365 development as more than writing code: organizations expect solutions that integrate across SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Graph, Azure and Microsoft 365 while staying scalable, secure and maintainable. In that context, PnPjs is one of the tools discussed alongside SharePoint Framework and Microsoft Graph for building such solutions.

policy-as-code.desc: Policy as code expresses governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code that is evaluated automatically to allow or block changes during deployment.

faq.a: Policy as code is the practice of expressing governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code that is evaluated automatically, for example during deployment, to allow or block changes.
faq.q: What is policy as code?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes name Azure Policy, which the episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" recommends for enforcing compliance across cloud resources at the right scope. Third-party tools are also mentioned as options.
faq.q: Which Microsoft tool is mentioned for policy as code?

faq.a: The episodes list Policy as Code alongside Infrastructure as Code, Golden Paths and platform engineering as ways to enforce governance consistently, so that standards are applied by the pipeline or platform rather than by manual review.
faq.q: How does policy as code relate to Infrastructure as Code and platform engineering?

policy-as-code.long:
Policy as code is the practice of writing governance, security and compliance rules as versioned code instead of keeping them in documents or relying on manual review. Because the rules are code, they can be stored in source control, reviewed, tested and evaluated automatically, for example during deployment, where the result decides whether a change is allowed or blocked.

The main purpose is consistency. When policies are embedded directly into the software delivery process, every deployment is held to the same standard regardless of who triggers it or which environment it targets. The episode "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" describes this approach: policies, security controls and quality gates belong inside the delivery pipeline rather than being added as an afterthought, so that every deployment follows the same trusted standards automatically. The episode lists Policy as Code alongside Infrastructure as Code, automated testing, security scanning, compliance validation, approval workflows and continuous monitoring, and contrasts this with manual reviews, noting that successful organizations build pipelines that enforce governance consistently across every environment.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Azure Policy is the tool most often named in connection with the practice. The episode "Compliance as Code: The Architect's Blueprint for Automated Trust" recommends using Azure Policy to enforce compliance across cloud resources and applying governance policies at the right scope through an inheritance system. It also mentions policy enforcement points that apply governance rules automatically, and presents policy as code as a way to enhance automation and consistency. The same episode pairs this with continuous monitoring, which gives ongoing visibility into compliance status and helps identify gaps quickly.

Policy as code also appears in infrastructure and security discussions. In "Azure Infrastructure as Code and DevOps with Maik van der Gaag [MVP]", it is mentioned as part of secure coding and access control practices. The episode suggests scanning code for vulnerabilities with Static Application Security Testing (SAST) to find problems early, and using Policy as Code to enforce rules and compliance, with Azure Policy and third-party tools named as options. It also recommends least-privilege access, giving users and services only the permissions they need, which reduces the risk of accidental changes or security breaches.

The concept extends beyond infrastructure to data and AI governance. In "How Probabilistic AI Changes Power Platform Design", policy as code is listed among practices for reliable AI outcomes that depend on data quality and governance. The episode suggests adopting it to manage access and retention, alongside active metadata and lineage, machine-learning-based classification of sensitive data, risk-based controls, human approvals and automated evidence collection for audits and compliance.

At the organizational level, "The DevOps Tax: Why Your Platform is Failing" places Policy as Code among the building blocks of Platform Engineering, together with Golden Paths, Infrastructure as Code and AI-ready governance. The episode frames the DevOps Tax as the hidden productivity cost created when developers spend most of their time solving infrastructure problems instead of building products. In that framing, encoding policy into the platform is one way to reduce the burden on individual teams, because standards are enforced by the platform rather than rediscovered by each developer.

Typical decisions around policy as code include where to evaluate rules (for example at deployment time in a pipeline), at which scope to apply them, which tools to use, and how to combine automated enforcement with human approval where judgment is needed. Standardized deployment templates, mentioned in the "Scaling CI-CD: The Governance Blueprint" episode together with platform engineering, are one way to help development teams move quickly while staying inside the same guardrails.

policy-tip.desc: A policy tip is a short notice in Outlook, Teams or other apps telling users that a data loss prevention rule applies to the content they are working with.

faq.a: A policy tip is a notice shown by a data loss prevention policy to tell users that the content they work with conflicts with a DLP rule. In Outlook it is shown to the sender while composing a message.
faq.q: What is a policy tip in Microsoft Purview DLP?

faq.a: According to the Microsoft Purview reference, they are not available in SharePoint and OneDrive desktop clients, mobile Office apps, third-party cloud apps or on-premises content. Teams files get no tips either.
faq.q: Where do policy tips not work?

faq.a: In Teams, a flagged message shows a prompt where users can review the detected sensitive information types and, if the admin allows it, override or report a mistake. Whether this is possible depends on how the administrator configured the policy.
faq.q: Can users override a policy tip?

policy-tip.long:
A policy tip is a short notice that a data loss prevention (DLP) policy shows to a user when the content they are working with conflicts with a DLP rule. In Outlook, for example, the sender sees the notice while composing a message and learns that a rule or policy applies to it. Policy tips are part of Microsoft Purview data loss prevention and are documented in the Microsoft Purview policy tips reference.

The main purpose of a policy tip is to make a compliance rule visible at the moment it matters. Instead of silently blocking an action or reporting it afterwards, the policy tip tells the user what has been detected, so that they can change what they are doing. The reference describes supported conditions that can trigger such a notice, including content shared from Microsoft 365, sensitive information types, sensitivity labels, keywords in the subject or body, and sender or recipient conditions.

How a policy tip looks depends on the application. According to the reference, Outlook offers default and customized oversharing dialogs, a wait-on-send dialog and a custom compliance link that can point users to further education, with availability depending on the client. In Teams, a flagged message triggers a prompt where users can review the detected sensitive information types and, if the administrator allows it, override the block or report a mistake. This means the tip can work both as information and as a point where the user may respond.

Support for policy tips varies widely between locations, and this affects how a DLP rollout is planned. The reference lists policy tips as working in SharePoint and OneDrive on the web, in Office apps on the web for documents already stamped by a policy, in Teams messages, on endpoint devices, and in Fabric and Power BI. They are not available in SharePoint and OneDrive desktop clients, in mobile Office apps, in third-party cloud apps or for on-premises content. Teams files get no tips, and Windows Office apps show them only for a limited set of conditions and actions. Administrators who rely on policy tips for user guidance should therefore check which client and workload their users actually work in.

The M365.FM episode "Configure Microsoft 365 DLP Policies in Purview" treats policy tips as an educational element of DLP. The episode advises adding helpful advice to the alert, reminding users about compliance rules and safe data handling, and using policy tips often. It describes DLP as a teaching tool and not just a way to block actions: when users see a policy tip, they understand the risk and can change their behavior, which the episode says builds a culture of security and responsibility.

The same episode places policy tips next to admin notifications. While the policy tip informs the person who triggers the rule, email notifications keep administrators informed about DLP incidents so that they can respond quickly to possible data leaks. Used together, the two give the user immediate guidance and give administrators visibility into what happened.

post-quantum-cryptography.desc: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) covers algorithms built to resist quantum-computer attacks, including NIST-standardized ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

faq.a: PQC is a set of cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers. Examples standardized by NIST include the lattice-based ML-KEM and ML-DSA and the hash-based SLH-DSA.
faq.q: What is post-quantum cryptography (PQC)?

faq.a: It is the risk that long-lived sensitive data is captured today and decrypted later, once quantum computers capable of breaking current public-key algorithms exist. It is a named driver for starting PQC planning early.
faq.q: What is the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk?

faq.a: Cryptographic agility is the ability to change algorithms quickly and safely. Microsoft Learn recommends it as the foundation, together with a cryptographic inventory, governance and review of vendor timelines, because migration is a multi-year program.
faq.q: Why is cryptographic agility important for PQC readiness?

post-quantum-cryptography.long:
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers. Among the algorithms standardized by NIST are the lattice-based ML-KEM and ML-DSA and the hash-based SLH-DSA. The concept is framed as preparation for the possibility that future quantum computers could break some of the public-key algorithms that security controls rely on today.

A central reason for acting early is the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk. In this scenario, long-lived sensitive data is captured now and decrypted once a sufficiently capable quantum computer exists. Data that must stay confidential for many years is therefore exposed earlier than the date on which quantum attacks become practical. Cryptography underpins authentication, digital signatures, software integrity and secure communication such as TLS, so the affected scope is broad. It spans applications, identity systems, VPN and network equipment, storage, IoT and operational technology, and partner integrations.

The guidance in Microsoft Learn, "Plan cryptographic agility and post-quantum readiness", treats cryptographic agility as the foundation. Cryptographic agility means being able to change algorithms quickly and safely, without rebuilding every system that depends on them. Alongside agility, the page recommends an inventory of cryptographic use and trust chains, clear governance, and a review of vendor timelines. These steps make it possible to know where vulnerable algorithms are in use and which suppliers can support new ones.

The suggested approach runs in several stages: discovering where vulnerable algorithms are used, evaluating vendor support, planning phased migration waves with rollback options, and implementing changes with testing and evidence tracking. High-value assets, identity systems and long-lived data are prioritized. Migration is described as a multi-year program rather than a single project, and some systems will need new libraries, certificates or firmware, or even replacement hardware.

The M365.FM episode "Cryptographic Agility for Post-Quantum Security" (2026-06-12) looks at how cryptographic agility can be used to defend against quantum risks. According to the episode, the platform follows a phased approach to upgrading its security. The first phase integrates PQC algorithms into foundational components such as SymCrypt, so that cryptographic security stays consistent across platforms. The second phase updates core infrastructure services, such as authentication and key management, to provide quantum safety, with the most sensitive components prioritized. The third phase extends PQC to all Microsoft services and endpoints.

In practice, decisions around PQC concern sequencing and readiness rather than a single switch. Organizations weigh which assets hold long-lived data, which identity systems anchor trust, and which vendors have published support timelines. Because some algorithms may need replacing in systems that were not designed for change, the emphasis on agility, inventory and governance is meant to reduce the effort and risk of each later migration wave.

power-apps-for-figma.desc: Power Apps for Figma is a Figma plugin by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka that moves designs, components and design systems to and from Power Apps canvas apps.

faq.a: It is a Figma plugin created by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka and published by Power Plugins. It moves designs, components and design systems between Figma and Power Apps canvas apps.
faq.q: What is Power Apps for Figma?

faq.a: Layers carry supported name prefixes, and the plugin turns them into YAML code shown in a Code view. The YAML is copied to the clipboard and pasted into the Power Apps builder, as described in the M365.FM episode with Lukas Pavelka.
faq.q: How does a design get from Figma into Power Apps?

faq.a: It comes in a free version and a pro version. The help article mentions extra settings and a Get PRO button for free users, but its own tab counts are inconsistent, so feature details should be confirmed in the plugin.
faq.q: Is Power Apps for Figma free?

power-apps-for-figma.long:
Power Apps for Figma is a Figma plugin that connects design work in Figma with app building in Power Apps. It was created by Microsoft MVP Lukas Pavelka and is published by Power Plugins. The plugin moves designs, components and design systems between Figma and Power Apps canvas apps, and it is available in a free version and a pro version. It is treated as part of the wider Power Apps ecosystem.

The core purpose, according to the plugin's help article, is to prepare Figma designs so they can be exported to Power Apps. Controls and screens in a Figma file carry name prefixes that the plugin recognizes as supported Power Apps control types. The plugin reads these prefixed layers and turns them into YAML code that can be pasted into the Power Apps builder. It also works in the other direction: an import function brings YAML and Base64 images into Figma, so existing app visuals can be brought back into a design file.

The interface is organized into tabs. The Editor tab manages designs before export. It offers a Layout view that lists the selected screens and controls with supported prefixes, and a Code view that shows the generated YAML. A theme and style tool works from design tokens or saved styles. A bottom action bar provides several functions: Compile, which adds prefixes automatically; a dependency model showing screen navigation; PDF export; YAML export, delivered as a ZIP when several screens are selected; resizing for mobile or tablet; translation; and a bulk manager for renaming layers. A Generate tab, described in the documentation as alpha, is an AI chat that creates modern Power Apps controls from prompts, with custom controls planned. Further tabs cover settings, help with the supported prefixes, and a history that compares versions.

The documentation separates a free version from a PRO version. Free users see extra settings and a Get PRO button, although the article's own count of tabs is inconsistent, so the exact split of features between the two versions should be checked in the plugin itself.

Typical situations involve a designer or maker who wants an app's look to be defined in Figma first and then carried into a canvas app, instead of rebuilding each screen by hand in the Power Apps builder. Decisions around the plugin include whether to start from a UI kit in Figma, how to name layers so the prefixes are recognized, whether to rely on the Compile function to add prefixes automatically, and whether the pro features are needed.

The M365.FM episode "Figma to Power Apps Development with Lukas Pavelka [MVP]" covers the workflow in practice. According to its show notes, the plugin has to be installed before starting. To edit a control, the user selects it in Figma with the right prefix, opens the AI chat in Figma, describes the edit as a prompt, opens Power Apps for Figma in the YAML Code Viewer, presses the copy-to-clipboard button and pastes the code into the Power Apps builder. The episode adds a tip that repeating these steps refreshes a design, so app visuals can be updated quickly. It also describes importing a Figma design into Power Apps after installing the plugin, starting with choosing a UI kit in Figma that fits the project.

power-apps-maker-portal.desc: The Power Apps maker portal is the browser-based, point-and-click environment in Power Apps where makers build apps, flows and solutions, and prototype quickly.

faq.a: It is the browser-based, point-and-click environment where makers build apps, flows and solutions. The episodes also describe it as the place to manage solution components, create and edit Dataverse tables, and add connections.
faq.q: What is the Power Apps maker portal used for?

faq.a: It is well suited to prototyping but offers limited control over moving work between environments. For deployments, the episodes point to solutions, environment variables, solution layering and ALM pipelines.
faq.q: Is the Power Apps maker portal suitable for moving work between environments?

faq.a: According to the episode "Design Scalable Dataverse Data Models", the maker portal is used to create and edit tables, columns, relationships, views and forms. Advanced tasks can be handled with tools such as the Dataverse Web API and Power Query.
faq.q: How is the maker portal used with Dataverse?

power-apps-maker-portal.long:
The Power Apps maker portal is the browser-based part of Power Apps in which makers build apps, flows and solutions through a point-and-click experience. It is part of Power Apps and acts as the main workspace where low-code work is created, edited and organized. Because it runs in the browser and relies on visual tools rather than code, it is well suited to prototyping, where an idea needs to be turned into a working app or flow quickly. At the same time, it offers only limited control over moving work between environments, which is why teams that go beyond prototypes usually look at additional deployment approaches.

In practice, the maker portal is used to view and manage the components that make up a solution. The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" describes solutions that contain items such as Power Automate cloud flows, connection references, APIs, plug-ins and workflows, as well as user interface components like web resources (HTML, JavaScript and images) and metadata for custom ribbon buttons. According to that episode, the Power Apps maker portal can be used to view and manage these components, and proper organization of them supports solution deployment and reduces errors during automation. The same episode stresses consistent naming and versioning across development, testing and production, which helps avoid problems such as case-sensitivity issues.

The maker portal also plays a central role in data modeling. In "Design Scalable Dataverse Data Models", the portal is named as the place to create and edit tables, columns, relationships, views and forms in Dataverse. The episode contrasts it with more advanced tools such as the Dataverse Web API for programmatic tasks and Power Query for data import and transformation, and it points to solutions as the way to package model changes. For validating a model, the episode suggests testing with model-driven apps and canvas apps, reporting with Power BI, and using test data to confirm that related data and business rules behave as expected. It also recommends solution layering and environment variables to manage deployments across environments so that data stays consistent across multiple applications.

Connections are another area where the maker portal appears. In "Replace Legacy RPA with Copilot Studio Computer Use", the portal is the place to create a new connection if the expected Copilot Studio connection is missing. The episode explains that a connection list should contain an entry with the API ID /providers/Microsoft.PowerApps/apis/shared_microsoftcopilotstudio, and that its presence means the connection exists. If it is absent, the connection can be added manually through the Power Apps maker portal. After that, the agent is published in Copilot Studio, the connection string and agent name are checked under the web app channel to confirm they match the Power Apps environment, and Power Automate flows triggered by the agent are tested.

Taken together, these episodes show the maker portal as the hands-on authoring surface of Power Apps: it is where tables, apps, flows, connections and solution components are created and inspected. A typical decision is when to stay in the portal and when to rely on more structured practices. For quick prototypes and everyday maintenance, the point-and-click experience is sufficient. When work has to move reliably between development, testing and production, the episodes point toward solutions, environment variables, solution layering, consistent naming and versioning, and ALM pipelines, since the portal alone gives limited control over that movement.

The maker portal therefore relates closely to several neighboring topics: Dataverse for tables and relationships, Power Automate for cloud flows and connection references, Copilot Studio for agents and their connections, and Dynamics 365 for solution-based customizations. Understanding what the portal covers well, and where other tools take over, helps makers choose an appropriate approach for each stage of an app's life.

power-apps-premium.desc: Power Apps Premium is a per-user Power Apps license for running apps that use Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors beyond Microsoft 365 rights.

faq.a: It covers apps that use premium capabilities such as Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors. These are not covered by the Power Apps rights included in Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What does Power Apps Premium cover that Microsoft 365 does not?

faq.a: According to the episode "Avoid the Dataverse Licensing Trap in Power Apps", the per-app plan covers one custom app or one Power Pages website per user, while Power Apps Premium is a per-user license for unlimited apps.
faq.q: How does Power Apps Premium differ from the per-app plan?

faq.a: Yes. The episodes on Power Apps Code Apps state that end users need a Power Apps Premium license to access Code Apps.
faq.q: Is a Power Apps Premium license needed for Code Apps?

power-apps-premium.long:
Power Apps Premium is a per-user license for Power Apps. It allows a user to run apps that rely on premium capabilities, such as Microsoft Dataverse, model-driven apps and premium connectors. These capabilities are not covered by the Power Apps rights that are included in Microsoft 365. The license is part of the Power Apps product family and is one of several licensing options for the platform.

The main purpose of the license is to give end users access to apps that go beyond the standard use cases covered by Microsoft 365. When an app uses a premium connector or stores its data in Dataverse, each user who runs it needs an appropriate license. The per-user model is aimed at people who work with several apps. A per-app plan, in contrast, covers a single application for each user.

The episode "Avoid the Dataverse Licensing Trap in Power Apps" compares the main plan choices. According to the episode, the free plan includes 2 GB of Dataverse space and up to 750 automation flows per month. The Power Apps Per App plan costs $5 per app per user and covers one custom app or one Power Pages website, with a 50 MB database and 400 MB file storage. Power Apps Premium is listed at $20 per user, or $12 per user for 2,000 or more users, with unlimited apps, 2 GB of files, 250 MB of Dataverse space and premium connectors. A pay-as-you-go option billed through an Azure subscription is also described. The episode summarizes the trade-off this way: the per-app plan suits a single app, while the per-user plan suits people who need many apps. These figures are attributed to the episode and may differ from current official pricing.

Licensing questions also arise with newer app types. The episode "Avoid the Generative Pages Power Apps Licensing Trap" says that using generative pages with Microsoft Dataverse brings licensing issues, because each viewer needs a Power Apps Premium license once a page has been created. According to the episode, this turns the app from a standard app into a premium one. To limit unexpected costs, it suggests keeping Dataverse components in separate environments so that other apps are not pulled into premium licensing.

Code Apps are another area where the license matters. The episodes "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" and "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" both state that a Power Apps Premium license is required for end users to access Code Apps. In the first episode, the license appears in a list of prerequisites alongside Visual Studio Code, Node.js (LTS version), Git, the Power Apps CLI and the Power Platform Tools extension for VS Code. The second episode says that a standard Power Apps Premium license is needed and describes it as ensuring access to advanced features within the Power Platform. It also notes that Code Apps can be deployed to a Power Apps environment with the command pac code push.

The license also comes up in discussions of scale. The episode "Power Platform Scalability Limits and Fixes" explains that licensed user types contribute different entitlements to tenant-level capacity and request limits. It says that for many users or many apps, appropriate licensing tiers such as Power Apps Premium and a suitable architecture should be considered, so that load is distributed across environments. Platform constraints named there include concurrent sessions, Dataverse capacity and environment-level limits.

In practice, the decision around Power Apps Premium usually involves three questions: whether an app uses Dataverse or premium connectors, how many apps each user needs to run, and how many users are involved. The answers determine whether a per-app plan, a per-user plan or pay-as-you-go billing fits better. The episodes consistently recommend checking licensing before building, since the cost model can change once premium features are added to an app.

power-bi-desktop.desc: Power BI Desktop is a free Windows application from Microsoft for connecting to data, modelling it and authoring reports before publishing to the Power BI service.

faq.a: It is used to connect to data, model it with relationships and measures, and design report pages and visuals. The finished reports are then published to the Power BI service for sharing.
faq.q: What is Power BI Desktop used for?

faq.a: Power Query is used in Power BI Desktop for loading and transforming data, and DAX is used for calculations in the data model. Both are part of everyday report authoring in the application.
faq.q: How do Power Query and DAX relate to Power BI Desktop?

faq.a: Yes, it is a free Windows application from Microsoft. Reports built in it are typically published to the Power BI service for sharing and refresh.
faq.q: Is Power BI Desktop free?

power-bi-desktop.long:
Power BI Desktop is a free Windows application from Microsoft for connecting to data sources, modelling the data and authoring Power BI reports. Report authors use it to shape data, define relationships and measures, and design visuals and pages. The finished report is then published to the Power BI service, where it can be shared with others and refreshed. It is part of Power BI, is classed as an analytics and BI tool, and is sometimes abbreviated as PBI Desktop.

The typical workflow in Power BI Desktop starts with getting data. Data is connected through the Get Data function, and loading and transforming it is done with Power Query. Calculations in the data model are written in DAX, so both Power Query and DAX are closely related to everyday work in the application. Once the model and the visuals are in place, the report is published to the Power BI service. This split between authoring on the desktop and sharing in the service is the central design of the product.

The M365.FM episodes describe several concrete data scenarios. "Connect Power BI Desktop to SharePoint Folders" deals with using SharePoint as a data source. SharePoint is described there as a place that can grow into a maze of lists, libraries, document versions, old folders and columns added by people who have since left. The episode frames the task as turning that jumble into something that can be reshaped, filtered, modelled and presented clearly, starting from the site URL. "Embed Power BI and Fabric Analytics in Dynamics 365" covers a Dataverse connection: open Power BI Desktop, choose Get Data, select Dataverse as the source, enter the Dynamics 365 organization URL, pick the entities needed and load them. From there, relationships, calculations and visuals can be added.

Power BI Desktop also appears in the episodes in the context of larger, team-based development. "Power BI DAX and Semantic Models with Bernat Agulló Roselló [MVP]" covers filter context, relationships and the difference between measures and calculated columns. The episode says advanced semantic models quickly become difficult to manage in Power BI Desktop alone, which makes automation and scripting with Tabular Editor important for scalable BI solutions. This points to a common decision: when a model outgrows manual work in the desktop application, enterprise tooling becomes relevant.

The lifecycle topics follow the same pattern. "Deploy Power BI with Development, Test, and Production Pipelines" describes the development workspace as the place where authors open Power BI Desktop, change tables, rebuild DAX calculations, try new visuals and adjust Power Query steps. Changes are promoted to a test stage and then to production, so that experiments do not affect other users. "Power BI Version Control with GitHub and Azure DevOps" notes that Power BI Desktop files use the binary PBIX format. According to the episode, teams therefore often rely on source control strategies, such as saving report parts as separate JSON files or using the ALM Toolkit. It also mentions workspaces, deployment pipelines and the XMLA endpoint as ways to mimic development, test and production branches.

Taken together, the episodes position Power BI Desktop as the authoring environment where data connection, Power Query transformation, DAX modelling and report design come together. It is the starting point for the Power BI service, deployment pipelines and version control practices, while the sources describe it as free to use on Windows.

power-bi-pro.desc: Power BI Pro is a per-user Power BI license for creating, publishing, sharing and collaborating on Power BI content, and part of the wider Power BI product.

faq.a: Power BI Pro is a per-user license that is part of Power BI. It lets users create, publish, share and collaborate on Power BI content.
faq.q: What is Power BI Pro?

faq.a: According to the episode "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]", you and your external users may need Power BI Pro or Premium licenses, so the organization's plan should be checked before sharing.
faq.q: Do external users need a Power BI Pro license to view shared reports?

faq.a: The episode "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals" says Fabric can be adopted alongside Power BI licensing and that organizations using Power BI Pro may evaluate upgrades depending on scale and governance needs.
faq.q: How does Power BI Pro relate to Microsoft Fabric?

power-bi-pro.long:
Power BI Pro is a per-user license within Power BI. It allows a licensed user to create, publish, share and collaborate on Power BI content such as reports and dashboards. Microsoft documents the differences between license types in its Power BI fundamentals material, which is the reference point for deciding what a Pro license covers compared with other options.

In practice, Power BI Pro is the license that turns Power BI from a personal analysis tool into a collaborative one. A user who builds a report in Power BI Desktop can publish it to the Power BI service and share it with colleagues. One of the M365.FM episodes summarizes the requirement list for embedded analytics in this way: a Power BI Pro license is essential for creating, sharing and collaborating on reports, report sharing allows distribution of reports to other Pro users within the organization, collaborative workspaces enable shared team spaces, and data refresh keeps reports current through scheduled refreshes. These are the capabilities most closely tied to the license in the episode material.

The license shows up in several typical scenarios. In the episode "Monitor Business Central Telemetry with Power BI", the Power BI app for Business Central is combined with a connection from Power BI Desktop to Application Insights. Custom dashboards then highlight KPIs such as performance bottlenecks, page load times, extension failures and user activity patterns. The episode states that with a Power BI Pro license, teams can publish and share these dashboards across the organization, supporting governance, capacity planning and decisions about performance tuning.

A second scenario appears in "Embed Power BI and Fabric Analytics in Dynamics 365". There, the episode lists licensing and permissions that need to be checked before starting an embedded analytics setup, and puts Power BI Pro first on that list. A third appears in "Power Platform - Simply Explained", where a Power BI Pro license is named among the prerequisites for sharing the Power BI report that is part of the CoE Starter Kit, alongside items such as access to an Office 365 mailbox for the Office 365 Outlook connector and an Azure app registration for collecting usage information.

Licensing also matters when content leaves the organization. In "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]", the answer to whether special licenses are needed to share Power BI reports externally is yes: both the sharer and the external users may need Power BI Pro or Premium licenses. The episode advises checking the organization's plan before sharing and notes, attributed to Nicholas Hayduk, that licensing affects both access and collaboration options. It also recommends reviewing shared data and permissions at least every quarter, with continuous monitoring for sensitive data.

Power BI Pro is also discussed in the context of larger-scale decisions. In "What Microsoft Fabric Means for Power BI Professionals", the episode explains that Microsoft Fabric can be adopted alongside Power BI licensing, that some Fabric capabilities overlap with Power BI Premium features, and that organizations using Power BI Pro may evaluate upgrades depending on scale and governance needs. Power BI Premium capacity combined with Fabric is described there as delivering enterprise-grade performance and management for BI at scale.

Taken together, the sources present Power BI Pro as the per-user entry point for authoring and sharing in Power BI. Questions about who needs the license, whether external recipients need one, and when capacity-based options become relevant are the main decisions that arise around it.

power-pages.desc: Power Pages is Microsoft's low-code service in the Power Platform for building secure, data-driven business websites such as customer and partner portals.

faq.a: Power Pages is used to build secure, data-driven business websites such as customer portals, partner portals and self-service sites. These let external visitors work with business data without direct access to internal systems.
faq.q: What is Power Pages used for?

faq.a: Dataverse usually stores the data that a Power Pages site displays and edits, while Power Fx is the formula language used across the Power Platform. Power Pages itself is part of the Power Platform.
faq.q: How does Power Pages relate to Dataverse and Power Fx?

faq.a: No. Power Pages is a paid Power Platform service, and the episode "Power Pages Licensing, Capacity Limits, and Alternatives" covers how its licensing and capacity limits compare with alternative solutions.
faq.q: Is Power Pages free to use?

power-pages.long:
Power Pages, also referred to as Microsoft Power Pages, is a low-code service for building secure, data-driven business websites. It is developed by Microsoft, belongs to the Power Platform and is classed as a low-code tool. It first appeared in February 2022 and is a paid service. Its focus is on external-facing scenarios: customer portals, partner portals, self-service sites and public-facing business applications in which visitors work with business data without having direct access to internal systems.

In practice, Power Pages is used when an organization wants to give people outside the company a controlled view of its data and processes. Typical examples named in the M365.FM material are customer portals, partner sites and self-service web experiences that can be created without heavy custom development. Data usually sits in Dataverse, the data platform that Power Pages is related to, so that a site can display and edit records that are already part of the organization's business data. Power Fx, the formula language used across the Power Platform, is a related topic for logic and configuration.

Because Power Pages sites are exposed to people outside the organization, security and architecture are recurring themes. The episode "Secure External Data Sharing with Power Pages and Nicholas Hayduk [MVP]" describes the risks of sharing data externally, such as data leaks and unauthorized access, and recommends double-checking permissions, classifying data into sensitive and non-sensitive categories and sharing only what is necessary. It presents Power Pages as a way to manage access while keeping compliance and user experience in focus, and argues that external users should not be treated like internal employees.

The episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" looks beyond simple portals and discusses what changes when a platform must support multiple customers, strict security boundaries, enterprise governance and large-scale growth. According to the episode, many Power Platform projects struggle when they move beyond a single environment, and it covers topics such as Microsoft Entra External ID, governance and ALM practices, and performance as architectural decisions that become critical at that stage.

Licensing and capacity are another decision area. The episode "Power Pages Licensing, Capacity Limits, and Alternatives" explains what Power Pages is, how it integrates with Dataverse and the Power Platform, why organizations use it for quick portal creation, and how its licensing, capacity limits and alternative solutions compare. Since it is a paid service, these points matter when planning a site that may grow in users or data volume.

Existing portals are also a topic. "Modernize Legacy Power Apps Portals and Power Pages" addresses the move from older portal implementations to Microsoft Power Pages and warns about shadow logic: business rules, automations or workflows that operate outside official oversight and can create a hidden security risk. The episode lists unofficial workflows, hidden automations and untracked logic as common forms and recommends recognizing them early in a migration.

For a general introduction, "Power Pages - Simply Explained" from the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series, presented by Mirko Peters, explains the platform in simple terms and shows how organizations can rapidly create customer portals, partner portals, self-service websites and public-facing business applications. It also frames the practical questions of architecture, adoption, security and governance that accompany such projects.

Taken together, the sources place Power Pages as the web-facing part of the Power Platform: a low-code way to publish business data externally, with Dataverse as the usual data layer and security, governance and licensing as the main points to settle before a site goes live.

power-pivot.desc: Power Pivot adds advanced data modeling to Microsoft Excel, relating multiple tables and using DAX calculations; introduced in 2010, it later became a Power BI building block.

faq.a: Power Pivot provides advanced data modeling in Microsoft Excel. It lets users relate multiple tables in a data model and write calculations in DAX, and it was introduced in 2010.
faq.q: What is Power Pivot?

faq.a: Power Pivot uses DAX for its calculations. The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" describes DAX as the calculation language behind Power BI, Excel Power Pivot, and SQL Server Analysis Services, and Power Pivot later became one of the building blocks of Power BI.
faq.q: How does Power Pivot relate to DAX and Power BI?

faq.a: The M365.FM episodes mention Power Query for transforming data, Power Pivot for data modeling with DAX, Power View for visualizations, and Power Q&A for natural language queries.
faq.q: Which tools are commonly mentioned alongside Power Pivot?

power-pivot.long:
Power Pivot is a data modeling feature in Microsoft Excel. It lets users bring several tables into a single data model, define relationships between them, and write calculations in DAX (Data Analysis Expressions). It was introduced in 2010 and later became one of the building blocks of Power BI.

The core idea behind Power Pivot is to move analysis beyond a single flat worksheet. Instead of combining everything into one large table, users keep related data in separate tables and connect them in a data model. Reports and PivotTables can then draw on that model. One of the M365.FM episodes describes this as relational data modeling, one of the capabilities that distinguishes Excel when work involves heavy data analysis.

Calculations in Power Pivot are written in DAX. The episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" describes DAX as the calculation language that powers Microsoft Power BI, Excel Power Pivot, and SQL Server Analysis Services. According to the episode, DAX is more than simply using Excel formulas inside Power BI, because it works across complete tables and data models rather than individual spreadsheet cells. The episode also covers the difference between calculated columns and measures, a distinction that matters when building calculations on top of a Power Pivot data model.

Power Pivot is often mentioned together with Power Query. In "Excel vs Google Sheets with David Benaim [MVP]", the two are presented as tools that let users manipulate and model data in complex ways: Power Query is associated with cleaning and transforming data from various sources, while Power Pivot is associated with relational data modeling. The episode frames these features as a reason Excel may be essential for users whose work involves heavy data analysis, in contrast to alternatives such as Google Sheets.

The pairing also appears in the context of data volumes. The episode "Fix Power Apps Excel Data Limits with Dataverse" says that Excel's data limitations are often overstated and that, with Power Query and Power Pivot, Excel can handle large datasets beyond the traditional one million row limit. The episode attributes these misconceptions to a lack of training on modern Excel capabilities. The same episode is nonetheless about the limits of Excel as a data source for Power Apps and the move to Dataverse, so Power Pivot is one part of a broader discussion about choosing the right data platform.

Power Pivot is also listed among the Microsoft tools relevant to reporting. In "Power BI Paginated Reports: Service vs Report Builder vs SSRS", the takeaways include using Power Query for data transformation, using Power Pivot for data modeling with DAX, creating visualizations with Power View, and using Power Q&A for natural language queries. The episode presents these as strategies for producing visually accurate, high-quality reports.

Typical decisions around Power Pivot involve where the data model should live and which tool should own the calculations. Because the same DAX language is used in Excel Power Pivot, Power BI, and SQL Server Analysis Services, skills in writing measures and understanding relationships carry across these products, as the DAX episode explains. Users who start with a data model in Excel can therefore recognize the same concepts when working in Power BI, which is consistent with Power Pivot's role as one of the building blocks of that product.

power-platform-center-of-excellence.desc: A Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE) is a team and set of practices that supports makers and governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption in an organization.

faq.a: It is a team and a set of practices that supports makers and administers, governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption across an organization, beyond tooling and dashboards.
faq.q: What is a Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE)?

faq.a: No. The CoE is the team and its practices, while the CoE Starter Kit provides tooling, templates and governance practices, such as dashboards and app inventories, that a CoE can use for monitoring and governance.
faq.q: Is the CoE the same as the CoE Starter Kit?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft 365 Admins: From Gatekeepers to Cloud Architects" lists CoE leadership, a governance architect, a security specialist and a training coordinator as example roles.
faq.q: Which roles can a CoE team include?

power-platform-center-of-excellence.long:
A Power Platform Center of Excellence (CoE) is a team and a set of practices that supports makers and administers, governs and nurtures Power Platform adoption across an organization. In the official guidance, the CoE is described as going beyond tooling and dashboards: it covers the people, responsibilities and routines that surround the platform, not only the technical assets used to monitor it. It sits within the broader Power Platform topic, which includes low-code apps and automation built by makers inside the business.

The purpose of a CoE is to bridge IT and business units. The episode "Microsoft 365 Admins: From Gatekeepers to Cloud Architects" describes the CoE as a team that guides governance efforts and helps organizations deliver value quickly while protecting their assets. The same episode lists example roles that such a team can include: CoE leadership, which oversees the CoE and its initiatives; a governance architect, who designs governance frameworks and policies; a security specialist, who ensures compliance and security measures are in place; and a training coordinator. These roles show that a CoE is organized around decisions about who does what, how data is protected and how apps keep running smoothly.

A CoE is often associated with the Power Platform CoE Starter Kit, although the two are not the same thing. The Starter Kit is tooling and templates, while the CoE itself is the team and the practices. The episode "Govern Power Platform Environments Instead of Disabling Them" says the Starter Kit provides tooling, templates and governance practices to govern Power Platform at scale. According to that episode, it helps implement governance controls, environment strategy, monitoring, app lifecycle management and adoption strategy, and it supports scaling low-code solutions while letting citizen developers deliver value without creating shadow IT or data governance issues. The episode's framing is to govern environments rather than disable them.

Monitoring and compliance are a recurring theme in the episodes. "Build Production AI Apps with Azure OpenAI and Power Platform" says the Starter Kit gives dashboards, app inventories and automation tools, and that these can be used to monitor usage, check compliance and document business reasons for settings. The episode adds that the kit can scan for new environments so that governance stays up to date, and it recommends reviewing policies regularly to support sustainable growth. It also lists related practices such as tagging resources, setting up a team structure for environments, and using activity logs and analytics to monitor usage.

The episode "Automate Microsoft 365 Compliance Tasks with Power Automate" places the CoE Starter Kit inside a wider governance checklist. In its monitoring, logging and auditing section, the episode lists enabling and centralizing audit logging for Power Platform activities, configuring the CoE Starter Kit for governance and monitoring, watching for flow run failures, performance anomalies and unusual usage patterns, and retaining logs according to regulatory and organizational retention policies. Other items in the same checklist include reviewing connector permissions and consent scopes regularly and mapping Power Platform components to applicable regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and SOC.

Taken together, the sources present a CoE as a combination of organizational structure and governance practice. Typical decisions around it include how to structure the team, which governance framework and policies to apply to environments, how to monitor usage and compliance, and how to support makers through training and adoption work. The official documentation is the reference for the full definition of the CoE and its role in Power Platform adoption.

power-platform-pipelines.desc: Pipelines in Power Platform is a built-in feature that moves solutions between development, test and production environments to simplify ALM for smaller teams.

faq.a: They are the native deployment pipelines built into Power Platform that move solutions between environments such as development, test and production. They are aimed at simplifying ALM for smaller teams.
faq.q: What are Pipelines in Power Platform?

faq.a: Per Microsoft Learn, they do not deploy Dataverse table data, handle one solution per deployment, do not support cross-tenant deployment, allow one development environment per solution and one host per environment.
faq.q: What limits apply to Pipelines in Power Platform?

faq.a: The sources do not say they replace them. The M365.FM episodes describe Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as popular tools for CI/CD in Power Platform projects, including automated testing, while the built-in pipelines simplify ALM with less setup.
faq.q: Do Pipelines in Power Platform replace Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions?

power-platform-pipelines.long:
Pipelines in Power Platform are the native deployment pipelines built into Power Platform. They move solutions between environments such as development, test and production and are aimed at simplifying application lifecycle management (ALM) for smaller teams. According to Microsoft Learn, the feature serves as a built-in way to handle ALM and CI/CD automation across Power Platform and Dynamics 365, without requiring a team to assemble its own tooling first.

The setup is organised around a central pipelines host environment. Administrators configure the deployment pipelines in that host, and the environments taking part are linked to it and typed as either development or target environments. Makers can then deploy solutions straight from their development environment, while developers can run pipelines with the Power Platform CLI. This split lets administrators keep control of the stages while makers carry out the day-to-day deployments.

Several checks and controls are part of how a deployment runs. Before deploying, the pipeline checks for missing dependencies and validates connections and variables. The same solution artifact moves through the stages in a fixed order without being exported again, so the package that was tested is the package that reaches the next stage. Approvals can be handled through delegated deployments. At each deployment, managed and unmanaged solutions are backed up in the host. An audit log and Power BI reports are included, and earlier solution versions can be redeployed when rollback is enabled.

Licensing and environment requirements affect planning. Developer-type development and test environments need no standalone license, while other environments must be managed environments, and a production target needs licenses with premium rights. Documented limits include that Dataverse table data is not deployed, that each deployment covers one solution, that cross-tenant deployment is not supported, that each solution has one development environment, and that each environment can be linked to one host. Teams that need to move reference data, span tenants or build more elaborate release flows will have to consider these boundaries.

Pipelines in Power Platform sit alongside other approaches to ALM rather than replacing all of them. The M365.FM episode "Automated Testing for Power Apps and Dataverse" discusses integrating automated testing with CI/CD pipelines and names Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions as popular tools for building such pipelines in Power Platform projects. The episode describes adding approvals, deploying with service principals for secure automation, and running tests as part of a workflow. That is a code-first, tool-driven route, in contrast to the built-in feature described above.

The episode "Deploy Dynamics 365 Customizations with ALM Pipelines" covers the same subject for Microsoft Dynamics 365. It states that pipelines in Power Platform simplify ALM for Microsoft Dynamics 365, bringing automation, continuous integration and continuous delivery, and it lists elements of a strong pipeline architecture: version control with Azure Repos, automated build and release steps, code review requests and minimum branching options for simplicity. It also stresses structuring environments and a branching strategy to support multiple development and deployment stages.

In practice, the choice comes down to team size, governance needs and how much customisation of the release process is required. Smaller teams that mainly need to promote a solution from development through test to production can use the built-in pipelines with limited setup. Teams that need automated testing gates, source control integration or more complex flows may combine them with, or choose, Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions, as the episodes outline.

power-platform-solution.desc: A Power Platform solution is a container that carries an app and its customizable components, such as flows, tables and connectors, between environments.

faq.a: It is a container in Power Platform that carries an app and its customizable components, such as flows, tables and connectors, between environments. It holds metadata and configuration, not business data.
faq.q: What is a Power Platform solution?

faq.a: No. A solution carries metadata and configuration only. Moving records stored in Dataverse is a separate task from deploying the solution package.
faq.q: Does a Power Platform solution contain business data?

faq.a: According to the episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely", customizations can be transferred and deployed across dev, test and prod environments using solution packages, which supports repeatable and automated migration pipelines.
faq.q: How are solutions used across development, test and production?

power-platform-solution.long:
A Power Platform solution is a container in Power Platform that carries an app together with all of its customizable components from one environment to another. Typical components include apps, flows, tables and connectors. A solution holds metadata and configuration, not business data, which makes it the unit that packages how an application is built rather than the information the application stores.

The main purpose of a solution is to move work between environments in a controlled way. Teams commonly separate development, test and production environments, and a solution is what travels along that path. Because everything that belongs to the application is grouped in a single package, the same set of components can be deployed repeatedly instead of being rebuilt by hand in each environment. Official documentation on solution concepts in application lifecycle management (ALM) describes this role in more detail, and solutions sit within the broader Power Platform family of low-code tools.

In practice, a solution is used whenever an app, a flow or a data model has to leave the place where it was created. A maker builds the components in a development environment, adds them to a solution, and then exports the solution as a package. That package can be imported into a test environment and later into production. The episode "Migrate Dataverse Data Between Environments Safely" connects this to migration work: it says that customizations can be transferred and deployed across environments (dev, test, prod) using solution packages, which enables repeatable and automated migration pipelines. The same episode treats Dataverse migration as a foundation for a Power Platform solution, noting benefits such as unified administration, an integrated platform that combines ERP, CRM and Power Apps, and fewer silos.

The distinction between configuration and data matters for planning. Since a solution carries metadata and configuration only, moving the records stored in tables is a separate task. This is why discussions of migration treat the transport of customizations through solution packages and the transfer of Dataverse data as related but different activities. Anyone planning a deployment needs to decide how components will be packaged and how any existing business data will be handled.

The term also appears in conversations about architecture and careers. In "Architecting Power Platform for Complex Enterprise Solutions with Ian Tweedie [MVP]", the host and a Power Platform Solution Architect discuss what happens when Power Platform applications become business-critical, highly integrated and more complex than a simple maker-first approach. The episode states that low-code does not mean low architecture, and that enterprise solutions almost always include requirements beyond standard low-code capabilities. Structuring components into well-defined packages is part of that kind of disciplined design, although the episode excerpt focuses on the broader architectural questions.

The phrase "Power Platform solution" is also used more loosely in other contexts. In "Microsoft Marketplace - Simply Explained", it appears as an example of something a business leader might look for when searching a global commerce platform that connects customers, software vendors, consultants, AI solutions and cloud services. In career-oriented episodes such as "From SharePoint Developer to Power Platform Architect with Michel Mendes [MVP]" and "Build a Power Platform Career with Nathalie Leenders [MVP-MCT]", the Power Platform Solution Architect Expert certification (PL-600) is described as testing the ability to design, secure and deliver Power Platform solutions. In these cases the wording refers to a delivered business solution in general, while the technical concept described above is the packaging container used for application lifecycle management.

For readers deciding how to approach the topic, the useful starting points are the environment strategy (which environments exist and how work moves between them), the components that belong together in one package, and the separation of configuration from business data. The linked official documentation on solution concepts in ALM covers the underlying model, and the M365.FM episodes above show how the idea appears in migration, enterprise architecture and certification contexts.

power-platform-tenant-isolation.desc: Power Platform tenant isolation is an admin setting that blocks Microsoft Entra ID-based connector connections to other tenants unless they are explicitly allowed.

faq.a: When switched on, it blocks cross-tenant connections made through Microsoft Entra ID-based connectors in both directions, except for tenants on an allow list. It affects only canvas apps and flows.
faq.q: What does Power Platform tenant isolation block?

faq.a: Exceptions are allow-list entries given as a domain or tenant ID, applied to inbound, outbound or both directions. A wildcard entry allows every tenant in a direction.
faq.q: How are exceptions to tenant isolation defined?

faq.a: At runtime, apps and flows that violate the policy fail. At design time, canvas apps cannot add the connection and flows are saved but suspended.
faq.q: What happens to existing apps and flows that use cross-tenant connections?

power-platform-tenant-isolation.long:
Power Platform tenant isolation is a Power Platform administration setting that controls cross-tenant connections made through connectors. It lets administrators decide which Microsoft Entra tenants may be reached from the tenant (outbound) and which external tenants may connect into it (inbound). The stated aim is to keep connector use secure within the tenant and to reduce the risk of data exfiltration. It is a feature of Power Platform and is configured as part of that platform's tenant-level security settings.

The setting applies only to connectors that authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID, such as Office 365 Outlook or SharePoint. It is separate from the Entra-wide tenant restrictions feature, so access outside Power Platform is not affected by it. According to the documentation notes, only canvas apps and flows are affected, and the Azure DevOps connector is not covered because it uses its own OAuth flow. These boundaries matter when judging what tenant isolation does and does not protect.

The behavior depends on whether the setting is switched on. According to the Microsoft Learn documentation, by default the setting is off, and cross-tenant connections work as long as valid Entra credentials are supplied. When isolation is switched on, all tenants are blocked in both directions except those on an allow list. Each allow-list entry can apply to inbound traffic, outbound traffic or both, and can be specified as a domain or as a tenant ID. A wildcard entry allows every tenant in a given direction. The short description of this topic states that the episode context describes the isolation as enforced by default, which can break cross-tenant flows that were never documented. That wording differs from the documentation notes, so the effective default in a given tenant is worth verifying in the admin center.

Administrators configure tenant isolation in the Power Platform admin center under the security and identity settings. The documentation mentions that a Power Platform administrator role is relevant for viewing and setting it. Because the effect is tenant-wide, a typical preparation step is to inventory which apps and flows rely on connections to partner or other tenants, then add those tenants to the allow list in the correct direction before enabling the restriction.

The consequences of a block differ between design time and runtime. At design time, canvas apps cannot add a connection that violates the policy, and flows can still be saved but are suspended. At runtime, apps and flows that violate the policy fail. This is why undocumented cross-tenant dependencies are a common source of surprises: a flow built years earlier that quietly reads a SharePoint site or sends mail through a connection in another tenant can stop working once isolation is enforced, even though nothing in the flow itself changed.

In practice, decisions around tenant isolation come down to balancing collaboration with data-exfiltration risk. Organizations that work with partners or subsidiaries in separate tenants need deliberate allow-list entries, while organizations without such needs can leave the allow list empty and block every external tenant. Using specific domains or tenant IDs is narrower than the wildcard, which opens a whole direction. Since the topic sits under the broader Power Platform area, it is usually reviewed together with other governance and data-protection settings for environments, connectors and flows.

power-virtual-agents.desc: Power Virtual Agents (PVA) was Microsoft's no-code chatbot builder in the Power Platform and has since been merged into Microsoft Copilot Studio.
