These options let an organization restrict where the agent operates while content structure and permissions are reviewed.

There are also stated limits. The agent is not available in GCC, GCC High, DoD, air-gapped clouds or the cloud operated by 21Vianet. Language support is limited to languages that appear in both the SharePoint and Copilot language lists. Organizations evaluating the agent therefore need to check their cloud environment and languages first, then decide on licensing, credit consumption and the level of human review applied to tagging and rule results.

sharepoint-premium.desc: SharePoint Premium is an add-on for SharePoint covering document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management, formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex.

faq.a: SharePoint Premium is the current name for the capabilities formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex. The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" describes Syntex being folded into SharePoint Premium.
faq.q: Is SharePoint Premium the same as Microsoft Syntex?

faq.a: It provides document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management for SharePoint. Examples from the episodes include extracting fields such as vendor, totals and dates, and supporting governance with SharePoint Advanced Management.
faq.q: What can SharePoint Premium do?

faq.a: The episodes say that structured, governed content gives Copilot better material to answer from. SharePoint Premium is presented as a way to prepare content so Copilot answers are grounded rather than guessed.
faq.q: How does SharePoint Premium relate to Copilot?

sharepoint-premium.long:
SharePoint Premium is a set of add-on capabilities for SharePoint, developed by Microsoft, that covers document processing, content AI, eSignature and advanced management. It was formerly marketed as Microsoft Syntex, and the older name still appears in some episodes and documentation. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool, and it is part of SharePoint rather than a separate platform.

The product is aimed at organisations that want to extract information from documents, automate content-heavy processes and govern content at scale. In practice this means turning files in SharePoint and OneDrive into structured, searchable content. The episode "End Content Silos with Microsoft Syntex" describes classifiers and extractors that tag details such as vendor, totals and dates, so that files can be organised automatically, drive Power Automate workflows and surface information across Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Purview.

One framing in the episodes is that SharePoint Premium brings three areas together: content experiences, content processing and governance. "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" describes this as a brain (content experiences), muscle (content processing) and bouncer (governance). The episode argues that folding Syntex into SharePoint Premium is Microsoft consolidating these areas into one platform, so that content becomes structured, governed and queryable, which in turn gives Copilot better material to answer from. For getting started, the episode recommends using prebuilt models first, measuring the time saved and then scaling.

Governance is a second major theme. "Reduce SharePoint Premium SAM and PAYG AI Costs" discusses SharePoint Premium together with SharePoint Advanced Management (SAM) as the governance backbone that keeps Copilot from turning oversharing into a data leak. The episode walks through Data Access Governance (DAG) to spot risky sites, Restricted Access Control (RAC) to limit visibility, Site Access Reviews to make site owners accountable, and AI Insights to prioritise fixes. Its title also points to cost considerations around SAM and pay-as-you-go (PAYG) AI usage.

"AI Contract Management with SharePoint Premium and Copilot" applies the same ideas to a concrete scenario. It describes how data drifts into disorder over time and how structure, governance and AI models give content purpose. The episode presents practical steps for deploying AI on content so that Copilot answers are grounded in governed, cleaner data rather than guesswork. Contracts are a typical example because they combine repeating fields, approval steps and compliance requirements.

SharePoint Premium is related to several other Microsoft offerings. AI Builder also offers document-oriented AI models, so teams choosing a document-processing approach often compare the two. Microsoft Purview supplies compliance and information protection that complement the governance side. SharePoint Advanced Management administers content and sites and is the part most closely tied to oversharing control.

"What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" gives an overview for readers new to the topic. It explains what the product is, where it fits in a SharePoint environment, and which practical questions to ask before using it for business processes and content at scale. It also lists features such as e-signatures and document processing as part of the add-on. Because it is an add-on, a typical decision is whether the volume and value of document-driven processes justify enabling it, and where to start.

site-access-reviews.desc: Site access reviews are a SharePoint Advanced Management feature that lets administrators delegate review of overshared sites to site owners.

faq.a: They are a feature that lets administrators delegate the review of overshared sites to site owners, who then confirm who should keep access. The sites are identified through data access governance reports.
faq.q: What are site access reviews in SharePoint Advanced Management?

faq.a: Data access governance generates reports on overshared sites based on link sharing, privacy and sensitivity labels. Site access reviews are the follow-up step in which owners check and confirm access to those sites.
faq.q: How do site access reviews relate to data access governance?

faq.a: According to the episode "Fix Wrong Microsoft 365 Copilot Answers with SharePoint Governance", the ability to trigger Site Access Reviews for OneDrive is limited, so manual clean-up is often needed there.
faq.q: Do site access reviews cover OneDrive?

site-access-reviews.long:
Site access reviews are a feature of SharePoint Advanced Management. They let administrators delegate the review of overshared sites to the owners of those sites. The sites in question are identified through data access governance reports, and the site owners then confirm who should keep access. Instead of an IT team trying to judge access for every site from the outside, the people closest to the content are asked to make the call.

The feature addresses oversharing, which is the situation where a site or its content is reachable by more people than intended. Oversharing matters more once tools such as Microsoft 365 Copilot can surface content that users can technically reach. The episode "Reduce SharePoint Premium SAM and PAYG AI Costs" describes SharePoint Advanced Management as a governance backbone that keeps Copilot from turning oversharing into a data leak. In that episode, Site Access Reviews are the part that makes owners accountable for the sites they run.

Site access reviews work together with data access governance (DAG). DAG generates reports on overshared sites and offers insights based on link sharing, privacy settings and sensitivity labels. The episode "Automate Document Processing with Microsoft Syntex" explains the division of labor this way: DAG helps spot sites that might be overshared, and Site Access Reviews let IT work with content owners to check who has access to important files. The stated goal of that process is to keep data safe and support compliance with company rules.

The same episode that introduces the feature uses a layered metaphor to place it among related controls. It describes role-based access control as the moat, Advanced Management as the walls, DAG and AI Insights as watchtowers, and site owners as the guards. Restricted Access Control is named alongside Site Access Reviews as another way to lock down visibility, while AI Insights help prioritize which fixes to tackle first. In this picture, the review is the step where a human owner actually decides who stays.

In practice, an administrator reviews the DAG reports, picks out sites that carry risky sharing settings, and starts a review so that the owners of those sites can confirm or remove access. This delegation is the central design choice: it spreads the work across owners rather than concentrating it in the IT team. The episode "What Is SharePoint Premium - Simply Explained" lists site access reviews among the governance capabilities of SharePoint Premium, next to data access governance reports, restricted access controls and AI recommendations. It contrasts this with the more basic access controls and content lifecycle management in the standard offering.

The episodes also note limits and alternatives. "Fix Wrong Microsoft 365 Copilot Answers with SharePoint Governance" says the ability to trigger Site Access Reviews for OneDrive is limited, which means manual clean-up is still needed there. It also stresses that AI cannot fix SharePoint problems on its own and that governance has to be in place for AI tools to work well. "Audit SharePoint Online Permissions at Scale" covers third-party audit tools that automate and schedule access reviews across thousands of sites, with document-level auditing and a single dashboard, as an option for organizations that want to scale permission reviews beyond what is built in.

For teams deciding how to use the feature, the episodes point to a sequence: identify risky sites with data access governance, narrow visibility where needed, and then ask owners to review access so that cleaning up oversharing becomes a recurring responsibility rather than a one-time project.

skype-for-business.desc: Skype for Business was Microsoft's enterprise unified communications product for messaging, presence, calling and meetings, now replaced by Microsoft Teams.

faq.a: Skype for Business was Microsoft's enterprise unified communications product for instant messaging, presence, calling and meetings. It was offered as an on-premises server and as Skype for Business Online.
faq.q: What was Skype for Business?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System", Skype for Business Online has been retired and its functionality has largely moved to Microsoft Teams. Some on-premises Skype for Business Server deployments still exist.
faq.q: Is Skype for Business still available?

faq.a: The episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire" recommends the Teams PowerShell module and the Graph API for modern management. Older modules exist for legacy Skype for Business Online tasks, but migrating to Teams is recommended.
faq.q: How should Skype for Business or Teams settings be managed with PowerShell?

skype-for-business.long:
Skype for Business was Microsoft's enterprise unified communications product. It brought instant messaging, presence, calling and meetings into one client for organizations. It was offered in two forms: as an on-premises server product, known as Skype for Business Server, and as a hosted cloud service, Skype for Business Online. Microsoft Teams has replaced it as the company's communications platform.

In practice, a product like Skype for Business gave employees a single place to see whether colleagues were available, send chat messages, start voice calls and join online meetings. The on-premises option let organizations run the infrastructure in their own environment, while the online option delivered the same kind of capabilities as part of a cloud subscription. That split between a self-hosted server and a cloud service shaped many deployment decisions, and it still explains why some environments behave differently from others today.

The M365.FM episodes treat Skype for Business mainly as part of a transition story. In the episode "Microsoft 365 as an Enterprise Operating System", the answer to the question of whether Skype for Business is still available is that Skype for Business Online has been retired and its functionality has largely moved to Microsoft Teams. Teams covers meetings, chat, calling and collaboration. The episode also notes that some on-premises Skype for Business Server deployments still exist, but that cloud-first enterprise subscriptions encourage Teams as the unified communications platform. For organizations still running the server product, this points to a migration decision rather than a new investment.

Administration is another area where the change is visible. In the episode "Run Your Full Stack Locally with .NET Aspire", a question addresses whether PowerShell can be used to interact with Skype for Business Online or Teams settings. The answer given there is that Skype for Business Online management has largely been replaced by Microsoft Teams and its PowerShell modules. The episode recommends using the Teams PowerShell module and the Graph API for modern management. Older modules exist for legacy Skype for Business Online tasks, but migrating to Teams and Graph-based administration is recommended for ongoing support. Administrators who maintain older scripts therefore have a practical reason to review which tooling they still depend on.

The product also has a place in the longer history of Microsoft collaboration. The episode "From Microsoft Lync to Teams with Carsten Lund Meilbak [MVP]" features a conversation between host Mirko Peters and Microsoft MVP Carsten Lund Meilbak. It follows the evolution of enterprise communication from the early days of Microsoft Lync and Skype for Business to the modern Microsoft Teams ecosystem. According to the episode description, collaboration platforms moved from simple messaging and voice solutions toward integrated hubs for meetings, telephony, teamwork, apps and AI-powered productivity. The discussion also covers how organizations adapted to major platform changes along the way.

For readers who encounter the name today, the relevant points are straightforward. Skype for Business describes a former product line with an on-premises and an online edition. The online edition has been retired, and Microsoft Teams is the successor for chat, meetings and calling. Any remaining on-premises Skype for Business Server environment should be understood as a legacy deployment, and planning around it usually centers on moving users, calling features and administration practices to Teams. The material in the M365.FM episodes supports that reading but does not give migration steps, dates or version details, so those would need to be checked against official Microsoft documentation.

smartart.desc: SmartArt is a Microsoft 365 feature in PowerPoint, Word, Excel and Outlook that turns text into diagrams such as lists, timelines and hierarchies.
smartart.long:
SmartArt is a feature of Microsoft 365 for creating diagrams from text. It is available in PowerPoint, Word, Excel and Outlook, and it is used to give plain text and bullet lists more visual impact. Typical diagram types include lists, timelines and hierarchies. Text can be converted to SmartArt, and a SmartArt graphic can be converted back to text or to shapes.

According to Microsoft Support, the basic workflow in PowerPoint starts with existing text. The user selects the text, uses the Home tab command for converting to a SmartArt graphic, and then picks a layout from a gallery. The layouts in the gallery are grouped into categories. Some layouts include picture placeholders: the user chooses a layout from the Picture category in the SmartArt gallery, clicks the picture icon and browses for an image to insert. The Microsoft Support article on this workflow states that it applies to PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 and to PowerPoint 2024, 2021, 2019 and 2016. That article is deliberately short; it does not cover converting a SmartArt graphic back into plain text or shapes, and it points to a separate, more general article on SmartArt graphics for such details.

The main decision when working with SmartArt is which layout fits the content. A sequence of steps, a set of people or an organizational structure each suggest a different layout, and the gallery makes it possible to try several layouts on the same text before settling on one. Because conversion works in both directions, SmartArt can be used as a quick way to visualize an existing bullet list and then be reverted to text or shapes if the diagram does not work.

SmartArt has been part of PowerPoint for years, and it is sometimes associated with a dated look. The M365.FM episode "PowerPoint Like a Pro- Hidden Features, Corporate Templates & Copilot with Fiona Walsh [MVP]" addresses this directly. In the section titled "SmartArt without the outdated look", Fiona explains how to keep SmartArt cleaner and more modern, including avoiding unnecessary 3D effects. The discussion also covers newer SmartArt options such as timelines, Meet the Team layouts and text cards, as well as converting ordinary text into SmartArt.

The same episode places SmartArt in a wider context of presentation design. It says that templates become increasingly important as organizations adopt Copilot, because Copilot relies heavily on the layouts available within the presentation template, and a poorly designed template can directly limit the quality of AI-generated slides. SmartArt therefore sits alongside template design and layout choices as one of the tools that shape how a presentation looks.

In practice, the feature is relevant wherever text benefits from structure: process descriptions in a PowerPoint slide, a hierarchy shown in a Word document, or a simple diagram in an Excel workbook or an Outlook message. The sources provided here describe the PowerPoint workflow in the most detail, and they do not go into the specific steps in the other applications.

soc-2.desc: SOC 2 is a System and Organization Controls audit report based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, used to assess the security controls of service and SaaS providers.

faq.a: SOC 2 is a System and Organization Controls audit report based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. Enterprise customers commonly request it to evaluate the security controls of service and SaaS providers.
faq.q: What is SOC 2?

faq.a: No. The episode "7-Step Microsoft 365 Sovereign Tenant Governance Framework" says certifications like SOC 2 or ISO 27001 do not equate to sovereignty, and organizations must assess their own sovereignty needs.
faq.q: Does a SOC 2 report mean an organization has data sovereignty?

faq.a: The episodes mention it as a standard behind documented access controls, for example in finance projects using Power BI, and as one of the standards that Microsoft Purview governance and SharePoint audit-ready document management should support.
faq.q: How does SOC 2 come up in Power BI and Microsoft 365 governance discussions?

soc-2.long:
SOC 2 is a System and Organization Controls audit report that is based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. It is commonly requested by enterprise customers who need to evaluate the security controls of service providers and SaaS vendors before trusting them with business data. Rather than being a product or a technical setting, SOC 2 is an independent attestation: it describes how a provider designs and operates its controls, and customers read the report as part of their vendor and risk assessment.

In practice, SOC 2 appears in procurement and compliance conversations. A provider that builds a software-as-a-service platform is often asked for a SOC 2 report by prospective customers, and an organization that handles regulated data may need to show that its own access controls and configurations stand up to the same kind of audit. The M365.FM episodes treat SOC 2 mainly in this role, as one of several compliance standards that appear next to GDPR, ISO 27001, HIPAA and CMMC when Microsoft 365 and Power Platform workloads are designed.

The episode "Building Multi-Tenant SaaS with Power Pages and Dataverse" mentions SOC 2 in the context of building a SaaS application. It describes the choice between single-tenant and multi-tenant models, where a single-tenant setup gives each customer a dedicated environment and a multi-tenant model serves many customers from one shared system. The episode says that Power Pages supports strong security and compliance with SOC 2 and GDPR standards, and it pairs this with points about continuous monitoring, shared infrastructure, auto-scaling and regular spending reviews.

In "Build Audit-Ready Document Management with SharePoint and Purview", SOC 2 is named alongside ISO 27001 and GDPR as a standard that an audit-ready Enterprise Content Management system in the cloud should align with. The episode outlines a structured approach that includes defining ownership, lifecycle management and data loss prevention (DLP) measures. It stresses clear policies, sensitivity labels and regular audits to support compliance and to reduce insider risks. Here SOC 2 is part of the audit pressure that document governance has to withstand.

The episode "Can Copilot Replace Power BI Developers?" places SOC 2 in the financial services setting. It states that in finance, access controls must be documented for SOC 2 audits, and that documenting access controls and AI instruction configurations is essential. The same passage contrasts this with HIPAA in healthcare, where the episode notes that row-level security bypass can expose protected health information and recommends implementing object-level security and keeping audit logs, and with government projects that require data to stay in approved regions. The takeaway offered is that a tool may support many compliance needs, but the organization still has to verify that its reports meet each requirement.

"AI-Powered Metadata Classification for Microsoft 365 Governance" lists SOC 2 among the standards, together with GDPR, CMMC and HIPAA, that can be addressed through Microsoft Purview. The episode links this to the Unified Catalog, which helps discover data and automate tag management, and to AI features such as auto-tagging, lineage insights and AI-based policy management working across Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive. The stated aim is to keep data ready for audits.

Finally, "7-Step Microsoft 365 Sovereign Tenant Governance Framework" draws a boundary around what SOC 2 means. The episode says that compliance certifications like SOC 2 or ISO 27001 do not equate to sovereignty, and that organizations must run their own assessments to confirm they meet their specific sovereignty needs. Taken together, the episodes present SOC 2 as a useful assurance signal for security controls and audit readiness, while making clear that it does not replace the organization's own governance decisions.

solutions-partner-designation.desc: Solutions Partner designation: Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program status per solution area, earned via the Partner Capability Score, replacing Silver and Gold competencies.

faq.a: It is a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program designation awarded per solution area, such as Modern Work, Security or Data & AI. A partner earns it by reaching the required Partner Capability Score.
faq.q: What is the Solutions Partner designation?

faq.a: It replaced the former Silver and Gold competencies. According to the M365.FM episode on partner designation restructuring, legacy designations no longer qualify for incentives.
faq.q: What did the Solutions Partner designation replace?

faq.a: By reaching the required Partner Capability Score in a given solution area. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" describes this as meeting specific customer outcome criteria.
faq.q: How does a partner earn a designation?

solutions-partner-designation.long:
The Solutions Partner designation is a status within the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program that is awarded per solution area, for example Modern Work, Security or Data & AI. A partner earns it by reaching the required Partner Capability Score for that area. The designation replaced the former Silver and Gold competencies, which means that the older competency model no longer serves as the basis for partner benefits.

The purpose of the designation is to show that a partner meets defined, measurable requirements in a specific solution area. Instead of a single general competency level, the model works area by area. A partner that is active in several areas can pursue a designation for each of them, and each designation is tied to its own thresholds. The M365.FM episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" notes that each solution area has specific thresholds that must be met, and that understanding these levels and criteria helps a partner position itself within the program.

The score behind the designation is the Partner Capability Score, which is introduced in Microsoft's partner documentation. Reaching the required score in a solution area is the condition for the designation. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Partner Journey: From Enrollment to Growth" describes this in terms of customer outcome criteria: partners can achieve a Solutions Partner designation by meeting specific criteria tied to customer outcomes. The same episode lists related building blocks of the partner journey, including access to training and marketing resources through the Microsoft Partner Program, the use of the Microsoft Partner Center to manage partnerships and track performance, and advanced specializations that can add credibility and open further business opportunities.

The transition away from Silver and Gold is a recurring theme in the episodes. According to "The FY26 Partner Designation Restructuring Is Coming — Most Partners Aren't Ready", legacy designations such as the Silver and Gold competencies no longer qualify for incentives, and from October 1, 2023 only partners who achieve the new Microsoft Solutions Partner designation are eligible for those benefits. The episode frames this as a reason to adapt partner strategy to the new requirements and lists anticipated benefits of the restructuring, such as enhanced market recognition. The episode "How to Become a High-Performing Microsoft Partner" states that the new model replaces the Silver and Gold standards by January 22, 2025 and that transitioning to the Solutions Partner designation is essential for continued benefits. The two episodes give different dates for the replacement, so partners should check the current dates in the official partner documentation before planning.

In practice, a partner deciding how to approach the designation typically has to identify which solution areas match its business, understand the Partner Capability Score thresholds for those areas, and track progress through Partner Center. The episodes also describe the program benefits as being organized into three packages, and they point to performance metrics as the way a partner demonstrates its standing. Because the designation depends on measurable results rather than on a one-time qualification, ongoing attention to customer success and to the underlying metrics is part of keeping the status.

In summary, the Solutions Partner designation is the current per-area recognition in the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program. It is earned by reaching the required Partner Capability Score, it superseded the Silver and Gold competencies, and it is the status that governs eligibility for program incentives and benefits. The related M365.FM episodes treat it as a central step in the partner journey, from enrollment through growth, and as the main point to address for partners still operating under the legacy competency model.

spec-kit.desc: Spec Kit is GitHub's open-source toolkit for spec-driven development with AI coding agents, using a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.

faq.a: Spec Kit is GitHub's open-source, MIT-licensed toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured processes, templates and documented outcomes. Its core process is Spec-Driven Development, built around a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.
faq.q: What is Spec Kit?

faq.a: It requires Python 3.11 or newer, uv and a supported AI coding agent, on Linux, macOS or Windows. Offline and air-gapped use and private catalogs are supported.
faq.q: What does Spec Kit require to run?

faq.a: The episode "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" describes it as the enforcement layer that binds architectural intent to executable rules. It says Spec Kit integrates with Microsoft Entra to lock identity policies and to support compliance reporting.
faq.q: How does the M365.FM episode describe Spec Kit?

spec-kit.long:
Spec Kit is an open-source, MIT-licensed toolkit from GitHub that gives AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates and documented outcomes. Its core process is Spec-Driven Development, in which a written specification, rather than an ad hoc prompt, drives what the agent builds. The toolkit is organized around four artifacts: a constitution, specifications, plans and tasks.

In the standard workflow, a constitution is set up once per project. It states guiding principles such as code quality, testing and maintainability. For each feature, commands are then run in the agent chat. The specify command describes what to build, plan sets the technical approach, and tasks breaks the plan into work items. The implement and converge steps build the code and check it until convergence is reported. Optional steps cover clarification, checklists and consistency analysis. This sequence moves from intent to executable work in a defined order.

Bundled extensions add further processes. A bug-fixing extension ends in a verified, partial or failed verdict, and an idea-assessment extension ends in go, needs-clarification or kill. Custom processes can be assembled from integrations, extensions, presets, workflows and bundles. Community catalogs can be searched, though the documentation warns that listings are not audits or endorsements. Spec Kit requires Python 3.11 or newer, uv and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS or Windows. Offline and air-gapped use and private catalogs are supported.

The M365.FM episode "How AI-Generated Identity Configuration Breaks Entra Security" (2025-12-31) places Spec Kit in a Microsoft identity context. There it is described as the enforcement layer that binds architectural intent to executable rules. According to the episode, architectural intent serves as a blueprint for system design, guiding technology choices and keeping them aligned with business goals. Enforcing that intent is said to improve reliability and security by validating that security controls function as intended.

The episode also says that Spec Kit integrates with Microsoft Entra to lock identity policies, supporting compliance with governance frameworks. It further says that automating compliance reporting with Spec Kit simplifies documentation and speeds up auditing, that strict permissions management minimizes unauthorized access to sensitive data and resources, and that real-time monitoring and alerts help identify compliance problems. These points are the episode's account of how the toolkit is used in that scenario, whereas the repository documentation describes the general spec-driven workflow.

Typical decisions around Spec Kit concern how much of a project's intent to capture in the constitution and specifications, which extensions or presets to adopt, and whether to use community catalogs or a private one. Teams working in restricted environments can rely on the offline and air-gapped support. Because the toolkit shapes how an AI coding agent produces code, it is relevant wherever AI-generated output, such as identity configuration for Microsoft Entra, needs to be checked against stated rules before it is accepted.

splunk.desc: Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data, used for log aggregation and SIEM, and discussed in M365.FM security episodes.

faq.a: Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data, used for log aggregation and SIEM. The M365.FM episodes mention it for centralized security monitoring and as a destination for telemetry and Azure data.
faq.q: What is Splunk used for?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" describes Splunk Enterprise Security as pay-per-ingested data plus a license, with a higher upfront cost but more control. Microsoft Sentinel is described as pay-per-data ingestion, with costs that rise with log volume.
faq.q: How does Splunk Enterprise Security pricing compare with Microsoft Sentinel in the episodes?

faq.a: The episode "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained" lists configuring integrations such as the Splunk Add-on as one step when working with Azure Event Hubs. Data is first sent to an Event Hub, for example using Azure Monitor.
faq.q: How can Azure data be sent to Splunk?

splunk.long:
Splunk is software for searching, monitoring and analyzing machine-generated data. It is typically used for log aggregation and as a SIEM (security information and event management) platform, where events from many systems are collected in one place so that security teams can search them, monitor them and look for anomalies. In the M365.FM episodes, Splunk appears mainly in a security operations context and as one of several tools that can sit alongside Microsoft services.

The episode "Microsoft Sentinel - Simply Explained" places Splunk Enterprise Security next to other SIEM and security options. In its pricing comparison, Microsoft Sentinel is described as pay-per-data ingestion, where costs rise with log volume. CrowdStrike Falcon is described as priced per endpoint, with a higher base price but lower add-on costs. Splunk Enterprise Security is described as pay-per-ingested data plus a license, with a higher upfront cost but more control. The episode lists data ingestion volume and retention settings as cost factors to consider when evaluating Microsoft Sentinel, noting that retention settings after the first 90 days may incur costs. The episode summary for this topic also frames a security operations stack being consolidated from Splunk into Microsoft Sentinel, which is a common decision point when organizations weigh a separate SIEM against a Microsoft-native one.

In "Azure Event Hubs - Simply Explained", Splunk shows up as an integration target. The episode's setup steps include creating an Event Hub namespace in the Azure portal, sending data to the Event Hub using Azure Monitor, setting up authentication with Azure AD, assigning roles for data access and configuring integrations such as the Splunk Add-on. This describes a pattern in which streaming data from Azure is forwarded to Splunk for analysis, so Splunk can remain part of the pipeline even when the data originates in Azure services.

Two episodes connect Splunk to Microsoft Copilot security. In "Protect Microsoft Copilot with Purview, DLP, and Insider Risk with Alan Cox [MVP]", Splunk Enterprise Security is named among the solutions to explore, together with Opsin, Wiz and CrowdStrike Falcon, to strengthen security posture alongside Microsoft Purview controls such as sensitivity labels, DLP and activity-log monitoring. In "Secure a Microsoft Copilot Rollout with Microsoft Purview", a table of tools describes Splunk Enterprise Security as providing centralized monitoring and analytics for Copilot activity and detecting anomalies and violations. In that table, Opsin helps security teams understand what Copilot can access and detect oversharing risks, while Microsoft Purview classifies and labels information. The episode pairs these with permission hygiene audits to enforce least-privilege access.

Splunk also appears in an automation context. In "Build Self-Healing Automation with Telemetry and Observability", it is listed among the connector options for telemetry integration, described as a source for logs and telemetry data. The same list includes Telegraf, NLog, Open Telemetry, Serilog, Fluent Bit and Logstash, and the episode notes that Microsoft Power Automate can link such sources to workflows so that responses can be automated based on real-time insights.

Across these episodes, Splunk is treated as one option in a wider tooling landscape rather than a Microsoft product. The recurring decisions are whether to keep Splunk as a separate SIEM, how its ingestion-based licensing compares with Microsoft Sentinel's pay-per-ingestion model, and how Azure Event Hubs or other connectors feed data into it.

sql-analytics-endpoint.desc: The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses.

faq.a: It is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses. It lets users query lakehouse data with SQL.
faq.q: What is the SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: No. It is described as read-only, so it is used for querying and analytics rather than for changing tables.
faq.q: Can the SQL analytics endpoint be used to write data?

faq.a: The episode says that using it as the default path for every workload is a major driver of capacity unit consumption, so routing all workloads through it can raise capacity use.
faq.q: Why does the SQL analytics endpoint matter for capacity?

sql-analytics-endpoint.long:
The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL surface over Delta tables that Microsoft Fabric provisions for items such as lakehouses. It gives people and tools a familiar SQL way to query data that is stored in OneLake, without requiring them to work through Spark. Microsoft documents the feature in its lakehouse SQL endpoint article under the Fabric data engineering section.

In practice, the endpoint is used for interactive analytics and for SQL-based reporting on lakehouse data. One episode describes the Lakehouse SQL Analytics Endpoint as a dedicated endpoint for running lakehouse SQL queries and interactive analytics. According to that episode, performance is helped by separating compute from storage, which allows compute resources to be scaled for query-heavy workloads, and by using optimized formats such as Delta tables to reduce IO and speed up query planning and execution. Because the surface is read-only, it is a way to read and analyze data, not a place where tables are written or transformed.

The endpoint also acts as a connection point for external tools. An episode on the Fabric data warehouse notes that the SQL analytics endpoint connects with third-party tools such as SQL Server Management Studio, so that users can run queries in an environment they already know. This is one reason the endpoint is often the first access path that SQL-oriented teams reach for.

The SQL analytics endpoint also has a cost dimension. The short description of the topic notes that, in the episode, using it as the default path for every workload is a major driver of capacity unit consumption. The takeaway is that the endpoint is convenient, but routing every workload through it is not neutral from a capacity standpoint. Choosing deliberately between SQL access and other ways of working with lakehouse data is part of managing capacity in Microsoft Fabric.

Governance and lineage are another area where the endpoint appears. The episode "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Governance and Data Lineage" explains that lineage is shown at the artifact level, with the lakehouse and the warehouse appearing as separate nodes even when they share data in OneLake. It adds that a SQL analytics endpoint in a lakehouse can sometimes create extra nodes in the lineage view, and that different connection methods can create multiple nodes for the same source or destination. The episode also states that the lakehouse and warehouse cannot currently be merged into a single lineage node.

The topic is covered in several M365.FM episodes. "Optimize Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Performance" discusses how the endpoint affects performance. "Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse - Simply Explained" places it within the wider lakehouse picture, alongside OneLake, Delta tables and the medallion flow from raw files to trusted tables. "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained" mentions it as the way third-party SQL tools connect. Together, these episodes frame the SQL analytics endpoint as a read-only SQL access layer over Delta data whose use should be weighed against capacity consumption, performance needs and lineage clarity.

sql-database-in-fabric.desc: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric is a transactional database on the Azure SQL Database engine whose data is automatically replicated into OneLake for analytics.

faq.a: It is a transactional SQL database inside Microsoft Fabric, built on the same SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database. It is part of the Fabric Database workload and serves as an operational OLTP store.
faq.q: What is SQL database in Microsoft Fabric?

faq.a: Data is automatically replicated into OneLake as Delta Lake parquet files, so it is available for analytics almost in real time. An SQL analytics endpoint is also created automatically in the workspace.
faq.q: How does its data become available for analytics?

faq.a: Billing runs through Fabric capacity. Access is authenticated with Microsoft Entra and requires read permission on the database item.
faq.q: How is SQL database in Microsoft Fabric billed and accessed?

sql-database-in-fabric.long:
SQL database in Microsoft Fabric is a developer-friendly transactional database that runs inside Microsoft Fabric. It is built on the same SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database and belongs to the Fabric Database workload. Its main role is that of an operational OLTP store: applications write and read transactional data in it, while the same data becomes available for analytics inside the Fabric platform.

The central mechanism is automatic replication. Data stored in the database is replicated into OneLake as Delta Lake parquet files, so it is available for analytical use almost in real time. An SQL analytics endpoint is created automatically in the workspace, which gives analytical workloads a way to query the replicated data without building a separate pipeline. This links transactional and analytical workloads in one environment, a combination that the documentation names as typical scenarios such as translytical applications, operational data stores and reverse ETL, alongside intelligent applications.

Developers can work with the database through several tools. The Fabric portal offers a web query editor, and SQL Server Management Studio, the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot are also supported. Further features described in the documentation include automatic tuning with automatic index creation, vector data types for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, a GraphQL API, and Git integration. On the security side, the documentation lists row-level and object-level security, customer-managed keys at workspace level, SQL auditing, and sharing without granting workspace access. Authentication uses Microsoft Entra, and access requires read permission on the database item.

Billing for the database runs through Fabric capacity rather than through separate Azure SQL pricing constructs. This matters when deciding between this item and a standalone Azure SQL Database, because consumption is tied to the capacity that the workspace already uses. The documentation also lists limits that influence that decision: only the default connection policy is supported, elastic pools in the Azure SQL sense do not exist, and some monitoring features are still in preview.

In the context of M365.FM, the product appears in the episode "Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Simply Explained". That episode points listeners to training material that includes a module titled "Get started with SQL Database in Microsoft Fabric", described as covering the basics of SQL databases within the platform. It sits in a list of learning resources next to modules on real-time data processing, data science, designing scalable semantic models and Microsoft Fabric IQ fundamentals. The episode frames these modules as a foundation for understanding and navigating Microsoft Fabric.

Taken together, SQL database in Microsoft Fabric fits situations where an application needs a familiar relational engine for transactions and where the resulting data should flow into OneLake without manual export steps. Because it shares its engine with Azure SQL Database, existing SQL skills and tools carry over, while the automatic mirroring into Delta parquet files connects it to the analytical side of Fabric.

sql-server-management-studio.desc: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is Microsoft's free environment for managing SQL Server and Azure SQL databases, writing queries and inspecting execution plans.

faq.a: SSMS is Microsoft's free integrated environment for managing SQL Server and Azure SQL databases. It is used to write queries and inspect execution plans, among other management tasks.
faq.q: What is SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)?

faq.a: The episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" suggests testing connectivity from the gateway server to the database with tools like SSMS. This helps confirm whether the database port, such as 1433 for SQL Server, is reachable.
faq.q: How can SSMS help troubleshoot Power BI gateway connection problems?

faq.a: The episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" recommends T-SQL for scheduled jobs, maintenance scripts and integration with SQL Server Agent or SSMS. It also names SSMS among SQL Server-specific tools for which T-SQL is the better fit.
faq.q: When do the episodes recommend SSMS together with T-SQL?

sql-server-management-studio.long:
SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is Microsoft's free integrated environment for managing SQL Server and Azure SQL databases. It is the tool database administrators and developers commonly use to connect to a database, write and run queries, and inspect execution plans. Official documentation for the product is published on Microsoft Learn.

In practice, SSMS serves as the working interface between a person and a SQL Server instance or an Azure SQL database. Queries are written in T-SQL, Microsoft's dialect of SQL, and executed from the tool; the results and the way the engine processed the query can then be examined. Looking at execution plans is one of the typical uses named in the product description, and it is a common step when a query behaves unexpectedly or needs to be understood in more detail.

The M365.FM episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" places SSMS within the SQL Server ecosystem. It recommends T-SQL for maintenance and automation work, such as scheduled jobs, maintenance scripts and integration with SQL Server Agent or SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). It also lists SSMS alongside Azure Data Studio and SQL CLR as SQL Server-specific tooling: teams that rely on these tools are advised to use T-SQL, while standard SQL is described as preferable for generic, cross-platform tools. In that framing, choosing SSMS goes together with choosing the SQL Server-specific T-SQL dialect.

SSMS also appears as a diagnostic tool in connectivity scenarios. The episode "Troubleshoot the Power BI On-Premises Data Gateway" suggests testing connectivity from the gateway server to the database using tools like SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). The idea is to confirm that the gateway server can reach the database port, such as port 1433 for SQL Server, before looking elsewhere. The same episode advises allowing outbound traffic on ports 443 (HTTPS) and 5671–5672 as well as 9350–9354 for Azure Service Bus, and recommends asking the IT team to review firewall and proxy settings if connection errors occur. Because SSMS connects to the database directly from the machine it runs on, a successful connection from the gateway server helps separate database-side problems from network or gateway configuration problems.

The episode "Connect Azure SQL to Copilot Studio Through a Data Gateway" mentions SSMS in the context of GitHub Copilot. Its troubleshooting steps include checking for a stable internet connection, checking whether the GitHub Copilot service is temporarily down, and refreshing credentials by selecting the option from the Copilot badge in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS). It also advises contacting the IT department to confirm whether Copilot has been disabled by an administrator. The same episode covers firewall settings that can block access to a SQL database and recommends making sure the firewall allows traffic from the necessary IP addresses.

Taken together, the episodes show SSMS in three roles: as the main tool for working with T-SQL on SQL Server and Azure SQL, as a quick way to test whether a database is reachable from a given machine, and as a place where Copilot-related features can be accessed and their sign-in state refreshed. Decisions around SSMS usually concern the surrounding ecosystem: whether the team works mainly with SQL Server-specific features, whether alternatives such as Azure Data Studio are needed, and whether network rules such as firewall and proxy settings allow the connection to be established at all.

stable-diffusion.desc: Stable Diffusion is a family of text-to-image and image-to-image generative models, available in Azure AI Foundry and discussed in M365.FM for GPU performance diagnosis.

faq.a: Stable Diffusion is a family of generative models that create images from text and can transform input images while keeping their basic structure. Versions such as Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large are offered through Azure AI Foundry.
faq.q: What is Stable Diffusion?

faq.a: Customers create an Azure AI Foundry project, deploy the models from the model catalog with managed compute, and call them through an API endpoint or the playground. Azure AI Content Safety is on by default and cannot be turned off.
faq.q: How is Stable Diffusion used in Azure AI Foundry?

faq.a: The episode "Diagnose GPU Underutilization and CPU Fallback in AI Systems" uses a Stable Diffusion workload to show how silent CPU fallback in ONNX Runtime, version mismatches across CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and ONNX Runtime, and container misconfiguration can leave a GPU underused.
faq.q: What does M365.FM say about Stable Diffusion performance problems?

stable-diffusion.long:
Stable Diffusion is a family of generative visual models that create images from text prompts and can also transform existing images. It is developed by Stability AI. According to a Microsoft Tech Community announcement, the models are available in Azure AI Foundry, which places them within the Microsoft ecosystem for teams that want to add image generation to their applications.

In the Azure AI Foundry announcement, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large is described as the most capable member of the Stable Diffusion family and as a model with several billion parameters. Two related offerings build on it and on earlier work: Stable Image Ultra builds on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, while Stable Image Core builds on an improved SDXL. The models generate images from text at roughly one megapixel. They also support image-to-image generation, which changes an input picture while keeping its basic structure, for example for style transfer or restoration. The post lists uses in advertising, media, gaming, education, e-commerce, and publishing. Performance claims in the announcement come from the vendor.

To use the models, customers need an Azure AI Foundry project. The models are deployed from the model catalog with managed compute and are then called through an API endpoint or tried in the playground. The announcement also names limits that affect how the models should be used. They are not trained to depict real people or historical events factually, so they suit creative work rather than tasks where authenticity is critical. Azure AI Content Safety is enabled by default and cannot be turned off, which matters for teams planning moderation and governance around generated content.

In M365.FM, Stable Diffusion appears mainly as a realistic example workload for performance engineering. The episode "Diagnose GPU Underutilization and CPU Fallback in AI Systems" treats a slow AI system as a forensic case. It walks through a Stable Diffusion workload under concurrency, with strict P95 latency objectives and GPU hardware that looks adequate on paper, even though dashboards look healthy and the models appear to work. Rather than blaming parameters or architectures, the episode follows the evidence through the whole compute pipeline. It traces how silent CPU fallback in ONNX Runtime, subtle version mismatches across CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and ONNX Runtime, and container misconfiguration combine into one problem that turns an accelerator into what the episode calls an expensive heater.

The episode "Enforce AI Agent Security Controls at Execution Time" also mentions stable diffusion models, though in a different context. In its excerpt, the term is used for an approach that integrates stylistic images with structural conditions to generate facade images that keep both aesthetic appeal and structural integrity. This is framed as part of a discussion about the difference between perception and reality, so it is a side reference rather than a description of the Azure offering.

Taken together, the sources point to two typical decisions around Stable Diffusion. The first is whether to consume it as a managed model through Azure AI Foundry, accepting the stated limits and default content safety, or to run it in a self-managed stack. The second, relevant to self-managed or containerised inference, is how to verify that the workload actually runs on the GPU and that runtime and driver versions are compatible, since the episode shows that a workload can appear to function while quietly falling back to the CPU and missing latency targets.

standard-channels.desc: Standard channels are the default Microsoft Teams channel type, visible to all team members and backed by folders in the team's SharePoint site.

faq.a: A standard channel is the default channel type in Microsoft Teams. It is visible and accessible to every member of the team, including invited guests, and is used for discussions, project updates, file sharing and announcements.
faq.q: What is a standard channel in Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: Files are stored in the team's SharePoint site, a Teams-connected site. Each channel appears as a folder in the document library, and the Files tab maps to that folder.
faq.q: Where are files in a standard channel stored?

faq.a: Standard channels are open to all team members, while private channels only reach explicitly added members and guests. Shared channels include channel members and B2B direct connect users across teams.
faq.q: How do standard channels differ from private and shared channels?

standard-channels.long:
Standard channels are the default channel type in Microsoft Teams. A standard channel is visible and accessible to every member of the parent team, including invited guests, and it serves collaboration around a topic, project or department. Because access follows team membership, no separate permission group has to be maintained for each channel.

Typical uses named in Microsoft's documentation include group discussions, project updates, file sharing, announcements, knowledge sharing and social topics. Every team also has a General channel, which stays at the top of the channel list and suits announcements and general conversation. Conversations and shared files can be searched within a channel and across teams, which supports finding earlier decisions and documents.

File storage works through SharePoint. All standard channels of a team use the same SharePoint site, a Teams-connected site. Each channel appears as a folder in that site's document library, and the Files tab in the channel maps to that folder. This is the main technical difference from private channels, which the episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works" describes as getting their own SharePoint site collection and a separate file library that only channel members can access. Standard channels, by contrast, map to folders inside the team's primary SharePoint site.

Standard channels differ from the other two channel types. Private channels only reach members and guests who were explicitly added, which makes them the option the documentation points to for sensitive content. Shared channels include channel members as well as B2B direct connect users across teams, which allows collaboration beyond a single team or organization. The episode "Microsoft Teams Channels vs Chat: When to Use Each" summarizes the three types in this way: standard channels let all team members join discussions and access files and suit general communication, private channels limit access to selected members for confidential topics, and shared channels enable collaboration with external users. It recommends choosing the channel type based on the needs of the project.

Permissions in a standard channel depend on the role. Owners can create or delete channels, add members, edit names and descriptions, and manage tabs and apps. Members can perform some of these actions if the owner enables it. Guests can do so only if an admin enables it in Entra ID. The episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works" also mentions channel moderation, where team owners can restrict who may start new posts while others can reply, which is useful for announcement-style channels.

In practice, the decision around standard channels is mostly about structure. Because every team member sees every standard channel, they fit topics where openness is wanted, while confidential discussions are better placed in private channels. The Microsoft Learn page names no licenses or numeric limits for standard channels, so those details are not covered here.

store-commerce-app.desc: The Store Commerce app is the point-of-sale app of Dynamics 365 Commerce for in-store staff, covering checkout, assisted selling and store operations on several platforms.

faq.a: It is the point-of-sale app of Dynamics 365 Commerce for in-store staff. Cashiers use it at checkout counters, and sales associates can use supported mobile devices around the store.
faq.q: What is the Store Commerce app?

faq.a: According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Commerce - Simply Explained", it supports Windows, iOS, Android and macOS. The documentation describes the Windows application in detail.
faq.q: Which platforms does the Store Commerce app run on?

faq.a: Offline mode is supported in the in-app deployment variant, where all components run locally and SQL Server is required. The hybrid variant loads its interface from the Commerce Scale Unit and does not support offline mode.
faq.q: Does the Store Commerce app work offline?

store-commerce-app.long:
The Store Commerce app is the point-of-sale application of Dynamics 365 Commerce. It gives physical store employees fast access to the information and functions they need while customers are standing in front of them. Cashiers can use it at traditional checkout counters, while sales associates can use supported mobile devices around the store. According to the episode "Dynamics 365 Commerce - Simply Explained", Store Commerce supports environments including Windows, iOS, Android and macOS, which gives retailers flexibility in how employees interact with the platform across desktop, tablet and phone form factors.

The documentation describes the Windows application as a WPF shell that hosts the Microsoft Edge WebView2 control to display Store Commerce for web. In this way it combines Modern POS and Cloud POS in one application and renders its interface with the Chromium engine instead of the UWP framework. The app serves several roles: cashiers, sales associates, inventory and warehouse staff, and store managers. Its functions include cash-and-carry sales, register and shift management, customer engagement, assisted selling, endless aisle, order fulfillment, inventory handling and reporting.

Two deployment variants are described in the documentation. In the in-app variant, all components run locally and offline mode is supported. In the hybrid variant, the interface loads from the Commerce Scale Unit and offline mode is not available. This difference matters when a store must keep trading without a stable network connection, so the choice of variant is a typical decision in a rollout. The documentation also notes that MPOS and hybrid apps were deprecated.

The documented requirements for the Windows app include a supported Windows 10, Windows 11 or Windows Server edition, WebView2, the listed .NET runtimes, and SQL Server for offline use. A Commerce headquarters environment is also needed, where the register and the device are configured before the app can be used. Several limits apply: ARM processors are unsupported, the app must not run with elevated rights, and UWP point-of-service devices are not supported, so OPOS drivers are needed for peripherals instead.

In the wider Dynamics 365 Commerce picture, the episode places Store Commerce in the physical store layer. The same episode points out that people still perform the physical work of picking, packing, shipping and handing products to customers, and Store Commerce is the tool that connects store staff to the commerce platform during that work. Planning for the app usually involves the target device types, the choice between in-app and hybrid deployment, the need for offline operation, and the setup of registers and devices in headquarters.

For current prerequisites, supported platforms and installation guidance, the official Microsoft documentation for Store Commerce in Dynamics 365 Commerce is the reference. The episode offers a plain-language introduction, while the documentation covers the technical details of the Windows application.

teams-admin-center.desc: The Microsoft Teams admin center is the admin portal for Microsoft Teams, used for usage reports, team templates and Teams policies.

faq.a: It is the admin portal for Microsoft Teams, used for usage reports, team templates and Teams policies. The episodes also describe using it for app setup policies, enabling Copilot and viewing activity and user metrics.
faq.q: What is the Microsoft Teams admin center used for?

faq.a: The episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane" says it is not. It describes the admin center as a downstream service console, while decisions about access and enforced policy come from upstream identity and compliance services.
faq.q: Is the Teams admin center the central place for Teams governance?

faq.a: According to "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards", an administrator opens Teams Apps and then Setup policies, edits the Global policy or creates a custom one, and adds Connections under Installed Apps and Pinned Apps.
faq.q: How is the Teams admin center used to pin an app such as Viva Connections?

teams-admin-center.long:
The Microsoft Teams admin center is the administration portal for Microsoft Teams. It is part of Microsoft Teams and gives administrators a place to review usage reports, work with team templates and manage Teams policies. Administrators open it when they need to see how Teams is being used or to change how specific Teams features behave for users in the organization.

In day-to-day administration, the admin center covers several recurring tasks. One is monitoring: the episode "Design a Microsoft Teams Structure That Actually Works" lists the admin center among the tools for tracking how teams use channels and meetings, noting that it shows activities and user metrics. The same episode places it next to Microsoft 365 Usage Analytics, the Teams Usage Report, the Audit Log and third-party dashboard tools, each of which answers a slightly different question about adoption, messages, meetings, active users or compliance actions.

Another recurring task is policy and app configuration. The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" describes pinning the Viva Connections dashboard in Microsoft Teams through the admin center. According to the episode, an administrator goes to Teams Apps and then Setup policies, edits the Global (Org-wide default) policy or creates a custom setup policy, adds Connections under Installed Apps and under Pinned Apps, and then moves the Connections app into the desired position. This shows how the admin center is used to decide which apps appear for users and where they sit in the Teams client.

Feature enablement is a third use. In "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step", enabling Copilot in the Teams admin center is listed as one of the steps for customizing settings for the organization, alongside having the right Microsoft 365 subscription, reviewing data permissions, assigning licenses to users, providing training and monitoring usage. The admin center is therefore one stage in a wider rollout rather than the only switch involved.

The admin center also comes up in troubleshooting. The episode "Find Missing Microsoft Teams and Channels" explains that a team may be missing from a user's list because of membership changes, Teams policies, or because the team is hidden or archived by an owner. It adds that global admin actions through the Teams admin center or Microsoft 365 can change visibility, and it suggests checking Teams settings and the Microsoft admin center for policy restrictions or removal when a team or channel cannot be found.

The most pointed discussion of the product's role is in "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane". The episode challenges the idea that the Teams admin center is the central command for controlling Teams behavior and enforcing governance. It describes the admin center as a downstream service console rather than the authority that decides who gets in, what gets blocked or what policy is enforced. According to the episode, those decisions come from upstream services such as identity and compliance tools, and treating the admin center like a control tower leads to a misunderstanding of where governance actually happens.

Taken together, the episodes position the Microsoft Teams admin center as the place for Teams-specific reporting, policies, app setup and feature settings, while pointing out that identity and compliance controls sit in other services. Administrators designing governance for Microsoft Teams therefore typically consider the admin center together with those upstream services instead of relying on it alone.

teams-developer-portal.desc: Developer Portal for Teams, formerly App Studio, is Microsoft's tool for configuring, distributing and managing Microsoft Teams apps and editing the app manifest.

faq.a: It was formerly called App Studio. Apps that come from App Studio can be managed in Developer Portal for Teams.
faq.q: What was Developer Portal for Teams called before?

faq.a: It is used to configure, distribute and manage Microsoft Teams apps, including editing the app manifest, importing existing apps, adding owners and linking to app usage analytics and app validation.
faq.q: What can be done with Developer Portal for Teams?

faq.a: No. It is not available in GCC High, Department of Defense and 21Vianet-operated tenants. The documented workaround is to create the app in a regular tenant and upload it through Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: Is Developer Portal for Teams available in all tenants?

teams-developer-portal.long:
Developer Portal for Teams is a Microsoft tool for configuring, distributing and managing Microsoft Teams apps. It was formerly known as App Studio and serves as the main place where a Teams app project is set up, adjusted and handed off for distribution. It also supports collaboration, so colleagues can work together on the same app project.

In practice, the portal covers several stages of an app's life. A developer can create a new app by giving it a name, or import an existing app from its manifest file. If an app has already been published in the Teams admin center and registered in the portal, it can be replaced during import. The portal is also where the app manifest is edited, and the manifest is a central part of any Teams app because it defines how the app is described to Teams. Apps built with Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit in Visual Studio Code can be managed in the portal, as can apps that originate from App Studio. Because signing in is required, the portal ties app management to an authenticated user account.

Ownership and governance are part of the tool as well. Owners can be added to an app, and Teams Administrators or Global Administrators can claim apps that have no owner. The portal also links to app usage analytics and to app validation, which places monitoring and quality checks close to the place where the app is configured.

The episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions" places the tool in a typical first-app workflow. According to the episode, a developer registers the app in Azure Active Directory, sets the required permissions, and then uses App Studio or the Developer Portal for Teams to generate the app manifest and package the app as a .zip file. The package is then submitted to Teams for testing and approval. The same episode points out that the Microsoft Teams Toolkit handles much of the configuration, so developers can concentrate on building features and improving the user experience. The episode also describes the app manifest as a key part of a first Teams app.

Several limits are documented. The portal is not available in GCC High, Department of Defense and 21Vianet-operated tenants. The documented workaround is to create the app in a regular tenant and upload it through Microsoft Graph. Importing can fail with an error when the package contains nested folders or is missing required files. Apps that are published but not registered in the portal cannot be imported until an administrator files a support ticket.

For teams deciding how to work, the choice usually comes down to where the manifest and packaging are handled. The portal offers a browser-based way to edit the manifest, manage owners and reach analytics and validation, while toolkits in the development environment can take over much of the configuration. The two approaches are related, since apps created with Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit can still be managed in the portal.

teams-phone.desc: Teams Phone is Microsoft's cloud telephony in Microsoft Teams, offering business phone numbers via calling plans, direct routing or operator connect.

faq.a: Teams Phone, also known as Microsoft Teams Phone or Teams Calling, is cloud telephony in Microsoft Teams. It provides business phone numbers so that Teams can serve as a business phone system.
faq.q: What is Teams Phone?

faq.a: The facts name three models: calling plans, direct routing and operator connect. The migration episode lists the choice between calling plans and direct routing as part of migration planning.
faq.q: How can Teams Phone connect to the public telephone network?

faq.a: The episode "Teams Phone Migration: Moving From a PBX to Cloud Calling Without Surprises" names inventory and number planning, calling plans or direct routing, devices, emergency calling and user adoption.
faq.q: What should be planned when moving from a PBX to Teams Phone?

teams-phone.long:
Teams Phone, also called Microsoft Teams Phone or Teams Calling, is cloud telephony built into Microsoft Teams. It gives an organization business phone numbers and lets the Teams client take over the role of a traditional phone system. Microsoft developed the product, and it is part of Microsoft Teams. It is classified as a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Teams Phone is licensed as an add-on to Teams rather than being part of the base Teams product.

The main purpose of Teams Phone is to replace a traditional PBX with calling inside the Teams client. Instead of running separate telephony infrastructure, an organization can handle internal collaboration and external voice calls from a single application. The earlier name for the capability was Teams Telephony, and the episode material notes that it is now known as Microsoft Teams Phone. Older documentation and discussions may therefore still use the previous terms.

Three connection models are named in the available facts for linking Teams to the public telephone network: calling plans, direct routing and operator connect. Each describes a different way of obtaining and connecting business phone numbers. The choice between them is one of the central decisions in a telephony project, and the migration episode lists "calling plans or direct routing" as part of the planning work, alongside inventory and number planning, devices, emergency calling and user adoption.

Typical situations in which Teams Phone comes up are PBX replacement and the cloud migration of an existing telephone setup. The episode "Teams Phone Migration: Moving From a PBX to Cloud Calling Without Surprises" describes such a move as rarely a pure technology project, because numbers, devices, sites and people each run on their own timelines. It covers how to plan a migration, including taking inventory of what exists today, planning numbers, deciding on a connection model, selecting devices, handling emergency calling and supporting user adoption.

Other M365.FM episodes treat the topic from different angles. "Microsoft Teams Phone and Telephony | Simply Explained" is presented by Mirko Peters and explains how organizations can replace traditional PBX systems with a telephony platform integrated with Microsoft 365, supporting both internal collaboration and external voice calling. "Microsoft Teams Phone - Simply Explained" is a further explainer, but only a short description is on record for it. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" touches on Teams Phone in its FAQ, stating that Copilot can assist in scenarios involving Teams Phone and hybrid meetings, for example by transcribing audio and generating recaps for attendees who joined by phone. It adds that availability may depend on the organization's configuration and on whether Teams Phone audio is captured for transcription.

Teams Phone also appears in a recommended-listening list in the episode "Shadow Data Discovery and Governance with Microsoft Purview", where the Teams Telephony explainer is suggested for understanding Teams calling and communication foundations. This reflects how the topic connects to governance and compliance subjects in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem. Official documentation for the feature is published by Microsoft on Microsoft Learn under the Teams Phone System overview.

teams-templates.desc: Teams templates are predefined or custom Microsoft Teams structures with channels, tabs, apps and settings, managed in the Teams admin center for creating new teams.

faq.a: A template can hold the type, name, description, visibility, team settings, channels, tabs and apps. It cannot hold members, the team picture, files, connectors, or private and shared channels.
faq.q: What can a Teams template contain?

faq.a: They are managed in the Teams admin center or with PowerShell. Developers can also create teams from templates through Microsoft Graph.
faq.q: Where are Teams templates managed?

faq.a: Microsoft's prebuilt industry templates can be duplicated but not edited. A duplicate can serve as the basis for a custom template, and custom templates can also be created from scratch or from an existing team.
faq.q: Can the prebuilt industry templates be changed?

teams-templates.long:
Teams templates are predefined or custom Microsoft Teams structures that include channels, tabs, apps and settings. They are managed in the Teams admin center, and new teams can be created from them. According to Microsoft Learn, a team template defines the structure of a team for a particular business need or project, so administrators can roll out consistent teams and users can start collaboration spaces with predefined settings, channels and apps.

A template can hold the team type, name, description, visibility, team settings, channels, tabs and apps. Several items are not part of a template: members, the team picture, files, connectors, and private and shared channels. Each template also has size limits on channels, tabs per channel and apps, although more of these can be added after a team has been created. Sensitivity labels are not supported in GCC environments.

Templates can be created and managed in the Teams admin center or with PowerShell. Custom templates can be built from scratch, from an existing team, or from another template. Microsoft also supplies prebuilt industry templates. These can be duplicated but not edited, and some of them are connected templates that add SharePoint pages and lists as tabs. Developers can create teams from templates through Microsoft Graph as well.

Which templates users see is controlled by template policies. These policies determine which templates appear for which users and groups, so different parts of an organization can be offered different starting points. Typical decisions around Teams templates include whether to duplicate a prebuilt industry template or create a custom one, which channels, tabs and apps belong in a standard structure, and which groups of users should be able to see a given template.

In the M365.FM episode "Automate Microsoft 365 Governance Beyond Static Checklists", Teams templates appear in a list of governance automation practices. The episode recommends using Teams templates and provisioning solutions to enforce standards, alongside automating user and group provisioning and deprovisioning, implementing group expiration and renewal, and standardizing on automation platforms such as Power Automate, Microsoft Graph and Azure Automation. In that framing, templates are one building block for making team creation consistent rather than relying on manual checklists.

The episode "Microsoft Teams Governance with Entra ID as the Control Plane" lists Microsoft Teams templates among its key strategies for managing the Teams admin center. The episode says to use Microsoft Teams templates to streamline team setups. The same list covers relying on groups for tailored policies, controlling private channel creation for sensitive discussions, customizing meeting policies, establishing messaging policies for different user groups, managing app access, using analytics, and controlling external and guest access. Templates are presented as one part of a broader approach to consistent, governed team setup.

teams-toolkit.desc: Teams Toolkit, also called Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, is free Microsoft developer tooling for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams and Copilot.

faq.a: Teams Toolkit is free developer tooling from Microsoft for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams. It is now also called the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and covers agents and Copilot extensibility in Microsoft 365.
faq.q: What is Teams Toolkit?
