faq.a: According to the episode "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", it simplifies development by providing tools for provisioning and deploying cloud resources. It is used together with Visual Studio Code, Node.js and Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: What does the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit do in a Teams app project?

faq.a: Both are ways to extend Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episode "Copilot Studio vs Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit" compares them and highlights production concerns such as grounding, governance, monitoring and cost control.
faq.q: How does the toolkit relate to Copilot Studio?

teams-toolkit.long:
Teams Toolkit is developer tooling from Microsoft for building apps and agents for Microsoft Teams. It is now also known as the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, a name that reflects its wider scope: besides Teams apps, it supports agents and Copilot extensibility across Microsoft 365. In the knowledge base it is classified as a Microsoft tool and a developer tool, and it is listed as free.

The toolkit is used to create, run and publish extensions. Developers reach for it when a project needs custom code and control rather than a purely low-code approach. Microsoft's documentation describes the fundamentals of the toolkit on its Microsoft Learn platform pages. In the M365.FM episodes, the toolkit appears mainly as part of a developer's starting kit, rather than as a standalone subject.

One episode, "Build Microsoft Teams Apps with Bots, Tabs, and Extensions", lists the toolkit in a table of main tools and their purposes. According to the episode, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit simplifies the development process by providing tools for provisioning and deploying cloud resources. It appears alongside Visual Studio Code, which the episode describes as essential for JavaScript, TypeScript or SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, and Node.js, described as the back-end JavaScript runtime needed for app functionality. Microsoft Teams itself is named as required for collaboration and testing, and Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome are recommended for their developer tools when debugging.

The same toolkit shows up in the episodes about extending Microsoft 365 Copilot. "Extend Microsoft 365 Copilot with Agents, Plugins, and Connectors" names the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and Copilot Studio as the first essential tools and resources for starting copilot development. It also mentions a Microsoft 365 subscription (with or without a copilot license), a development environment setup, and admin permissions for sideloading custom apps. The Microsoft 365 Developer Program is described there as giving access to a dedicated sandbox environment suited to testing and prototyping copilot extensions. "Build Custom Microsoft 365 Copilot Plugins" lists the toolkit, together with the Yeoman Generator for Office Add-ins, as a way to scaffold and manage projects, and advises installing the latest version of Visual Studio with the Office/SharePoint development workload. It further notes that a Microsoft 365 developer account is needed for plugin development.

"Microsoft 365 Copilot Extensibility with Gautam Sheth [MVP]" describes custom tools that automate tasks, integrate apps and personalize workflows. The episode says that the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, connectors and APIs can be used to create agents that streamline daily work, and it gives examples of repetitive tasks that custom agents can handle.

A typical decision around the toolkit is whether to build with code or with a low-code tool. "Copilot Studio vs Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit" compares the two paths. The episode argues that rolling out Microsoft 365 Copilot is only the starting point and that production exposes harder challenges: grounding answers in authoritative sources, governance to prevent agent sprawl, monitoring for reliability, and licensing and cost controls. It suggests thinking in layers, from the foundation model and orchestrator to grounding, and mentions that agents can use the conversational reasoning of Microsoft 365 Copilot through the Search MCP server.

Because the toolkit targets Microsoft Teams as a host, it is closely related to Microsoft Teams, where many of the apps it produces run, including bots, tabs and extensions. Its alias, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, is the name used in most of the more recent episode material.

terraform.desc: Terraform from HashiCorp is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool that describes infrastructure in readable files and manages Azure through a provider.

faq.a: Terraform is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool from HashiCorp. It describes infrastructure in readable files that can be reviewed and run again, and it manages platforms such as Azure through providers.
faq.q: What is Terraform?

faq.a: Bicep is Azure-only and made by Microsoft, while Terraform works across several clouds, including Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The episodes also note that Terraform relies on a state file that must be managed carefully, whereas Bicep does not.
faq.q: How does Terraform differ from Bicep?

faq.a: The episode "Terraform - Simply Explained" describes plan and apply as a safety net. Terraform first shows what it intends to change, and the change is carried out only in the apply step.
faq.q: What do the plan and apply steps do in Terraform?

terraform.long:
Terraform, also called HashiCorp Terraform, is a multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code tool from HashiCorp. It describes infrastructure in files that can be read, reviewed and run again, and it connects to cloud platforms through providers, including a provider for Azure. It is classified as a developer tool and is closely tied to the practice of infrastructure as code.

The core idea is that infrastructure should not depend on manual steps. The episode "Terraform - Simply Explained" puts it this way: Terraform exists because Azure portal clicks cannot be rebuilt twice. Writing the infrastructure down as a file makes it repeatable, reviewable and easy to run again. That episode walks through the main building blocks in order: what Infrastructure as Code really means, what Terraform actually is, how providers let Terraform talk to a cloud, the plan and apply steps described as a safety net, the state file as Terraform's memory, modules for avoiding rebuilding the same thing, remote state for working with other people, and drift, where reality quietly diverges from what was written.

Several of these parts are what set Terraform's day-to-day use apart. Providers are the layer through which Terraform reaches a platform such as Azure, AWS or Google Cloud. The plan and apply workflow separates previewing a change from carrying it out. The state file records what Terraform manages, which is why the episodes stress handling it carefully. One of them warns that state files must be managed carefully to avoid issues, and another says Bicep's lack of native state management is a limitation, so state is a recurring point in the comparisons. Modules support reuse, and remote state matters once more than one person works on the same infrastructure.

In the Microsoft ecosystem, Terraform is most often compared with Bicep. Bicep is Azure-only and made by Microsoft, while Terraform spans several clouds. The episode "Terraform vs Azure Bicep: Which IaC Tool Should You Choose?" says Terraform stands out when multi-cloud infrastructure as code is needed, since the Terraform CLI and configuration files offer the same workflow across Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and many other platforms. The same episode describes Bicep files as simple to read and write, and notes that Bicep avoids the state-file handling that Terraform requires. It does not name a universal winner; the right choice depends on the organization's architecture and cloud strategy.

The episode "Bicep vs ARM Templates vs Terraform for Azure" places Terraform in a wider comparison with ARM templates and Bicep. It refreshes the role of ARM templates as a long-standing standard, introduces Bicep as a cleaner and more maintainable alternative, and compares readability, modular design and parameter handling. The episode "Infrastructure as Code - Simply Explained" covers the same tools, including Azure Bicep, ARM Templates, Terraform and PowerShell, and explains where each fits within the Microsoft ecosystem. It also links infrastructure as code to Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions, CI/CD pipelines, governance and security policies.

Another episode, "Azure Bicep at Scale: Modular Infrastructure as Code", lists limitations of Bicep such as no native state management and a smaller ecosystem than Terraform or Pulumi. Taken together, the episodes suggest that Terraform is a candidate when work spans more than Azure or when a mature provider ecosystem and a state-based workflow are wanted, while Bicep is the Azure-focused option.

threat-explorer.desc: Threat Explorer is a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 tool for searching email detections, delivery actions and campaigns across a tenant.

faq.a: Threat Explorer is a near real-time reporting tool in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2. It lets security teams search email detections, delivery actions and campaigns, and take actions such as remediating messages.
faq.q: What is Threat Explorer?

faq.a: Real-time detections, available in Plan 1, show only the state of a message at delivery. Threat Explorer offers more views, filtering with saved queries and actions, and also shows post-delivery activity.
faq.q: How does Threat Explorer differ from real-time detections?

faq.a: A Defender for Office 365 licence and suitable permissions are required. Permissions can come through Defender XDR roles, email and collaboration roles, or Entra roles, with least privilege advised.
faq.q: What is needed to access Threat Explorer?

threat-explorer.long:
Threat Explorer is a near real-time reporting tool in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 that helps security operations teams investigate and respond to threats. It is included in Plan 2 of Defender for Office 365. A lighter report, real-time detections, is available in Plan 1. Threat Explorer offers more views, more filtering including saved queries, and more actions than that real-time report. The tool is used to search email detections, delivery actions and campaigns across a tenant.

The tool is organized into views that cover all email, malware, phish, campaigns, content malware, and URL clicks. Analysts can filter by date range, message properties, file properties and threat properties. Charts can be pivoted by values such as delivery action, sender domain, and detection technology, which makes it possible to look at the same set of messages from several angles. Data can be exported as CSV for further analysis or reporting outside the portal.

Beyond reading data, Threat Explorer supports action. Admins can remediate selected messages, preview or download an email, or move into hunting. Preview and download work only while the message still exists in a cloud mailbox or quarantine. This is one practical difference from the real-time detections report, which shows only the state of a message at the time of delivery. Threat Explorer also shows post-delivery activity, so an investigation can follow what happened to a message after it reached the mailbox.

Access requires a Defender for Office 365 licence and suitable permissions. These can be granted through Defender XDR roles, email and collaboration roles, or Entra roles, and least privilege is advised. Teams that only hold Plan 1 work with the real-time detections report rather than the full Threat Explorer experience, which is a typical licensing decision to check before planning investigation workflows.

The M365.FM episode "Tune Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Against Phishing" places Threat Explorer in the context of ongoing tuning. According to the episode, Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing and mail flow rules are often not tuned together. It recommends layered policies per risk group, dynamic delivery, tighter impersonation protection, removal of conflicting transport rules, and weekly reviews that use Threat Explorer together with Message Trace. The episode frames Defender as a living system rather than a checklist, with Threat Explorer serving as one of the review tools.

The episode "Build Better Phishing Reports with Defender and Power BI" uses Threat Explorer from a reporting angle. It says that surface statistics do not equal risk, and that Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response (AIR), and user submissions reveal the narrative behind "blocked" totals. The episode points to near-miss telemetry, such as who clicked, who reported and how fast an incident was contained, as more informative than raw block counts. It also covers feeding this data into Power BI dashboards and normalizing data before visualizing it.

In practice, Threat Explorer is the place where analysts check what was detected, how a message was delivered, which campaign it belongs to and whether further remediation is needed. Its filtering, pivoting and export functions make it suited to both ad hoc investigations and recurring review routines.

transact-sql.desc: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL, used by SQL Server, Azure SQL Database and related SQL products and services to query and manage data.

faq.a: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL used by Microsoft SQL Server and related SQL products and services. According to Microsoft Learn, all tools and applications that talk to a SQL Server database do so by sending T-SQL commands.
faq.q: What is Transact-SQL (T-SQL)?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn reference lists SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Synapse Analytics and several Microsoft Fabric items such as the warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. Individual articles may apply only to certain products, as shown in their applies-to notes.
faq.q: Which Microsoft products does T-SQL apply to?

faq.a: The episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" suggests T-SQL when using Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL Database, when portability across vendors is not required, and when procedural logic is needed. Standard SQL is preferred for cloud-agnostic or multi-vendor systems.
faq.q: When should a team choose T-SQL over standard SQL?

transact-sql.long:
Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL, the structured query language for relational databases. It is the dialect used by Microsoft SQL Server and by related SQL products and services. The Microsoft Learn reference for the Database Engine states that all tools and applications that talk to a SQL Server database do so by sending T-SQL commands, which makes the language central to the Microsoft data platform.

In practice, T-SQL covers the statements that most people associate with working in a relational database. The reference names SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE as common statements for reading and changing data. Beyond these, the documentation links to system objects that administrators and developers query or call, including catalog views, dynamic management views, system functions and system stored procedures. Related languages such as XQuery and MDX are also referenced from the same documentation area.

The scope of T-SQL extends across several Microsoft products. According to the reference, it applies to SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Synapse Analytics and several Microsoft Fabric items, such as the warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. Individual articles may be valid only for certain products, which is indicated by the applies-to notes shown on each page. Checking those notes is therefore part of using the documentation correctly, especially when moving workloads between an on-premises SQL Server instance and a cloud service.

Several tools are built around T-SQL. The reference lists SQL Server Management Studio, the MSSQL extension for Visual Studio Code, SQL Server Data Tools and sqlcmd as tools that use the language. In SQL Server Management Studio, pressing F1 on a keyword opens the matching reference article, which gives a quick path from a statement in an editor to its documented syntax and behavior. Details on how T-SQL relates to SQL standards are covered in a separate document rather than on the reference entry page.

A recurring decision for data teams is whether to write standard SQL or to use T-SQL features. The M365.FM episode "SQL vs T-SQL: Key Differences for Microsoft Data Teams" addresses this with a checklist under the keyword t-sql vs sql. According to the episode, a team using Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL Database should prefer T-SQL, while multi-vendor or cloud-agnostic systems point toward standard SQL. On portability, the episode says standard SQL fits queries that must run across different relational database systems such as Oracle, MySQL and PostgreSQL, whereas T-SQL is the choice when portability is not required. The excerpt also lists procedural logic as a reason to use T-SQL, and the episode advises consulting Microsoft's documentation and testing T-SQL features in the target environment to get reliable and well-performing database operations.

For teams working with Microsoft data services, T-SQL is therefore both the everyday query language and a platform-specific layer on top of SQL. Understanding which statements and system objects are available in a given product, and which are portable, helps when planning migrations, choosing tooling and deciding how tightly to tie code to the Microsoft platform.

typescript.desc: TypeScript is a Microsoft programming language that adds static types to JavaScript to catch mistakes early, and it is used for Power Apps code components.

faq.a: TypeScript is a programming language from Microsoft that builds on JavaScript with static types to catch mistakes early. It is used, among other things, to write Power Apps code components.
faq.q: What is TypeScript?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Code Apps let teams build custom web applications with technologies such as React and TypeScript, developing locally and running within the Power Platform. App logic can be written in TypeScript or JavaScript using Visual Studio Code and the Power Apps SDK.
faq.q: How is TypeScript used in Power Apps Code Apps?

faq.a: The episode on PnP React Controls describes TypeScript as providing stronger typing and compile-time checks within a modern SPFx stack that also includes React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls.
faq.q: What role does TypeScript play in SharePoint Framework development?

typescript.long:
TypeScript is a programming language from Microsoft that builds on JavaScript by adding static types. The aim of those types is to catch mistakes early, before code runs, rather than leaving them to surface at runtime. In the Microsoft ecosystem it is used to write Power Apps code components, and it appears across other developer scenarios covered by M365.FM, including SharePoint Framework (SPFx) development, Power Apps Code Apps, infrastructure as code and AI-assisted software engineering.

Because TypeScript is built on JavaScript, teams that already know JavaScript can work with it without learning an entirely separate language. The core idea is stronger typing combined with compile-time checks. The episode "Stop Reinventing SPFx- Building Better SharePoint Solutions with PnP React Controls with Siddharth Vaghasia [MVP]" describes TypeScript as providing stronger typing and compile-time checks, and places it alongside React, Fluent UI, PnPjs and PnP React Controls as part of a modern SPFx technology stack. In that breakdown, no single framework carries a project; several technologies each play a defined role. TypeScript contributes the typing layer, Fluent UI helps custom solutions keep the familiar Microsoft user experience, and PnPjs simplifies interaction with SharePoint, Microsoft Graph and other Microsoft 365 services by replacing repetitive REST request code with reusable abstractions.

TypeScript is also central to Power Apps Code Apps. The episode "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" explains that Code Apps let teams create custom web applications using familiar coding tools within the Power Platform, drawing on modern web technologies such as React and TypeScript. These apps can be developed locally and run within the Power Platform. According to the episode, the significance lies in better control over architecture, user interface and complex business logic, which makes them suitable for advanced applications and sets them apart from Canvas and Model-Driven Apps. Teams are advised to understand these characteristics before adopting Code Apps in a Microsoft environment.

The episode "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" adds the tooling side. It describes writing app logic in languages such as TypeScript and JavaScript, using frameworks such as React and Vue for the user interface, and working in Visual Studio Code, which integrates with the Power Apps SDK so that code apps can be developed, tested and packaged within the editor. The episode also mentions access to more than 1,500 connectors for data integration, including Dataverse and SQL data sources.

TypeScript is not limited to application front ends. In "Bicep vs ARM Templates vs Terraform for Azure", Pulumi is presented as an option for teams that prefer languages they already know: it allows infrastructure as code to be written in Python, TypeScript, Go, C# or Java. The episode lists benefits such as using familiar languages, fitting into current development workflows and not needing to learn a new syntax, and notes that this applies to Azure resources and other cloud platforms.

TypeScript also comes up in discussions of AI-assisted development. In "GitHub Copilot, Clean Context, Automated Testing & AI Coding Agents with Lars Gyrup Brink Nielsen [MVP]", Mirko Peters and the guest cover GitHub Copilot, AI coding agents, developer experience, automated testing, TypeScript, JavaScript, Nx, monorepos, Polygraph, GitHub Actions and Playwright, along with the architectural foundations needed for agentic software engineering at enterprise scale. In that context TypeScript is one of the languages and ecosystems around which such workflows are discussed.

Typical decisions around TypeScript concern where it fits in a given solution: as the language for Power Apps code components, as the typed layer of an SPFx project, as the language for a Power Apps Code App built with React, or as an alternative to a domain-specific language for infrastructure code. In each case the shared reasoning in the episodes is the same: familiar web tooling combined with typing that surfaces errors early.

unity-catalog.desc: Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI in Azure Databricks, providing access control, auditing, lineage and discovery across workspaces.

faq.a: Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI in Azure Databricks. It controls access, tracks lineage automatically and records activity for auditing across workspaces.
faq.q: What is Unity Catalog in Azure Databricks?

faq.a: Tables, views, volumes, functions and models use a three-level namespace of catalog, schema and object. Privileges on these securable objects are granted to users, service principals or groups.
faq.q: How are objects organized in Unity Catalog?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, it is on automatically for workspaces created after November 2023. Workspaces created before that must be upgraded to use it.
faq.q: Is Unity Catalog enabled by default?

unity-catalog.long:
Unity Catalog is the governance layer of Databricks. In Azure Databricks it is described as the unified governance layer for data and AI. Once it is enabled for a workspace, it works underneath all data and AI interactions there. It provides centralized access control, auditing, lineage and discovery across workspaces, so that rules about who may see or change data are defined in one place instead of being repeated in each workspace.

The documentation describes how this works in practice. Unity Catalog controls access whenever a table is queried or a model is called. It tracks lineage automatically and records activity for auditing. Access to the catalog is available through Catalog Explorer, SQL, the Databricks CLI and REST APIs. Everything that is governed is a securable object, and privileges on these objects are granted to users, service principals or groups. Tables, views, volumes, functions and models are organized in a three-level namespace made up of a catalog, a schema and the object itself.

A distinction that matters for storage decisions is the one between managed and external objects. Tables and volumes can be managed, in which case Unity Catalog handles the storage lifecycle as well as governance. They can also be external, in which case Unity Catalog handles governance only and the storage stays outside its lifecycle management. Choosing between the two is a typical design decision when data already lives in existing storage locations.

The functional areas named in the Microsoft Learn documentation go beyond basic permissions. They include access control with attribute-based policies and row and column filters, discovery, lineage, audit logs exposed as a system table, data classification, data quality monitoring, data sharing across organizations and clouds, and AI governance. This means one layer covers both analytical data and AI assets such as models, rather than treating them as separate governance problems.

On availability, Unity Catalog is turned on automatically for workspaces created after November 2023. Workspaces created earlier must be upgraded to use it. The documentation also notes that an open-source implementation of Unity Catalog exists, and it points to a separate page for requirements and limitations that should be checked before planning a rollout.

The M365.FM episode "Azure Databricks - Simply Explained" places Unity Catalog within its overview of the platform. Its outline covers what Azure Databricks is, why the lakehouse idea exists, Apache Spark, notebooks, clusters and Delta Lake, and then groups "Workspaces, Accounts, and Unity Catalog" together as one topic. The episode also closes with guidance on when to use Databricks, Fabric or Synapse. In that framing, Unity Catalog is the part that explains how several workspaces under one account can share a consistent governance model, which is relevant when comparing Databricks with other Microsoft data platforms.

For people searching for the term, the short version is that Unity Catalog answers the questions of who can access which data or model, where that data came from, who used it, and how it can be found or shared. Because it is enforced at the point where tables are queried or models are called, and because lineage and audit records are generated automatically, it forms the basis for governance in Azure Databricks rather than an optional add-on.

vertipaq.desc: VertiPaq is the in-memory columnar storage engine behind Power BI import models, compressing data column by column to support fast queries.

faq.a: VertiPaq is the in-memory columnar storage engine used by Power BI import models. It compresses data column by column so queries run fast.
faq.q: What is the VertiPaq engine?

faq.a: The episodes say VertiPaq processes star schema models faster because they need fewer joins and simpler queries, and that it compresses data better with star schemas, reducing memory use.
faq.q: Why do star schemas matter for VertiPaq?

faq.a: According to the episodes, Direct Lake queries are processed by the VertiPaq engine, giving performance comparable to Import mode without scheduled refresh cycles.
faq.q: How is VertiPaq related to Direct Lake?

vertipaq.long:
The VertiPaq engine is the in-memory columnar storage engine used by Power BI import models. Instead of storing data row by row, it compresses data column by column, which allows queries to run quickly against data held in memory. It sits beneath the semantic model layer, so report authors rarely interact with it directly, but its behavior shapes how fast reports respond and how much memory a model consumes.

One point made in the M365.FM episode "Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) - Simply Explained" concerns how VertiPaq treats data. The episode states that the engine operates independently of data types: strings, floating-point numbers and dates use similar memory and perform at comparable speeds because of dictionary encoding. It also notes that mixing data types in expressions can force conversions. Some of these conversions are efficient, while others place more demand on the formula engine, which can affect performance. In practical terms, this means data type choices matter mostly where DAX expressions combine or convert values.

Model design has a direct effect on how well VertiPaq performs. The episode "Build a Power BI Star Schema for Faster Reports" says the engine processes star schema models faster because they require fewer joins and less complex queries. Its recommendations include aggregating data before loading to reduce size, avoiding many-to-many relationships that can produce incorrect results and slow performance, and flattening snowflake structures into a star schema to minimize joins. The episode "Reduce Power BI Premium Costs with Better Data Models" makes a related argument: VertiPaq compresses data better with star schemas, which speeds up queries and reduces memory use, and a clear model is also easier to maintain.

The same episode warns against overly complex models. Cramming too much data into wide tables or adding unnecessary calculated columns is described as a common mistake that can hurt report performance. Keeping relationships simple and clear, and avoiding circular or ambiguous links, is presented as part of the same approach. Because memory use is tied to Premium capacity costs in that discussion, efficient modeling for VertiPaq is framed as a way to reduce those costs.

VertiPaq also appears in the Microsoft Fabric context. The episodes "Build Reusable Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric" and "Speed Power BI with OneLake and Direct Lake" explain that Direct Lake queries are processed by the VertiPaq engine. According to these episodes, this gives performance comparable to Import mode without scheduled refresh cycles, since data is queried directly from OneLake without being moved or duplicated. The episodes add that only the necessary data is loaded into memory, which makes it possible to analyze data volumes that exceed memory limits, and that Direct Lake fits into existing Fabric investments, such as the gold analytics layer in a medallion lakehouse architecture.

Taken together, the episodes treat VertiPaq as the common query engine across Import mode and Direct Lake. Decisions about schema shape, relationship types, calculated columns and data types are all discussed in terms of how they help or hinder this engine, which makes it a central concept for anyone tuning Power BI or Fabric semantic models.

visio.desc: Microsoft Visio is a paid Microsoft diagramming application for flowcharts, org charts, network and process diagrams, offered as a desktop app and as Visio for the web.

faq.a: Microsoft Visio is a diagramming application used for flowcharts, org charts, network diagrams and process diagrams. Typical uses are documenting business processes, mapping IT infrastructure and presenting organisational structures.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Visio used for?

faq.a: No. Visio is a paid product and not part of the standard Microsoft 365 licence. It is licensed through the Microsoft 365 platform and has to be assigned to the users who need it.
faq.q: Is Visio included in the standard Microsoft 365 licence?

faq.a: Yes. Visio is related to SharePoint and Microsoft Teams, where diagrams can be stored, shared and discussed with colleagues.
faq.q: Does Visio work with Teams and SharePoint?

visio.long:
Microsoft Visio is a diagramming application developed by Microsoft. It is used to create flowcharts, organisational charts, network diagrams and process diagrams. The product is available in two forms: as a desktop app and as Visio for the web, which runs in the browser. Visio is classified as a Microsoft tool and is a paid product rather than a part of the standard Microsoft 365 licence.

The typical purpose of Visio is to turn information that is hard to explain in text into a visual representation. Common situations include documenting a business process step by step, mapping IT or network infrastructure, and presenting how a team or company is structured. Because diagrams of this kind are often shared and maintained over time, they are usually created with the audience and the review process in mind, not only the person drawing them.

Visio is related to several parts of the Microsoft ecosystem. It is connected to Microsoft 365, the platform through which Visio is licensed and used alongside other apps. It is also related to SharePoint and Microsoft Teams, where diagrams can be stored, shared and discussed with colleagues. In practice, this means a diagram does not have to stay in a single file on one computer; it can be placed where a team already works and collaborates.

The licensing side matters for administrators. Since Visio is a paid product that sits outside the standard Microsoft 365 licence, it has to be assigned deliberately to the users who need it. Visio plans are mentioned in M365.FM episodes in exactly this licensing context, as one of several add-on products that organisations have to track.

The M365.FM episodes assigned to Visio touch it only indirectly. The episode "Set Up Microsoft Copilot in Teams Step by Step" lists Visio Plan 1 and Plan 2 among the other eligible plans that can qualify a user for Copilot, and states that one of these plans is needed for each user who will access Copilot. The episode stresses that activating Copilot is not enough and that setup, licensing, permissions and governance decide its value. Anyone unsure which plan their organisation uses is advised to check with their IT administrator.

The episode "Fix Automated Microsoft 365 Licensing Failures" approaches Visio from the licence-management side. It describes why automatically assigned licences can seem to disappear, pointing to brittle dynamic group rules, drifting attributes and slow recalculation. As part of right-sizing, it recommends reviewing add-ons such as Audio Conferencing, Project and Visio, and Power BI Pro, removing unused SKUs, adding missing base SKUs, and tracking reclaimed licences and monthly savings so the results can be shared with Finance. This is relevant wherever Visio licences are handed out through groups rather than assigned manually.

In summary, Microsoft Visio is the diagramming option within the Microsoft ecosystem for process, organisational and infrastructure diagrams. Decisions around it usually concern which form to use (desktop app or Visio for the web), where to store and share the diagrams (SharePoint and Microsoft Teams), and how to license and review its use alongside the rest of Microsoft 365.

visual-studio.desc: Visual Studio is a Microsoft development product; M365.FM episodes cover its Dev Tunnels feature for testing Microsoft 365 apps, alongside related tooling.

faq.a: According to the episode "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels", Dev Tunnels in Visual Studio expose local Teams, SharePoint, or Power Platform services to the internet without an Azure deployment, so changes can be tested quickly.
faq.q: What does Visual Studio do in the context of Microsoft 365 testing?

faq.a: The episode recommends a named, persistent tunnel with Private, authenticated access tied to Microsoft Entra ID, and warns that leaving a tunnel Public or anonymous can expose the whole development machine. It also advises logging and shutting the tunnel off when done.
faq.q: How should a Dev Tunnel be secured?

faq.a: The episodes treat them separately. Dev Tunnels are described in Visual Studio, while the Bicep, ARM template, and Power Apps Code Apps episodes refer to Visual Studio Code as an editor with extensions and IntelliSense.
faq.q: Is Visual Studio the same as Visual Studio Code in these episodes?

visual-studio.long:
Visual Studio is a development product from Microsoft. In the M365.FM episodes that mention it, it appears in two roles: as the environment that hosts the Dev Tunnels feature for testing Microsoft 365 apps, and as a point of reference in discussions of related developer tools such as Visual Studio Code. This page summarizes only what those episodes state and does not describe the full product.

The clearest use case in the source material is Dev Tunnels. The episode "Test Microsoft 365 Apps with Visual Studio Dev Tunnels" explains that Dev Tunnels in Visual Studio let developers expose local Teams, SharePoint, or Power Platform services to the internet within minutes, without an Azure deployment. The episode recommends configuring a named, persistent tunnel and using Private, authenticated access tied to Microsoft Entra ID. According to the episode, this keeps tests secure and keeps OAuth redirect URIs stable. It also describes real-time feedback in Microsoft 365 as a way to shorten iteration loops, and it mentions that tunnels can be managed with the Dev Tunnels CLI.

The same episode raises a security warning. It names leaving a tunnel Public or anonymous as the biggest risk, because one missed setting can expose an entire development machine. Its guidance is to lock the tunnel down, log activity, and shut the tunnel off when testing is finished. For anyone deciding how to test a locally running Microsoft 365 app, the practical choice described is between an authenticated, Entra ID-bound private tunnel and an anonymous public one, with the episode favoring the former.

Other episodes in the source set mention Visual Studio Code rather than Visual Studio itself. The episode "Bicep - Simply Explained" notes that IntelliSense in Visual Studio Code helps catch errors and improves coding speed when working with Bicep, a language that compiles to ARM templates for Azure infrastructure. The episode "ARM Templates - Simply Explained" lists Visual Studio Code as a lightweight editor with Azure extensions that offer code completion and error highlighting, next to the Azure CLI and the ARM template test toolkit. These references show how editors in the Visual Studio family fit into infrastructure-as-code workflows, although they concern Visual Studio Code specifically.

Power Platform development is a further area where the family appears. The episodes "Power Apps Code Apps - Simply Explained" and "Power Apps Code Apps with Carike Botha [MVP]" describe Code Apps as a way for developers to build modern web applications, for example with React, using familiar tools like Visual Studio Code. These apps still draw on Power Platform capabilities such as Dataverse, Microsoft Entra authentication, connectors, security policies, and managed deployments. The episodes also mention source control with GitHub for collaboration, versioning, and deployment management, and AI-assisted development for generating code. They present Code Apps as an extension of the platform for scenarios that need full control over user experience and architecture, not as a replacement for low-code development.

Taken together, the episodes position Visual Studio and its related editor as everyday tools for developers working across Microsoft 365, Azure, and the Power Platform. Choices that recur in the material include whether to test locally through a tunnel or deploy first, how to secure that tunnel with Microsoft Entra ID, and which editor to use for infrastructure code and custom apps. Details beyond these points, such as editions, versions, or pricing, are not covered in the available sources.

viva.desc: Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps in Teams and Microsoft 365, covering communities, work patterns, learning and a branded employee start point.

faq.a: Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps inside Teams and Microsoft 365, including Viva Engage, Viva Insights, Viva Learning and Viva Connections. It is developed by Microsoft.
faq.q: What is Microsoft Viva?

faq.a: Most Viva experiences are surfaced in Microsoft Teams, for example as apps or as the employee portal provided by Viva Connections.
faq.q: How does Microsoft Viva relate to Microsoft Teams?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained", the first view it opens is meant for the individual user, covering topics such as focus time and quiet time, before manager and leader views are explained.
faq.q: Is Viva Insights only a tool for managers?

viva.long:
Microsoft Viva is a set of employee-experience apps inside Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365. It is developed by Microsoft and classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Rather than being one single application, Viva bundles several services under one name, including Viva Engage for communities, Viva Insights for personal and team work patterns, Viva Learning for training content and Viva Connections for a branded start point in Teams. It was released in February 2021, and organizations use it to support communication, learning and well-being at work. Product documentation is published by Microsoft on its Learn site.

The modules address different parts of daily work. Viva Engage focuses on communities, leadership communication and knowledge sharing. Viva Insights shows work patterns and gives individuals, managers and leaders different views of the same underlying data. Viva Learning brings learning content and discovery into the flow of work across Microsoft 365 and Teams. Viva Connections acts as a central hub within the Viva suite. In the description quoted in the M365.FM episode on it, Microsoft calls Viva Connections "a gateway to other Viva apps and services" that can curate specific content and tools and give easy access to resources, news, announcements and popular destinations. Viva Topics is another part of the family; it uses AI to build topic pages from content across Microsoft 365, including SharePoint, and can show topic cards inside apps such as Outlook and Teams.

Viva is closely tied to Microsoft Teams, because most Viva experiences are surfaced there, for example as apps or as the employee portal that Viva Connections provides. Because the modules sit inside tools people already use, adoption decisions often concern which modules to switch on, who owns each one, and how they fit with existing communication and learning practices.

The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained" notes that Viva Insights may already be switched on inside a Microsoft 365 account. It addresses the assumption that the tool exists for a manager to watch employees, and says the first view it opens is the one meant for the individual user. The episode outline covers four views of the same data: your own insights such as focus time, quiet time and switching off, what a manager sees, what leaders see across the company, and the analyst role, where more detailed questions can be explored.

The episode "Viva Engage - Simply Explained" is aimed at decision-makers who need a practical introduction to Viva Engage and its implications for adoption, operations and governance. It recommends related listening on Viva Connections as the employee-experience entry point that can complement communities, and on Microsoft Viva Learning as a way communities can reinforce learning and skills development.

"Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained" gives a quick answer: Viva Learning brings learning content and discovery into the flow of work across Microsoft 365 and Teams. The episode explains how the service supports employees and learning teams, which content and governance choices matter, and how to position learning as an ongoing work habit. It also cites studies suggesting that a strong learning culture can contribute to better employee satisfaction, easier onboarding and lower turnover.

"Viva Connections - Simply Explained" describes the module as part of efforts to streamline communication and foster a sense of community and inclusion among employees, and mentions security measures such as data encryption and regulatory compliance. The episode "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint" adds that proper licensing and planning are essential for adopting Viva Topics, and that integration with search and SharePoint can save time and improve productivity.

In practice, Viva is approached module by module. Teams typically decide which employee-experience needs matter most, such as communities, learning, personal work insights or a company portal, then plan governance and licensing for those modules accordingly.

viva-connections.desc: Viva Connections is a Microsoft Viva app that acts as the employee experience front door, bringing news, resources and tools into a dashboard inside Microsoft Teams.

faq.a: Viva Connections is a Microsoft Viva app that serves as the employee experience front door, bringing company news, resources and tools into a dashboard inside Microsoft Teams.
faq.q: What is Viva Connections?

faq.a: According to the M365.FM episodes, Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs) are cards built with the SharePoint Framework that surface live business data and actions in Teams and Viva Connections, such as approving, submitting or tracking items.
faq.q: What are Adaptive Card Extensions in Viva Connections?

faq.a: The episode on governing Adaptive Card Extensions says cards can become orphaned with no owner or lifecycle, spread across departments and create data silos with inconsistent dates, labels or retention rules, which leads to stale content and compliance gaps.
faq.q: Why does governance matter for Viva Connections?

viva-connections.long:
Viva Connections is a Microsoft Viva app that serves as the front door to the employee experience. It brings company news, resources and tools into a single dashboard inside Microsoft Teams, so employees can reach what they need from one branded place instead of searching across separate sites and applications. The Microsoft documentation describes it as part of the Viva family, which focuses on connecting people with information, learning and communities in the workplace.

The M365.FM episode "Viva Connections - Simply Explained" describes Viva Connections as creating a branded employee experience in Microsoft Teams that combines news, resources, navigation and dashboard cards. The episode explains that it integrates with Microsoft Teams and SharePoint, placing essential resources and personalized news within easy reach. It also stresses that the experience needs governance decisions to stay useful over time, rather than being switched on once and left alone.

A central building block is the dashboard, made up of cards that surface information and actions. The episode "Customize Microsoft Viva Connections Dashboards" argues that Viva Connections can be more than a decorative SharePoint homepage. According to that episode, a solid foundation of navigation, targeting, permissions and mobile support should be paired with SharePoint Framework (SPFx) web parts and Adaptive Card Extensions (ACEs). ACEs are described as a way to surface live business data and actions inside Teams, so that tiles can do work such as approving, submitting or tracking items. The episode also recommends role-based personalization, performance discipline and a measured change approach to drive adoption.

The same episode and the related "Govern SPFx Adaptive Card Extensions in Teams and Viva" episode treat the cards as more than interface elements. The governance episode says Adaptive Card Extensions can age quickly: a simple announcement card or dashboard widget may become an orphaned solution with no owner and no lifecycle. It warns that cards can spread across Teams and Viva Connections, multiply by department and create data silos that disagree on dates, labels or retention rules. The episode frames these cards as a distribution channel that surfaces content on mobile and caches data offline, which can raise risk when the underlying data is not governed. Ownership, lifecycle management and compliance are therefore presented as part of the design, not an afterthought.

Automation is another theme. The episode "Automate Viva Connections, Topics, Learning, and News" argues that many Viva rollouts stall at the point of turning features on and hoping for adoption. It covers authentication scopes, payload shapes and batching approaches for publishing content programmatically, including auto-targeting organization-wide news, and mentions authentication errors such as 401 responses as a common stumbling block. This positions Viva Connections within a broader set of Viva services that can be driven through APIs rather than only through the user interface.

Viva Connections also sits alongside other Viva and Microsoft 365 components. The episode "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint" describes Viva Topics as a knowledge discovery service in the Viva employee experience platform that uses Microsoft Graph and AI to organize content and expertise across Microsoft 365, including SharePoint Online. It discusses how Viva Connections, Viva Engage and SharePoint web parts relate to each other and notes that licensing and cost implications should be reviewed for Viva Topics, SharePoint Syntex and any connector services.

In practice, decisions around Viva Connections include which employee needs the dashboard should address, how navigation and targeting are structured, who owns each card, and how mobile use and performance are handled. The episodes consistently point to governance, ownership and role-based design as the factors that determine whether the experience stays relevant after launch.

viva-engage.desc: Viva Engage is the enterprise social network in Microsoft Viva and the successor to Yammer, used for communities, leadership communication and knowledge sharing.

faq.a: Viva Engage is the successor to Yammer and is part of Microsoft Viva. According to the episode "Viva Engage - Simply Explained", it launched in 2023, retained Yammer's core features and added new functionality.
faq.q: What is the difference between Viva Engage and Yammer?

faq.a: It is used for conversations, leadership communication and knowledge sharing across an organization, mainly through communities. The episodes position it as the organization-wide social layer next to Outlook for email and Microsoft Teams for real-time chat.
faq.q: What is Viva Engage used for?

faq.a: Yes. "Viva Engage - Simply Explained" highlights governance and clear participation habits, and "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" names Viva Engage among the channels where compliance policies can address risks such as misconduct and inappropriate communication.
faq.q: Do compliance and governance apply to Viva Engage?

viva-engage.long:
Viva Engage is the enterprise social network in Microsoft Viva and the successor to Yammer. It gives organizations a place for conversations, leadership communication and knowledge sharing across departments and teams. Microsoft developed the product, and it is classed as both a Microsoft tool and a collaboration tool. Because the older name Yammer remains in use as an alias, the term is often searched under both names, particularly when people look for older documentation or discussions.

The central idea is the community: a space that people can join and follow, where topics, questions and announcements can be shared beyond the boundaries of a single team. The episode "Viva Engage - Simply Explained" describes Viva Engage as Microsoft's community experience for conversations, leadership communication and knowledge sharing across an organisation. It explains how the product fits into Microsoft 365 and how communities create value. According to the episode, it was launched in 2023 and evolved from Yammer, keeping the core features while adding new functionality, with the stated aim of improving the employee experience. The episode names Storyline among these features.

Viva Engage is part of Microsoft Viva, the suite of employee experience services. Within that suite, other services cover areas such as topics or insights, while Viva Engage is where the exchange between employees takes place. It is often described alongside the other Microsoft 365 communication tools rather than as a replacement for them. The episode "Microsoft 365 Data Sovereignty Beyond Technical Custody" lists Outlook for email, Microsoft Teams for real-time chat in sub-groups, and Viva Engage as the enterprise social experience for connecting across the organization. In that framing, each tool serves a different communication pattern, and Viva Engage is the one aimed at organization-wide conversations.

The same idea appears in "Fix a Failing Microsoft 365 Rollout", which mentions Viva Engage as a way to build community by letting employees share experiences and crowdsource solutions. The episode says this sense of belonging helps people feel valued. In that context Viva Engage is treated as one part of a rollout that also involves Microsoft Teams and SharePoint, with the point being that tools work better when paired with a supportive environment.

Viva Engage also connects to knowledge management. The episode "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint" notes that integrated search helps people find relevant content quickly, including content within Viva Engage communities. Centralized topic pages in SharePoint and permission settings for who can access and manage topics are part of that picture. In practice, community conversations can feed a wider body of findable knowledge when search and topics are configured together.

Governance is a recurring theme. "Viva Engage - Simply Explained" stresses that governance and clear participation habits matter for sustainable engagement, which suggests that a community platform needs defined expectations rather than only a technical rollout. On the compliance side, "Communication Compliance - Simply Explained" lists Viva Engage among the digital channels, together with Microsoft Teams chats, Outlook email and Microsoft 365 Copilot, where risks such as workplace misconduct, regulatory issues, sensitive information, insider threats and inappropriate communication can arise. The episode explains Microsoft Purview Communication Compliance as a way to create targeted compliance policies instead of reviewing communication indiscriminately.

Typical decisions around Viva Engage therefore include which communication needs belong in communities rather than in email or Teams chats, how leadership will use it to reach the organization, how knowledge shared there is made searchable, and which governance and compliance measures apply to the conversations that take place in it.

viva-glint.desc: Viva Glint is a Microsoft Viva app for employee engagement surveys and listening, offering ready-made program types, templates, benchmarking and analytics.

faq.a: Viva Glint is a Microsoft Viva app for organization-wide employee engagement surveys with benchmarking and analytics. It is built around frequent feedback that organizations turn into concrete improvements.
faq.q: What is Viva Glint?

faq.a: According to Microsoft Learn, there are four program types: recurring or special topic programs, employee lifecycle programs, ad hoc programs and always-on programs. Each offers ready-made templates and a blank one.
faq.q: Which survey program types does Viva Glint offer?

faq.a: The episodes say Viva Glint helps assess employee sentiment and track sentiment during Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption, and that its feedback helps guide the next steps in the rollout.
faq.q: How do the M365.FM episodes connect Viva Glint to Copilot?

viva-glint.long:
Viva Glint is a Microsoft Viva app for organization-wide employee engagement surveys. It is built around frequent employee feedback that organizations turn into concrete improvements, and it combines survey programs with benchmarking and analytics. The Microsoft Learn documentation defines engagement as the degree to which employees direct their cognitive, emotional and behavioral energy toward positive organizational goals, and the survey design in Viva Glint follows that idea.

The technology is configurable rather than a fixed formula. The Microsoft people science team updates the survey items and templates, so organizations can start from maintained content instead of writing every question from scratch. Administrators decide on the survey rhythm, and several surveys can run in parallel. The documentation points to survey fatigue as a concern, which makes the choice of frequency and the number of concurrent programs a practical planning topic.

Viva Glint organizes its surveys into four program types. Recurring or special topic programs allow trend comparison over time. Employee lifecycle programs are triggered by dates such as hire or exit. Ad hoc programs cover a single occasion, and always-on programs can be answered at any time. Each type offers ready-made templates as well as a blank one, and only templates with cycles can recur. The listed templates include engagement, onboarding, exit, productivity, culture, diversity and inclusion, manager effectiveness and team effectiveness. For rollout, six introduction email templates are available to announce a survey to employees. Licensing and numeric limits are not covered on the documentation page used here, so those details need to be checked separately.

Typical situations for Viva Glint include measuring overall engagement across an organization, gathering feedback from new hires during onboarding, collecting exit feedback, and assessing manager or team effectiveness. Choosing between a recurring program and a one-time ad hoc survey depends on whether the organization wants to compare results across cycles. Lifecycle programs suit moments tied to an individual's employment dates, while always-on programs suit situations where feedback should be possible at any point.

In the M365.FM episodes, Viva Glint appears mainly in the context of Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption. The episode "Microsoft 365 Copilot Adoption with Chris Hinch [Microsoft]" says that tools like Viva Insights and Viva Glint help track sentiment and usage, and that organizations should measure employee awareness and motivation. The same episode says that open communication increases excitement about AI, stating that when plans are shared, 75% of employees feel more positive about new technology, and it links psychological safety to people sharing concerns and trusting the process.

The episode "Is Your Organization Structurally Ready for Microsoft Copilot?" makes a related point about measurement. It says that progress and outcomes need to be tracked to see how a culture evolves, and that Microsoft Viva Glint helps assess employee sentiment and identify areas for improvement. In the same episode, local leaders use Viva Pulse to gather insights on AI value and learning needs, and the feedback from these tools guides the next steps. Taken together, the episodes treat Viva Glint as a way to listen to employees during technology change, alongside other Viva tools such as Viva Insights and Viva Pulse.

viva-insights.desc: Viva Insights is a Microsoft Viva service that shows work patterns and wellbeing insights for individuals and teams, built on Microsoft 365 data.

faq.a: Viva Insights is a Microsoft Viva service that shows work patterns and wellbeing insights for individuals and teams. It was developed by Microsoft and is part of Microsoft Viva.
faq.q: What is Viva Insights?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained", the first view it opens is the one that is just for the individual user. The same data is also presented in separate views for managers and for leaders across the company.
faq.q: Is Viva Insights only a tool for managers to monitor employees?

faq.a: The episode "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot" names Viva Insights, including the Copilot Dashboard in the Viva Insights web app, as a way to measure adoption, track active users and analyze license utilization.
faq.q: How does Viva Insights relate to Microsoft 365 Copilot?

viva-insights.long:
Viva Insights is a service within Microsoft Viva, developed by Microsoft, that shows work patterns and wellbeing insights for individuals and teams. It looks at how working time is spent across areas such as meetings, email and focused work, and it offers suggestions for healthier working habits. Because it draws on activity in a Microsoft 365 account, it is closely tied to the data layer of the suite.

A frequent concern is that Viva Insights is a tool for managers to watch employees. The episode "Microsoft Viva Insights - Simply Explained" addresses this directly. It notes that the service is probably already switched on inside a Microsoft 365 account, and that the first view it opens is the one that is just for the individual user. The episode describes four views of the same data: the personal view, what a manager sees, what leaders see across the company, and an analyst role where more detailed questions are asked. The personal view covers topics such as focus time, quiet time and switching off.

The layered approach matters for anyone deciding how to introduce or communicate about the service. The same underlying data is presented differently depending on who looks at it, so the audience for each view shapes how employees understand the purpose. According to the episode, the personal view is the starting point rather than a management dashboard, which is relevant when explaining the service to staff who may expect monitoring.

Viva Insights also appears in the context of Microsoft 365 Copilot. The episode "Secure and Govern Microsoft 365 Copilot" lists Viva Insights among the tools Microsoft offers for measuring Copilot adoption, together with Copilot Business Impact reports and Copilot Analytics reports. It also mentions the Copilot Dashboard in the Viva Insights web app, alongside the Microsoft 365 admin center. The episode says these tools help measure adoption, track active users and analyze license utilization, and that regular audits can reveal inefficiencies in license usage so that licenses can be reclaimed and reallocated.

Adoption and sentiment are another use. In "Microsoft 365 Copilot Adoption with Chris Hinch [Microsoft]", Viva Insights and Viva Glint are named as tools that help track sentiment and usage when an organization measures employee awareness and motivation around new AI tools. The episode ties this to building psychological safety and aligning organizational goals with measurement strategies.

On the technical side, Viva Insights connects to Microsoft Graph. The episode "How Microsoft Graph Connects Microsoft 365 Data and Context" lists Viva Insights among the services that can be reached through Microsoft Graph, next to Teams, Outlook, SharePoint, Planner and others. In "Microsoft Graph: The Enterprise Nervous System", a dataset named VivaInsightsDataset_Report_v1 with the Viva Insights query name appended is described as containing metrics according to a query authored by the user in Viva Insights. The episode presents this as a way to analyze employee interactions and support decisions about productivity and collaboration.

Taken together, the sources place Viva Insights as a Microsoft tool inside Microsoft Viva that serves several audiences: individuals who want to understand their own work patterns, managers and leaders who see aggregated perspectives, and analysts or administrators who work with query-based metrics and Copilot usage reporting.

viva-learning.desc: Viva Learning is a Microsoft Viva service that surfaces learning content such as LinkedIn Learning inside Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365, in the flow of work.

faq.a: Viva Learning is a Microsoft Viva service that brings learning content, such as LinkedIn Learning, into Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 so employees can discover and start courses in the flow of work.
faq.q: What is Viva Learning?

faq.a: According to the episode "Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained", the main choices are which learning content to offer and how it is governed, along with treating learning as an ongoing work habit.
faq.q: Which decisions matter when introducing Viva Learning?

faq.a: The episode "Automate Viva Connections, Topics, Learning, and News" describes bulk-loading external courses into Viva Learning through APIs, including the authentication scopes, payload shapes and batching tactics involved.
faq.q: Can external courses be loaded into Viva Learning automatically?

viva-learning.long:
Viva Learning is a Microsoft Viva service that brings learning content, including LinkedIn Learning, into Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365. Developed by Microsoft and part of Microsoft Viva, it is meant to let employees discover and start courses where they already work, instead of visiting a separate learning site. For learning teams, it offers a way to present content from several sources in one place.

The core idea is learning in the flow of work. Because the service is related to Microsoft Teams, learning content appears next to the collaboration tools that employees use every day. Employees can find courses and begin them without leaving that environment, and learning teams can make selected content visible to the people who need it. The M365.FM episode "Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained" describes it as an integrated platform that brings learning content and discovery into the flow of work across Microsoft 365 and Teams.

Two decision areas come up repeatedly when organizations introduce Viva Learning: which content to offer and how that content is governed. Content choices determine what employees actually see, whether that is LinkedIn Learning material or other sources, and governance choices determine how that content is managed over time. The episode "Microsoft Viva Learning - Simply Explained" says these choices matter and also frames learning as an ongoing work habit rather than a one-off activity. It points to a strong learning culture as linked to improved employee satisfaction, easier onboarding and decreased turnover, presenting these as findings from studies cited in the episode.

Viva Learning also has an administrative side. The episode "Integrate Viva Topics with Search and SharePoint" notes that broader Viva features such as Viva Connections and Viva Learning require additional admin setup beyond what is needed for Viva Topics. This means that turning on the service involves configuration work by administrators and is not purely an end-user feature.

For larger environments, automation becomes relevant. The episode "Automate Viva Connections, Topics, Learning, and News" focuses on moving past manual setup into API-driven work. It covers reliable authentication, the authorization scopes and payload shapes involved, and batching tactics. In the Viva Learning context, it describes bulk-loading external courses into the service so that learning content held in other learning management systems does not stay in separate silos. The episode also discusses avoiding common errors such as 401 and 403 responses and rate-limit problems when working at scale.

Viva Learning sits alongside the other parts of Microsoft Viva. Episodes on OneDrive Sync and Viva Connections mention it as a related topic: the OneDrive Sync episode links accessible files and structured content to employee learning, and the Viva Connections episode notes that its integration with Microsoft 365 lets people use tools like Microsoft Teams and Viva Learning together. Taken together, the episodes position Viva Learning as one component of a connected employee experience in which learning, news, topics and collaboration are available from the same working environment.

windows-365.desc: Windows 365 is Microsoft's Cloud PC service that streams a personal Windows desktop from the Microsoft cloud to many devices at a fixed monthly price.

faq.a: Windows 365 is Microsoft's Cloud PC service that streams a personal Windows desktop from the Microsoft cloud to devices such as laptops, tablets, Macs or a web browser, on a fixed monthly price.
faq.q: What is Windows 365?

faq.a: The episodes describe the two as solving different business challenges, with the choice depending on who runs the platform and how the workload behaves. They compare management effort, cost behavior, scaling, image handling and user experience.
faq.q: How does Windows 365 differ from Azure Virtual Desktop?

faq.a: According to the episode "Windows 365 Link - Simply Explained," it is a purpose-built access device that connects users to their Cloud PC and does not store applications, files or user profiles locally.
faq.q: What is Windows 365 Link?

windows-365.long:
Windows 365 is a Cloud PC service from Microsoft. It streams a complete, personal Windows desktop from the Microsoft cloud to a user's device. The operating system, applications, files and settings live in the cloud rather than on local hardware, so the same personalized desktop can be reached from a laptop, a tablet, a Mac or a web browser. The service is offered on a fixed monthly price, which makes the cost per user predictable, and it is classified as a paid Microsoft tool and cloud platform. It is also referred to as Cloud PC or Windows 365 Cloud PC.

The core idea is that each user receives their own dedicated Cloud PC. This differs from a shared virtual desktop in which many users draw on a pooled set of machines. Because a Cloud PC behaves like a normal personal computer that happens to run in the cloud, it is typically used when an organization wants a familiar desktop experience without depending on the performance or condition of the device a person happens to hold. Typical situations include people who switch between devices, who work on hardware that is not powerful enough for their applications, or who need access to the same environment from different locations. The episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained" in the Microsoft Knowledge Nuggets series describes the service in exactly these terms: a Windows desktop streamed from the Microsoft cloud to virtually any device.

Windows 365 sits next to Azure Virtual Desktop, another Microsoft service for delivering Windows desktops from the cloud, and the two are frequently compared. The episode "Windows 365 or Azure Virtual Desktop: Choosing the Right Cloud PC Model" frames the decision as less about features and more about who will run the platform and how the workload behaves. It compares the operating models behind both options, looking at management effort, cost behavior, scaling, image handling and user experience. The episode "AVD vs Windows 365: Which Virtual Desktop Strategy Wins" with Microsoft MVP Shabaz Darr makes a related point: although the two are often compared, they solve different business challenges, and the discussion covers architecture and licensing with practical guidance for IT leaders, cloud architects, administrators and consultants.

Management is the other main connection. Windows 365 is related to Microsoft Intune, the endpoint management tool many organizations already use for physical devices. Managing Cloud PCs with the same tooling is one reason the service can fit into existing administration practices. The episode "Agentic AI for IT Operations: Windows 365, Intune & Microsoft's AI Vision" with Christiaan Brinkhoff of Nerdio discusses Windows 365 and Intune in the context of AI agents, governance, security and Microsoft's vision of an agentic operating system, and describes agentic AI for IT operations as goal-driven AI agents combined with governed workflows, observability, identity and human oversight.

A further part of the Windows 365 family is Windows 365 Link, covered in the episode "Windows 365 Link - Simply Explained." According to that episode, Windows 365 Link is a purpose-built access device for Windows 365 Cloud PCs. It is designed to deliver a secure, simplified desktop experience without storing applications, files or user profiles locally. Rather than working as a traditional Windows PC, it acts as a secure gateway that connects employees directly to their personal Cloud PC running in Microsoft's cloud.

When evaluating Windows 365, the episodes point to a few recurring questions: who will operate the platform, how predictable the cost needs to be, how the workload scales, how images are handled, and what experience users should have. The official documentation for the product is published on Microsoft Learn under the Windows 365 section. Taken together, the linked episodes treat Windows 365 as a per-user, fixed-price option within a wider choice of cloud desktop models rather than as a one-size-fits-all answer.

windows-365-frontline.desc: Windows 365 Flex, formerly Windows 365 Frontline, is a Windows 365 option for shift workers in which one license serves Cloud PCs used by several people in turn.

faq.a: They refer to the same product. Windows 365 Flex is the current name, and Windows 365 Frontline is the former name that still appears in older documentation and episodes.
faq.q: What is the difference between Windows 365 Flex and Windows 365 Frontline?

faq.a: One license can serve Cloud PCs used by several people at different times, so cost follows concurrency rather than headcount. The number of licenses per policy depends on peak concurrent use, and license requirements follow those of Windows 365 Enterprise.
faq.q: How does licensing work in Windows 365 Flex?

faq.a: According to the product FAQ, users who need access to a Cloud PC at any time are better served by Windows 365 Enterprise. Flex is aimed at workers who need a Cloud PC only during scheduled working time.
faq.q: When is Windows 365 Enterprise a better fit than Windows 365 Flex?

windows-365-frontline.long:
Windows 365 Flex is a version of Windows 365 designed for shift workers and part-time staff. It was formerly named Windows 365 Frontline, and the older name still appears in documentation and in podcast episodes. The central idea is that one license can serve Cloud PCs used by several people at different times, so an organization pays for concurrency rather than headcount. It is part of the wider Windows 365 family of Cloud PCs.

The product targets employees and contractors who need a Cloud PC only during scheduled working time, such as shift, seasonal or part-time workers. Because these users rarely need a desktop at the same moment, a shared pool of licenses can cover many more people than a one-license-per-person model. The number of licenses needed per policy depends on peak concurrent use, meaning how many people are connected to a Cloud PC at the same time.

Two modes are described in the product material. In dedicated mode, one license allows up to three personalized Cloud PCs that keep their apps, data and settings, although only one of them is active at a time. In shared mode, one license maps to one Cloud PC that several users take in turn, never at once, and administrators control personalization. Shared mode is also the basis for Cloud Apps, which deliver single applications instead of a full desktop. Cloud Apps run only in shared mode, are managed through Intune and are reached through the Windows App.

License requirements follow those of Windows 365 Enterprise. Concrete prices are not set out in the product description and are left to a separate pricing page. According to the FAQ cited in the product material, users who need access to a Cloud PC at any time are better served by Windows 365 Enterprise, since Flex is built around scheduled, non-overlapping use. This makes the main decision a question of usage patterns: whether staff work in distinct shifts or need an always-available desktop.

The M365.FM episode "Windows 365 – Simply Explained" touches on this scenario under the Frontline name. The episode describes Windows 365 Frontline as allowing multiple users to share a Cloud PC, which it calls a good fit for shift workers and for optimizing resource allocation. It also mentions that each employee can log in and reach personalized resources right away, and it lists security features such as automatic lock screens, auto sign-out and an auto reset feature that restores the Cloud PC.

The episode "AVD vs Windows 365: Which Virtual Desktop Strategy Wins: with Shabaz Darr [MVP]" places Windows 365 Frontline in a broader discussion of virtual desktop strategy. According to its description, the conversation covers Windows 365 Frontline alongside Windows 365 Reserve, GPU-enabled Cloud PCs, AI workloads, automation, Infrastructure as Code, Nerdio management capabilities and the future evolution of Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365, with attention to performance, cost optimization and governance.

In practice, Windows 365 Flex fits situations such as retail, support or seasonal operations where staff are scheduled in shifts and where licensing every person individually would be inefficient. Choosing between dedicated mode, shared mode and Cloud Apps depends on whether users need a persistent personalized desktop, a shared desktop with admin-controlled personalization, or only individual applications.

windows-365-link.desc: Windows 365 Link is a Microsoft device that connects users directly to a Windows 365 Cloud PC, with no local apps, user files or local admin account.

faq.a: Windows 365 Link is a purpose-built Microsoft device that connects users directly to their Windows 365 Cloud PC. It has no local apps, no local data storage and no local user with administrator rights.
faq.q: What is Windows 365 Link?

faq.a: Organizations manage the device with Microsoft Intune, together with their other devices. A Windows 365 license for the Cloud PC is also required.
faq.q: How is Windows 365 Link managed?

faq.a: The Microsoft Learn overview lists a discrete TPM, Secure Boot, virtualization-based security, hypervisor-protected code integrity and BitLocker encryption. It also names a strict application control policy, default security baseline policies and the Microsoft Defender endpoint detection sensor.
faq.q: Which security features does Windows 365 Link include?

windows-365-link.long:
Windows 365 Link is a purpose-built Microsoft hardware device that lets users connect directly to their Windows 365 Cloud PC. It belongs to the Windows 365 family and is designed as a dedicated access point to a Cloud PC rather than as a conventional Windows computer. After a user signs in on the device, the connection to the Cloud PC virtual machine is established through the Windows 365 service.

The central design idea is that the device acts only as a client for the cloud session. According to the Microsoft Learn overview, this means it has no local user with administrator rights, no local data storage and no local apps. The M365.FM episode "Windows 365 Link - Simply Explained" describes it in similar terms: a secure gateway that connects employees directly to their personal Cloud PC running in Microsoft's cloud, delivering a simplified desktop experience without storing applications, files or user profiles locally.
